  - (Action) evaluate `SpeedCalibration.run_still_valid(train_id)` for the open calibration run (lighting or speed) and end the run when it is false (step `26f5`, `SimulationController._reevaluate_calibration_run`)

  The gating, latch-clear-on-no-op, and inclusive higher-level deferral rules are owned by the **Latch Table** and the **Action latched-cancel consumption** subsection.
- **Batched block entries.** If a tick advanced the head across several blocks, those block entries arrive batched in that tick's final no-boundary report, ordered by `sequence_index` (per **Path And PathDispatcher**, Multiple resource boundaries in one tick). The drain fires one head-advance callback per entry, so the entries consume their waypoints in order.
**SimulationController runtime surface**

- `SimulationController` is the construction and per-tick orchestration owner, and the only owner of the public `add_train(...)` and `remove_train(train_id)` APIs.
- `SimulationController` is optional in editor mode. A pure map-editor session (geometry placement, connectivity wiring, static field edits that do not affect runtime occupancy or locks) runs with no `SimulationController`, no `BlockManager` runtime, no dispatcher, and no controllers. An editor session that wants geometry/connectivity validation through `BlockManager` MAY create the lightweight `SimulationController` with its manager dependencies fully wired (`BlockManager` wired, no runtime route/dispatcher/trains), but no runtime component receives a general controller back-reference. The choice is all-or-nothing per editor session. Wiring `BlockManager` makes the `Switch.position` mutation workflow reachable, but a live operator switch throw is subject to the operating-throw gate: `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)` throws only while an operating environment is active (`SimulationController.environment_active`), which is distinct from whether the session is running (see **Session state** and the operating-throw gate under **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**).
- **Exposed surface.** The surface exposes the services and registries orchestration owns, including: `network`, `block_manager`, `path_dispatcher`, `route_executor`, `notification_center`, `speed_calibration`, the controller registry keyed by `train_id`, the physics registry keyed by `train_id`, `safe_state_generation`, `enter_output_safe_state()`, `layout_emergency_cut_out()`, `reset_layout_cut_out()`, `hold_all()`, `_freeze_lost_train_controller(train_id)`, `get_train(train_id)`, `get_or_create_controller(train_id)`, `get_or_create_physics(train_id)`, the public train-addition API `add_train(...)`, and the public train-removal API `remove_train(train_id)`. Components receive only the narrow dependencies listed below; this surface is not a service locator.
- **`SpeedCalibration` access.** `SimulationController` owns the one `SpeedCalibration` instance for the network run and exposes it on this surface. `TrainController.tick(...)` reads `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` through it as the selected driving source while a calibration leg or run is open (see **Speed calibration**, Where it runs, and **Lighting-voltage calibration**). `TrainPhysics` applies the effective output as the block track voltage; it holds no reference to `SpeedCalibration` and reaches into no run registry.
- **`safe_state_generation`.** `safe_state_generation` is a runtime-only integer initialized to `0`. `enter_output_safe_state()` increments it exactly once before delegating to `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`; every request for the runtime's safe state made under `AppState.simulation_lock` uses this wrapper. A Setup tool's closing sequence is not such a request (per **Power**, Hardware setup, Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state). The Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` is the sole direct-call exception, because its daemon may not mutate runtime state: it calls `OutputSafety` directly and records its own trip generation. The next runtime-thread tick increments `safe_state_generation` when it consumes that trip record.
- **`layout_cut_out_active`.** `layout_cut_out_active` is a runtime-only boolean on `SimulationController`, initialized to `False`. `layout_emergency_cut_out()` is its only writer of `True`; `reset_layout_cut_out()` and a successful activation are its only writers of `False` (see **Session state**).
- **Route-target readers.** A caller that needs the route's currently acquired target uses `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`; a stop-completion caller uses `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id)`. The private planning resolver is not a cross-component read surface.
- **Dispatcher projections.** `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) -> Optional[str]` and `PathDispatcher.get_active_path(train_id) -> Optional[Path]` are the dispatcher projections.
- **`add_train(...)` effects.** `add_train(...)` constructs the `Train`, ensures the controller exists, calls `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` — the placement-time `Block.occupied_by` writer (see **Power**, Placement is seeded, not re-detected) — and writes the initial `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` before any tick.
- **Threading model.** API/UI/admin runtime mutations run between ticks while the request holds `AppState.simulation_lock`, which the runtime loop holds for every whole tick; the safety-only `OutputWatchdog` exception is defined under **Power**, Hardware interface boundary. Because ordinary mutations are serialized between ticks, consumers recompute live through the named projections rather than trusting cached values.
- **`add_train(...)` atomicity.** `add_train(...)` is synchronous and all-or-nothing, and a duplicate `train_id` fails without mutation.
- **`remove_train(...)` effects.** The refusals and step order of `remove_train(train_id)` are defined in **Train Entity**, Deleting a train.
- **Same workflow as internal code.** External operation surfaces (routes/API/UI/admin code) follow the same stage workflow as internal code.
- **Cancel/revoke requests.** A request to cancel or revoke a live path resolves the target train/controller, calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(error, kind, deviation=False)`, and returns success once that accepted/pending payload is written.
- **Abort requests.** A request to abort the whole route run calls `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(train_id, None)`. With a `RUNNING` run, that method clears the held assignment stashes and then calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_route_abort(...)` (per **Route assignment writers**). No request service calls `set_route_abort(...)` directly.
- **Operator-command requests.** A request that sends an operator command returns the command's own result (see **Operator-command processing slot**). A request that writes an Action handoff returns success once the handoff is written; any later failure is emitted through `NotificationCenter` by the dispatcher operation when Action consumes the handoff.
- **Action is the sole explicit-cancel and teardown committer.** The per-train Action pass is the only place that consumes a retained cancel request through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` and that removes route runs for abort, power-off, or deactivation. There are two exceptions, and both run between ticks while no stage is running to consume a latch: environment activation, which cancels every live path and ends every running run directly (per **Activation starts the railway over**), and the layout emergency cut-out, which cancels every live path directly (per **Emergency cut-out**, Layout emergency cut-out). Observe separately truncates invalid reservation, commits physical entry and tail-vacate, and releases the resources those Observe operations own; Plan settlement completes an arrived path and runs its completion route callback, all per the Observe, Plan, and Action Table.
- **No inline state changes.** Request handlers must not change dispatcher path records, controller reservation, route-run state, block reservations, or switch locks directly.
- **Switch-position exception.** A request service may drive a `Switch.position` change between ticks only through `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)`, subject to that method's operating-throw gate (see **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**); handlers never write it.
- **Config-level exception.** Request services may commit entity availability flags and route-assignment requests between ticks. Handlers only parse and map transport data.
- When a `SimulationController` instance is created for a runtime session, it constructs and owns the runtime registries and components in dependency order. Ownership does not grant every component a back-reference to the controller. Each component receives only the narrow registry, projection, writer, or callback surface it uses:
  - `TrainController` receives the active-path projection reader, the route-assignment reader `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` (read only by **ATO go**), its `NotificationCenter` adapter, and its own controller-local latch store. It receives no `SimulationController`, `PathDispatcher`, or `RouteExecutor` object.
  - `PathDispatcher` receives `RailwayNetwork`, `ResourceCoordinator`, a controller registry read for the target `train_id`, the two named route callbacks it invokes: `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)` and `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)`, and one injected read-only route resolver, the single dependency behind its two reads of route state: `RouteExecutor.find_next_move_target(train_id)` (the reversal-trap exclusion under **Path And PathDispatcher**) and the override-aware `effective_priority` of the two runs it compares (**Preemption**). The head-advance callback `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` is not a `PathDispatcher` dependency: `RouteExecutor` invokes it itself in Plan settlement (step `640a`).
  - `RouteExecutor` receives the route registry, a `PathDispatcherPort`, the controller registry, and `NotificationCenter`. `PathDispatcherPort` is the narrow request/projection interface that is constructed before `RouteExecutor`, bound exactly once to the later-created `PathDispatcher`, and raises a construction error if called before that binding. It exposes no runtime owner or unrelated service.
  - `BlockManager` receives `RailwayNetwork`, a narrow `notification_emitter` callback, a `fatal_conflict_reporter` callback, and the same `active_path_getter` `SwitchManager` receives (see **Block-manager model** for how runtime construction binds each and what the getter fills).
  - `SwitchManager` receives `RailwayNetwork` and four narrow injected callbacks — the same `notification_emitter` and `fatal_conflict_reporter` callbacks `BlockManager` gets, plus an `environment_active_getter` and an `active_path_getter` (see **Switch-manager model** for what each does and how `SwitchManager` reaches `BlockManager` and `SwitchPowerController`).
  - `ResourceCoordinator` receives `BlockManager` and `SwitchManager`, the two managers it routes to.
- `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)` may create a controller only after those narrow dependencies are available. Any later-created entity is registered with its owning registry before it may participate in runtime state. A missing dependency fails construction instead of leaving a partially wired object.
- Controller-owned release and removal commands do not call dispatcher or route teardown inline; they only write the Action handoff in the Latch Table. `SimulationController`'s Action orchestration consumes those latches and calls the narrow request interfaces in Action step order.

**Session mode and operating environment**

A session has exactly one **session mode**: **Editor** or **Operation** (the ban on editing geometry while operating is recorded under **Out of Scope**). Editor places and wires geometry, with no `SimulationController` by default or with the lightweight one (per **SimulationController runtime surface**). Operation runs the railway: it brings up the full runtime — the `SimulationController` and its per-tick loop, with dispatcher, route executor, and controllers — and drives the trains. The header names this session mode **Operate** regardless of operating environment. `SimulationController` keeps its name in all three environments.

An operation session chooses exactly one **operating environment** when it is built:

- **Simulation** is the algorithm-focused in-memory run. It requires no Hardware Setup and has no chips, ports, buses, or bindings. `SimulatedTrackDriver` and `SimulatedSwitchDriver` accept every command, and `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` derives current-present readings from calculated train spans. Train physics owns movement. Simulation is the environment for ATC, ATO, routing, interlocking, timetable, and multi-train scenarios under happy hardware assumptions.
- **Virtual Hardware** is the hardware-integration run. It requires a complete, valid Hardware Setup and builds the same chips, binding maps, HAL interfaces, occupancy selection, and Setup tools as Real Hardware, but the transport is an in-memory device. The operator may control raw detector/current inputs, device responses and failures, or a higher-level virtual train scenario that translates movement into those raw inputs. Virtual Hardware never opens the physical controller and never mutates operational occupancy as a shortcut; the ordinary hardware pipeline must observe and attribute its inputs.
- **Real Hardware** is the physical-layout run. It requires the same complete Hardware Setup, and every required device and binding must be available. Its interfaces talk only to the physical device. Missing or failed hardware blocks activation or enters the latched hardware-failure state; it never falls back to Simulation or substitutes an individual simulated interface.

All three environments share one operational core: the per-tick stage loop, train ordering, ATC, ATO, routing, interlocking, notifications, and the occupancy read–debounce–attribute–reconcile pipeline. The environment changes only the physical-world boundary and pacing:

1. **Hardware boundary** — Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware construct all required interfaces as one transaction: a Virtual/Real builder either returns the complete interface set or fails. A `None` slot never means "substitute Simulation" outside the Simulation environment.
2. **Pacing** — Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware advance in real wall-clock time because they exercise hardware timing, so their `simulation_speed` is `1.0`: a successful Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware activation writes `simulation_speed = 1.0`, and `POST /api/simulation/control`'s `set_speed` action, the one other writer, is accepted only while Simulation is the active environment. Simulation is not bound to real time; its tick cadence and speed multiplier are runtime concerns. A stopped session runs no authoring step in any environment, and the two hardware environments go on reading their detectors in Setup and after Emergency stop (see **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs). No environment replays or time-travels (held **Out of Scope**).
3. **Occupancy reservation** — Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware read the configured occupancy interface and apply the two reconciliation rules under **Power**, Block occupancy detection: "Physical detection outranks the calculated position" and "The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector". There is no Real/Virtual environment with model-derived occupancy.

- **`active_environment`** names the environment the session was last built for: the one the most recent activation attempt, Setup entry, or boot was for. Deactivation leaves it unchanged, so it still names that environment while no environment is active; `environment_active` says whether it is active now.

The selected environment and `active_environment` are both explicit session truth, and neither is inferred from an interface type or from whether one chip happened to initialize. They differ while the operator has selected an environment the session has not yet activated, because selecting changes no session flag (per **Session state**). Each reader uses the one that matches its question:
- **The selected environment** says what the operator means to run next. The environment control, the readiness report, and Setup entry read it.
- **`active_environment`** says what the session is running now. The runtime loop's choice of pass, detector polling, unidentified-train adoption, and every environment-dependent safety gate (such as the operator-initiated per-train emergency cut-out, per **Emergency cut-out**) read it, as does every "in Simulation" condition (per **Session state**, "In Simulation" means the active environment). The selected environment is stored separately from Hardware Setup: loading layout wiring does not silently select or activate Real Hardware.

**Activation starts the railway over.** `POST /api/operation/activate` is accepted only while the session is stopped and not Halted for `runtime_failure` (see **Session state**). Before the new environment's first tick, it drops the railway's runtime state and keeps only what describes the layout.

- **An open Setup tool is closed first.** When activation passes its readiness check in Setup while a Setup tool holds the outputs, it closes that tool before anything else, which completes the tool's safe-state sequence (per **Power**, Hardware setup, Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state). Only then does it build the new environment's interfaces, so the outputs pass from the tool to `BlockPowerController` and `SwitchPowerController` through the safe state and never have two owners.

It keeps **all three** of these:

- the layout and the Hardware Setup;
- every train, with its last position (`physics_sync.current_span`);
- every `Route` definition and its `Route.assigned_train_ids`.

It drops the rest, in this order:

1. **Every live `Path`.** `PathDispatcher` cancels each one through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` with `error.origin = "revoked"` and `kind = "info"`, which releases its block reservations, locks, and switch claims; the route-side callback is the ordinary no-op branch.
2. **Every `RUNNING` `RouteRun`.** `RouteExecutor` moves each one to `_historical_runs` as `DEACTIVATED` and leaves `Route.assigned_train_ids` unchanged, so the next eligible Plan after the train is powered on allocates a fresh run per **Run start-mode seeding**.
3. **Every train's power.** Each controller goes `OFF` through `TrainController.complete_power_off()`. A train that was still rolling stops by itself on its next running pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**).

Pending teardown latches and held assignment requests are left alone. Each is consumed by its ordinary Action step on the first Live tick, because the Action teardown consumers run for an `OFF` train too (per **`SimulationController._act_train(...)` flow**): a pending path cancel finds no live path and clears; a pending abort or power-off removes the train's stored assignment and commits any held replacement (per **Route assignment writers**); a pending deactivate unassigns the train only from a route pending deletion and commits any request it was holding.

The one latch activation clears itself is the emergency request. It calls `phase_latches.discard_emergency_request()` on every controller, because a request latched on a stopped pass — for example when a Setup tool moved a locomotive into the next block — describes the railway before it started over. Discarding it is safe: a train with no reservation cannot move, and a real conflict re-latches on the next detector read (per **Power**, An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out).

- **Activation goes Live.** After the reset, a successful activation writes the session flags its row in the **Session state** transition table lists, and the session is Live. Every train is `OFF`, so nothing moves until the operator starts a train.
- **A refused or failed activation leaves no environment active.** The session reads Setup if it was in Setup, and otherwise Halted for `hardware_failure` or `not_activated` (per **Session state**). It never falls back to Simulation.
- **Boot activates no hardware environment.** At boot the runtime activates Simulation when Simulation is the selected environment, and the session boots Paused. A Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware selection is not activated at boot: the session boots Halted for `not_activated`, and the operator activates it. Boot runs no readiness check of its own.

**Fail-closed environment lifecycle.** A requested Real Hardware session that cannot validate or initialize is not activated, and the session reads Halted for `not_activated` with its readiness blockers (or Setup, or Halted for `hardware_failure`, per **Session state**), before anything drives. A failure after activation reports to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`, which attempts the full safe state and latches the **hardware failure** halt; the runtime does not keep ticking and retrying the failing I/O. Virtual Hardware follows the same logical fault lifecycle against its fake device so the fault handling can be tested. Simulation may report injected happy-interface faults when a test explicitly supplies them, but ordinary Simulation assumes success.

**Canonical runtime procedures**

These named procedures are the canonical home for ordering-sensitive cross-component workflows. Later sections may restate local consequences, but they must cross-reference these procedures rather than inventing a second order.

- **Physical progress / deviation procedure**:
  1. `e3e6` — During Observe, for a train whose movement is calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` emits one ordered `PhysicsSpanUpdate` per crossed resource boundary, plus one final no-boundary callback so Observe has a deterministic progress-commit point. For a train whose movement is not calculated, that commit point follows the three-way split in that same subsection: `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` on a stopped pass, the OFF branch of `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` on a running `OFF` pass, and no report for a ghost-frozen train.
  2. `35d0` — `TrainController.on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)` writes the new controller-owned span/speed, converts the tile delta into one typed `ControllerProgressReport`, and appends that report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`). It does not call `PathDispatcher` directly.
  3. `3e9b` — Later in that same train's portion of the same Observe batch, `SimulationController` drains the progress mailbox in FIFO order by calling `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each report, then clears the mailbox.
  4. `83a2` — `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` handles entered resources before any path bookkeeping by resolving `path_id = PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` and calling `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, path_id, route)` for each one; `path_id` is optional because a detector-delayed block entry may arrive after reservation ended. `route` is the unordered `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` the train uses through a switch tile (derived from the controller's `ResourceEvent.entry_edge` + `switch_exit_edge`); it is ignored for blocks. The coordinator routes block events to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks([block_id], train_id)`. For switch events, `path_id` and `route` must both be present: the coordinator routes them to `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)`, whose clean-entry effects and ordered conflict cases are defined under **SwitchManager**. A switch entry with `path_id is None` is a fatal physical-entry conflict, because no live path can own the required compatible main lock. Physical occupancy is the top-priority truth for clean entry: if recording it would not overwrite another owner's live route or block claim and the switch-entry lock check succeeds, the resource state records it even when later path bookkeeping has nothing to update.
  5. `018a` — When the routed manager returns `False`, it has already detected the overwrite of another train's current physical/reservation owner, reported it through the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**, and left the prior owner intact. `PathDispatcher` runs no ownership test of its own — the `bool` return is all it reads — and stops processing the report.
  6. `389a` — If `report.deviation == true`, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` latches cancellation instead of committing it inline: it calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(error=report.deviation_error, kind="warning", deviation=True)` per the **Writer-helper rule**. That `ErrorRecord` rides the latch payload into the `cancel_path` event defined in the **Cancellation** subsection. The deviated path stays `ACTIVE` and keeps its not-yet-entered reservations and switch locks until the latched cancel commits under its `is_stopped()` gate — resources acquired for a train are never released ahead of it while it is still rolling, so a braking train still consumes its own locks cleanly at each entry instead of intruding. The next eligible Plan after the committed cancel reruns ordinary covered-task index advance plus `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` from the train's current physical position.
  7. `640a` — Head progress splits across stages. In Observe, the dispatcher applies ordinary active-path head progress for entries that map into the live `resource_sequence` (per the monotonic `current_resource_index` rule) and records each such head-entry on `physics_sync.entered_blocks_this_tick`; the route head-advance callback itself runs in Plan settlement (this same step `640a`), under these rules:
     - **When it applies.** Observe records, and Plan settlement runs the callback, while the train has an active route run and the entry carried `current_head_sequence_index is not None` — including ticks where a cancel latch is pending.
     - **No-op cases.** A reported block that does not match the next task is a no-op on the route side. An entry the controller could not map under the **Head-mapping rule** (`sequence_index` is `None`) advances no path index and is not recorded for settlement.
     - **Deviation reports skip progress.** On a `deviation == true` report — which always carries `current_head_sequence_index = None` per the **Head-mapping rule** — the dispatcher records physical entry and tail-vacate only: `Path.current_resource_index` does not advance, and nothing is recorded on `entered_blocks_this_tick` for settlement.
     - **Per-block advance procedure.** In Plan settlement, for each recorded head-entry (in `sequence_index` order), the route side compares that single reported block/direction with the current next task on the `RouteRun` directed walk. If that task is a `waypoint` whose resolved target block and direction match the reported block and direction (the predicate in the **Dispatcher progress/completion flow**), the callback records it through `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(i)` and returns. The next recorded entry discovers the next task through a fresh `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` call.
     - **Callback prohibitions.** The callback must not call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` or `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`, must not arm a future planning cursor, must not write `RouteRun.direction`, and must not consume more than one task. Fresh target resolution for a new reservation waits for the next eligible Plan.
  8. `02bb` — Dispatcher processes `tail_vacated_resources` after all entered-resource handling.
- **Stop-arrival procedure**: Observe commits this tick's position; **Plan settlement** — the first half of `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`, before the planning half resolves and acquires the next target — decides route progress and finishes completed tasks. Finishing and re-planning therefore happen in one Plan pass, so a train can finish its stop and acquire the next reservation on the same tick.
  1. `e564` — Stop arrival is decided in Plan settlement, not in Action: `TrainController.tick(...)` maintains lookahead in Action, but it does not latch or emit task completion.
  2. `e4ad` — In Observe, `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` moves the train for that tick, and `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` writes the post-move span/speed and appends any resource/deviation observations to the progress mailbox (per steps `e3e6` and `35d0` of the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**).
  3. `4e0e` — Later in that same train's portion of the same Observe batch, `SimulationController` drains the mailbox by calling `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each report. Each call commits physical block/switch entry and tail-vacate through `ResourceCoordinator`, latches any movement-derived deviation, and records the tick's head-entered blocks (in `sequence_index` order) on the controller-owned within-tick field `physics_sync.entered_blocks_this_tick` for Plan settlement; it finishes no route task.
  4. `640a` — In Plan settlement, `RouteExecutor` consumes the head-entered blocks step `4e0e` recorded by calling `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` once per entered block in `sequence_index` order — each finishing at most one `waypoint` task per the **Dispatcher progress/completion flow** — then clears `physics_sync.entered_blocks_this_tick`.
  5. `9d8b` — Still in Plan settlement, after the head-advance consumption, if an active dispatcher path still exists for that train AND `pending_path_cancel_request` is `None` (a pending cancel — deviation or explicit — outranks arrival and skips this check), `RouteExecutor` calls `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` through its injected dispatcher port. The Action teardown latches `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, and `pending_route_deactivate` are consumed after this settlement, in Action. That order gives a pending teardown no arrival chance whenever a live path exists, because each teardown helper also latches the inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request`, which skips this check.
  6. `8df5` — **Stop-arrival check.** This is the canonical home for the predicate. `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` commits an arrival when **all three hold**:
     - `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id)` returns a `CompletionTaskProjection` whose `task_kind == "stop"` — an expired `run` row is presented with `task_kind == "stop"` by that projection (per the **`CompletionTaskProjection` schema** and **Run task resolution**), so it completes through this same check
     - the live reservation's terminal block is that projection's `stored_resolved_target.requested_destination_block_id`
     - `TrainController.is_stopped_at_reservation_end()` is true — the controller-owned derived read the dispatcher calls, reading no controller internals of its own. That helper completes on **either** of its two arrival conditions: `4a`, the train braked to rest at its braking target, **or** `4b`, the head physically in the terminal block (both defined, with their reasons, under **TrainController**, Read accessors).

     A train stopped short of its terminal block with clearance left in front of it does not satisfy the check and has not arrived, even when its distance-`0` reason code is `"reservation_stop"` (per **TrainController**, `is_stopped_at_reservation_end()`). The check runs no exact-position test beyond `4a` and `4b`. Because the live reservation for a `stop` task terminates at that stop's target block (the **Reservation termination rule**), a train inside that terminal block has nothing further ahead of it within the reservation.
  7. `f8c6` — If the stop-arrival check is false, no task is finished for that train on that tick and the live path stays `ACTIVE`.
  8. `09b0` — **Canonical terminal-teardown orders.** After the step-`8df5` predicate succeeds, release and cancellation share the same lower-layer prefix and differ in release mode and route-side callback. Release: `ResourceCoordinator.release_path_resources(..., completed=True)` → `Path.status = COMPLETED` → the injected completion callback `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`. Cancellation: `ResourceCoordinator.release_path_resources(..., completed=False)` → `Path.status = CANCELLED` → the injected cancellation callback `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)`. Neither order writes controller state: `train_status` and `ato_status` are derived, so once `received_path_plan` reads `None` the train holds no live reservation (a paused or idle ATO train reads `ato_status == READY`), or stays held under EB (`train_status == EB`) until `eb.release()`. `control_mode` is untouched: with `received_path_plan` now `None` the ATO output is `0` until the next reservation is granted. Neither order calls a controller hook.
  9. `bc55` — The completion callback delivered by step `09b0` (the injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`) records the stop as finished through `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`. This step owns only the route commit; reservation release and `Path.status = COMPLETED` already happened in `09b0`. The `stop` task and any following `dwell` task are independent rows. Because settlement runs before the planning half of the same Plan pass, a following `dwell` row's timer starts in that same pass at Plan step `70c3` — the train is already standing at the platform, so its `started_at` is sampled correctly. Timestamps that record this transition (`Path.last_status_updated_time`, the stop's `task_runs[walk_position].finished_at`, the stop's `task_runs[walk_position].finished_at_operating`, and any related notification `event_time`) are sampled fresh by their own writer at the moment of the write per **Time sampling** under the **Units contract**; the route-side and dispatcher-side wall timestamps are independent samples.
- **Power-off procedure**: The `pending_power_off` latch coordinates a four-step teardown across `PathDispatcher`, `RouteExecutor`, and `TrainController`.
  1. `98d3` — `TrainController.commands.power_off_cmd()` runs between ticks and accepts only while stopped. `_apply_power_off_request()` sets `control_mode = "manual"`, sets `pending_power_off`, and writes the inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request` with an `ErrorRecord` whose `origin` is `"power_off"` when reservation exists. While `pending_power_off` remains set, the **Propulsion cap step** applies a ceiling of `0` at the service rate on every tick, so `TrainController.tick(...)` may compute diagnostics but emits no non-neutral propulsion command. It does not mutate dispatcher or route state inline.
  2. `278a` — Step `7b40` (the `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer) consumes the inclusive cancel through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` on the first Action pass whose `is_stopped()` gate holds: the first pass after acceptance, unless the voltage the previous Action emitted moved the train in that tick's Observe, in which case the power-off ceiling brakes it to a stand first. The Observe ghosted-train writer (see **Power**, Ghosted trains) is not stopped-gated, but its rising-edge freeze forces the train's speed to `0` before Action runs, so its `is_stopped()` gate holds and both latches commit on that same tick's Action pass too. If no live path existed at acceptance, no inclusive cancel was written and the step is a no-op.
  3. `534f` — After step `7b40` has run (or no-opped), Action reaches the `pending_power_off` consumer step `9a81`. That step calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` through `SimulationController.route_executor`. The power-off consumer never calls `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` itself.
  4. `886a` — Finally that same Action step calls `TrainController.complete_power_off()`, which performs the OFF cleanup defined in **TrainController** (its full effect set, the callability rule, and its other callers live there) and takes the controller to `OFF`. After that call returns, the step clears `pending_power_off`. The earlier steps `7b40` (the inclusive cancel) and `534f` (`RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)`) have already left no route or reservation live; `complete_power_off()` itself performs only the controller OFF cleanup.
- **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**:
  1. `cd5e` — `SimulationController` owns the failed-runtime flag and fatal diagnostic payload; the halt is released only whole, through step `7c41`.
  2. `16e0` — `BlockManager` (for block conflicts) or `SwitchManager` (for switch conflicts) builds a typed `FatalPhysicalEntryConflict` and calls its injected `fatal_conflict_reporter`. Runtime construction binds that callback to `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`. This happens when a block entry encounters another train's `occupied_by` or `reserved_for_train` (see **Fatal-conflict `origin` labels**), a switch route conflicts with a different train's route in `Switch.physical_occupants`, a train enters a disabled block/switch, or a train enters a switch without a compatible reservation for its route. A physical entry into a manual (but not also disabled) resource is not fatal; clean-entry rules apply. The payload carries exactly `resource_type: "block" | "switch"`, `resource_id: str`, `incoming_train_id: str`, `prior_owner_train_id: Optional[str]`, `incoming_path_id: Optional[str]`, `prior_owner_path_id: Optional[str]`, and `error: ErrorRecord`. `incoming_path_id` is the active path dispatcher resolved for the entering train, or `None` when entry arrived without live reservation. `prior_owner_train_id` names the conflicting owner for `reserved_for_other_train`, `switch_occupied_by_other_train`, and `occupied_by_other_train`; it is `None` for `disabled_resource_entry`, `malformed_route_key`, and `switch_intrusion`. `prior_owner_path_id` is the conflicting reservation's stored path ID for `reserved_for_other_train`; for the two physical-owner conflicts it is that owner's currently active path ID when one exists; it is `None` for the remaining origins. No other field is optional or implied.
  2a. `6e4a` — **Fatal-conflict `origin` labels.** Every fatal physical-entry conflict halts the runtime the same way and is consumed only by `enter_failed_runtime(...)` diagnostics, so no code branches on which conflict it was and there is no conflict enum (per **Errors and diagnostic classification**). The reporting manager builds one `ErrorRecord` with a `text` naming the train, the resource, and the prior owner, and one of these reference `origin` labels, which `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)` — not the manager — later emits at `kind = "error"` (see step `b9a2`):
    - `"reserved_for_other_train"` (`f3f2`) — entry against another train's future reservation, before physical co-occupancy was recorded. Reservation exclusivity at acquisition time (`BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`) and Observe's resolution of any foreign reservation on a just-entered block before it commits the entry (per **Reservation truncation**) together mean this label reports an exclusivity-invariant violation, not an ordinary workflow outcome.
    - `"switch_occupied_by_other_train"` (`c0bf`) — a physically entering train's route conflicts (per `switch.routes_conflict(...)`) with a route a different train already holds in `Switch.physical_occupants`.
    - `"disabled_resource_entry"` (`b0f5`)
    - `"malformed_route_key"` (`a37e`) — a switch physical-entry event arrived with `route is None`. `PathDispatcher` derives a non-`None` route for every switch tile in the interior of a path (see step `83a2` of the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**); this label reports a break of that invariant, so the manager reports it as a fatal conflict instead of writing occupancy state from an unresolved route.
    - `"switch_intrusion"` (`d51c`) — a train physically entered a switch while holding no compatible reservation in `Switch.locks` for the route it occupies (the intrusion check defined in the **Switch entity** section).
    - `"occupied_by_other_train"` (`e2c7`) — a block entry committed for a train onto a block whose `occupied_by` belongs to another train. Attribution never produces one: a block already in a train's block list resolves as `held` for that train (rank 1 of the match order, see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), and adoption refuses a consist that reaches a block another train holds (see **Power**, Adoption is refused when any of these holds). So this label reports an exclusivity-invariant violation, not an ordinary workflow outcome. A locomotive that physically runs onto a block another train holds is not detected at all (see **Block**, One train per Block).
  3. `b9a2` — `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`, not the reporting entity, is the only writer of `failed_runtime = True`. It first calls `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`. The delegated safe-state write touches outputs and the recorded block voltages only (per **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe). The wrapper also ends every open calibration run (per **What ends a calibration run**). All other controller/path/route/resource/occupancy state remains available for inspection. `enter_failed_runtime(...)` then stores the fatal payload, latches `failed_runtime`, emits one `kind = "error"` event with `operation = "enter_failed_runtime"`, and aborts the transaction. The session then reads Halted for `runtime_failure` (per **Session state**).
  4. `525b` — Fatal conflict is not an ordinary cancellation branch. `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)` must not call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)`, or `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)`, because those APIs are recoverable workflow callbacks and would incorrectly clear state or replan while the runtime is failed.
  5. `ee19` — `SimulationController.update(...)` always refuses advancement while `failed_runtime` is set. It refuses advancement while `hardware_failure` is set only when `active_environment` is `virtual_hardware` or `real_hardware`; an active `simulation` environment runs its full Observe → Plan → Action loop while retaining and reporting the hardware-failure latch. The sole operation `update(...)` performs through either applicable gate is consuming the `OutputWatchdog` trip record (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**). Separately, the runtime loop closes a Setup tool whose idle timeout has passed on every iteration, gate or not (see **Power**, Hardware setup, A timeout closes the tool on time); that close only drives the tool's outputs toward the safe state, so the gate does not hold it back. When a gate applies, the session reads Halted, or Setup for a hardware failure latched while in Setup (per **Session state**), neither `AppState.operating_time` nor `SimulationController.simulation_time` advances, and no train pass or stopped pass runs (per **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs).
  6. `7c41` — **Clearing the halt.** `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()` is the only writer of `failed_runtime = False`. It is refused unless `failed_runtime` is set. On success it calls `TrainController.complete_power_off()` on every controller, clears the flag and stored payload, and emits one informational event. It writes no speed. A train the halt froze while rolling stops by itself once it is `OFF`: its next running pass reports speed `0` (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**). Clearing writes no other session flag, so the session state is derived again from the flags the halt left unchanged (per **Session state**): a session halted while Live is Live again with every train `OFF`, and one halted while Paused is Paused. Path, route, reservation, and occupancy state remain for inspection: an `OFF` train keeps its live path and its `RUNNING` run until an ordinary cancel or route teardown ends it (see **Authority to run is live reservation**). There is no force-clear of an individual resource.
**Path completion notification flow**

- `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` gives a spent reservation back and then hands the arrival to the route, which records the arrival that ended it. It evaluates the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) and invents no acceptance test of its own; on success it performs the step-`09b0` teardown, in that step's release order (per the **Stop-arrival procedure**).
- `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` returns a `PathCompletionResult` with these fields:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `success` | `bool` | Whether this call performed the `ACTIVE -> COMPLETED` transition. |
  | `path_id` | `Optional[str]` | The active path this call examined; `None` when the train has no active path. |
  | `new_status` | `Optional[PathStatus]` | `PathStatus.COMPLETED` when committed; `PathStatus.ACTIVE` when the stop-arrival predicate was false; `None` when no active path exists. |
  | `reason` | `Optional[str]` | `None` when committed; otherwise a diagnostic such as `"no active path"` or `"stop-arrival check not satisfied"`. |

  `RouteExecutor` calls this from Plan settlement step `9d8b`, which already guards the call on an active path existing, so that caller never sees the `(False, None, None)` no-active-path return; the return stays in the method's contract because the method resolves the active path itself. The one unsuccessful return `9d8b` can see is `(False, active_path_id, PathStatus.ACTIVE)`, for an active path whose stop-arrival predicate is false. An already-terminal row cannot be reached, because `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train()` returns only `ACTIVE` rows. A resolved active-path ID with no `paths_by_id` row is an internal invariant break and raises.
- Runtime components hold no general `SimulationController` back-reference. `SimulationController` owns construction and orchestration, then supplies the narrow registries, projections, writer interfaces, and callbacks listed under **SimulationController runtime surface**. A component may call only the named methods on the dependency it received; it may not discover unrelated services through a shared owner object.
- Wiring order follows those dependencies: create the network, `SwitchPowerController`, `BlockManager`, and `SwitchManager`; then create `ResourceCoordinator` and an unbound `PathDispatcherPort`; construct `RouteExecutor` with that port; construct `PathDispatcher` with the route executor's two named callbacks (`handle_path_completion`, `handle_path_cancellation`) and its one read-only route resolver; bind the port to that dispatcher exactly once; and only then create any `TrainController`. `ResourceCoordinator` holds only `BlockManager` and `SwitchManager`.
- `TrainController` instances are created on demand through `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)`, which runs only after the **SimulationController runtime surface** is fully registered. Each new controller receives only its controller-local modules, the read-only path projection, the route-latch writer interface, and the notification interface; it does not receive `SimulationController`. Controller-owned release/removal commands (for example, `TrainController.commands.power_off_cmd()`) write the Action handoff latches through controller-owned state rather than reaching into `PathDispatcher` or `RouteExecutor`.
- The conditions for recognizing path completion, and the rule that the controller safety margin outranks reaching the requested destination block, are defined under **Completion ownership and timing** and **Controller-mediated progress**.
- After reservation release, route-level waypoint and dwell logic must follow the **Stop-arrival procedure**: settlement step `bc55` records the finished stop, and the planning half of that same `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(train_id, delta_seconds)` pass either starts the dwell timer at step `70c3` (when the next row is a `dwell`) or resolves the next target. The train holds no live reservation throughout; an engaged ATO train on a following dwell row reads `ato_status == DWELLING`.

**`SimulationController._act_train(...)` flow**

1. Get or create a `TrainController`.
2. Get or create a `TrainPhysics`.
3. On first pairing only, initialize any controller-owned bootstrap values that come from persisted train data, then establish the runtime 1:1 `Train` <-> `TrainController` pairing for that `train_id`.
4. Call `TrainController.tick(delta_seconds, early_action_callback)`. The controller applies any latched emergency request (step `01f2`), then calls the supplied `early_action_callback` exactly once, even when it is `OFF`; `SimulationController` binds that callback to the early-Action consumer, the stopped-gated `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer (step `7b40`, per **Controller tick order**). When the controller is powered on, it lets the selected driving source produce its command against the post-cancel live reservation and lowers it through the **Propulsion cap step**. The callback exposes no dispatcher object to the controller.
5. Have `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` set the train's block track voltage for the next tick's Observe movement. This write runs for every train and self-gates: a powered train's blocks carry the propulsion output, and an `OFF` train's blocks are driven to the safe `0` V (a de-energize, never an energize — see **Running and stopped**, An observing step may remove power and must not apply it). Do not calculate movement or write the span here.
6. Consume `pending_route_abort` (`5d2c`), `pending_power_off` (`9a81`), and `pending_route_deactivate` (`4f6e`) after the voltage write, then run the calibration-run re-evaluation (step `26f5`). The `early_action_callback` already handled the path-cancel latch. **These steps run for every train.** They run whether or not the controller is powered; each is gated only by its own latch (and, for the teardown consumers, the inclusive cancel having been consumed). A teardown needs no power: it releases route state, and `TrainController.complete_power_off()` is idempotent on a train that is already `OFF`.
7. Sync only persistent train data back to `Train` (per **Ownership split**).

Movement and dispatcher feedback are not part of `SimulationController._act_train(...)`: before this Action call begins, the Observe batch has already run `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` and `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` and drained the progress mailbox, and this train's Plan settlement has already consumed head-entries and evaluated stop arrival.

**`SimulationController._act_train(...)` calls**

- The per-train Action calls are `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)`, `SimulationController.get_or_create_physics(train_id)`, `TrainController.tick(delta_seconds, early_action_callback)`, the physics-owned block-voltage application, the three later teardown consumers, and the calibration-run re-evaluation. The two accessors are orchestration methods; other components use their injected `ControllerRegistry` / physics registry dependency rather than calling back into `SimulationController`.
- **Controller creation binds only persistent data.** A newly created controller may bind only to the persistent train data needed for that 1:1 pairing. It does not seed `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span`; `SimulationController.add_train(...)` does, before any simulation tick (per **Train Entity**, Initial placement of `current_span`).
- **No seeded `received_path_plan`.** `Train` carries no live reservation or position/span fields, so this constructor path does not seed `received_path_plan`. `received_path_plan` resolves the dispatcher's active `Path` on each read, returns `None` before any path exists, and has no `receive_path_plan(...)` setter; its derived reads `assigned_path_id`, `ato_path_id`, and `ato_destination_block_id` are never written directly (per **received_path_plan schema** and **Dispatcher/route-executor inputs**).
- **Runtime reservation is route-backed.** `RouteExecutor` creates every path in Plan through `PathDispatcher.create_path(train_id=..., ...)`, using either the train's ordinary assigned route or a dedicated one-off route for ad hoc, operator, or speed-calibration movement. Every live path has a matching `RouteRun`; there is no other standalone non-route dispatcher-reservation mode.
- **Controller existence precondition.** `RouteExecutor` must already have ensured the controller exists before any Plan path creation: it calls its injected `ControllerRegistry.get_or_create(train_id)` before `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` or `extend_path(...)`. The registry owns the 1:1 binding and the persisted-data bootstrap callback supplied at construction; `RouteExecutor` sees neither `SimulationController` nor the `Train` registry. Controller bootstrap must not recreate reservation from train-side runtime mirrors. There is no late-controller recovery hook, and `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)` only makes sure the controller exists (per **Controller invariants**).
- Consumers read live target-speed data from controller lookahead at distance 0 and live operational state from `TrainController.ops.train_status` (and the read-model `ato_status` projection, per **ATO status**).
- Initial power/control runtime state comes only from the controller defaults and later explicit `TrainController` commands; live power/control state is never re-synced from `Train`.

**`PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` signature**

- `report: ControllerProgressReport` — payload per the **ControllerProgressReport schema**.
- Returns `None`. Side effects only; ordering follows the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**.
- On a fatal physical-entry conflict, the manager calls its injected `fatal_conflict_reporter`, which runtime construction binds to `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`; the call does not return a recoverable failure code.

**Dispatcher progress/completion flow**

**ControllerProgressReport schema**: This is the home of the `ControllerProgressReport` field set. Its producers are `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` and, for a detection-only report, `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()`; its consumer is `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`. It carries these fields:

- `train_id` (`str`)
- `event_time` (`float`, system-time Unix seconds; `TrainPhysics` samples it once per movement pass and passes it into `on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)`, and the controller stores it unchanged. A detection-only report from `build_detected_progress_report()` has no movement pass, so that method samples `time.time()` once when it builds the report)
- `entered_resources` (ordered list of resource-entry events)
- `tail_vacated_resources` (ordered list of tail-vacate events)
- `current_head_sequence_index` (`Optional[int]`, the train head's `sequence_index` in the active `resource_sequence`, resolved by the **Head-mapping rule**)
- `deviation` (`bool`)
- `deviation_error` (`Optional[ErrorRecord]`, required when `deviation == true` and `None` otherwise; diagnostic only, must not be used for branching)

The report does not carry `path_id`; `PathDispatcher` resolves the active path from `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)`.

Each resource event in `entered_resources` and `tail_vacated_resources` carries `sequence_index` (when known), `resource_type`, and `resource_id`, plus these type-specific fields:

- block tail-vacate events additionally carry `exit_edge` (`Optional[edge]`, the vacated block's forward exit edge `N`/`E`/`S`/`W` for the traversal by which the train left that block, or `None` per its definition under **BlockManager**); `PathDispatcher` passes this value as the `direction` argument to `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(...)` and `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)`
- switch events (both entry and tail-vacate) additionally carry `entry_edge` and `switch_exit_edge` (the traversal-frame edges `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` copies from the switch tile's `TileTraversal`), from which `PathDispatcher` derives the unordered `route` key — both are required non-`None` on switch events and are `None` on block events

**Head-mapping rule**: This is the single rule for how `TrainController` turns the train head's physical position into the `sequence_index` values it reports.

- **Why one resource can appear twice.** One `resource_id` may appear at more than one `sequence_index` in a single live `resource_sequence`, because the **repeated-resource rule** under **Path invariants** allows an extension to take reservation back into a resource the train has already passed and released; a run that laps through the same block carries that block at two indices.
- **Resolution algorithm.** The controller must not resolve the head by taking the first entry whose `resource_id` matches. It resolves the head to the lowest `sequence_index` at or after its own progress anchor. That anchor is the last `sequence_index` this controller reported for the current `received_path_plan.path_id`; it is 0 for a path whose head has not been reported yet, and it resets to 0 whenever `path_id` changes. The resolved index is what the report carries in `current_head_sequence_index` and in that entered event's `sequence_index`. This always picks the occurrence the train is physically in, because an earlier duplicate of the same resource exists only where the train already passed it and the path released it, so every duplicate lies behind the anchor.
- **Outcomes.** Resolution produces one of two outcomes:
  - When the only matching occurrence lies behind the anchor, the controller reports that occurrence's `sequence_index` and the entry is a no-advance — the monotonic `Path.current_resource_index` rule leaves the stored index unchanged — and the controller must not set `deviation = true` for it.
  - A head that matches no entry anywhere in the `resource_sequence` is the mapping failure that sets `deviation = true`, and that is the only thing that makes a report a deviation; its `deviation_error` carries `origin = "out_of_sequence"`.

- `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` is the runtime progress API for the **ControllerProgressReport schema** payload; a deviation report's required fields and its treatment as deviation input rather than ordinary active-path progress are defined under **Controller-mediated progress**. For a single report, processing order is the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**: entered resources first, then deviation latching, then tail-vacated resources.
- `PathDispatcher` uses `deviation` to decide whether to latch cancellation of the active path. On a deviation report, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` writes `pending_path_cancel_request(error=report.deviation_error, kind="warning", deviation=True)` during the Observe drain per step `389a`; the explicit-cancel step commits `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(path_id, error=..., kind="warning", deviation=True, latch="path_cancel_request")` once the train is stopped, and that `ErrorRecord` is preserved on the `cancel_path` event payload (per **Cancellation**) for diagnostics. Replanning after the cancel (including after an EB) and power-off teardown follow the **route path-event callback schema** and the **EB workflow state machine**. Planning and routing logic do not read anything inside `error`.
- `deviation = true` has exactly one predicate: live reservation exists and the train head is in a resource that appears nowhere in the active `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` (per the **Head-mapping rule**).

  A head that runs past `Path.get_reservation_end_block_id()` is covered by that same predicate, because the resource it runs into is not in the `resource_sequence`. Where the head sits relative to the reservation end is not part of the deviation decision.

- `TrainController` owns progress interpretation and the stored span. It applies each `span_update` from `TrainPhysics`; derives only switch entered/tail-vacated observations from ordered `added_tiles` / `removed_tiles`; takes block entered/tail-vacated observations only from `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` (folded and cleared per **Controller-mediated progress**); and compares the updated `current_span` with `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` when live reservation exists. `PathDispatcher` owns path progress/status, resource release, cancellation/completion, and route callbacks.
- For entered resources, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` must first record clean physical entry as defined in the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**. Only after those physical writes succeed, and only when `report.deviation == false` and an active path still exists for `train_id`, may dispatcher resolve the dispatcher-owned path record and update `Path.current_resource_index` from the reported `sequence_index` when the train head enters a resource in that live `Path.resource_sequence`.
- After that entry and index update, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` (in Observe) records the head-entry `resource_event` on `physics_sync.entered_blocks_this_tick` for the path's active route execution, if any, and only when `report.current_head_sequence_index is not None`. A report carrying `None` — a deviation report, a stopped-pass report, or a running-`OFF` detected-only report — records physical entry and tail-vacate only, and contributes no head-entry event. Observe does not call the route head-advance callback. In Plan settlement (step `640a`), `RouteExecutor` invokes the single route-facing head-advance callback `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(train_id, path_id, resource_event)` once per recorded event, in `sequence_index` order, then clears the list; `path_id` is re-resolved from `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` (stable within the tick, since cancellations commit only in Action). `resource_event` is a structured payload carrying `resource_type`, `resource_id`, and `traversal_direction: Optional`. For block resources, `resource_event.traversal_direction` is the block-relative `"forward"` / `"reverse"` traversal direction computed by the block-direction helper from the entered `resource_sequence` block entry against `Block.ordered_tiles`; for switch resources it is `None`. `RouteExecutor` must not poll `TrainController.get_current_span()` or `TrainController.get_lookahead()` inside `RouteExecutor.update(...)` to discover head movement. `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` is a Plan-settlement route-progress callback that consumes at most one task per call:
  - If `resource_type != "block"`, return; switches are no-ops on the route side.
  - Call `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` to live-resolve the next non-finished task on the directed walk. This default form is read-only over existing rows, does not invoke the `after_walk_position` append branch, and does not write `task_runs[i].resolved_target`.
  - If the resolved next task's `task_kind == "waypoint"` and its resolved-target block and direction match the callback's reported block and direction, the callback consumes that task: call `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(i)`; return. The next eligible Plan step `592a` / `66aa` sets `RouteRun.direction` from the `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` it consumes. The next report in the same local progress drain discovers the next task via the same live recompute.
  - If the resolved next task's `task_kind == "stop"`, the callback is a no-op on the route side whether or not the reported block matches: entering the block is not arriving at it. A stop is served by the **Stop-arrival check** in Plan settlement step `8df5`, or by the head-anchored covered-stop case in Plan when no reservation exists. The head-advance callback must not record `finished_at` for a `stop` task.
  - If the resolved next task's `task_kind == "run"`, the callback finishes no task on the route side whether or not the reported block matches: only Plan run step `6a0d` accumulates a run's timer, and the run finishes per **Run task resolution**. While a `run` is the active (next non-finished) task, the callback additionally records passed-behind waypoints: when the reported block equals the resolved target block of a not-yet-finished `waypoint` task ahead of that run on the directed walk, it adds that waypoint's walk-position to `RouteRun.run_passed_waypoint_positions` (see that field and **Covered-task index advance**). Recording a passed-behind waypoint is a `RouteRun` write, not a task completion, so it neither consumes a task nor counts against the one-task-per-call limit.
  - If the reported block does not match the next task's target block, the callback is a no-op on the route side. Coverage of an intermediate task that the train physically passed through without entering is reconciled by the next Plan's covered-task index advance, not by Observe.
  - The callback must not call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` or `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`, must not arm a future planning cursor, must not write `RouteRun.direction`, and must not write any controller state.

  Head-entry route progress is not gated by controller state: whatever the train's `train_status` (or the read-model `ato_status`), a head entering a `waypoint` task's resolved block consumes that task.
- When the entered resource is a block, that same dispatcher-owned entry handoff calls `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry("block", block_id, train_id, path_id, route=None)`, which routes to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks([block_id], train_id)` — the only normal runtime path that marks a block physically `OCCUPIED` (per **ResourceCoordinator** and **BlockManager**). When live reservation still exists, clean entry consumes any same-train dispatcher reservation for that block.
- When the entered resource is a switch, the same dispatcher-owned entry handoff calls `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry("switch", switch_id, train_id, path_id, route)`, which routes to `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(switch_id, train_id, path_id, route)`; both `path_id` and `route` are optional at the facade boundary so malformed input can be reported deterministically. The missing-argument fatal cases, the clean-entry semantics, and the flank-lock conversion are owned by the **SwitchManager** section and step `83a2` of the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**. `route` is the unordered `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` the train uses through the switch tile, derived by `PathDispatcher` from the controller's `ResourceEvent.entry_edge` + `switch_exit_edge`.
- A detector-delayed block occupancy update still commits when no `ACTIVE` path remains for that train (the old reservation was completed or cancelled): `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` passes `path_id=None` through `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(...)`; a block event still records physical occupancy through `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`, then dispatcher skips path-progress and completion bookkeeping. A switch entry has no detector-lag exception: it must arrive with the live path that owns its compatible lock, so a switch event with `path_id=None` enters the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure** and writes no occupancy state, with its `origin` set by the **SwitchManager** `on_physical_entry(...)` ordered precedence. Any conflicting physical entry likewise enters the fatal procedure — no silent overwrite, recoverable-cancellation treatment, or continued dispatcher bookkeeping. Every train stays halted until the operator clears the gate through step `7c41`.
- A live path's lifecycle while it progresses follows **Path invariants** and **Controller-mediated progress**.
- **Tail-vacate release flow.** Tail-vacate release is resource-local and dispatcher-mediated. After processing a report's `entered_resources`, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` releases each `tail_vacated_resources` entry by calling `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, direction, route)`; the coordinator alone routes the release to the block or switch manager (per **ResourceCoordinator**).
- **`direction` and `route` parameters.** `direction` is the block event's `exit_edge` as the **ControllerProgressReport schema** defines it, and is ignored for switches. `route` is the unordered `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` the train used through the switch tile, the key into `Switch.physical_occupants`, and is ignored for blocks. The dispatcher must always pass a non-`None` route for switch tail-vacate events. Entry removal, the flank-release walk, and the route-drift fallback are defined under **SwitchManager**, `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`.
- **Release survives reservation loss.** Active progress resolves through `PathDispatcher`'s registries rather than from `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan`, but tail-release logic after reservation release must resolve from the resource itself, so it still works when there is no active dispatcher reservation. `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` is not a deferred-release hook.

**Controller/train sync**

- `TrainController.tick(delta_seconds, early_action_callback)` owns ATC, ATO, and manual-control runtime calculations; target speed and speed-limit reason live only in the controller lookahead payload, never as standalone scalars (see **Design Direction**).
- `Train` must keep only persistent train data in sync from the simulation loop.

**Tick-order dependency**

- For one train's transaction, Plan must run before Action because the controller must read path tiles that already exist.
- Within Observe, the movement calculation must run before the occupancy commit, because the commit reads positions the movement has just produced.
- Physics progress and occupancy commit run inside the Observe batch, not in a per-train physics-then-feedback pass: every train's movement calculation (`TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`) and the one global detector attribution run first, then each train's progress-mailbox drain (`PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`) commits that train's boundary crossings later in the same batch, and the whole Observe batch commits before any train's Plan and Action begin. Route reactions to those crossings — the head-advance consumption (step `640a`) and stop arrival (step `9d8b`) — run in each train's Plan settlement, not in Observe.
## Design Direction

**Ownership split**

- `TrainController` owns live operational state: ATC/ATO/manual mode, handle position, manual `power_percent`-mode inputs, and the live lookahead data series. "Target speed" and "speed-limit reason" MUST NOT be stored as standalone fields anywhere. They are the value and the reason metadata at position 0 of the lookahead series.
- `TrainController` also owns live power and control state: the stored `powered` flag (from which the derived `train_status` reads `OFF` when off), the `control_mode` selection, and the ATO `engaged` bit. The travel direction is not an operator selection: it is derived from the live reservation per **Reservation-side head derivation**.
- `Train` owns only persistent train data: identity, consist, capability/profile references, and other non-live train fields. It does not mirror any live state — not live position or span, live speed, ATO/ATC/path-runtime state, power/control state, or operational state.
  - Initial live placement comes through `SimulationController.add_train(...)` before the first simulation tick (per **Train Entity**, Initial placement of `current_span`).
  - The frontend/API input shape is `id`, optional `position: {x, y}`, `direction`, `max_speed`, `length`, and other persistent train fields.
  - Bootstrap data must enter through `add_train(...)` or explicit controller commands.
- The manual model has no `manual_target_speed` field.
- Manual control has two controller-owned submodes:
  - `simulation`: the user drives with handle notches. The handle command flows to `TrainPhysics`, which turns it into a speed change over time.
  - `power_percent`: the user drives with a power percentage. The controller maps the percentage through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` to one commanded speed, and the **Propulsion cap step** (see **TrainController**) lowers it under any active ceiling. `TrainPhysics` applies the effective operating point right away, with no momentum model: `track_voltage` comes from the inverse of `SpeedProfile.voltage_power_curve`, and the calibrated current speed comes from `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve`.
- `TrainPhysics` and `BlockPowerController` MUST NOT decide manual-mode policy. They run whatever command the controller produces, convert command to speed, and emit voltage.

**Errors and diagnostic classification**

- Every error, failure, and cancellation reason has one of two shapes, decided by one question: does code branch on which one it is?
  - **Branched.** Some caller changes behavior based on the value. It stays a small closed set — an enum or a `bool` — and the branch that reads it must be named where the set is defined. The members of this shape are:
    - `PathAcquisitionFailureKind`
    - `TargetResolutionFailureKind`
    - the `deviation` field on `ControllerProgressReport` (read by `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(...)` to decide whether to latch a cancel)
    - the branched subset of the `atc_limit_reason_code` enumeration (see **the canonical lookahead payload**): `reservation_stop` (read by the **Stop-arrival check**) and `deviation` / `no_reservation` (read by the zero-limit EB escalation applied at controller tick step `914f`, under the step `826a` protocol)
  - **Not branched.** The value exists so a person can read it in a log, a notification, or the UI. It is carried as one `ErrorRecord` and never as an enum, and no runtime code may switch on its text.
- A new closed-set value requires a caller that branches on it. A set whose values all lead to the same behavior is one value plus an `ErrorRecord`, not a taxonomy. One set carries a stated exception: the three caller-contract-violation values of `PathAcquisitionFailureKind`, and its `blocked_before_target` outcome, are named without a branching caller, for the reasons given at that set's definition site (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, **`create_path()` / `extend_path()` return contract**).
- `ErrorRecord` is the single diagnostic-error object. It carries exactly:
  - `text` — `str`, the human-readable failure detail
  - `origin` — `str`, a free-form label naming what produced the error (`"eb"`, `"out_of_sequence"`, `"switch_intrusion"`, `"operator_cancelled"`, `"planning_failed"`, `"no_viable_path"`, `"reservation_truncated"`). Diagnostic only: no runtime branch reads it, and writers may use labels beyond the ones this document names. It is the field a reader groups errors by when `operation` alone is too coarse.
- An `ErrorRecord` is always written whole: both fields are present together, or the whole record is `None`. Ordinarily it rides in the `error` field of one runtime event, and that event owns the time and the level: the event's `event_time` is when the error happened, and the event's `kind` is how bad it is (see **Runtime notifications**). An `ErrorRecord` therefore carries no timestamp and no severity of its own. The only across-tick carriers are the bounded Action-latch and `SimulationController.failed_runtime_payload` exceptions defined under **Error events**; both retain the same whole record. It is the diagnostic carried by `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, by every latch write that defers a failed or interrupted action, and by the fatal physical-entry conflict payload.
- A plain `reason: Optional[str]` field on a *result* object (what an operation did) is not an error record and stays a free-form string; `ErrorRecord` is for the diagnostic a writer hands forward for a person to read later.

## Layered Architecture

**Layered responsibilities**

- `PathDispatcher` carries out the route plan: it acquires future blocks, locks future switches, and manages movement reservation. It plans for the controller by giving it the dispatcher-owned reservation geometry and the current reservation-end block. The controller then works out the braking target from that boundary, using its safety-margin policy.
- `PathDispatcher` is the only owner of dispatcher path records. `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` is a read-only property. It returns the dispatcher's current movement-reservation projection for that train. It is not controller-owned state, has no setter, and keeps no copy of its own.
- `PathDispatcher` stores each path record by `path_id` in a dispatcher-owned registry such as `paths_by_id[path_id]`.
- `PathDispatcher` exposes a derived read `active_path_id_by_train(train_id) -> Optional[str]`. It scans `paths_by_id` for the one path whose `train_id` matches and whose `status == ACTIVE`. There is no separate registry to keep in sync; this index is a view of `Path.status`. Each train has at most one `ACTIVE` path at a time (per **Same-train create rejection**).
- **Retained path history.** Cancelled or completed paths may stay in `paths_by_id[path_id]` as history. They are not active reservation: their `Path.status` is not `ACTIVE`, so `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` skips them, and the controller's `received_path_plan` property returns `None`. There is no path-owned deferred-release flag.
- **Future-only reservation ownership.** `PathDispatcher` owns only future reservation resources — the blocks and switches the train has not entered yet. When the train head enters a resource, that future reservation or lock is consumed, and physical occupancy becomes resource-local state through dispatcher-mediated writes.
- **Release on cancellation or completion.** Cancellation and completion release only the not-yet-entered dispatcher-owned reservations and locks, and they change `Path.status` in the same step.
- **Motion continues after release.** Retained path rows do not stop physical motion after completion or cancellation. `TrainPhysics` keeps moving the train using live network geometry and state, and physical `occupied_by` state is cleared by later tail-vacate release events (detector-confirmed for blocks per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; controller-reported traversal for switches) and, for blocks, by the three `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` teardown clears (ghosted-train teardown, adoption re-key, and train deletion, see **BlockManager**). Train deletion also releases the train's switch occupancy through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` (see **Train Entity**, Deleting a train).
- **Same-train create rejection.** `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` rejects a same-train request while that train already has an `ACTIVE` path. The active-path guard in the **`create_path()` flow** and the **`create_path()` / `extend_path()` return contract** own the rejection rule, its no-side-effect guarantee, and its `failure_kind`. Once the old path is not `ACTIVE`, later creation follows only the ordinary live resource conflicts.
- **Span/speed ownership and computation.** `TrainController` owns the stored span and speed.
