- A `Block` is the power + occupancy + reservation unit: a switch-free connected run of one or more segments wired to one power feed, carrying one `track voltage` and admitting one train at a time (see **One train per Block (power domain)**). The block stores its members as `segments` — the ordered `Segment` objects it owns — and the derived read `segment_ids -> List[str]` gives their IDs in that order.
- `state` is a computed read-only property derived from these primitive fields:
  - `occupied_by: Optional[str]` — physical train presence (non-None means a train is in the block).
  - `caution: Optional[CautionState]` — physical safety-margin record; `None` when not in caution. `CautionState` carries exactly `exit_edge: "N" | "E" | "S" | "W"` (the departing train's exit edge). It is written only by `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()`, and cleared only by one of these:
    - `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()`;
    - `occupy_blocks(...)` on clean entry;
    - `release_path_block_reservations(completed=True)`.

    A reservation never changes it (see **BlockManager**, A reservation never changes a block's caution).

    Storing the flag and the exit edge as one Optional record makes them all-or-nothing by structure. Convenience reads: `_is_caution` (= `caution is not None`) and `caution_exit_edge` (= `caution.exit_edge` or `None`).
  - `reservation: Optional[BlockReservation]` — the one active path's dispatcher reservation on this block, or `None` when no path holds it. `BlockReservation` carries exactly:
    - `path_id: str` — which active path holds the reservation;
    - `train_id: str` — the train the reservation is intended for, stored on the reservation because `occupied_by` is physical-only; `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`'s reserved-for-other-train safety check needs the intended train without reading occupancy;
    - `exit_edge: "N" | "E" | "S" | "W"` — the direction reserved by the dispatcher through the block.

    `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` always writes the three fields together, and `Block.release_path_reservation()`/`occupy_blocks(...)` clear them together; as for `caution`, the one Optional record keeps them all-or-nothing by structure. Convenience reads `reserved_by_path`, `reserved_for_train`, and `reserved_direction` are derived from `reservation.path_id`, `reservation.train_id`, and `reservation.exit_edge` respectively (each `None` when `reservation is None`).
  - `locked_by_path: Optional[str]` — the `path_id` that has locked this block, or `None` when no path has. A block is locked only by the path that already reserved it, so whenever it is set `locked_by_path == reservation.path_id`. The lock is that path's braking-distance commitment on the block (the **Braking-distance lock**), a written, readable flag **peer to the reservation**, not a value derived from it. It is written by `BlockManager.lock_blocks_for_path(...)`. It is cleared by the surplus-lock release (which keeps the reservation) and by every release that drops the block's future reservation:
    - `BlockManager.unlock_blocks_for_path(...)` — the **Stopped-run lock shrink**'s surplus-lock release;
    - `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)` on clean head-entry — the head consumes the lock together with the reservation, so an entered block is never left locked;
    - `ResourceCoordinator.release_reservation_tail(...)` on a **Reservation truncation** or **Preemption** tail-release;
    - `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)` on whole-path completion or cancellation.

    `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` clears any residual lock on the vacated block. A locked block is uncancellable: **Preemption** may take a reserved block from a lower-priority train only when `locked_by_path is None`. Convenience read: `is_locked` (= `locked_by_path is not None`).
  - `disabled: bool = False` — physical-absence availability flag inherited from `TrackResource` (rules per **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**).
  - `manual: bool = False` — virtual-disable availability flag inherited from `TrackResource` (rules per **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**).
  - `allowed_travel_directions: Set["forward", "reverse"]` — static block-level travel policy for this block, defaulting to both directions allowed. It is not a reservation field and is not stored on `Tile`; `Block.reserved_direction` is only the temporary dispatcher reservation direction for one path.
    - **Manual override bypass.** Operator-initiated `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` calls that carry `manual_override = True` bypass this filter (per **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**).
    - **Effect on prefix-scan truncation.** The **Junction-fouling exclusion** reads this set: a block restricted to a single direction is exempt from that exclusion.
- The computed `state` property must use priority order: OCCUPIED > CAUTION > RESERVED > FREE.
  - Return `OCCUPIED` if `occupied_by is not None`.
  - Return `CAUTION` if `caution is not None`.
  - Return `RESERVED` if `reserved_by_path is not None`.
  - Return `FREE` otherwise.
- This makes composite physical+reservation states directly representable:
  - OCCUPIED with no path reservation (start-block / occupied-seed scenario): an occupied seed block appears in `Path.resource_sequence` for geometry and progress only; `Block.occupied_by` names the train and `Block.reservation` stays `None`, because clean entry consumes any same-train reservation (see **BlockManager**, `occupy_blocks(...)`, and the occupied-seed rule in `reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`). `state` reads `OCCUPIED`.
  - CAUTION + `reserved_by_path` set (path holds block through safety margin): see **`CAUTION` vs reservation independence**.
- `Block.ordered_tiles` is a derived read-only property: the concatenation of its member `Segment.ordered_tiles` in `segment_ids` order. The segments in a block join end-to-end into one connected switch-free walk (an invariant of `segment_ids`), so this concatenation is a single well-defined block-local tile order; the block stores no tile list of its own. `Block.allowed_travel_directions` is the static allowed-direction policy over that order, and that same order is the frame the block's commanded voltage sign is expressed in (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction). For a direct block target, `requested_destination_direction == "forward"` means movement in the increasing direction of `Block.ordered_tiles`, and `"reverse"` means the decreasing direction. Before `RouteExecutor` accepts the request with the run's `Route.manual_override = False`, and before `PathDispatcher` accepts a request with `manual_override = False`, the concrete `"forward"` or `"reverse"` value must be present in the target block's `allowed_travel_directions`. Both entry points skip this check when the override is `True`, per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home.
- Block direction is computed only by the **canonical block-direction helper** defined under **Segment**, using this derived `Block.ordered_tiles` view. The pathfinder reads tile order and geometry fields from each member `Segment` along a candidate block.
- `occupied_seconds: float = 0.0` is the block's cumulative occupied time, a runtime-written persisted counter; the rules and its single writer live in **Maintenance counters**.
- `is_holding_point: bool = False` is a manually-set persisted layout flag marking this block as a safe place for a train to wait. The operator sets it; it is saved with the layout and never written by runtime. It does not affect availability, reservation eligibility, pathfinding, the computed `state`, or physical entry. It has three consumers: the holding-point chunking of the **Reservation termination rule** (per **Holding-point chunking**); the truncation **Holding-point preference** (a truncation-terminal rule under **Path And PathDispatcher**); and **Meet coordination**'s passing places, where a train waits while another goes by (see **Meet coordination**, Passing place). Marking a block a holding point asserts that a train may wait there without fouling a switch throat or blocking a single-track corridor; that placement is the operator's responsibility.
- Because acquisition decisions need to check all blocks at once, `BlockManager` must be the sole mutator of Block runtime state (`occupied_by`, `caution`, `reservation`, `locked_by_path`) on the runtime path; the one exception is pre-first-tick placement through `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` (see **Power**, Placement is seeded, not re-detected). `Block` is a data container.
- There is no admin-side direct-mutation surface for Block state. Admin endpoints that need to drive block state for testing must drive it through real flows (place a train, create a path, and so on) so the canonical writers run. The `PATCH /api/blocks/<block_id>` endpoint rejects `state` mutations with HTTP 410.

**Block grouping**

- Block membership — creating a block, adding or removing a `Segment` from the stored `Block.segments`, and deleting a block — lives in `BlockGroupingManager` (file `block_grouping_manager.py`). `RailwayNetwork.create_block / delete_block / add_segment_to_block / remove_segment_from_block` are forwarders to it. `BlockGroupingManager` edits only the power-grouping axis (`Block.segments`, the derived `segment_ids` following it); it never writes runtime state (that is `BlockManager`) and never writes segment geometry (that is `SegmentGeometryManager`).
- A block is a switch-free connected run of segments joined end-to-end (an invariant of `segment_ids`, see **Block model**), so grouping edits preserve that run. `add_segment_to_block` and `remove_segment_from_block` may add or remove a `Segment` only at either end of `Block.segments`, and only when the result is still one connected switch-free walk whose member `Segment.ordered_tiles` orientations all align with increasing block order. Backend edit validation rejects middle insertions, removals, reorders, and an end-add that would require reversing the stored segment order — the same end-only rule as `Segment.ordered_tiles` (see **Segment**) and the platform tile extent (see **Platform And Station**).
- **Grouping infers member order, never member geometry.** `BlockGroupingManager.create_block()` and `add_segment_to_block` both derive member order from stored geometry, not from an unordered caller-supplied set. When a segment is oriented against the run, grouping rejects and names it; the operator first calls `SegmentGeometryManager.reverse_segment_orientation(segment_id)` through the explicit segment endpoint and then retries grouping. Grouping never reverses geometry itself.
- Grouping never leaves a segment without a block, because every segment belongs to exactly one block (see **Segment**). At creation, `RailwayNetwork.create_segment(...)` / `create_segment_with_tracks(...)` (see **SegmentGeometryManager**) complete by calling `BlockGroupingManager.create_block(...)` for that one new segment in the same operation: the segment create and the block create commit together, so a rejected block create rejects the segment create as a whole, and `RailwayNetwork` never returns a segment with no block. This is the default one-block-per-segment rule; the new block's id is derived from the segment's under **One id per record**. After creation, a segment the operator has not grouped into a larger block remains its own single-segment block under that same rule. `add_segment_to_block` moves a segment out of its prior block (deleting that block if it thereby empties, through the **Non-empty parent rule** under **Tile**); `remove_segment_from_block` returns the segment to its own single-segment block; on a block whose only member is that segment it is a no-op; and `delete_block` re-homes every member segment the same way. Removing a block's last member segment deletes the block through the same **Non-empty parent rule**.
- **One id per record.** This is the canonical home for how the two axes are identified. A `Block` id and a `Segment` id must never be equal. The two are separate records with separate lifetimes, so one string naming both is ambiguous wherever either is displayed, addressed, or bound — a panel row, an event `entity_id`, a `block_id` key in the **Power** binding table. The default one-block-per-segment rule still pairs them, and the pairing is spelled as a matched prefix pair: a segment `SEG_<suffix>` is owned by block `BLK_<suffix>`, and a platform's segment `<platform_id>_SEG` by its block `<platform_id>_BLOCK`. The pairing must be derived from the id alone and must not change across a save, a load, or a re-bake of the same layout, because the `block_id` keys in the **Power** binding table name blocks that outlive any one session. When one axis already carries the id an outside record names, that id stays put and the other axis takes the derived one: `create_segment(...)` / `create_segment_with_tracks(...)` mint the segment and derive its block, and a caller that must pin an exact block id states it. Splitting a segment whose children each get their own block suffixes the parent BLOCK's id (`PARENT_1`, `PARENT_2`), and each child segment takes the matching derived id.
- **One name per record.** This is the canonical home for how the two axes are named. `Segment.name` and `Block.name` are separate display names, and no create, split, group, or re-home step copies one onto the other. `create_segment(...)` / `create_segment_with_tracks(...)` name the segment they mint and leave the new block unnamed; `create_block(...)` names the block and leaves every member segment's name as it stands; splitting a segment names the child segments after the parent segment and leaves the child blocks unnamed; and a segment re-homed by `remove_segment_from_block` / `delete_block` keeps its name and lands in an unnamed block. Each name says what its own record is: a segment's names a run of track geometry, a block's names a power feed. A record with no name is displayed by its id, so a reader always sees which of the two they are looking at.

**`CAUTION` vs reservation independence**

- `CAUTION` is a safety state indicating the block ahead (in the departing train's direction) is still occupied; it is independent of path reservation.
- A block can be simultaneously `CAUTION` and `reserved_by_path` (path still holds it for a future or in-progress train), or `CAUTION` with no reservation (train has passed and path is done). The `state` property returns `CAUTION` in both cases, and `reserved_by_path` can be cleared by a plain field write with no state guard.
- `CAUTION` by itself does not make a block unreservable. `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` must still allow a `CAUTION` block when the **Block eligibility** predicate in **BlockManager** is satisfied. The operational effect of `CAUTION` is that `TrainController` lookahead applies `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` when it samples the block and the train's traversal leaves it through `block.caution.exit_edge`; a train crossing the block out of its other end is not limited (see **TrainController**, ATC speed limit).
- Setting `Block.disabled = True` is rejected while occupancy, reservation, or `CAUTION` remains; the caller must wait for ordinary tail-vacate/CAUTION clearing or cancel the holding path, then retry. There is no force-cleanup workflow, and train deletion is refused while a train holds a live path or a `RUNNING` run (see **Train Entity**, Deleting a train); a fatal halt is released whole through step `7c41` of the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**, not repaired resource by resource. `Block.manual` remains an unconditional future-planning flag.
- The `OCCUPIED → CAUTION → FREE` lifecycle is driven purely by physical train movement through `BlockManager`; it does not depend on whether a path reservation exists.
- `CAUTION` is directional: `block.caution.exit_edge` records the compass edge through which the departing train left (the direction it was moving). The `CAUTION → FREE` decision — which forward neighbour is consulted and when the protection chain is stale — is owned by `BlockManager._reevaluate_caution_blocks()`; see **`on_block_tail_vacated()` behaviour (directional CAUTION evaluation)** under **BlockManager**.

**Block methods**

- Path reservation and physical occupancy are separate concerns with separate `BlockManager` entry points: reservation eligibility is owned by `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` and physical entry by `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`, both defined in the **BlockManager** section.
- `Block.reserve_for_path(path_id, train_id, exit_edge)` is an internal helper called only by `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`. It writes `block.reservation = BlockReservation(path_id=..., train_id=..., exit_edge=...)`. The reservation never overwrites `occupied_by` (which stays physical-only).
- `Block.release_path_reservation()` is an internal helper called only by `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)`. It clears `block.reservation` with no state guard. It must NOT touch `block.caution` (that field is the physical-lifecycle owner's, `BlockManager`).

**Block invariants**

- Runtime physical entry is written only through `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(block_ids, train_id)` (full contract in the **BlockManager** section). The single-writer rule, its commit stage (Observe, for every train including an unidentified train, plus the between-tick adoption re-key), and the initial-placement exception are reconciled in **Power**, Block occupancy detection. On clean entry the primitive fields move together: `occupied_by = train_id`, `caution = None`, any same-train `reservation = None`, and any same-path `locked_by_path = None`. `OCCUPIED` overrides `CAUTION` on clean entry; stale caution metadata must not survive an intervening clean entry.

**One train per Block (power domain)**

- A block owns the one `track voltage` its member segments share; there is no separate per-segment voltage. The canonical home for the voltage value itself is `TrainPhysics` (see the `track voltage` glossary term and **Power**, Block power-controller role); the block is the set of segments one emitted value lands on. A switch between blocks has no feed of its own and runs on its `switch feed block` (see **Power**, Switch power-controller role). A block the operator has not grouped from a larger run is its own single-segment feed, independently powered, so a layout with no grouping applied behaves as one feed per segment; grouping models real shared-power wiring.
- **Detection isolation is separate from geometry.** A block is one occupancy section with its own current detection (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). Its member segments are geometry only and are not independently detected.
- A block carries one train's `track voltage` at a time, so a block is a single-train power domain. Two trains cannot be controlled independently on one shared feed: one voltage cannot produce two target speeds, and two locomotives with different speed profiles on one feed close on each other until they collide.
- The one-train-per-block rule is just the ordinary block-exclusion check: a block already occupied or reserved by another train is not eligible for a second train's reservation, so `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` rejects it the same way it rejects any occupied or other-reserved block (see the reservation-eligibility rule in **BlockManager**). A path is therefore never reserved into a block another train holds.
- **A second train on a held block is not detected.** When a locomotive physically runs onto a block another train already holds, nothing records it: the block already reads current, so the detector reports no change, and attribution keeps the block with its holder (rank 1 of the match order, see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). Two rules keep a second train out instead: no reservation ever reaches a held block (the bullet above), and a block past a train's authority end is never energized (see **Power**, A block past the authority end is never energized). A locomotive that coasts past both is not seen. Telling a second motor from the size of the current a block draws is out of scope (see **Out of Scope**, Collision modeling): it could show only while the block is driven, and a block whose train is standing still carries too little current to tell.
- Running several trains on one layout therefore uses several blocks, one powered train each.
## BlockManager

**Block-manager model**

- `BlockManager` is the lock manager for block resources and the single serialization point for atomic block acquisition.
- `BlockManager` holds:
  - the network;
  - an injected narrow `notification_emitter(operation, kind, message, entities, error=None, payload=None)` callback;
  - the injected `fatal_conflict_reporter` callback;
  - the same `active_path_getter` `SwitchManager` receives, used only to fill a fatal block-conflict payload's `incoming_path_id` (always) and its `prior_owner_path_id` for the physical-owner conflict (`occupied_by_other_train`) only; the `reserved_for_other_train` conflict reads `prior_owner_path_id` from `block.reservation.path_id` per the payload contract in the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**.

  It never receives or looks up `SimulationController`. Runtime construction routes the notification callback into `NotificationCenter` and binds the fatal callback to `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`; what that method does is defined in the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**. `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)` and `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` emit their manager-owned warnings through `notification_emitter`.
- `occupy_blocks(block_ids, train_id)` is the atomic occupy helper and sole physical-entry writer. Clean entry sets `block.occupied_by = train_id`, clears `block.caution`, consumes any same-train reservation, and clears any same-path `block.locked_by_path`. When a target block fails clean entry it reports a fatal physical-entry conflict:
  - occupied by another train -> `error.origin = "occupied_by_other_train"`;
  - reserved for another train -> `error.origin = "reserved_for_other_train"`;
  - `disabled == True` -> `error.origin = "disabled_resource_entry"`.

  All three call the injected `fatal_conflict_reporter`, and none writes occupancy or overwrites the prior owner. A block whose `occupied_by` already equals `train_id` is an idempotent no-op: no field is written and no conflict is reported. Returns an `OccupyResult(outcome: str, reason: Optional[str])` whose `outcome` is `"clean_entry"`, `"idempotent_noop"`, or `"fatal_conflict"`. `bool(result)` is `True` for `"clean_entry"` and `"idempotent_noop"` and `False` for `"fatal_conflict"`, and every caller uses it as a bool: on a fatal conflict the callback has already entered failed runtime, and the caller stops processing.
- `ReservedBlockTraversal` is the value type for `directions` in `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`. It carries exactly `exit_edge` (`"N" | "E" | "S" | "W"`) and `block_direction` (`"forward" | "reverse"`). `block_direction` is derived from the block's immutable internal tile order, not from train-end labels: if the directed in-block traversal advances to higher indices in `Block.ordered_tiles`, it is `"forward"`; if it advances to lower indices, it is `"reverse"`; if the traversal stays within one ordered tile, it is `"forward"` when the traversal enters through that tile's stored `entry_edge` and `"reverse"` otherwise.
- `reserve_blocks_for_path(block_ids, path_id, train_id, directions, manual_override=False)` reserves a path's blocks atomically.
- `directions` must be a mapping keyed by `block_id`, where each value is one `ReservedBlockTraversal`. `PathDispatcher` owns building that mapping from the chosen path geometry before calling `BlockManager` and must use the same canonical block-direction helper used by route callbacks. `ReservedBlockTraversal.exit_edge` is written to `block.reservation.exit_edge` (read as `Block.reserved_direction`); `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction` is used for `Block.allowed_travel_directions` validation, and it is also the direction the emission layer signs that reserved block's voltage with (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction).
- The `manual_override` parameter of `reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` is propagated from the calling `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**. The method must first check eligibility for every future block in the candidate block set before writing any fields. Blocks already physically occupied by the train may appear in `Path.resource_sequence` for geometry/progress, but they are not included in the future reservation candidate set.
  - **Block eligibility.** A candidate future block is eligible when **all of these hold**:
    - `block.disabled == False`
    - `block.occupied_by is None`
    - `block.reserved_by_path is None or block.reserved_by_path == path_id`
    - `manual_override == True`, or the candidate `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction` is present in `block.allowed_travel_directions`
    - `block.manual == False`, or `manual_override == True`

    These conditions are the whole of the one-train-per-block rule in **Block** — no separate cross-train test is applied.
  - `block.caution is not None` is not an eligibility failure by itself.
  - When any block in the candidate set fails eligibility, the entire call is rejected and no state changes are made.
  - `PathDispatcher` owns choosing how much of that candidate set to attempt atomically — the full requested route when it is all acquirable, or the longest acquirable forward prefix otherwise, bounded by the reservation cap.
- `reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` writes the reservation by calling `Block.reserve_for_path(path_id, train_id, reserved_exit_edge)` with the mapping value's `exit_edge` for each future block; the helper sets `block.reservation` in one step. It must not create path-owned reservations for blocks the train already physically occupies. An occupied block the path does store is the seed's start-side block at `resource_sequence[0]` or a forward block the head has since driven through; every other occupied resource is pure physical occupancy on `Block.occupied_by`, outside `resource_sequence`. Returns `ReserveResult(success: bool, failed_block_id: Optional[str], reason: Optional[str])`. On success `failed_block_id = None`. On failure no field is mutated, `failed_block_id` is the first block that failed eligibility, and `reason` is a free-form diagnostic string.
- **A reservation never changes a block's caution.** `reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` writes no caution: reserving a caution block, for a traversal out of either end, leaves `block.caution` as it was. A caution clears only through the ordinary tail-vacate cascade, on clean entry, or by the completion-time exception (per the `caution` field in **Block**). Which trains a caution limits is decided where it is read, not by clearing it: the caution speed cap applies only to a train whose traversal leaves the block through `block.caution.exit_edge` (see **TrainController**, ATC speed limit).
  - **A following train is limited.** A train that leaves the block the way the departing train went still has the protected chain ahead of it, so it gets the `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` cap and cannot close on the train ahead at line speed.
  - **A train crossing the other way is not.** A train that leaves the block out of its other end is moving away from the protected chain, so that safety margin can restrict nothing ahead of it. This keeps a train that reverses out of the block it was protecting from crawling back through its own stale safety margin.

  Because no reservation writes the caution, a reservation that is later rolled back, truncated, or cancelled before the train enters the block leaves nothing to restore.
- **`matching_path_reservation_ids(block_ids, path_id) -> List[str]`.** This read-only projection returns, in input order, exactly the block IDs that exist and currently satisfy `block.reserved_by_path == path_id`. `ResourceCoordinator.release_path_resources(...)` uses it to filter out expected already-released blocks.
- **`release_path_block_reservations(block_ids, path_id, completed=False)`.** Releases not-yet-entered reservation ownership during completion and cancellation, without modifying physical occupancy state.
  - It clears only blocks matching **both** of these:
    - the block belongs to that path's dispatcher-owned future reservation set
    - the block currently satisfies `block.reserved_by_path == path_id`
  - A mismatched block is ignored and must emit one `kind = "warning"` event whose `message` reads `release <block_id> but it's not reserved for <path_id>`, rather than being treated as a hard release failure.
  - Because `Block.release_path_reservation()` is a plain field clear with no state guard, this method can call it for each matching owned block whether the block is currently `CAUTION` or `RESERVED`.
  - When `completed=True` (path completed with the train fully stopped at terminal), it additionally force-clears `block.caution = None` on any still-`CAUTION` matching owned blocks.
  - When `completed=False` (path cancelled mid-flight), physical `CAUTION` state is left untouched, because the train is still moving and the safety margin must be preserved.
  - Returns `bool`: `True` if at least one matching reservation was released; `False` if none.
  - Head-entry consumption of a block reservation happens through the physical-entry path, not this release path.
  - This is the single reservation-release entry point. Its callers are path completion, path cancellation, and the acquisition-failure / truncation releases (`ResourceCoordinator.rollback_probe(...)` and `ResourceCoordinator.release_reservation_tail(...)`); every caller except path completion passes `completed=False`.
  - It also clears `block.locked_by_path` on each released block.
- **`lock_blocks_for_path(block_ids, path_id)`.** Sets `block.locked_by_path = path_id` on each listed block — the train's per-tick braking-distance lock write (the **Braking-distance lock**). A block may be locked only by the path that already reserves it, so the method requires `block.reserved_by_path == path_id` for each block and skips (with one `kind = "warning"` event) any block not reserved by that path. Re-locking an already-locked own block is an idempotent no-op. It never touches `reservation`, `occupied_by`, or `caution`.
- **`unlock_blocks_for_path(block_ids, path_id)`.** Clears `block.locked_by_path` on each listed block that currently satisfies `block.locked_by_path == path_id` — the release side of `lock_blocks_for_path(...)`, used by the **Stopped-run lock shrink**. A block not locked by that path is ignored. It never touches `reservation`, `occupied_by`, or `caution`, so the block stays reserved (and reserved-but-not-locked blocks are what **Preemption** may take).
- `on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)` is the block tail-vacate entry and the only normal entry point for a train physically vacating a block. It also clears any residual `block.locked_by_path` on the vacated block; clean head-entry normally already consumed that lock with the reservation. Its write set, no-op cases, and cascade are defined in **`on_block_tail_vacated()` behaviour (directional CAUTION evaluation)**. Returns `bool`: `True` on a clean tail-vacate; `False` on the no-op cases. No exception raised.
- `BlockManager` must read `network.blocks`, `network.switches`, and one shared network-topology adjacency helper from the owning `RailwayNetwork`, which owns the block registry, switch registry, and topology graph/traversal helpers. It must not keep its own copied block/switch registries, rescan unrelated entity lists, or invent a second topology cache of its own.

**`on_block_tail_vacated()` behaviour (directional CAUTION evaluation)**

- `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(...)` is the only normal runtime caller of `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)` for block resources (per **Tail-vacate release flow**). `TrainPhysics` does not call `BlockManager` directly.
- `BlockManager` does not decide by itself whether to release a block resource; that instruction comes from `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` after a tail-vacate observation whose attribution result is `vacate` (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection and A clear read from under the train is a detection fault). For normal runtime release, `train_id` must still match the current physical owner. If `block_id` is not present in the `BlockManager` registry (e.g. during early bootstrap or after teardown), `on_block_tail_vacated()` is a no-op that returns `False` and emits no event. If the block exists but `block.occupied_by != train_id`, `on_block_tail_vacated()` must leave the block unchanged and emit one `kind = "warning"` event whose `message` reads `block <block_id> release for train <train_id> skipped: currently occupied by <other_train_id>`.
- `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)` is one-shot: the tail-vacate fires on the single tick that first satisfies both halves of the release gate — the detector confirms the block clear, and the block is an end block that can clear for the train. A clear the detector confirmed earlier is re-offered on later reads only while the train still holds the block (see **Power**, A held clear is re-offered until it is an end block), so the release commits at most once per `(train_id, block_id)`. If `block.occupied_by != train_id`, the diagnostic emits exactly once for that pair, because that same holding condition keeps the block out of every later re-offer.
- `BlockManager.on_switch_position_changed(switch_id)` is safe to call once `BlockManager` is constructed, even before any blocks/switches have been registered. Empty-registry calls are a no-op.
- `direction` on `on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)` is `Optional[edge]`. It is the vacated block's forward `exit_edge` (`N`/`E`/`S`/`W`) for the traversal by which the train left that block, or `None` when no calculated traversal supplies an exit edge. A train whose movement the runtime calculates this pass always supplies an edge; `None` arises when movement was not calculated — an unidentified train's last held block clears, or one of its middle blocks clears and splits it (see **Power**, Unidentified trains), or a detection-only report built on a stopped pass by `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` or on a running `OFF` pass by the OFF branch of `on_physics_updated(...)` (see **Running and stopped**, the stopped pass).
- If `block.occupied_by == train_id` and `direction` is an edge, `on_block_tail_vacated()` clears `block.occupied_by` and sets `block.caution = CautionState(exit_edge=direction)`, so the block's `state` property returns `CAUTION`.
- If `block.occupied_by == train_id` and `direction` is `None`, `on_block_tail_vacated()` clears `block.occupied_by` and writes no `caution`, so the block's `state` property returns `FREE`. With no known exit edge, `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()` has no forward neighbour to consult and there is no direction to protect.
- `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()` iterates all blocks currently in `CAUTION`. In the normal reevaluation path, a `CAUTION` block advances to `FREE` unless the forward protection chain is both reachable AND ends in an `OCCUPIED` block. The forward block is found this way: start from the vacated block's exit edge given by `block.caution.exit_edge`, inspect the neighbouring resource in network connectivity, and keep following live tile connectivity through any intervening switch tile using the current `Switch.position` until the next block resource is reached. That next reachable block resource is the only block consulted for the `CAUTION -> FREE` decision. A disabled block reached by the walk is treated like any other block resource: the walk stops there. A disabled block is never `OCCUPIED` — a block cannot be disabled while occupied, and a train entering a disabled block is a fatal physical-entry conflict — so the block advances to `FREE`. Blocks behind the vacated block or off the currently selected switch branch are ignored. Occupancy of that one forward block is the whole test: the reevaluator reads no train, controller, or `travel_direction` state. This shape prevents a following train (entering from behind) from keeping a caution block alive, and lets a later switch throw invalidate the old protected chain. A margin the protecting train has reversed away from needs no retiring by this walk: the caution speed cap never limits a train crossing the block out of its other end (see **A reservation never changes a block's caution**), and the margin clears once its train enters the block or the chain ahead empties.
- If `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()` cannot resolve any reachable forward-adjacent block in `block.caution.exit_edge`, if live connectivity no longer reaches the block that was previously being protected, or if that forward block is not `OCCUPIED`, there is nothing ahead left to protect. In that case it must clear `block.caution = None` immediately, so the computed state becomes `RESERVED` if `reserved_by_path` is still set, otherwise `FREE`.
- **Reevaluation triggers.** Reevaluation is triggered by manager-owned state changes, not by a periodic scan. The trigger list is closed at **exactly three entries**:
  - `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` must call `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()` after updating the vacated block.
  - Every successful `BlockManager.on_switch_position_changed(switch_id)` call must call it too. A `Switch.disabled` toggle arrives through that same callback, per **Switch entity**.
  - `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` must call it too.

  Those three cover every input to the clear predicate. Connectivity comes from switch position and switch availability. The forward block's `occupied_by` is cleared by `on_block_tail_vacated()` on the ordinary detector-confirmed path, and by `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` on the three teardown paths that have no detector observation to wait for: the ghosted-train teardown (**Power**, Ghosted trains), the unidentified-train adoption re-key (**Power**, Unidentified trains), and train deletion (**Train Entity**, Deleting a train). Block availability is not an input, so toggling `Block.disabled` cannot change the result.
- `release_train_occupancy(train_id)` clears `occupied_by` on every block that train holds, writes no `caution`, queues those just-cleared holdings for de-energize through `BlockManager`'s own occupancy-release writer (`_mark_for_deenergize`, into `_blocks_pending_deenergize`; see **Power**, De-energize against the same source), and then runs `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()`.
- `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)` is not a trigger: writing `occupied_by` can only make the reevaluator keep a caution it would otherwise clear, and this walk never re-adds caution.
- `Switch` does not clear block caution state; it only changes connectivity, and `BlockManager` is the sole owner of the `CAUTION -> FREE` decision on this path.
- `reserved_by_path` is NOT checked as a condition for `CAUTION → FREE`: the physical safety margin and the dispatcher reservation are independent, so a block whose caution clears while it is still reserved reads `RESERVED`, not `FREE`, until the dispatcher clears the reservation via `release_path_block_reservations()`.
- Exception: `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(..., completed=True)` may force-clear `block.caution = None` during terminal completion release for owned blocks, outside this neighbour-based reevaluation.

## SwitchManager

**Switch-manager model**

- `SwitchManager` is the lock manager for switch resources and the single serialization point for atomic multi-switch lock acquisition, whether the dispatcher is acquiring the full requested route or a shorter forward prefix. It mirrors `BlockManager`'s contract on the switch side.
- `SwitchManager` holds `RailwayNetwork` plus four narrow injected callbacks only, and never receives or looks up `SimulationController`. The callbacks are:
  - **Notification emitter.** `notification_emitter(operation, kind, message, entities, error=None, payload=None)` routes a manager-owned event into `NotificationCenter`.
  - **Fatal-conflict reporter.** `fatal_conflict_reporter` takes one `FatalPhysicalEntryConflict` and is runtime-bound to `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`.
  - **Operating-environment gate.** `environment_active_getter` returns whether an operating environment is active and gates the operating throw in `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)` (see the operating-throw gate under **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**). It is required: every construction that wires a `SwitchManager` — the full runtime and the lightweight editor runtime alike — binds it to `SimulationController.environment_active`.
  - **Active-path lookup.** `active_path_getter` takes a `train_id` and returns that train's active `Path` (resolved live through `PathDispatcher.get_active_path`), used only to fill a fatal switch-conflict payload's `incoming_path_id` (always) and its `prior_owner_path_id` for the physical-owner conflict (`switch_occupied_by_other_train`) only. `BlockManager` receives the same getter for its block-conflict payload (per **Block-manager model**); see the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure** for the per-origin payload contract.
- `SwitchManager` reads `switches`, `BlockManager` (for the `on_switch_position_changed(switch_id)` notify), and `SwitchPowerController` live off `RailwayNetwork` rather than holding them as captured handles, because the runtime rebinds `BlockManager` and `SwitchPowerController` on each interface bind/release. `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)` and `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` emit their manager-owned events through `notification_emitter`. In a pure editor session these runtime dependencies are not constructed; a lightweight editor runtime constructs the complete set.
- `SwitchLockRequest` is the value type for one requested switch lock.
  - Every request is a main-usage request: `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)` is the sole entity that derives flank-protection claims, expanding each request internally per **Path And PathDispatcher**, Resource acquisition, **Per-switch main claim and flank acquisition**.
  - `SwitchLockRequest` carries exactly `switch_id`, `locked_state`, and `route: FrozenSet[str]` (required, non-`None`) — the unordered `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` the path uses through the switch.
  - `PathDispatcher` populates `route` from the chosen candidate's switch step (`GraphWalkStep.entry_edge` / `exit_edge`). The manager copies it onto the main claim it builds for `Switch.acquire_lock(claim)`, and rejects a request whose `route` is `None` per the cross-train co-locking rule under **Switch entity**.
- `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(requests, path_id, train_id, manual_override=False)` attempts every requested switch lock atomically.
  - **`manual_override` propagation.** The `manual_override` parameter is propagated from the calling `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**; the manager sets `claim.manual_override = manual_override` on every `Switch.acquire_lock(claim)` call it issues.
  - **Transaction insertion journal.** `SwitchClaimKey` is the exact stored identity `(holding_switch_id, path_id, source_switch_id)`, where `source_switch_id is None` identifies a main claim. Before each `Switch.acquire_lock(claim)` call, the manager checks that key and records it only when it was absent and this call inserted it. An idempotently pre-existing claim may make acquisition succeed, but it never enters this call's journal. On failure the manager calls `rollback_inserted_claims(...)` with only this journal.
  - **Return contract.** The call returns `LockAcquireResult(success: bool, failed_switch_id: Optional[str], reason: Optional[str], inserted_claim_keys: List[SwitchClaimKey])`. On success the list is exactly the keys this call inserted, in insertion order. Callers concatenate those lists across a probe and never replace them with main-switch IDs.
- `SwitchManager.rollback_inserted_claims(path_id, inserted_claim_keys)` removes only the exact listed keys whose stored `path_id` matches. It is the only switch release used for a failed acquisition probe, so an idempotently pre-existing main or flank claim cannot be removed by rollback.
- `SwitchManager.release_path_locks(path_id) -> List[str]` releases every lock owned by `path_id` across every switch and returns the main-switch IDs it released a claim from. `SwitchManager.release_segment_locks(path_id, main_switch_ids)` is used only when valid reservation is deliberately shortened. For every source main-switch ID it removes the main `(path_id, None)` claim and every stored flank `(path_id, main_switch_id)` claim. Stored claim identity is authoritative; current flank geometry is not. All three release methods are idempotent and preserve every unlisted key.
- `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)` is the switch tail-vacate entry, called by `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for switch tail-vacate events through the `ResourceCoordinator` facade, and between ticks by `SimulationController.remove_train(train_id)` for each `Switch.physical_occupants` entry a deleted train still holds (per **Train Entity**, Deleting a train). `route` is required (non-`None`) and is the key into `Switch.physical_occupants`.
  - **Physical-occupant release.** `SwitchManager` performs the release itself: it removes the `Switch.physical_occupants` entry whose key equals `route` and whose value equals `train_id`.
  - **Flank-protection release.** Only when no `physical_occupants` entries remain for that train on this switch, `SwitchManager` also releases train-owned protection — by stored claim identity, not by the switch's current `flank_protection` neighbour list. It scans every switch in the network for a `train_protection_claims` entry keyed `(source_switch_id=switch_id, train_id=train_id)` and calls `Switch.release_train_protection_from(source_switch_id=switch_id, train_id=train_id)` on each one it finds, per the **Switch entity** tail-vacate contract.

    `RailwayNetwork.recompute_all_flank_protection()` can rewrite `Switch.flank_protection` between acquisition and tail-vacate (see **Flank Protection Computation**), and a neighbour dropped from that live list must not strand its claim unreleased.

    `Switch` never walks neighbours itself; the neighbour iteration is manager-owned (see **Switch entity**).
  - Returns `bool`: `True` on a clean tail-vacate, or on a route-drift salvage that still removed one owned entry. `False` only when nothing was released — the route-drift fallback where `train_id` owns no `physical_occupants` entry on this switch. No exception is raised.
  - **The route-drift fallback.** This is the canonical home for the fallback. A supplied `route` that matches no `physical_occupants` entry owned by `train_id` is a contract violation: the controller emits the same `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` key on tail-vacate that it recorded on entry, so a mismatch means a stale or malformed `ResourceEvent` (the entry-side analogue is the `"malformed_route_key"` fatal contract violation).
    - A release is safe to degrade rather than freeze the runtime. When `train_id` still owns at least one entry on this switch, `SwitchManager` emits one `kind = "warning"` event naming the train, the switch, and the mismatched route, then removes exactly one entry: the first owned entry under the route-key ordering (route frozensets compared as sorted edge tuples). This keeps the release deterministic and strands no entry, because the train's remaining vacate events release the rest. The same flank-release walk runs after the removal.
    - When `train_id` owns no entry at all on this switch, `SwitchManager` emits the same `kind = "warning"` event and releases nothing.
- `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(switch_id, train_id, path_id: Optional[str], route: Optional[FrozenSet[str]])` is the physical-entry entry point for switches. Clean entry requires both `path_id` and `route`. A `route is None` or `path_id is None` argument is reported through the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure** and returns `False` without writing occupancy state; the reported `error.origin` follows the single ordered precedence in **Conflict cases** (so a `path_id is None` argument reports `"switch_intrusion"` only when no disabled-switch or route-conflict case ranks ahead of it).
  - **Clean-entry effects.** On clean entry it owns the flank-lock conversion: it records `Switch.physical_occupants[route] = train_id`, consumes the entering train's compatible main switch lock for that switch, and converts every required flank-protection claim on neighbours into train-owned `train_protection_claims` per the **Switch entity** flank-protection contract.
  - **Conflict cases.** `on_physical_entry(...)` is reported through the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure** and returns `False` when any of these holds, evaluated in this order with the first match deciding the reported `error.origin`:
    - the `route` argument is `None` — reported with `error.origin = "malformed_route_key"`. It ranks first because the route-conflict and intrusion checks cannot be evaluated without a valid route key.
    - the switch is disabled — reported with `error.origin = "disabled_resource_entry"`. A disabled switch has no acquirable lock (per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**), so it always also satisfies the intrusion case; it is reported ahead of it.
    - the route conflicts with a route held by a different train, per `switch.routes_conflict(...)` — reported with `error.origin = "switch_occupied_by_other_train"`
    - the intrusion case — `path_id is None`, or the entering train/path holds no compatible lock for its route (see the intrusion check in the **Switch entity** section) — reported with `error.origin = "switch_intrusion"`
  - **The `manual` flag adds no conflict case and removes none.** The route-conflict, disabled, and intrusion checks run unchanged on a manual switch, so a manual switch entered without a compatible lock is still a fatal intrusion. Physical entry into a manual (but not also disabled) switch is not itself a conflict case: it is ordinary clean entry per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**, provided the entering train holds the compatible lock the intrusion check requires. Only the flag's own filter — pathfinding and lock acquisition without `manual_override = True` — is skipped by the flag; present occupancy is unaffected.
- The `Switch.position` write goes through the mutation workflow on `Switch` (per **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**); `SwitchManager` calls into that workflow and never mutates `Switch.position` directly.
- `SwitchManager` owns the physical throw emission as part of that same paired operation: after the `Switch.position` write + `BlockManager` notify, it drives the throw through `SwitchPowerController.set_throw(...)` for every switch this call acquires, per **Acquisition always throws**. It never calls `SwitchOutput` itself. The throw contract, including how an unissued throw is handled, is defined in **Power**, Switch power-controller role.

## ResourceCoordinator

**Resource-coordinator model**

- `ResourceCoordinator` is the facade `PathDispatcher` calls to reserve, release, and route physical-entry / tail-vacate events for an entire `PathSegment`. It owns no state; it is a pure composition layer over `BlockManager` and `SwitchManager`. The only manager-routing `resource_type` branches live inside `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(...)` and `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(...)`. `PathDispatcher` does not branch on `resource_type` for reserve / release / rollback / tail-vacate / physical-entry. This does not prohibit block-only interpretation in `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)`, which consumes only block events for route-task progress.
- `ResourceCoordinator.reserve_segment(future_block_ids, block_traversals, switch_requests, path_id, train_id, manual_override=False)` runs the switch-lock phase first, then the block reservation phase.
  - **Parameters.** `future_block_ids: List[str]`, `block_traversals: Dict[str, ReservedBlockTraversal]` (keyed by `block_id`, matching `reserve_blocks_for_path`'s `directions` contract in the **BlockManager** section), `switch_requests: List[SwitchLockRequest]`, `path_id: str`, `train_id: str`, and `manual_override: bool = False`. `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` pass them positionally.
  - **`manual_override` propagation.** The `manual_override` field is propagated per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**, and forwarded to `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` and `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)`.
  - **Rollback on failure.** The coordinator records only block reservations and exact switch claim keys newly inserted by this call. A switch-phase failure leaves the coordinator nothing to roll back, because `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)` already removed the keys it inserted. A block-phase failure reserves no block, because that phase is all-or-nothing, so the coordinator then calls `SwitchManager.rollback_inserted_claims(...)` with the exact switch keys this call inserted. On a failed return both lists are empty because the coordinator has released its own journal.
  - **Return contract.** Returns `SegmentReserveResult(success: bool, failed_resource_type: Optional[str], failed_resource_id: Optional[str], reason: Optional[str], reserved_block_ids: List[str], inserted_switch_claim_keys: List[SwitchClaimKey])`; on success, both lists contain only holds newly inserted by this call.
- `ResourceCoordinator.rollback_probe(block_ids, inserted_switch_claim_keys, path_id)` releases the exact holds of one prefix-scan acquisition attempt that dispatcher discards — a whole-prefix attempt that acquired but was set aside so the scan could look for a nearer holding point. It releases the listed block reservations and then the exact switch keys through `SwitchManager.rollback_inserted_claims(...)`, in reverse acquisition order.
- `ResourceCoordinator.release_reservation_tail(block_ids, main_switch_ids, path_id)` is used when a stage deliberately shortens live reservation — Observe **Reservation truncation** and **Preemption** (the dispatcher releasing a lower-priority victim's reserved tail). It has one caller that drops a single block rather than a tail: the locked case of **Reservation truncation** passes the one taken block and no switch IDs, so every switch claim the reserving train may still roll into is kept. It releases the dropped block reservations, clearing their `Block.locked_by_path` with the reservation, and then calls `SwitchManager.release_segment_locks(...)` for the dropped main-switch families. The **Stopped-run lock shrink** is not a caller: it releases only lock flags, through `BlockManager.unlock_blocks_for_path(...)`, and shortens no reservation.
  - Separating this from `rollback_probe(...)` is required: truncation removes whole no-longer-valid families, while a discarded acquisition attempt removes only the keys that attempt inserted.
- `ResourceCoordinator.release_path_resources(path_id, block_ids, completed)` composes `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)` and `SwitchManager.release_path_locks(path_id)`.
  - The coordinator first calls `BlockManager.matching_path_reservation_ids(block_ids, path_id)` and passes only that returned subset to `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)`. This is because expected already-released blocks must not emit mismatch warnings during completion or cancellation — for example a path whose ahead reservations Observe reservation truncation already released through `ResourceCoordinator.release_reservation_tail(...)`.
  - Returns `(released_block_ids, released_switch_ids)`: `released_block_ids` is exactly the matching subset, and `released_switch_ids` is `SwitchManager.release_path_locks(path_id)`'s returned list, passed through unchanged.
  - `ResourceCoordinator` never reads the network or a manager's registry directly.
- `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, direction, route)` is the single entry called by `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each `tail_vacated_resources` event. It routes to `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` for blocks (using `direction`, ignoring `route`) and `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)` for switches (using `route`, ignoring `direction`). It returns the routed manager's `bool` (`True` on a clean release, `False` on a no-op). `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` does not branch on that return: tail-vacate release is non-fatal, so it always continues to the next event, in contrast to the entry side's `False`-stops-the-report rule (step `018a`).
- `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, path_id: Optional[str], route: Optional[FrozenSet[str]])` is the single entry called by `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each `entered_resources` event.
  - Blocks ignore both optional routing fields and go to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks([resource_id], train_id)`, including detector-delayed entry after reservation ended.
  - Switches require both fields for clean entry and go to `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(switch_id, train_id, path_id, route)`; that manager reports a missing `path_id` as `switch_intrusion` and a missing `route` as `malformed_route_key`.
  - The facade returns the routed manager's `bool`: `True` on clean entry, including an idempotent no-op, and `False` after a fatal physical-entry conflict. On `False`, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` stops processing that report per step `018a`.
## Path And PathDispatcher

**Path model**

- The dispatcher path lifecycle has three states, `ACTIVE`, `COMPLETED`, and `CANCELLED`, stored on `Path` as `status: PathStatus` (transitions per the **Path status state machine**).
- The core identity and routing fields on `Path` are `path_id`, `status`, `train_id`, and `resource_sequence`. `reservation_end_block_id`, `path_tiles`, and `reaches_target(block_id)` are derived functions (`get_reservation_end_block_id()`, `get_path_tiles()`, `reaches_target(...)`) computed from `resource_sequence` on each call (per the **Path field schema**).
- `RouteExecutor` owns route scheduling priority through `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` (the override-aware read of the shared `Route.priority`; see **RouteRun overrides**) once a run exists, and the run-phase scheduling tier through the derived `RouteRun.is_starting`. Dispatcher path records carry no copied `priority` field and no phase-tier field.
- Resource acquisition is synchronous inside `create_path()`. Terminal-approach behavior is represented by progress and completion predicates, not by a separate live status.
- `RouteExecutor` platform-end resolution, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` start-side selection, and `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` suffix search all use `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)`, the single source for candidate ranking, direction filtering, and the comparison keys callers use for current-span end selection and tie-breaking (per the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload**). Every train-context caller — `RouteExecutor` platform-end resolution, `create_path(...)` start-side and forward candidate selection, `extend_path(...)` suffix search — must pass the routed train's `train_max_speed_kmh` on every query whose candidates it will compare against each other, so a single comparison never mixes a populated and an absent travel-time estimate. Only geometry-only callers with no train context omit it.
- **Two acquisition interfaces.** The dispatcher path-acquisition API is exactly `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` for a new reservation and `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for growing an existing live reservation. Code must not add a third acquisition wrapper, or a route code path with a third acquisition contract.

**Path field schema**

`Path` is the dispatcher-owned resource-sequence reservation record, and this table is its one field set (per **Authoring Rules**).

**Why this shape.** `resource_sequence` is the single source of truth for path geometry, and `reservation_end_block_id` and `path_tiles` are derived from it, so an update to live reservation is one change to one list, not several stores to keep in sync. `reaches_target(block_id)` is measured from `current_resource_index`, the head-progress anchor, so "reached" means reached *ahead of the train*, not merely present somewhere in the sequence. The requested target itself is not stored here: it is an argument to `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` and an echo in their result, while the run's own copy lives in `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`. Keeping one stored copy, on the side that owns the task, stops the reservation record and the run from drifting apart. The one stored control flag beyond geometry is `zero_reservation_end_standoff`, kept here because lookahead must read a **Speed calibration** leg's zero standoff live on every tick and the projection has no other live carrier for it.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path_id` | `str` | Unique dispatcher path identifier |
| `status` | `PathStatus` | One of `ACTIVE`, `COMPLETED`, `CANCELLED` |
| `train_id` | `str` | Assigned train |
| `path_tiles` | `function (read-only): get_path_tiles() -> List[path_tile]` | Returns the full ordered path-origin -> current-reservation-end traversal history by concatenating `resource_sequence[*].path_tiles` in `sequence_index` order on each call. Not stored, not cached, no writers, no rebuild step. |
| `resource_sequence` | `List[resource_sequence entry]` | Ordered interleaved block/switch resources (per the **resource_sequence entry schema**). The single source of truth for path geometry. |
| `current_resource_index` | `int` | `sequence_index` of the current path-progress anchor resource, not the first matching raw resource ID; the controller resolves the reported index by the **Head-mapping rule** in the **ControllerProgressReport schema**. Strictly head-based once live reservation establishes a head (per **Reservation-side head derivation**) or live progress updates establish a true head. Before that, initialized to the reservation-side resource at the physical train end closer to the path end, under the same comparison the head derivation uses. |
| `reaches_target` | `function (read-only): reaches_target(block_id) -> bool` | Returns whether the live reservation reaches `block_id`: `True` when `block_id` appears as a `block` entry in `resource_sequence` at a `sequence_index` at or after `current_resource_index`. Not stored; no writers. This is the test for "is this reservation still short of that target?", and no consumer answers that question by comparing the target against `reservation_end_block_id`, with one exception: the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) tests terminal-block equality, which the **Reservation termination rule** makes exact for an unserved `stop` (a live reservation for a `stop` target never legitimately runs past it), so the two agree in every reachable state. It is deliberately not an equality test against the terminal block: a target the reservation already runs past is reached, not missed. Entries before `current_resource_index` are retained traversal history or currently covered geometry behind the head, so they never count as reached. |
| `reservation_end_block_id` | `function (read-only): get_reservation_end_block_id() -> str` | Returns `resource_sequence[-1].resource_id` on each call (the **Path invariants** rule requires the terminal `resource_sequence` entry to always be a `block` entry). The controller brakes toward this block's forward boundary using its safety-margin policy. Not stored, not cached, no writers, no setter: updates to live reservation are made on `resource_sequence` itself, and the function reflects the new terminal block automatically. |
| `lock_end_block_id` | `function (read-only): get_lock_end_block_id() -> str` | Returns the furthest-forward block in `resource_sequence`, at or after `current_resource_index`, whose `Block.locked_by_path == path_id`. When no block ahead of the head is locked, it returns the head's block instead: the last `block` entry of `resource_sequence` at or before `current_resource_index`. The fallback gives a train standing in its reservation-end block a lock end, because entering a block clears that block's lock flag (per `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`). Not stored; no writers. It derives from the per-block `Block.locked_by_path` flags the **Braking-distance lock** writes and from `current_resource_index`, so it reflects the current lock automatically. It is always at or behind `reservation_end_block_id`, because a block is locked only after it is reserved. Consumers: the **Holding-point chunking** extend trigger (the reservation holds at each chunk terminal until the lock end reaches it; a train stopped inside the terminal reaches it through the head-block fallback), the **Stopped-run lock shrink** floor test, the **Reservation truncation** cut floor (the cut never enters the lock), and the **Preemption** floor (a switch at or before the lock end is never preempted). |
| `last_status_updated_time` | `float` | System-time Unix timestamp of the last `status` change, sampled fresh for that transition (see **Time sampling** under the **Units contract**). Each status writer calls `time.time()` itself when it writes `Path.status`: `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` for `ACTIVE`, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` for `CANCELLED`, and `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` for `COMPLETED`. A call that commits no status transition writes no status and therefore does not resample this field: an idempotent `cancel_path(...)` no-op on an already-terminal path, or a `try_complete_active_path(...)` call that finds no active path or whose step-`8df5` (Stop-arrival check) predicate is false. When that same writer also emits a notification carrying an `event_time` for the same transition, it samples `time.time()` once locally and uses that one value for both the status timestamp and the notification field. |
| `zero_reservation_end_standoff` | `bool` | When `True`, `TrainController` lookahead uses a zero safety margin at this path's reservation end in place of the terminus-type value from **Safety margin globals**. A **Speed calibration** leg's one-off route sets it (see **Speed calibration**, A calibration leg holds no reservation-end standoff); every other path leaves it `False`. Set once by `create_path(...)` and carried unchanged by `extend_path(...)`. |

**Path status state machine**

The state machine for `Path.status`, the path lifecycle enum. Shared contracts must not invent extra path lifecycle states or path-owned pending cleanup flags.

| From `status` | Trigger | To `status` | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (none) | `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` succeeds | `ACTIVE` | The path record is inserted into `paths_by_id` and indexed as the train's active reservation. Writes `last_status_updated_time` with the synchronous create-time system-time Unix timestamp. |
| `ACTIVE` | `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` is invoked from Plan settlement step `9d8b` (Stop-arrival evaluation); its step-`8df5` (Stop-arrival check) predicate succeeds | `COMPLETED` | Step `09b0` (Canonical terminal-teardown orders) owns release/status/callback ordering, and callback step `bc55` (Finished-stop route commit) records route progress. Dispatcher evaluates the predicate but invents no separate acceptance test. |
| `ACTIVE` | `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(path_id, error, kind, deviation=False, latch=None)` | `CANCELLED` | Not-yet-entered reservation resources are released synchronously; controller reservation is cleared; the transition to `CANCELLED` makes `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` return `None` by definition; `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error)` is notified with the cancellation `ErrorRecord` only; the `deviation` classification rides the `cancel_path` event payload, not the callback. |
| `COMPLETED` | any | `COMPLETED` | Terminal. `cancel_path(...)` on a `COMPLETED` path is an idempotent no-op: it returns `committed = False` with `new_status = COMPLETED` and mutates nothing. |
| `CANCELLED` | any | `CANCELLED` | Terminal. `cancel_path(...)` on a `CANCELLED` path is an idempotent no-op: it returns `committed = False` with `new_status = CANCELLED` and mutates nothing. |

- `status` is set once per lifecycle transition by the originating synchronous call. No later stopped cleanup pass re-transitions status or writes a pending field.
- Physical `occupied_by` (block or switch) is outside this state machine and is never cleared by a `status` transition. It and train-owned switch protection change through resource entry and tail-vacate observations committed by `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`: detector-confirmed for blocks (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), controller-reported traversal for switches. Three documented exceptions change `Block.occupied_by` without an observation, all through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` (see **BlockManager**): the Observe ghosted-train teardown, the unidentified-train adoption re-key between ticks (`release_train_occupancy(...)` then `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`), and train deletion between ticks. Train deletion also releases the deleted train's `Switch.physical_occupants` entries and switch protection through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` (see **Train Entity**, Deleting a train), so the switch's derived `occupied_by` read no longer names it. The `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` seed also changes this occupancy and protection state, at initial placement and, for switch occupancy only, during adoption.
- A train may have at most one `ACTIVE` path at a time (the active-path guard in the **`create_path()` flow** rejects a same-train create while one exists). Retained `COMPLETED` / `CANCELLED` rows do not by themselves block a fresh `create_path(...)` once the old path is no longer active; only ordinary live resource conflicts remain.
- A path may contain switch resources internally, but in a stored live path `resource_sequence[-1]` must always be a `block` entry, so `reservation_end_block_id` never names a terminal switch.

**path_tile entry schema**

The schema of one tile step inside `Path.get_path_tiles()` and inside each `resource_sequence[*].path_tiles` slice; shared contracts must not use bare `(x, y)` tuples in its place.

- Each `path_tile` entry carries exactly:
  - `x`
  - `y`
  - `entry_edge`
  - `exit_edge`
  - `resource_sequence_index` — the parent `Path.resource_sequence[*].sequence_index`.
- `entry_edge` and `exit_edge` are required on every tile entry; shared contracts must not infer them later from neighboring coordinates.

**resource_sequence entry schema**

The schema of one `resource_sequence` entry. Its per-resource tile slices, with explicit entry and exit edges at both the resource and the tile level, are the geometry contract for controller and UI consumers. Every site that describes the `received_path_plan` projection, dispatcher/UI reservation projections, the `to_dict()` exports, or any other projection of reservation geometry refers to this schema by name rather than restating it.

**Why this shape.** Each entry carries both the resource identity (`resource_type`, `resource_id`) and the directed traversal frame (`entry_edge`, `exit_edge`, plus the nested `path_tiles` slice). Ordered tiles alone are not enough: a single tile can be traversed in either direction, and the stop frame changes with the chosen entry side. Storing the directed frame explicitly, instead of letting consumers infer it from tile coordinates, makes every traversal unambiguous and gives downstream lookahead and braking math the geometry it needs without re-walking the tile graph. Storing `entry_edge` and `exit_edge` at both the resource and the tile level lets resource-level consumers read the frame without unpacking the tile slice, while per-tile detail stays available.

- Each `resource_sequence` entry carries exactly these fields, with every ordering and edge direction taken in path-origin -> current-reservation-end traversal order:
  - `sequence_index` — position of the entry in traversal order.
  - `resource_type` — `"block"` or `"switch"`.
  - `resource_id` — stable network resource ID for the block or switch.
  - `path_tiles` — the contiguous ordered slice of `path_tile` entries belonging to that resource. Every nested tile entry in this slice has `resource_sequence_index == sequence_index`.
  - `entry_edge` — the directed traversal-frame entry edge for that resource.
  - `exit_edge` — the directed traversal-frame exit edge for that resource.
- No other fields are required.
- `entry_edge` must equal the first nested `path_tiles[0].entry_edge`, and `exit_edge` must equal the last nested `path_tiles[-1].exit_edge`.
- For switch resources, the required switch state is not stored as a field on the entry. It is derived at acquisition time from the planner-facing `Tile.enumerate_traversals(entry_edge)` contract on the switch tile, using the `(entry_edge, exit_edge)` pair selected for that resource's `path_tiles` slice.
- Flank protection lives on the switch entity (acquired automatically when the switch is locked); `Path` does not store its own flank-protection list.
- `Path` does not carry the requested target. `requested_destination_block_id` and `requested_destination_direction` are call arguments: dispatcher uses the direction during the call to filter compatible terminal candidates and to choose a legal terminal traversal frame, then stores only the resulting `resource_sequence`. The direction is the caller's already-resolved block-relative constraint and is always `"forward"` or `"reverse"`. No stop-centimetre field is passed or stored. Arrival direction is guaranteed at acquisition instead of re-checked later: candidate search rejects any candidate whose terminal traversal does not satisfy the caller's `requested_destination_direction`, so a stored reservation that reaches a target reaches it in a legal frame by construction.
- The live terminal frame always comes from the explicit directed geometry on the terminal `resource_sequence` block entry (`path_tiles`, `entry_edge`, `exit_edge`); the spec must not rely on readers inferring direction from tile coordinates alone or from `requested_destination_direction` alone.
- `PathDispatcher` must treat each `Path` record as the authoritative dispatcher-owned database entry, keyed by `path_id` in `paths_by_id[path_id]`, with `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` deriving the train's one active reservation path, and its retained path database must be the authoritative historical store for every path it has created. The controller-facing reservation is only a read-only projection of the current dispatcher record.
- Dispatcher-owned path records must remain available while active and, after termination, as retained `CANCELLED` or `COMPLETED` records for history and inspection, kept indefinitely rather than aged out. Reservation release must not depend on any controller-side copy surviving.
- After `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` has been cleared, controller progress reports resolve active reservation only against the new active reservation, while delayed release or occupancy reporting for a block or switch that remains under the train resolves from the resource itself (`BlockManager` state for blocks, `Switch.occupied_by` / `Switch.train_protection_claims` for switches).
- `train_id` is mandatory for every dispatcher reservation path, including ordinary route-driven paths, one-off operator routes, and speed-calibration one-off routes (see **Speed calibration**). Frontend and API callers supply it; anonymous reservation paths are out of scope. Future reservation on reserved resources is tracked through `Block.reserved_by_path` (written by `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`) and `Switch.locks` (keyed by `(path_id, source_switch_id)`, where main claims use `source_switch_id = None`; each claim stores `path_id`, `source_switch_id`, `train_id`, `locked_state`, and `route`).

**Path acquisition and cancellation API**

- **Canonical write interfaces.** The acquisition and cancellation request interfaces are `PathDispatcher.create_path(requested_destination_block_id, train_id, requested_destination_direction, manual_override=False, zero_reservation_end_standoff=False, reservation_cap_block_id=None, required_candidate_resource_keys=None)`, `PathDispatcher.extend_path(path_id, requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction, manual_override=False, reservation_cap_block_id=None, required_candidate_resource_keys=None)`, and `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(path_id, error, kind, deviation=False, latch=None)`. `extend_path(...)` is the same request contract as `create_path(...)` plus the leading `path_id` of the live path it grows in place. `required_candidate_resource_keys`, used only by **Meet coordination**, is either `None` or the exact ordered `(resource_type, resource_id, entry_edge, exit_edge)` list of the candidate that the tick-start meet calculation selected, which is one of the walks this call itself enumerates (see **Meet coordination**, Conflict detection). When the list is present, dispatcher filters to that candidate before applying acquisition rules and returns the ordinary blocked/no-growth result if it is no longer viable; it never falls through to another candidate. `PathDispatcher.truncate_path_before_resource(...)` (see **Reservation truncation** and **Preemption**) and `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` (see **Stop-arrival procedure**) are the other two `Path`-mutating request interfaces; they are not acquisition or cancellation requests and are not part of this closed set. The **Stopped-run lock shrink** does not mutate the `Path` at all: it clears per-block `Block.locked_by_path` flags through `BlockManager.unlock_blocks_for_path(...)` and leaves `resource_sequence` and every reservation intact. The Observe progress-commit callback `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` also advances `Path.current_resource_index`, but it is a commit callback, not a request interface.
  - **`manual_override`.** This is the operator-override flag defined under **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**. It defaults to `False`, and is `True` only when the requesting run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True` (operator-initiated routes such as Quick Route). `RouteExecutor` forwards that route-stored flag; request handlers never call these interfaces directly.
  - **`error`.** The diagnostic `ErrorRecord` the writer populated for the `cancel_path` event. Callers must not branch on anything inside it when deciding planning or routing behavior.
