It drains the controller-owned progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`) in order, calls `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each one, records each head-entry on `physics_sync.entered_blocks_this_tick` in `sequence_index` order, and clears the mailbox. Observe finishes no route task. In Plan settlement, `RouteExecutor` then consumes the recorded head-entries (step `640a` of the **Stop-arrival procedure**) and runs the stop-arrival check under **Only Plan settlement may finish a `stop` task against a live reservation**.
- **Multiple resource boundaries in one tick.** When physical movement crosses multiple resource boundaries within one simulation tick, `TrainPhysics` must fire multiple sequential `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` calls — one per resource boundary crossed, in physical traversal order — rather than batching them into a single multi-resource report.
  - `TrainPhysics` computes each incremental `span_update` up to the next boundary, calls `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` for that boundary, then computes the next boundary update and repeats. Each call appends that step's report to the progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`).
  - The boundary `event_time` on each returned `ControllerProgressReport` is the timestamp `TrainPhysics` sampled once for that movement pass (per the **ControllerProgressReport schema**); the controller stores it unchanged and never resamples per report. The `ControllerProgressReport` is a within-tick transient, so this sits outside the stored-field **Time sampling** rule under the **Units contract**.
  - The per-boundary reports carry the switch observations (calculated traversal, this tick). The detector-confirmed block observations are folded into that tick's final no-boundary report instead, ordered by `sequence_index` when the entries map into the active `resource_sequence` — each such `sequence_index` resolved by the **Head-mapping rule** — and by physical entry order otherwise (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). Consumers must tolerate the one-tick detector lag between block and switch observations; the monotonic `Path.current_resource_index` rule absorbs the skew.
  - After the last boundary in that tick, or on a tick with no boundary crossing, `TrainPhysics` must still emit one final callback for that tick. When no resource boundary was crossed, that final update carries `added_tiles=[]` and `removed_tiles=[]`; when nothing changed physically, it may be an explicit no-change callback.

  This guarantees that the Observe progress-mailbox drain (step `3e9b`) always has a final report to drain and one deterministic pass every tick, whether or not movement crossed a boundary, and that downstream side effects (lock consumption, tail-vacate release, switch state notifications, and the head-entry records Plan settlement's head-advance later consumes) commit in the same physical order as the local progress reports.

  Within any single `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` call, `entered_resources` and `tail_vacated_resources` typically carry one entry each at most. When a single call needs to carry more (for example simultaneous head entry and tail vacate at the same boundary), events within each list must still be ordered by physical traversal / vacate order.
- Entry ownership is resource-typed and dispatcher-mediated. `PathDispatcher` does not branch on `resource_type`: it routes every entry through `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, path_id, route)`, which routes it per step `83a2` of the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**:
  - on block entry, to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks([block_id], train_id)`; this is the only normal runtime path that writes `Block.occupied_by`
  - on switch entry, to `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(switch_id, train_id, path_id, route)`, whose clean-entry effects and conflict cases are defined under **SwitchManager**. A conflict must not overwrite the prior owner
- **Monotonic `current_resource_index`.** Dispatcher progress must update `Path.current_resource_index` using the reported path-step `sequence_index`, not by searching for the first matching raw `resource_id`. The producer-side companion is the **Head-mapping rule** in the **ControllerProgressReport schema**, under which a lapping path's second visit to a block reports the later index and so advances progress. `Path.current_resource_index` is head-based progress only; it advances when the train head enters a new resource and does not wait for the later tail-based release of earlier resources. Because switch observations (calculated, same tick) and block observations (detector-confirmed, one tick later) interleave, `current_resource_index` is monotonic: an entry whose `sequence_index` is at or behind the current value leaves it unchanged (`current_resource_index = max(current, reported sequence_index)`).
- A live path must remain `ACTIVE` after creation, through intermediate resources, and after entering the final block/resource. Entering the terminal resource must not change lifecycle state by itself.
- **Only Plan settlement may finish a `stop` task against a live reservation.** After Observe has committed this tick's position, if an active path still exists for that train and `pending_path_cancel_request` is `None` (a pending cancel outranks arrival), Plan settlement step `9d8b` has `RouteExecutor` call `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)`. Step `8df5` is the predicate. If it is true, step `09b0` releases future resources, writes `Path.status = COMPLETED`, and delivers the `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)` callback; step `bc55` is the route callback's finished-stop commit (timestamps per **Time sampling**). Dispatcher invents no additional acceptance test.
  - **Reservation is the only "moving" signal.** A train has authority to run whenever it holds live reservation — `received_path_plan is not None` (per **Authority to run is live reservation**). Under that reservation the selected driving source moves the train (per the **Propulsion cap step**).
  - **A pending teardown skips this arrival check.** The teardown latches (`pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, `pending_route_deactivate`) are consumed in Action, after this settlement. Each of their helpers also latches `pending_path_cancel_request` whenever a live path exists, so a pending teardown skips the arrival check (per step `9d8b` of the **Stop-arrival procedure**).
- A distance-0 ATC limit at its floor is not by itself stop completion: no-reservation, deviation, EB, and truncated reservation all drive the distance-0 limit to zero without being stop completion. Stop completion requires the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`), whose two arrival conditions, `4a` and `4b`, are defined under **TrainController**, `is_stopped_at_reservation_end()`.
- For a `task_kind == "stop"` task whose live reservation already reaches its requested target block, a post-physics controller stop at the safety-margin-adjusted usable reservation stop satisfying the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) completes the path normally. The head may be short of the physical requested block when the safety margin/ATC boundary requires that; ATC remains the higher-priority rule and there is no "go back and try again" prompt for a within-block or before-block safety-margin stop.
- EB activation latches `pending_path_cancel_request` when a live path exists (per the **canonical EB activation effects**), and the same train's Action consume pass commits it through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` once the train is stopped. Once the cancel has committed, the route continues through a fresh `create_path(...)` on the first Plan pass where `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` holds (per **Route And RouteExecutor**, Planning Kernel eligibility).
- Controller-reported deviation produces a `cancel_path` event carrying the report's own `ErrorRecord` unchanged on the event's `error` field, with `deviation = true`, per the **Cancellation** subsection. A `task_kind == "waypoint"` target the train has entered, passed, or later covers counts as served and does not produce a separate overshot-waypoint deviation.
- A path capped or truncated short of its requested target must not complete just because the train has stopped at the current reservation boundary while the target is still farther on. In that case the same path remains `ACTIVE`, the train keeps its live reservation, and `RouteExecutor` keeps trying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on that same `path_id` as the track ahead clears. A run stopped short is locked over only its floor block: step `66aa`'s **Stopped-run lock shrink** releases every surplus lock past that floor without cancelling the path or releasing the reservation.
- Completed paths must release only not-yet-entered block reservations through `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(..., completed=True)`, because reservations for already-entered blocks were consumed on head entry. That reservation release may force-clear terminal `CAUTION` only for matching still-reserved owned blocks, but it must not force-clear any physical `OCCUPIED` block early. The retained record may remain in `paths_by_id` for history, but physical release of a switch or block still under the train resolves from the resource itself when a later tail-vacate event arrives. `RouteExecutor` records the arrival in step `bc55` and does not re-check safety-margin projection itself.
- On extension, the only stored `Path` update is `Path.resource_sequence`. On creation, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` initializes every stored field in the **Path field schema** — `path_id`, `status`, `train_id`, `resource_sequence`, `current_resource_index`, `zero_reservation_end_standoff`, and `last_status_updated_time`; path geometry has only one stored source, `resource_sequence`. `Path.get_reservation_end_block_id()` and `Path.reaches_target(block_id)` are derived reads of that list and update automatically. The controller's `received_path_plan` property reads them live on the next access; there is no separate controller write step. An extension that appends nothing stores nothing, and the caller learns the outcome from `appended_resource_count` and `reached_target` in the result rather than from any refreshed field on the record.
- Drive resource release from tail-vacate observations (detector-confirmed for blocks per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; controller-reported traversal for switches). `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` routes every vacate through `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, direction, route)` (the single `resource_type` branch lives inside the coordinator; `PathDispatcher` does not branch on it):
  - vacated blocks go through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)`
  - vacated switches go through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)`. The manager removes this train's matching `Switch.physical_occupants[route]` entry first, and only when no `physical_occupants` entries remain for that train on this switch does it clear the train-owned protection sourced from that switch (per **SwitchManager**). The physical-vacate handler never decides which lock to drop; the manager does, keyed by `(path_id, source_switch_id)`, so a switch that holds both a main lock and a flank lock for the same route releases the correct one (per the **Switch entity** tail-vacate contract)
- All normal block release goes through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` so `OCCUPIED -> CAUTION -> FREE` stays a single-manager state machine.

**Path extension**

- Path updates have no per-controller invalidation step, because the controller has no lookahead cache: it computes lookahead live on each read.
- A change to `Block.allowed_travel_directions` (static config edit) does **not** invalidate any already-active path's reservations. The block-direction eligibility test in `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` ran once at acquisition against the candidate `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction`, and the stored `Block.reservation` carries only `path_id`, `train_id`, and `exit_edge`, so there is nothing on the block for a policy edit to invalidate. The new direction policy takes effect only at the next `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` call. Operator/admin code must not edit `allowed_travel_directions` to indirectly cancel a live path; cancellation goes through `pending_path_cancel_request`.
- Truncated reservation where the train physically stops at the temporary boundary while no resolved target is armed (the one-tick gap between task-completion and the next Plan target arm) is permissible: the train keeps its live truncated reservation with zero ATC clearance, and the next Plan may extend reservation once the next target resolves.
- Extension is forward-only. **`RouteExecutor` must call `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` with the `stored_resolved_target` returned by `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` for the live planning chain.** Extend identity is the target block alone. Any other target block is a route-side invariant violation expressed through cancel-and-replan. Plan resolves the direction once per armed target block (per **Direction is resolved once per armed target block**); when the path already reaches a newly armed block, **Already-reached success** applies.
- `extend_path(...)` appends only the new suffix's resources (with their nested `path_tiles` slices) to `resource_sequence`; `Path.get_path_tiles()` reflects the growth on its next call. The existing prefix's entries — including the connecting tile the new suffix starts from, already seeded by the prior `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` call — are not re-appended.
- **Already-reached success.** When `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` is already true there is nothing to append: return `success = True` with `appended_resource_count = 0` and `reached_target = True`, and leave `resource_sequence` unchanged. This covers both shapes — the target is the live reservation end, or it sits behind the reservation end on the stored walk — because in both the reservation already runs to that block. It is reached whenever Plan arms a target block the live path already holds, which the **Waypoint lookahead** produces routinely.
- `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` must take the same argument contract as `create_path(...)`, except that a leading `path_id`, which identifies the existing live path, takes the place of `train_id` (signature per **Path acquisition and cancellation API**). `manual_override` and `required_candidate_resource_keys` act on the appended suffix exactly as they do on create (both per **Path acquisition and cancellation API**). It has no `zero_reservation_end_standoff` parameter, because `create_path(...)` sets that once and `extend_path(...)` carries it unchanged (per the **Path field schema**). `reservation_cap_block_id` caps the appended suffix per the **Reservation-cap rule**. The live path identified by `path_id` is the fixed already-acquired prefix; `extend_path(...)` grows that existing path forward from its current reservation end toward the caller-supplied requested target for this extend attempt. Dispatcher does not run a separate shared-walk prefix-compatibility test. When the requested extension cannot continue forward from the existing live path without breaking the ordinary path rules, the **viable-but-unavailable rule** decides between a `no_viable_path` failure and the `0` / `False` retry result. Neither outcome changes the existing path's `resource_sequence`.
- Beyond that shared request contract, `extend_path(...)` requires a live `path_id`, and the newly appended suffix must continue forward from that live path's current reservation-end edge in the same travel direction the existing prefix was built in. The caller-supplied `requested_destination_direction` applies only to the new terminal block `requested_destination_block_id`; it is not a license to reverse at the current reservation end. A `requested_destination_direction` that would require the train to reverse 180 degrees at the current reservation end (for example, the requested new terminal block lies behind the current reservation-end edge on the existing prefix's travel frame, or reaching it would require exiting the reservation-end block backward out of its current `exit_edge`) is invalid for `extend_path(...)` and must be rejected with `success = False`, `failure_kind = no_viable_path`, and a diagnostic `reason` such as `"extend would reverse at reservation end"`. The existing live path must remain unchanged in that rejection. Callers that need the train to turn back at the current terminal must cancel the existing path and issue a fresh `create_path(...)` from the train's current span.
- A `path_id` that does not exist, or that references a path which is not currently `ACTIVE`, is a caller-contract violation and fails with `failure_kind = missing_or_inactive_path` per the **`create_path()` / `extend_path()` return contract**. `RouteExecutor` passes the id it just read from `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id)`, so it cannot reach this case in normal operation.
- `extend_path(...)` must keep the same `path_id` and append the furthest forward acquirable suffix it can add to the current path, bounded by `reservation_cap_block_id`, so the `resource_sequence` grows in place on the same live path instead of creating a new path. No outcome stores the caller's requested target on the `Path`; the record holds only the geometry actually acquired.
  - When at least one resource is appended, return `appended_resource_count > 0`, with `reached_target` reporting whether `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` is now true.
  - When no resource can be appended but the dispatcher can prove the existing path is still a legal prefix to the requested target, return `success=True` with `appended_resource_count = 0` and `reached_target = False`, leave `resource_sequence` unchanged, and let `RouteExecutor` retry later. Every unavailability cause in the **viable-but-unavailable rule**, including the cap, lands here. The requested target this call echoed is recorded route-side on `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`, never in the **received_path_plan schema** projection.
  - When no legal forward suffix to the requested target exists at all, return `success=False` with `failure_kind = no_viable_path` and leave the existing path unchanged.
- The truncation-terminal rules that govern `create_path(...)` — the holding-point preference (a terminal choice among eligible prefixes), the reversal-trap exclusion, and the junction-fouling exclusion — also govern the appended suffix and Observe reservation truncation (see **Reservation truncation**), and their canonical home owns each of them. Growth's terminal must not land on an excluded block, whatever holds the reservation short — an occupied block ahead, a truncation exclusion, or a meet ceiling (per the **Reservation-cap rule**): dispatcher truncates to the nearest legal terminal instead. Where the truncation-terminal rules would fail a create because no legal terminal remains, `extend_path(...)` instead appends nothing and returns the `appended_resource_count = 0` / `reached_target = False` success, because the existing live path is still valid and the right caller behavior is to keep it and retry.
- Extend outcomes are branchable without parsing `reason`. Every `success=True` result preserves a valid live path: `reached_target = True` means there is nothing left to extend, and `reached_target = False` means `RouteExecutor` keeps the path and retries later, whether or not the call appended anything. `success=False` with `failure_kind = no_viable_path` means no legal walk from the live reservation end reaches the requested target, so waiting cannot clear it, and `RouteExecutor` must latch cancellation before a fresh create attempt (per the **Structural failure_kind rule**).

**Cancellation**

- `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(path_id, error, kind, deviation=False, latch=None)` is the single cancellation entry point. `error` is the diagnostic `ErrorRecord` that flows directly into the `cancel_path` event's `error` field for logs/UI and is required on every call; nothing inside it may be used as a condition by planning or routing logic. `deviation` is the one structured classification: `True` for a movement deviation, `False` for every other cancellation. `latch` names the latch this cancel consumes and rides the event as `payload.latch`: the Action explicit-cancel step passes `"path_cancel_request"`, and the two direct callers, environment activation and the layout emergency cut-out, leave it `None`. A cancellation ends the path and nothing else: the train brakes to a stand under the no-reservation ATC limit, and the planner creates a fresh path on the first Plan pass where `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` holds (per **Route And RouteExecutor**, Planning Kernel eligibility). Nothing records that a cancellation happened except the `cancel_path` event.
- Release owned blocks through `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)` instead of direct `block.release()` calls.
- Path cancellation or revocation effects are owned entirely by `PathDispatcher`, and a latched cancellation commits only in Action. The two between-tick callers named in **Action is the sole explicit-cancel and teardown committer** call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` directly and consume no latch. `RouteExecutor` or `TrainController` may request cancellation only by recording controller-owned Action handoff state such as `pending_path_cancel_request`; they must not call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, clear reservation, or release a live path's resources as a cancellation directly from Plan, from the controller's own tick, or from operator-command code running between ticks. The one sanctioned non-cancellation release from Plan is the **Stopped-run lock shrink**, which releases a stopped run's surplus `Block.locked_by_path` lock flags while keeping the path `ACTIVE` and its reservation intact. If Plan route logic decides that the current live path must be revoked, it records or refreshes that cancel request and then stops planning for that train for that tick; later eligible Plan passes follow the same latch-only rule while the incompatible live path still exists. A later eligible Plan may resume ordinary create/extend planning only after **both** have happened:
  - the same train's later Action consumes that request, clearing `pending_path_cancel_request`
  - `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` completes, so `received_path_plan` reads `None`

  With those done, `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` is the only gate between the train and a fresh `create_path(...)`.
- Power-off uses this same dispatcher cancellation workflow through the inclusive-latch fan-out: see the **Power-off procedure** for the four-step sequence (`98d3` → `278a` → `534f` → `886a`).
- On `ACTIVE -> CANCELLED`, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` follows the cancellation-specific order in step `09b0`.
- Future switch/flank release for both `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` and `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` goes through `SwitchManager.release_path_locks(path_id)`. The manager removes every still-future main and flank claim in the stored `Switch.locks` collections whose stored `claim.path_id` matches; stored claim identity is authoritative, so it neither recomputes flank neighbours from the switch's current fields nor infers releases from `Path.resource_sequence` (per **SwitchManager**). It must not clear `Switch.physical_occupants` or `Switch.train_protection_claims`; those remain physical/train-owned until later controller-reported switch tail-vacate.
- Reservation / physical state ownership must be read literally:
  - dispatcher-owned future reservation state: `Block.reserved_by_path`, `Block.reserved_for_train`, `Block.reserved_direction`, `Switch.locks`, flank-protection lock ownership for resources the train has not entered yet
  - block physical state owned by `BlockManager` and mutated only through `BlockManager` entry/tail-vacate APIs invoked by `PathDispatcher` on detector-confirmed observations (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection): `Block.occupied_by`, `Block.caution`. The exceptions that change `Block.occupied_by` without a detector observation are the ones the physical entry / tail-vacate item of this list names
  - dispatcher-mediated switch physical state, written by `PathDispatcher` on controller-reported resource-entry / tail-vacate observations rather than directly by `TrainPhysics`: `Switch.physical_occupants` and `Switch.train_protection_claims` (the `Switch.occupied_by` read is a derived projection of `physical_occupants`, not a separately written store)
  - a block has at most one physical `occupied_by` train at a time. Switch occupancy is different: `Switch.physical_occupants` may contain multiple trains on mutually non-conflicting routes, and conflict is decided by `switch.routes_conflict(...)`, not by the single-value diagnostic `Switch.occupied_by` projection. A single train may hold multiple path records layered over physical ownership; path membership stays on dispatcher `Path` records.
  - cancellation / completion release clears only future block reservations and future switch locks that have not already been consumed by head entry
  - physical entry / tail-vacate observations committed through `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` are the only runtime path that clears or sets `BlockManager`-owned block physical state or dispatcher-mediated switch physical state (block observations are detector-confirmed per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; switch observations are controller-reported traversal), except for the Observe ghosted-train teardown clear through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` (see **Power**, Ghosted trains); the unidentified-train adoption re-key, an operator request between ticks (`release_train_occupancy(...)` then `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`, plus adoption's `place_train(...)` seed of `Switch.physical_occupants`; see **Power**, Unidentified trains); train deletion, an operator request between ticks (`release_train_occupancy(...)` for blocks and `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` for switches, per **Train Entity**, Deleting a train); and the pre-first-tick `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` seed (see **Power**, Placement is seeded, not re-detected)
  - once a resource is physically occupied, later tail-vacate clears physical occupancy and train-owned protection rather than path-owned residue
- A latched cancellation commits only on a stopped train (the latch's `is_stopped()` gate). The layout emergency cut-out forces every train's speed to `0` first, so its direct cancels also commit at rest; environment activation may cancel the path of a train whose stored speed is still above `0` in a Paused Simulation, and powers that train `OFF` in the same act, so it stops by itself on its next running pass. On the latched path the controller therefore observes `received_path_plan` turn `None` at rest: the canonical lookahead becomes the no-reservation empty payload and ATC holds the train there. When the cancellation was deviation-driven, the stop itself was forced earlier by the deviation stop — the `overrun_entry` emergency cut-out on a fresh entry, or the zero-limit / EB protocol in step `826a` of the **Controller tick order** otherwise (see **Route And RouteExecutor**, Deviation braking). The operator clears EB through `TrainController.eb.release()` once the cancel has committed (per **EB release**).
- After a `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` call commits its lower-layer mutation, dispatcher calls its injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error)` callback. A `committed = False` idempotent no-op delivers no callback at all. The callback writes no `RouteRun` field: the run↔path link is dispatcher-owned and already gone (`active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` now returns `None`), and the cancellation's `ErrorRecord` rides the `cancel_path` event, which `RouteRun.display_state` reads to show `"CANCELLED"` while the run has no live path (see **Route-run state**, `display_state`). It writes no `RouteRun` latch and does not choose a target.
- **`cancel_path` event.** This is the one event surface for cancellation diagnostics, which UI/log consumers read. `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` emits one `cancel_path` event through `NotificationCenter` as the last step of the cancellation flow, after the dispatcher mutation has committed and the route-side `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` callback has been invoked. Only a call that returned `committed = True` emits it; an idempotent no-op emits nothing, so a path is never announced as cancelled twice. The notification carries:
  - `notification_id` — assigned by `NotificationCenter` per the canonical notification rule
  - `event_time` — system-time Unix seconds. Immediately before writing `Path.status = CANCELLED`, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` samples `time.time()` once and stores that value locally. It uses the same retained value for `Path.last_status_updated_time` and for this event after the route callback returns; it does not resample at emission time.
  - `source` — `"PathDispatcher"`
  - `operation` — `"cancel_path"`
  - `kind` — the level the writer declared on the `pending_path_cancel_request` payload, or the level a between-tick direct caller passed, unchanged. `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` derives nothing: it does not inspect `error` or `deviation` to pick a level. Because the whole most-recent same-tick payload wins, all fields describe the request actually committed.
  - `entities` — refs naming the train, the cancelled path, and the train's `RouteRun` when it has one
  - `message` — one line naming the train, the path this call cancelled, and what ended it in plain words: `deviation` when `deviation` is `true`, and otherwise the plain-words form of the writer's `error.origin` (emergency brake, operator cancelled, power off, revoked). This is where a reader sees "deviation"; `error.origin` stays the machine label `"out_of_sequence"` and no code reads either one
  - `error` — the diagnostic `ErrorRecord` the writer committed, regardless of `kind`. It is never `None`.
  - `payload`:
    - `deviation: bool` — `True` only for movement-derived deviation
    - `latch: Optional[str]` — `"path_cancel_request"` when this event is the consumption of that latch, so a log reader can group it with the latch's other diagnostics; `None` for a direct cancel from environment activation or the layout emergency cut-out, which consumes no latch
    - `origin: str` — the machine label the writer put on `error.origin` (for example `"out_of_sequence"`, `"operator_cancelled"`, `"power_off"`, `"revoked"`). This is the machine-readable twin of the plain-words cause in `message`
**Path invariants**

- In v1 the dispatcher path lifecycle is exactly `ACTIVE` / `COMPLETED` / `CANCELLED` (see the **Path status state machine**): acquisition is synchronous inside `create_path()`, so a live path has the single state `ACTIVE`. Whether the train has started moving, entered the terminal resource, or is stopped at the stop point is represented by the derived `train_status` / `ato_status` reads and `is_stopped()`, `current_resource_index`, and explicit completion predicates, not by separate path lifecycle values.
- A path must not hold the same resource twice at once. Both `create_path()` and `extend_path()` must reject any candidate whose walk would put one block or switch into the path's live holdings a second time. This is the **repeated-resource rule**, and this bullet is its canonical home. For `extend_path(...)`, a candidate whose only walk to the requested target would revisit a resource the path still holds fails with `no_viable_path`, and `RouteExecutor` cancels the path and re-plans; by the next eligible plan the train's tail may have cleared that resource, letting a fresh `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` take it. Dispatcher does not distinguish a revisit whose hold would clear as the train advances from one that never could — there is no own-length feasibility filter that measures the walk against the train's length, so every revisit of a still-held resource is a viability failure, not an availability retry. Because a path may still take reservation back into a resource the train has already passed and released, one `resource_id` may appear at more than one `sequence_index`; the **Head-mapping rule** resolves the train head to the right occurrence.
- What counts as held is the live claim, not the traversal record. `Path.resource_sequence` keeps every resource the path has ever reserved, including ones the train has already rolled through; tail vacate never trims this history or renumbers its `sequence_index` values. A block is held while `Block.reserved_by_path` names this path or while this path's train still occupies it; head entry consumes the reservation and tail vacate clears the occupancy (see `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()`), after which the block is free and any path, this one included, may acquire it again. A switch is held while a live claim on the switch names it: a `Switch.locks` claim whose stored `claim.path_id` is this path, or an entry in `Switch.physical_occupants` / `Switch.train_protection_claims` owned by this path's train. Held is computed from the claims stored on the resource; there is no path-owned hold flag, and a path only ever manages the claims it placed. Head entry consumes this path's main switch lock and converts its flank locks into train-owned protection (see `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)`), and switch tail vacate removes the train's `physical_occupants` entry and clears that train-owned protection (see `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`), after which the switch carries no claim from this path and any path, this one included, may acquire it again.
- Reading the rule against live holdings is what lets a `CIRCULAR` route close its lap. The route walk wraps back to the resources the run started from; by then the train has entered and vacated them, so no live claim from this path remains and taking reservation into them again is an ordinary acquisition. A seam that falls on a switch closes the same way, since a vacated switch carries no claim either; where the stored reservation may end is set separately by the block-terminated live reservation rule under **Resource acquisition**.
- A switch resource contributes its active leg length to forward-distance accumulation, the same way a block contributes `Block.length_cm`: `Switch.main_length_cm` when the switch is aligned to main (`position == 0`) or `Switch.diverge_length_cm` when aligned to diverge (`position == 1`), read at the alignment the path locks the switch into so the value is static across the traversal. Both leg lengths default to `0 cm` when the operator has not set them, so a switch with no configured leg length adds nothing and the cumulative axis continues across it. Any helper that sums per-resource physical length reads this active leg length for a `resource_type == "switch"` entry.
- `FLANK_PROTECTION_DISTANCE_CM` must be a global config, not a per-path setting.
- Switch locks are a multi-owner compatibility set: multiple paths may hold compatible same-state lock claims on the same switch, but conflicting required states are not allowed.
- `PathDispatcher` does not run a behind-train release sweep.
## Route And RouteExecutor

**Route data**

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `route_id` | `str` | Unique route identifier |
| `name` | `str` | Display name |
| `tasks` | `List[RouteTask]` | Ordered route definition — see **RouteTask data** |
| `mode` | `RouteMode` | One of `ONE_OFF`, `CIRCULAR`, `ROUND_TRIP` |
| `assigned_train_ids` | `List[str]` | Trains assigned to the route. Written only through `Route.assign_train(train_id)` and `Route.unassign_train(train_id)`, both idempotent — see **Route assignment writers**. |
| `created_at` | `float` | System-time Unix timestamp of construction — see **Route edit timestamps**. |
| `last_edited_at` | `Optional[float]` | System-time Unix timestamp of the last route-definition edit; `None` until the first edit — see **Route edit timestamps**. |
| `priority` | `int` | Route-executor scheduling priority, `0..9` where `9` is highest and `0` is lowest (default `5`) |
| `timing_basis` | `"operating" \| "realtime"` | Which clock this route's duration-based dwell and `delay_class` calculations measure against (default `"operating"`; see **Task time semantics** and **Clocks**). It never governs an absolute `target_time` or a `run` task's `run_elapsed_seconds`. Only full-snapshot load sets it. A change takes effect on the next evaluation with no run teardown, because every `RouteTaskRun` row stores both stamps. |
| `manual_override` | `bool` | Operator override for `manual` resources (default `False`). Set `True` only on operator-initiated routes (the Quick Route tool offers it). `RouteExecutor` passes it into every `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` call for the run (per **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags**), and `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` applies it to its `manual` target filtering and its `Block.allowed_travel_directions` direction filtering. Edits take effect on the next create/extend attempt with no run teardown. |
| `start_mode` | `RouteStartMode` | Which stop a fresh run begins at: `FIRST` (default), `NEAREST`, or `SPECIFIC`. Read once, when Plan allocates a fresh run — see **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `start_task_index` | `Optional[int]` | Index into `Route.tasks` of the stop to begin at when `start_mode == SPECIFIC`; `None` otherwise. |

**Route assignment writers**

`Route.assigned_train_ids` changes only through these writers:

- `Route.assign_train(train_id)` and `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` are the two stored-list helpers. Request services never call them directly; they go through **Assignment request entry**.
- **The speed-calibration leg route.** Plan step `c9e1` assigns a speed-calibration pass's own one-off leg route through `Route.assign_train(train_id)`, outside the request entry, because the pass owns the train while it is open (per **Speed calibration**).
- **Assignment request entry.** Every HTTP/UI/admin assignment writer calls `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(train_id, requested_route_id: Optional[str], start_override=None)`. `requested_route_id = None` means unassign.
  - **A calibrating train refuses assignment.** When the train reads `CALIBRATING`, the method commits nothing, holds nothing, and returns a refusal naming the open run, for an unassign too. The operator ends the run first (per **What ends a calibration run**).
  - **A route that is being deleted or is unknown refuses assignment.** When `requested_route_id` names a route in `RouteExecutor.pending_route_deletions` or a route not in the active route registry, the method commits nothing, holds nothing, and returns a refusal naming the route (per **Route deletion waits for live teardown**).
  - **A pending teardown holds the request.** When the controller reports `ControllerCondition.ROUTE_DEACTIVATE_PENDING`, `ROUTE_ABORT_PENDING`, or `POWER_OFF_PENDING`, the method commits nothing and writes no second teardown latch. It discards any held `RouteExecutor._pending_reassign[train_id]` and overwrites `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]` with `{requested_route_id, start_override}`. The teardown consumer already in flight then applies this latest request: the abort or power-off consumer when it removes the run (per **Action commits a replacement**), and the deactivate consumer through that same removal or, with no `RUNNING` run, through `RouteExecutor.settle_deactivate_without_run(train_id)` (per **Action latched-cancel consumption: stopped-train gating and no-active-path skip**). Holding the request means a later same-tick teardown consumer never discards a freshly committed assignment.
  - Otherwise, when no teardown latch is pending:
    - When no `RUNNING` run exists, the method clears older pending route/start state and any held `_pending_reassign[train_id]`, removes the train from any old route, assigns the requested route when non-`None`, and stores the new start override. When that leaves the old route a `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route with no assigned trains and no live run, the method deletes it (per **`RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`**, An emptied one-off route is deleted).
    - When a `RUNNING` run exists and the request names that same route, the request is an idempotent no-op; a supplied start override is rejected because the run already consumed its start mode.
    - For a different route or `None`, the method clears `_pending_start_overrides[train_id]`, `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]`, and `_pending_reassign[train_id]`, calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_route_abort(...)` — which writes only the abort latch and its inclusive cancel — and stores `{requested_route_id, start_override}` in `RouteExecutor._pending_route_assignments[train_id]`. Neither route's `assigned_train_ids` changes yet.
  - **A route assignment resets `commands.engaged`.**
    - When the method commits a new route immediately (the no-`RUNNING`-run branch), it clears `commands.engaged` itself, as an operator-initiated write between ticks.
    - When a live run must tear down first, `commands.engaged` stays set and `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` clears it in Action. The aborted train therefore runs to its current reservation end before the cancel commits.
    - When a held request commits with no run to tear down, the commit clears it in Action.
    - Either way the fresh run starts not engaged (`ato_status == READY`) and the operator issues `/ato/go` to start it; the same-route no-op clears nothing (per **ATO status**).
  - **A dropped one-off request route is deleted.** When the method overwrites or clears a held `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]` entry whose route is a `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route with no assigned trains and no live run, the method deletes that route (per **`RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`**, An emptied one-off route is deleted).
- **Action commits a replacement.** `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` changes the old run to its historical `DEACTIVATED` state, calls `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` on that run's route, then consumes `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]`. When the stored `requested_route_id` is non-`None`, it calls that route's `assign_train(train_id)` and moves the stored start override to `_pending_start_overrides[train_id]`; when it is `None`, the train stays unassigned. These writes are one Action procedure, so no stored assignment points at the new route while the old run is still live.
- HTTP/UI/admin entry points that use the request method:
  - `POST /api/train-routes` requests the route for each train in its `assigned_train_ids` body.
  - `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>` diffs the existing list against the requested list and requests each change.
  - `PUT /api/trains/<train_id>/assign-route` requests the named route. `PUT /api/paths/<path_id>/extend` uses the same method for operator retargeting.
- Internal teardown writers that call `Route.unassign_train(train_id)`. Each runs only when the train has no `RUNNING` run left, so the request-entry rules above do not apply to them:
  - `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`, called by the Action abort, power-off, and deactivate consumers after their latch has torn the run down.
  - `RouteExecutor.settle_deactivate_without_run(train_id)`, called by the Action deactivate consumer when no `RUNNING` run exists. It unassigns the train only from a route pending deletion, or to commit a request the deactivate was holding. It also deletes a one-off route emptied by an earlier abort or power-off whose re-assignment it drops.
  - `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)`, called by Plan terminal-walk completion. It unassigns the train in the same step that deletes its run.
  - `RouteExecutor.forget_train(train_id)`, called by `SimulationController.remove_train(train_id)` when the operator deletes a train; deletion is refused while the train has a `RUNNING` run. It drops the train's held request instead of committing it, because a deleted train must not be assigned a route (per **Train Entity**, Deleting a train).
- **Structural-edit re-assignment writer.** When the Action `pending_route_deactivate` consumer owned the run teardown, it calls `Route.assign_train(train_id)` directly to re-apply a held same-route re-assignment (`RouteExecutor._pending_reassign[train_id]`, set by `RouteExecutor.record_pending_reassign(...)`) — see **Shared-route edit teardown**. This stash and call site are separate from the `_pending_route_assignments` consumption in **Action commits a replacement**.
- Operator retargeting and route swap call `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(...)`; they do not mutate either route list around a live run.

`RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` returns, in order:

- `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id).route_id` when a live `RUNNING` run exists;
- otherwise, the route whose stored `assigned_train_ids` contains the train.

While a live run tears down, both sources name the old run's route; a held `_pending_route_assignments` request is not reported as an assignment. The live run and stored list must agree whenever both are present; disagreement is an invariant violation, not a third lookup rule.

- **Single-assignment rule.** A train appears in at most one `Route.assigned_train_ids` at a time. A requested replacement lives only in `_pending_route_assignments` until Action removes the old run and stored assignment.
- **The assign-to-allocation window.** After a route is stored in `assigned_train_ids` and before the next eligible Plan step `9c4f`, the train has that assignment and no `RUNNING` run. That condition is the signal for allocating the fresh run. It occurs immediately for a train without a live run, or after Action commits a held replacement.
- **Start-mode stash timing.** A per-assignment start-mode input stays beside a held replacement in `_pending_route_assignments`. It moves to `RouteExecutor._pending_start_overrides[train_id]` only when the stored route assignment commits; Plan step `9c4f` then consumes it (see **Run start-mode seeding**).

**Route edit timestamps**

`Route.created_at` is sampled once, via `time.time()` inside `Route.__post_init__` (per **Time sampling** under the **Units contract**). No other writer touches it.

`Route.last_edited_at` is sampled via `time.time()` only by request services that change the route definition, and only for these fields: `name`, `tasks`, `mode`, `priority`, and `manual_override`. `Route.start_mode` and `Route.start_task_index` do not bump it, because they are read only when a fresh run is allocated (see **Run start-mode seeding**), so editing them changes nothing already recorded. `Route.timing_basis` does not bump it, because only full-snapshot load sets it. Assignment changes do not bump it.

The route-definition edit entry points are:

- `POST /api/train-routes` — its service writes `last_edited_at = time.time()` once when at least one edit field is supplied. A bare create leaves it `None`.
- `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>` — its service writes `last_edited_at` once, only when an edit field actually changed.

`last_edited_at` records the time of the last definition write, not of the last structural change, so `Route.priority` and `Route.manual_override` edits bump it even though they cause no structural-edit teardown (see **Route Edit And Reconciliation**).

**Canonical ownership split**

- `Route` is the shared plan definition only: ordered tasks plus route-level policy such as mode and priority. It carries no per-train execution state and no runtime progress fields.
- A route may be assigned to multiple trains. Each assigned train has at most one `RUNNING` `RouteRun` at a time, read through `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)`; how live and historical runs are stored is defined in **Route-run state**. That `RouteRun` is the train's runtime instance of the shared plan: its `route_id` names the `Route` it follows, and it owns only per-train state — the task cursor, the current traversal direction, per-task timing and resolved-target state (`task_runs`), route-version reconciliation state, and the current route status. No execution state is shared across trains. Consumers read per-train progress from each `RouteRun`; a route-level progress summary is out of scope (see **Out of Scope**).
- `Route` is live shared input, not a snapshot copied into each run: active runs read the current `Route` through `RouteRun.route_id`. A structural route edit latches teardown of every assigned train's `RUNNING` `RouteRun`, followed by fresh `RouteRun` allocation (per **Route Edit And Reconciliation**).
- When an active-run helper below takes a `route` parameter, it is the current shared `Route` resolved from `RouteRun.route_id`, unless the paragraph says a new dedicated route assignment is being created.
- Per-train route/path errors are error events with `kind = "warning"` and `ErrorRecord.origin = "planning_failed"` (per **Error events**); neither `Route` nor `RouteRun` stores an error summary.
- Departure is not a route-level policy: `RouteExecutor` writes nothing to start movement. Once live reservation exists for the current target, the selected driving source moves the train — in ATO per the **ATO driving rule**, in manual by the driver with ATC capping the input to the reservation. The one operator action that gates ATO movement is `/ato/go` (which sets `commands.engaged`); manual has no such gate.
- Effective priority — `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)`, the override-aware read of `priority` (per **RouteRun overrides**) — has two uses: the per-tick runnable-train order (per **Per-train tick transaction**, Ordering criteria) and **Preemption**.
- `ResolvedRouteTarget` (defined under **RouteTaskRun schema**) pairs `requested_destination_block_id` with `requested_destination_direction`.
  - **Direction is block-relative.** `requested_destination_direction` is always the block-relative direction for `requested_destination_block_id`. `Platform` has no direction field, no platform-frame direction, and no direction-conversion helper.
  - **Platform/station resolution.** `PlatformTarget` and `StationTarget` resolution chooses a concrete platform-end block, derives the direction from `Block.ordered_tiles`, and validates it against `Block.allowed_travel_directions` unless the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`.
  - **No persistent cache.** Every route-side attempt that arms a new target block resolves its candidate live through `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` (per **Canonical Next-Target Selection**). While the same target block stays armed, Plan reuses the stored `resolved_target` pair instead (per **Live-path target re-resolution**). A failed `extend_path(...)` with `failure_kind == no_viable_path` does not retry candidates; it follows the **Structural failure_kind rule**.
  - **Canonical writer.** Plan's reservation-acquisition step is the only writer of `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`. After a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`, it records the accepted pair the result returns. The `Path` record stores only `resource_sequence`; the live reservation end is read through `Path.get_reservation_end_block_id()` (see **Path field schema**).
  - **Operator edits don't rewrite a live segment.** Operator/admin edits to platform/block target-resolution inputs (for example platform block membership/order, the `disabled` / `manual` toggles on `Block`, `Platform`, and `Station`, or `Block.allowed_travel_directions`) do not rewrite an already-successful live segment. They take effect the next time Plan commits a new successful create/extend attempt.

**Canonical Next-Target Selection**

- **`ResolvedNextTaskProjection` schema.** `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=None, after_walk_position=None)` returns `Optional[ResolvedNextTaskProjection]`. `exclude` is a caller-owned set of already-attempted `ResolvedRouteTarget` values for the current planning problem; the helper itself stores no per-tick state. With `after_walk_position = None` (the default), the helper projects the next non-finished walk-position and never appends. With `after_walk_position` set, it projects the first non-finished walk-position strictly after that index on the directed walk; when that position would be one row beyond the current tail, it calls `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=after_walk_position)` once to append that row, and it never appends more than one row per call. This is how the **Waypoint lookahead** in step `66aa` reaches past the task the train is physically working on. A `None` return means no next task on the current directed walk (terminal); otherwise the projection carries:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `walk_position` | `int` | Index in `RouteRun.task_runs` of the next non-finished walk-position on the directed walk. Its `RouteTask` is `Route.tasks[task_runs[walk_position].task_index]`. |
  | `task_kind` | `"waypoint" \| "stop" \| "dwell" \| "run"` | Copied from the underlying `RouteTask.task_kind`. |
  | `direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | The projected row's `walk_direction` (it may have flipped at a `ROUND_TRIP` reflection). |
  | `resolved_target` | `Optional[ResolvedRouteTarget]` | The resolved block and direction for a `waypoint`, `stop`, or `run` task (for a `run`, per **Run task resolution**). `None` for a `dwell`, for a `run` whose timer has elapsed with no live reservation, and for a task whose target cannot be resolved in the current attempt. |
  | `failure_kind` | `Optional[TargetResolutionFailureKind]` | Why resolution produced no target; set exactly when the task cannot be served. `None` for a `dwell` whose `task_location` is present, for a `run` whose timer has elapsed with no live reservation (per **Run task resolution**), and whenever `resolved_target` is present. Drives the broken-vs-unreachable split in **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
  | `failure_reason` | `Optional[str]` | Human-readable diagnostic accompanying `failure_kind` when `resolved_target is None` for a non-dwell task (e.g. `"Block <block_id> is set to manual"`, `"all platforms in station <station_id> are disabled or manual"`, `"every candidate for <station_id> already attempted this tick"`); `None` for dwell projections. Plan copies it into the `ErrorRecord.text` of the error event it emits (see **Error events**). Consumers branch on `failure_kind`, not on this string. |

  `TargetResolutionFailureKind` has two values. `missing_target`: the `task_location` ID (block, platform, or station) is not present in the network — a **broken** task. It applies to every `task_kind`, including `dwell`, because a dwell names a location too. `target_unavailable`: the target is present but cannot resolve to a usable block this tick — it is `disabled`, or `manual` under the run's `Route.manual_override = False`, or a `StationTarget`'s platforms are all filtered or held by other trains. It is never set for a `dwell`, which carries no dispatcher target to acquire. The enum classifies target resolution failures only; a target that resolves but whose reservation cannot be acquired is classified by `PathAcquisitionFailureKind` instead and is always treated as unreachable, never broken (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**).

  The helper is **read-only over existing rows**: it never writes an existing row's `resolved_target` or any other `RouteTaskRun` field, and never writes `RouteRun.direction` — it reports the projected row's `walk_direction`, and Plan commits that value after successful reservation acquisition (see **Route-run state**, the `direction` row). Its one permitted `RouteRun` side effect is the single-row append of the `after_walk_position` form. The only writer of `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` is Plan's reservation-acquisition step: after a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that task, it writes the `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair the call returned, with `walk_position` taken from the same Plan pass's projection. It writes the returned pair because that pair names the reservation the dispatcher actually holds, which later stop-completion lookup must match. Callback-time code may call the helper to recompute live; the stored `resolved_target` stays whatever Plan's last successful create/extend wrote.

- **`CompletionTaskProjection` schema.** `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id) -> Optional[CompletionTaskProjection]` is the public read used only by `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path()`. It returns the lowest non-finished walk-position, without appending or resolving a new target, carrying `walk_position`, `task_index`, `task_kind`, and `stored_resolved_target = task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target`. `task_kind` is `Route.tasks[task_index].task_kind`, except that a `run` row whose `task_runs[walk_position].run_elapsed_seconds >= task_time` is presented with `task_kind == "stop"` (its `stored_resolved_target` is the armed-target block Plan step `66aa` has already written, per **Run task resolution**); a `run` whose timer is still running is presented with `task_kind == "run"` and is not completable. It returns `None` when no `RUNNING` run or no unfinished row exists. `PathDispatcher` never indexes route storage itself.
- **`ArmedTaskProjection` schema.** `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id) -> Optional[ArmedTaskProjection]` is the public derived read for the task the live reservation was most recently acquired toward. It requires a `RUNNING` run and an active dispatcher path, and selects the greatest non-finished walk-position whose `resolved_target` is non-`None`. Because walk order is append-only and step `66aa` (Reservation acquisition) is the single writer of `resolved_target`, that is the most recently acquired row, including a waypoint-lookahead row ahead of the physically served task. It carries `walk_position`, `task_index`, `task_kind`, and `stored_resolved_target`, and never resolves, appends, or writes. It returns `None` when there is no live reservation or no acquired row.
- **Separate cursor model.** `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target()` resolves the next planning candidate, `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task()` identifies the next physical task eligible for stop completion, and `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task()` identifies the acquired reservation target. `RouteRun.current_waypoint_index` is only the derived physical-progress cursor. Callers use the named projection matching their question; none derives an armed row through raw index arithmetic.
- For a station task with several compatible platform-end candidates on the current tick, `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=...)` returns one candidate per call: it enumerates the current candidate ordering, skips any candidate present in `exclude`, and returns the next untried one. The caller (Plan's per-tick retry loop) owns the `exclude` set and passes it on each call. When every candidate has already been attempted this tick, the helper returns the ordinary `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` for that walk-position with `resolved_target = None` and `failure_kind = target_unavailable` — never `None`, because a next task still exists on the walk (per the **Failure-shape rule**). A `PlatformTarget` or `BlockTarget` task has only one candidate per tick. Callers other than Plan's reservation-acquisition retry loop — for example the **Dwell timer step** (`70c3`), steps `c481` / `592a`, and the Plan-settlement head-advance callback — pass `exclude=None` and receive the first candidate in the candidate ordering, which is deterministic for the same shared `Route`, physical progress, and platform availability.
- **Terminal-walk rule.** When `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns no next task on the current directed walk, the current walk is terminal.
  - **Live path still exists.** This is reachable only when every remaining task was broken-skipped, per **Unreachable and broken task handling**. Plan latches the ordinary cancel instead of finishing the run and returns for the tick. A later eligible Plan pass, once that cancel has committed and no live path remains, reaches this same check again.
  - **No live path exists.** Plan calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` and returns for that tick (per **Terminal route completion**). In the ordinary case the step-`09b0` stop-completion has already cleared the matching live path (per **Stop-arrival procedure**), so `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(...)` itself needs no new dispatcher cancel.
  - **`CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` exemption.** For `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`, `_find_next_task_target` never returns `None` — it wraps or reflects instead — so this rule never fires for those modes.
  - **All-broken cyclic walk.** When every task on a `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` walk is broken, the run does not finish; it holds in the no-reachable-task stall once no live path remains (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**).
- **Failure-shape rule.** When a next task exists but no legal concrete platform/block target can be resolved under the task's targeting policy on this attempt — including when the retry loop has exhausted every same-tick `exclude` candidate — the helper returns a `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` whose `walk_position`, `task_kind`, and `direction` describe that walk-position and whose `resolved_target` is `None`. The helper returns `None` only for the `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` terminal case of the **Terminal-walk rule**. When no live reservation exists and Plan has exhausted all same-tick candidates, Plan stops for that train for that tick. When live reservation exists, Plan leaves the live path and route status unchanged unless a later `extend_path(...)` result proves structural incompatibility.
- **Run task resolution.** `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` resolves a `task_kind == "run"` task from the row's stored `task_runs[walk_position].run_elapsed_seconds` (a simulated-time accumulator whose only writer is Plan step `6a0d`) against the task's `task_time`. A run is a stop whose location is decided by time:
  - **Timer running** (`run_elapsed_seconds < task_time`): the task is a waypoint. Its `resolved_target` is its `task_location` resolved through the ordinary chain (a direction seed), and Plan creates or extends reservation toward it and onward through the route's next geometry as for a `waypoint`, including the **Waypoint lookahead** in step `66aa`. Head entry, coverage, and the head-advance callback never finish a run; only the timer changes what it resolves to. A `waypoint` the train passes while the run's timer is still running is not finished then, because the run is the next non-finished task; head-advance step `640a` records its walk-position in `RouteRun.run_passed_waypoint_positions`, and covered-task index advance finishes it after the run finishes (see **Covered-task index advance**, the covered-waypoint rule).
  - **Timer elapsed, live reservation exists** (`run_elapsed_seconds >= task_time` and `received_path_plan is not None`): the task is a stop whose `resolved_target` is the run's currently armed target — the `waypoint` the **Waypoint lookahead** armed past the run while its timer was still running, when one was armed (the target `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` reports), and otherwise the run's own reservation end block (`received_path_plan.reservation_end_block_id`, with the block-relative direction of the live path's terminal frame). Step `66aa` writes the run row's `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` to that armed pair and keeps extending the reservation toward it under the ordinary extend-retry, while the **Waypoint lookahead** arms nothing past it, so the armed target is the reservation terminal. The train runs to that target and brakes to it under ordinary reservation-end braking, and the **Stop-arrival check** finishes the run row there through `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`: `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` finds the reservation terminal equal to the run's `resolved_target`, because both are that armed target. A train already stopped at that target when the timer elapses needs no further movement; the next **Stop-arrival check** finishes the run.
  - **Timer elapsed, no live reservation** (`received_path_plan is None`): the projection carries the run's `walk_position` and `task_kind` with `resolved_target = None`, `failure_kind = None`, and `failure_reason = None`. Plan step `66aa` finishes the task through `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(walk_position)` and returns for the tick. The train is already at a stand with nothing granted, so the run is over.

  A run that must hold after stopping is authored as a `run` followed by a `dwell`.
- Callers must not rewrite `direction` or `task_runs[i].resolved_target` through raw increment/decrement index arithmetic or by indexing `Route.tasks` outside the helper. Next-task selection comes from `_find_next_task_target(...)`; committed progress advances through the head-advance callback and the **Dwell timer step** (`70c3`), each recording `finished_at`, and through Plan's covered-task index advance for already-passed `waypoint` tasks and covered stopped-at-destination `stop` tasks.
- `Route.mode` is consumed when the directed walk grows through `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)`:
  - `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`: if no next task exists, return `None` (terminal).
  - `RouteMode.CIRCULAR`: wrap from the last task to the first task.
  - `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`: reflect task groups at the route ends and flip `walk_direction` when moving to the next group after an end.
- A **task group** is one non-`dwell` task followed by all of its contiguous `dwell` rows. Reflection changes group order, never row order inside a group. For groups `[A, B, C]`, the walk is `A forward → B forward → C forward → B reverse → A reverse → B forward`; the apex group is not repeated. If `B` is `[B(stop), dwell(B)]`, both rows run in that order on both visits.

**RouteTask data**

`RouteTask` is the one schema for every entry in `Route.tasks`.

| Field | Type | Applies | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `task_kind` | `"waypoint" \| "stop" \| "dwell" \| "run"` | all | Required task behavior discriminator. `waypoint` is a pass-through traversal (no stop, no dwell). `stop` is a platform stop served by the **Stop-arrival check**. `dwell` is a hold at a location after a stop. `run` is a timed roll: the train keeps rolling while reservation permits for `task_time` simulated seconds, then stops at the target it is armed for when the timer elapses — see **Run task resolution**. |
| `task_location` | `BlockTarget \| PlatformTarget \| StationTarget` (tagged union) | all | The concrete target for this task: `BlockTarget(block_id: str)` for a direct block target, `PlatformTarget(platform_id: str)` for a fixed concrete platform, `StationTarget(station_id: str)` for a logical station resolved at runtime. For a `run` task it is only a direction seed — the block the train heads toward while rolling — never an arrival target; the run ends on its timer, not on reaching it. |
| `task_time` | `Optional[float]` | all | Meaning depends on `task_kind`. For `waypoint`/`stop`: expected travel time in seconds from the previous task's location to this task's location; used to classify arrival as early/on-time/late when the `RouteTaskRun` timing data is available; omit when no timing classification is needed. For `run`: required finite duration greater than `0`, in seconds of **simulated** time, not wall-clock — measured by `RouteTaskRun.run_elapsed_seconds` as per-tick `delta_seconds` accumulated by Plan step `6a0d` while the run is the next non-finished task, `controller.eb.active == False`, and the train is not a paused ATO train (per the **ATO engage gate**). For `dwell`: how long in seconds to remain at the location; omit to allow departure immediately. |
| `task_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse" \| "either"]` | all | Route-level block-relative traversal preference; defaults to `"either"` when omitted. `RouteExecutor` resolves `"either"` to a concrete direction before any dispatcher call. |
| `target_time` | `Optional[float]` | `waypoint`, `stop`, `dwell` | Optional absolute wall-clock Unix timestamp. For `waypoint` / `stop` it is the expected arrival time: informational (schedule-adherence / ETA classification) and gates nothing. For `dwell` it is the scheduled **departure** time (see **Task time semantics**); a `dwell` row carrying a `target_time` does not read its own `task_time`. A `run` task must omit `target_time`. |

Route-task authoring rules:

- A platform stop with a hold is authored as two consecutive tasks: `stop(task_location=PlatformTarget(platform_X), task_time=expected_travel_seconds)` followed by `dwell(task_location=PlatformTarget(platform_X), task_time=hold_seconds)`. The `stop` is served by the **Stop-arrival check**; the `dwell` withholds reservation until the dwell timer elapses, per the **Dwell timer step**.
- A terminal stop with no hold is authored as a single `stop` task with no following `dwell` task.
- A pass-through is a single `waypoint` task. For target resolution and path acquisition, `waypoint` and `stop` tasks use the same resolution chain and the same dispatcher target contract, and both resolve to a `ResolvedRouteTarget` for reservation planning. Their completion differs: a `stop` arrival is decided by the **Stop-arrival check**, while a `waypoint` is completed by head entry into its resolved block, with no stop and no dwell logic.
- `task_kind` is required. Missing, null, or unrecognized `task_kind` is a validation error at task creation time; `RouteExecutor` must never infer a default kind.
- A terminal task must not be `waypoint`. If the train must stop and reverse immediately with no dwell, the terminal task is `stop`. A `run` may be a terminal task: it brings the train to rest at its armed target when its timer elapses.
- A `dwell` task does not create or require new dispatcher reservation. It is served by the **Dwell timer step** (`70c3`): while its timer runs, the step returns without a target, so Plan creates and extends nothing, and the train stands at the platform with no reservation while ATC holds it; once `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` is satisfied (per **Task time semantics**), the step sets `finished_at` through `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(...)` and Plan continues to the next target in the same pass.
- **`run` task lifecycle.** Plan step `6a0d` accrues a `run` task's timer; how the timer changes the task's resolved target, and how the **Stop-arrival check** finishes it, is defined once in **Run task resolution**. A missing or currently unavailable seed follows the ordinary broken/unreachable handling.
- Station/platform distinction:
  - `Station` is a logical grouping of platforms used by route planning and platform selection.
  - `Platform` is the concrete physical stop. When a waypoint's task_location is a `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget`, dispatcher path requests, block IDs, and directions are always derived from one resolved concrete platform (`platform_id`) for the current attempt, never from a station group directly.
- `Platform.ordered_segments(network)` is derived from the platform's stored tiles (per **Platform And Station**); backend platform-creation/edit logic validates that those tiles form one connected switch-free run of matching orientation. `Platform` carries no direction, no platform-side helper, and no user-facing directional option. To make a platform serve only one direction, the user must configure the underlying end block's `Block.allowed_travel_directions` so only that traversal is allowed.
- `requested_destination_direction` is the resolved traversal constraint at the requested target.
  - **Route-authored input is block-relative.** Task authors express the route-level preference as `forward`, `reverse`, or `either` on `RouteTask.task_direction`; those values are block-relative preferences, not platform-relative ones. Before path creation, by the time `RouteExecutor` builds `ResolvedRouteTarget`, it must have resolved that preference into one concrete block-relative `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for the chosen `requested_destination_block_id`.
  - **Platform-resolved filtering.** For a task that resolves through a concrete platform, the candidate comparison defined in **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload**, applied by the per-platform end-block selection, evaluates terminal traversals through the platform end block(s):
    - when `task_direction == "forward"` or `"reverse"`, it filters out candidates whose terminal traversal does not match that authored block-relative direction, or is not allowed by `Block.allowed_travel_directions`;
    - when `task_direction == "either"`, it applies no route-authored direction filter, but every candidate must still satisfy `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, and `RouteExecutor` still stores the chosen block-relative concrete direction.
  - **BlockTarget resolution.** When the task_location is a `BlockTarget`, `"forward"` / `"reverse"` are read directly in that block's immutable internal traversal order, and `"either"` means `RouteExecutor` picks whichever block-relative direction is reachable under the same current-span comparison and allowed by `Block.allowed_travel_directions`.
  - **`manual_override` relaxation.** When the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`, `RouteExecutor` skips every `Block.allowed_travel_directions` check named above, per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home. The route-authored `task_direction` filter still applies.
  - **Dispatcher never sees `"either"`.** `RouteTask.task_direction` (the route-author input, which may be `"either"`) and `ResolvedRouteTarget.requested_destination_direction` (the strict subtype `"forward" | "reverse"` passed to the dispatcher) are two distinct types. Implementations must reflect this difference in their static types, so that handing an unresolved `RouteTask.task_direction` to `PathDispatcher.create_path()` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path()` is a type error rather than a runtime branch.
- Waypoint targets resolve through one chain: `station -> platform -> block`. When the task_location is a `PlatformTarget`, resolution starts at `platform`. When it is a `BlockTarget`, resolution skips station/platform lookup and targets that block directly, with no platform resolution.
- When a task_location is a `StationTarget`, `RouteExecutor` must resolve one concrete platform before path creation. Platform availability is evaluated relative to the train for this route attempt: a platform is unavailable when any linked block is held by another train's physical occupancy or another train/path's live reservation. `CAUTION` by itself does not make a platform unavailable, because a caution block may still be reserved/acquired when ordinary reservation rules allow it. The current train's own physical occupancy or current live reservation must not make that platform unavailable to itself; same-train coverage is handled by Plan's covered-task index advance, and same-train path conflicts by the shared pathfinder/acquisition rules. Deterministic tie-breaking is required and follows the `StationTarget` candidate order in the next bullet.
- Platform/station target selection:
  - For a `PlatformTarget`, `RouteExecutor` resolves that one platform for this tick. For a new path, `RouteExecutor` picks its single best compatible platform-end candidate by the graph comparison; when that `create_path(...)` attempt fails, the run waits until the next eligible tick.
  - For a `StationTarget` with no live path, `RouteExecutor` builds the complete ordered transient list of all compatible available platform-end candidates across every platform in `Station.platform_ids`, sorted by the cross-query comparison defined in the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** home. In that same Plan pass, `RouteExecutor` may try `create_path(...)` once for each distinct resolved `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair, stopping at the first success, which arms that pair.
  - For a `BlockTarget`, `RouteExecutor` resolves that block/direction for this tick. When the create/extend attempt fails without creating or growing reservation, the run waits until the next eligible tick rather than inventing alternatives.
  - Later retries re-enumerate platform/station candidates only when no live path exists. A live path freezes the armed pair until completion or cancellation: every retry uses the armed `stored_resolved_target`, calls only `extend_path(...)`, and never tries another platform end or station candidate. A stored target that becomes unavailable is handled by the **Live-path target re-resolution** cancellation flow, never by silently extending toward another platform. When no concrete platform/block candidate can be resolved for a create retry, target resolution fails for that tick.
- A `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget` task with `task_kind == "waypoint"` is satisfied by the ordinary **covered-waypoint** test (per **Covered-task index advance**) and by the head-advance callback on its live-resolved target block; the platform/station identity carries no separate satisfaction rule, and no stop-at-station procedure runs for a `waypoint`. A `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget` task with `task_kind == "stop"` counts as satisfied when the **Stop-arrival procedure** commits it in Plan settlement through `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`. For a `stop`, `RouteExecutor` uses the actually served compatible block/platform only to decide satisfaction and to report diagnostics; it must not force resolution to some other platform or store a second served-platform choice.
- For each concrete platform being considered, `RouteExecutor` resolves the terminal candidate end blocks and picks among them.
  - **Gathering candidate end blocks.** `RouteExecutor` gathers the terminal candidate block at each end of that platform by calling the same shared network-graph walk query that `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` uses, passing the run's `Route.manual_override` as the query's `manual_override` field. For a multi-segment platform, the candidate end blocks are the blocks owning the first and last segments of `Platform.ordered_segments` (through the segment -> block reverse index); for a platform whose segments all lie in one block, both platform ends collapse to that one block, so only it participates.
  - **Which train ends participate.** When the train has live reservation, only the current head-side start locator (the reservation-facing end, per **Reservation-side head derivation**) participates in this stop-planning comparison.
