Rolling stop under EB | Physics integrates EB deceleration | `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement()` | When `eb.cut_out` is set, the **Propulsion cap step**'s momentum-free zero applies the same tick in every submode and `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` de-energizes the train's blocks (see **Emergency cut-out**). Otherwise, in ATO and manual `simulation` submode, the train decelerates at `SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate`; in manual `power_percent` submode the momentum-free model writes the capped zero speed the same tick instead, per the **Propulsion cap step**. `current_span` and `current_speed_kmh` keep updating normally either way. No reservation completion or cancellation side effect fires during rolling beyond the earlier EB-cancellation request, but physics stays authoritative: `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` keeps emitting span updates, and the same train's Observe pass keeps committing physical entry and tail-vacate resource updates while EB is latched. |
| 3 (`9f74`). Full stop under EB | `TrainController.is_stopped()` returns `True` | `TrainController.tick()` | Controller remains in the EB early-exit loop with `eb.active == True`; no state transition yet. Dispatcher path completion cannot commit while `eb.active == True`, for two reasons: the **Stop-arrival check** calls `TrainController.is_stopped_at_reservation_end()`, which requires `eb.active == False`; and EB activation latched `pending_path_cancel_request` per the **canonical EB activation effects**, so step `9d8b` skips the arrival check entirely while that latch is set. |
| 4 (`ad04`). EB release | `TrainController.eb.release()` called under its four conditions (**EB release**): powered, latched, stopped, no live reservation | operator | Sets `eb.active = False` and `eb.cut_out = False` (**Emergency cut-out**), returns the handle to neutral through `OperationalStateMachine.reset_handle_to_neutral()`, and returns the retained power percentage to `0` through `ManualDriving.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`. It writes no `train_status` or `ato_status` (both derived). The command does not call `RouteExecutor`, inspect or complete a cancelled path, or re-select ATO. After release the train reads its stored `control_mode` again, which EB left unchanged: `MANUAL`, or `ATO` with `ato_status == READY`. Plan creates fresh reservation whenever `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` holds and the route has a next target; for an ATO train that is after the operator issues `/ato/go`. |

- `eb.active` is controller-owned, but EB activation must request dispatcher cancellation through `pending_path_cancel_request` immediately when a live path exists. The cancellation side effects run only inside `PathDispatcher`, during the same train's later Action consume pass; `TrainController` never releases resources itself.
- An EB cancellation is an ordinary cancellation: the train brakes to a stand and waits, and only the diagnostic event records that it happened. No EB-specific route hook or flag exists.
- `eb.active` while `OFF`: `TrainController.eb.activate()` is accepted in `OFF` and latches `eb.active = True` with no live path to cancel. The latch survives power-up: `power_on_cmd()` does not clear it, so a train powered on with EB latched reads `train_status == EB` until the operator issues `TrainController.eb.release()`, after which it reads its stored `control_mode` again (row `ad04`). There is no separate OFF-state EB clear path; `eb.release()` is rejected while `OFF` per its `powered` gate. `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()` shares this OFF-state acceptance (per **Emergency cut-out**).

**Emergency cut-out** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

An **emergency cut-out** is an emergency stop that removes the train's traction power: it de-energizes the train's blocks — track voltage `0`, both rails floating — and drops the commanded speed to `0` on the train's next Action, with no brake curve, so the physical locomotive stops in the shortest distance. A model locomotive has almost no momentum and stops as soon as its power is removed; the emergency brake's `SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate` curve models a full-size train and cannot express that faster stop, so the cut-out is a separate command.

- **The cut-out is the emergency-brake latch with `eb.cut_out` set.** `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()` performs the **canonical EB activation effects** and also sets `eb.cut_out = True`, so a cut-out reads `train_status == EB` and shares every emergency-brake effect. It differs from an emergency brake in only two ways, both defined below: how the train stops, and when the command is accepted.
- **Three trigger paths.** Three sites raise the cut-out, all by calling `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()`:
  - **Operator-initiated** — the API calls it between ticks (per **Operator-command processing slot**).
  - **Observe overrun/conflict** — Observe latches a cut-out request (`phase_latches.emergency_request = "cut_out"`) for a train whose attribution result is `overrun_entry` — except a train with a speed-calibration pass open, whose pass fails as a measurement fault instead — and for every candidate of a `conflict` (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection, An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out); the same tick's Action step `01f2` calls it.
  - **Layout emergency cut-out** — the Emergency stop button calls it on every powered train between ticks (see **Layout emergency cut-out**).
- **Method gate.** `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()` is accepted only when `eb.active == False`, the same duplicate-rejection gate as `TrainController.eb.activate()`, so a cut-out on an already-latched train is a no-op. Like `eb.activate()`, it is valid while moving, while `OFF`, and on a ghosted train. The method itself is not environment-gated.
- **The operator-initiated path is gated to hardware environments.** The operator-initiated cut-out (the API call between ticks) is accepted only when the active operating environment is Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware (`active_environment` is `virtual_hardware` or `real_hardware`, see **Session mode and operating environment**); otherwise it returns `success=False` and changes nothing. It reads the active environment, not the selected one, because the gate is about the run the session is driving now. In Simulation the operator-initiated cut-out is not offered, because there is no physical locomotive to stop faster than the modeled brake curve and no output boundary to de-energize. The Observe-latched request carries no such gate: an overrun or a conflict must cut the train out in every environment.
- **The stop is immediate, in every submode.** While `eb.active == True and eb.cut_out == True`, the **Propulsion cap step** holds the ceiling at `0` applied the same tick in every submode (the momentum-free drop the `power_percent` submode already uses) instead of the `emergency_brake_rate` deceleration of a plain emergency brake. The emitted `track_voltage` is `0`, fully de-energized with both rails floating, not the stopped-but-lit `lighting_voltage` a zero ceiling otherwise emits. The block then sits in the **idle** zone, where the digital occupancy detector decides (see **Hardware setup**, Occupancy source follows drive state), so a cut-out train stays detected and attributed on the same detection path a powered-off block uses, rather than being ghosted.
- **Release is the ordinary EB release.** `TrainController.eb.release()` clears `eb.cut_out` together with `eb.active` under its four conditions (**EB release**), so a cut-out resets exactly as an emergency brake does. `TrainController.eb.clear()` clears both during OFF cleanup.
- **Layout emergency cut-out** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name). `SimulationController.layout_emergency_cut_out()` is the one kill switch for the whole layout, in every environment; its button is labeled Emergency stop. It runs between ticks, called by `POST /api/simulation/emergency-cut-out` while the request holds `AppState.simulation_lock`.
  - **When it is accepted.** It is accepted while the session state is Live or Paused (see **Session state**).
    - **In Setup** it is also accepted: it closes whichever Setup tool holds the outputs, and each close completes the safe-state sequence (see **Power**, Hardware setup, Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state). The session stays in Setup.
    - **While Halted** it is accepted and changes nothing, because no train is driven and every block already sits at `0` V.
  - **What it does.** On acceptance it does these, in order:
    1. It calls `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`, so every block voltage goes to `0`, every point motor de-energizes, and every open calibration run ends (see **What ends a calibration run**).
    2. It forces every train's retained speed to `0`.
    3. It cancels every live path through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` with `error.origin = "eb"` and `kind = "warning"`, which releases its block reservations, locks, and switch claims. The route-side callback is the ordinary no-op branch, so each train keeps its route assignment and its `RUNNING` run.
    4. It calls `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()` on every powered train. No live path is left, so the **canonical EB activation effects** latch no cancel. A train already under EB rejects the call as a duplicate and keeps its latch.
    5. It sets `SimulationController.layout_cut_out_active = True`, so the session reads Halted for `layout_emergency_cut_out` (per **Session state**).
  - **What it leaves.** A latch that was already set, such as a deviation cancel, finds no live path once the session is Live again, and its own consumer clears it (per the **Latch Table**). While Halted in Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware, the stopped pass keeps reading the detectors, unless no detector interface is open or a hardware failure is latched (see **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs).
  - **Why it stops and cancels directly.** No Action pass runs while the session is Halted, so steps 2 and 3 do at once what Action would do for a cut-out train. A model locomotive stops as soon as its power is removed, so forcing the speed to `0` records the stop the power cut makes, and each cancel then commits at rest. This is the second direct exception beside environment activation (see **Action is the sole explicit-cancel and teardown committer**).
  - **Why it works in Simulation.** Unlike the per-train operator-initiated cut-out, the layout emergency cut-out is offered in every environment, so the operator has one kill switch to learn and Simulation runs the same stop and the same Reset as a hardware session.
- **Reset** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name). `SimulationController.reset_layout_cut_out()` is the way back from Halted for `layout_emergency_cut_out`, called by `POST /api/simulation/reset` between ticks. It is accepted only in that state; otherwise it returns `success=False` and changes nothing. On acceptance it does these, in order:
  1. It calls `TrainController.eb.release()` on every powered train with `eb.active` that is not ghosted. Every such release passes its four conditions (**EB release**): the cut-out stopped every train and left none holding a live path, and no Plan pass ran while the session was Halted to grant a new one. A ghosted train (`presence_unknown`) refuses `eb.release()`, so Reset leaves it alone; its pending power-off takes it `OFF` on the first running pass (see **Power**, Ghosted trains).
  2. It discards every pending emergency request through `phase_latches.discard_emergency_request()` (per the **Latch Table**, Clear/consume access). A request the stopped pass latched while the session was Halted — for example for a locomotive pushed by hand into the next block — would otherwise cut the train out again on the first Live tick. Discarding it is safe: a train with no reservation cannot move, and a real conflict re-latches on the next detector read.
  3. It clears `SimulationController.layout_cut_out_active`.

  The session then reads Live, or Paused when it was Paused before Emergency stop (per **Session state**). Every train is stopped, holds no reservation, keeps its assigned route, and reads the mode it had: a manual train reads `MANUAL` with its driver input at rest, and an ATO train reads `ATO` with `ato_status == READY`. Nothing moves until the operator acts: `/ato/go` for each ATO train the operator wants to run, and driver input for each manual train.

Other sites must cross-reference this subsection by name and must not restate the effect list.

**received_path_plan schema**

- This is the schema for `received_path_plan`, the controller's only active path-plan payload. Every producer and consumer must refer to this subsection by name instead of restating the field list elsewhere.
- **Why this shape.** The controller brakes to the live reservation boundary using its safety margin and computes speed restrictions live from the network and the reserved corridor. That needs the corridor geometry (`resource_sequence`) and the boundary (`reservation_end_block_id`), not the requested target the create/extend call carried. A narrow projection keeps the controller decoupled from dispatcher-side completion logic and lets `received_path_plan` regenerate as a pure read with no caching.
- `received_path_plan` carries exactly `path_id`, `resource_sequence`, `reservation_end_block_id`, and `zero_reservation_end_standoff`.
  - `zero_reservation_end_standoff` is the `Path` field of the same name (see **Path field schema**), projected live so `get_lookahead()` selects a zero reservation-end safety margin for a **Speed calibration** leg; it is `False` on every ordinary path.
  - `resource_sequence` uses the **resource_sequence entry schema**, and each nested `path_tiles` slice uses the **path_tile entry schema**, so the controller can extend lookahead along the actual geometry without inferring terminal-frame direction from tile coordinates alone.
  - The requested target (`requested_destination_block_id`, `requested_destination_direction`) is a `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` argument recorded route-side (per **Path field schema**) and is never in `received_path_plan`; the controller does not see those fields.
  - Arrival enforcement against the requested target belongs to the **Stop-arrival check**, which reads route-owned state.
- `reservation_end_block_id` is always the current reservation boundary the controller brakes toward, whether or not that reservation has reached the run's armed target. The controller does not know the armed target and does not need to: `Path.reaches_target(block_id)` answers that question for the route side.
- `received_path_plan` carries no separate head-side field.
  - Its ordered `resource_sequence` is the retained history from the path origin (the start-side block at `resource_sequence[0]` where the create seed began) to the reservation end. Controller geometry reads locate the current physical span's reservation-side end within that history and ignore entries wholly behind the current tail; the remaining suffix carries the head-forward covered blocks the path stores plus forward reservation.
  - Occupied resources behind the path origin are physical occupancy on `Block.occupied_by`, outside `resource_sequence` (per the start-side seed in the **`create_path()` flow**).
  - "Tail" means the physical end of the current span farther from `reservation_end_block_id`; "reservation side" means the physical end closer to the destination, pointing into the path reservation.
  - The **Reservation-side head derivation** takes as head the end facing the reservation side, by comparing `TrainSpan.end_a` and `TrainSpan.end_b` against that live suffix, for ATO and manual trains alike. `end_a` is not a general preferred end. It has only two roles: the final dead-heat tie-break when every reservation-side comparison between the two physical ends is exactly tied, and the head of a span no reservation has framed yet.
- `assigned_path_id`, `ato_path_id`, and `ato_destination_block_id` are computed reads derived from `received_path_plan`, not independently written runtime fields. The aliases are:
  - `assigned_path_id := received_path_plan.path_id`
  - `ato_path_id := received_path_plan.path_id`
  - `ato_destination_block_id := received_path_plan.reservation_end_block_id`
  When `PathDispatcher` clears reservation by moving `Path.status` to `COMPLETED`/`CANCELLED`, the controller's `received_path_plan` property returns `None` on its next read and all three disappear with it.
- The canonical lookahead is a pure derived value computed live on every read. It is exposed as the `lookahead` property (the per-block `LookaheadPoint` list, read at index `0` for the distance-0 anchor) and as `get_lookahead()` (the Dict payload).
- Target speed and ATC limit are lookahead reads at distance 0 (per **canonical lookahead payload**); the controller does not store standalone `target_speed` or `effective_limit` scalars.

**canonical lookahead payload**

- `TrainController.get_lookahead()` is the one exported lookahead payload for ATC, ATO, UI, and monitor consumers. Every producer and consumer must refer to this subsection by name instead of restating the field list elsewhere.
- **Why this shape.** Lookahead combines reservation geometry, network state, signals, and current motion into one ordered forward projection. ATC, ATO, monitor UI, and stop-completion all sample the same payload, so a forward-projected datapoint is added or changed in one place. Speed-curve metadata (including `atc_limit_reason_code`) lives on the same payload so that "why is the train holding at zero?" is answered by one read instead of three.
- `get_lookahead()` carries exactly:
  - top level: `train_id`, `head_tile`, `head_distance_cm`, `travel_direction`, `speed_limit_reason`, `lookahead`
  - nested `lookahead`: `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, `stations`, `clearance_cm`, `safety_margin_cm`, `target_stop_cm`, `reservation_boundary_delta_cm`, `speed_curves`
- `head_tile` is the current train head tile coordinate, or `None` when unavailable. `head_distance_cm`, `clearance_cm`, `safety_margin_cm`, `target_stop_cm`, and `reservation_boundary_delta_cm` are centimeters. `head_distance_cm` is the head end's precise in-tile distance from its `entry_edge` — the head end's `SpanEndLocator.distance_cm` (see **TrainSpan schema**) — and `0.0` when no span is available. `target_stop_cm` is the braking-target distance from the head (`clearance_cm` minus the effective `safety_margin_cm`, floored at 0; equal to `max(0, -reservation_boundary_delta_cm)` under the sign convention of `reservation_boundary_delta_cm`). `travel_direction` is the train's current forward travel direction in the frame used by movement and traversal, derived from the live reservation per **Reservation-side head derivation**, or `None` when there is no live reservation.
- `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, and `stations` are ordered forward projections for UI/debug consumers. They are informational read models only; control decisions come from the same payload's clearance and speed-curve data.
- `lookahead.stations` is the payload name for the ordered forward platform projection: each entry refers to a concrete physical platform ahead on the track, not to a logical multi-platform station group.
- Each `lookahead.blocks` entry carries exactly:
  - `id`
  - `name`
  - `state`
  - `start_cm`
  - `end_cm`
  - `length_cm`
  - `tile_count`
  - `speed_limit_kmh`
- Each `lookahead.signals` entry carries exactly:
  - `id`
  - `name`
  - `state`
  - `distance_cm`
- Each `lookahead.switches` entry carries exactly:
  - `x`
  - `y`
  - `name`
  - `position`
  - `distance_cm`
  - `locked`
  where `position` is the live switch alignment at that tile, `"main"` or `"diverging"`, and `locked` is the exported boolean monitor view of whether that switch currently has any future lock claim or train-owned protection claim that blocks conflicting acquisition.
- Each `lookahead.stations` entry carries exactly:
  - `platform_id`
  - `station_id`
  - `name`
  - `distance_cm`
  - `length_cm`
  - `tile_count`
  - `top_speed_kmh`
- `platform_id` is the concrete physical platform identifier on the track.
- `station_id` is the logical station-group identifier that owns that platform, or `None` when no station group exists. `station_id` must not be reused as the physical platform identifier anywhere.
- Each `lookahead.speed_curves` entry carries exactly:
  - `distance_cm`
  - `atc_limit`
  - `operational_limit`
  - optional `atc_limit_reason_code`
  - optional `atc_limit_reason_detail`
  The limit fields are in `km/h`.
- **The canonical `atc_limit_reason_code` enumeration** is the enum `AtcLimitReasonCode`; each member serializes as the lowercase string shown. Every consumer (the **Stop-arrival check**, the no-reservation braking diagnostic, and monitor/UI display) cross-references this set by name and must not use arbitrary strings or redefine the values elsewhere. `TrainController.is_stopped()` is speed-only and consumes no reason code.
  - `"reservation_stop"` (`f169`) — zero-speed restriction at the safety-margin-adjusted end of live reservation, including a head that has rolled past that boundary while still mapping into `resource_sequence`
  - `"caution"` (`39ed`) — approaching or inside a caution zone (block in `CAUTION` state or forward block occupied)
  - `"speed_limit"` (`5c1d`) — a posted segment speed limit (`Segment.speed_limit_kmh`) ahead, below the train's current maximum
  - `"no_reservation"` (`7f1a`) — no live path reservation; `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 regardless of block geometry, so ATC holds a stopped train at rest. Step `914f` escalates to EB the fail-safe case of a train still rolling under it, which ordinary operation does not reach because reservation clears only on a stopped train (see step `826a`)
  - `"deviation"` (`4e2b`) — live reservation exists but the train head cannot be mapped into `received_path_plan.resource_sequence`; `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 so ATC stops the train (escalating a rolling train to EB per step `826a`) while the latched deviation cancel waits for the stop
  - `"eb"` (`c3ea`) — emergency brake latched; ATC limit is zero
  - `"no_train"` (`7b09`) — the train or network object is not yet wired; the empty distance-0 anchor still reports this structured code rather than a free-form string
  - **Tie-break.** When more than one category above produces the distance-0 minimum, the reported code is the first match in this order: `no_train`, `eb`, `no_reservation`, `deviation`, `reservation_stop`, `caution`, `speed_limit`. So `reservation_stop` never masks a zero-limit condition that is not an arrival, which keeps the **Stop-arrival check**'s first arrival condition exact.
- **A changed reason code is an event.** The reason code answers "why is this train limited right now", so the runtime records when that answer changes.
  - **Comparison and emission.** Tick substep `4d7c` compares this tick's distance-0 `atc_limit_reason_code` against the stored `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code`. When they differ, it emits one event through `controller.notifications` per the **Event schema** — `operation = "tick"`, `entities` naming the train, `message` one line naming the previous and new code, and `payload` carrying the previous code, the new code, the new `atc_limit`, and the `atc_limit_reason_detail` — and then writes the new code to `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code`.
  - **Kind selection.** The substep declares `kind` itself, like every other writer, choosing **either of these two**:
    - `"info"` for `"deviation"` and `"no_reservation"` — because those hold the train at zero and an operator wants them in the stream
    - `"debug"` for every other code — because they are ordinary driving restrictions a developer reads back

    The level is written into the emit call, never computed from the code value at run time.
  - **No `ErrorRecord`.** The event carries no `ErrorRecord`: it reports what the limit is, not that something failed, and the failure that caused the restriction is reported by its own emitting operation. Keeping it below `"warning"` also keeps it out of `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)`, so the no-reservation banner still answers with a real failure.
  - **Change basis.** The comparison is against the last emitted code, not the last tick's code, so a code that flickers back and forth emits on each real change and a steady code emits nothing. The substep does its own change detection because the event carries no `ErrorRecord` and `NotificationCenter`'s suppression covers only error-carrying events (see **Error events**, Emit on change, not per tick). An error-free per-tick emitter that must not repeat owns its own last-emitted state this way.
  - **Payload completeness.** The payload is the whole record: nothing else stores a reason-code history, and the live value stays the lookahead read.
- The **Stop-arrival check**'s first arrival condition must key on `atc_limit_reason_code == "reservation_stop"`, not on arbitrary reason strings; its second arrival condition reads head position and no reason code.
- `reservation_boundary_delta_cm` is the live signed separation from the train head to the safety-margin-adjusted reservation boundary, on the same forward distance axis as the `speed_curves[*].distance_cm` samples and the reservation-boundary projection helper. With a live path it is derived from `reservation_end_block_id` plus the terminal frame; without a live path it is `0.0`. It is diagnostic/control lookahead data, not a route-authored stop-position field.
- Consumers asking "what is the target speed right now?" sample `get_lookahead()`'s nested `lookahead.speed_curves` at distance `0`: `operational_limit` there is the controller target speed, and `atc_limit` plus its reason metadata there is the controller ATC limit and reason. The top-level `speed_limit_reason` field surfaces the same distance-0 reason metadata for monitor/UI reads.
- The empty/no-train form must preserve this same top-level and nested key shape, with empty lists and zero distances, instead of returning a different payload shape, so consumers do not branch on payload variant. If a producer cannot compute one of the nested boundary/safety fields on an empty payload, it must still emit the key with `0.0` rather than omitting it.
**Controller tick order**

1. `01f2` — Apply any pending `phase_latches.emergency_request` as the first substep of `TrainController.tick(...)` (per **Operator-command processing slot**).
1a. `7b40` — Invoke `early_action_callback` exactly once. The callback binds to the early-Action consumer, the stopped-gated `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer. This runs even when the controller is `OFF`, as the later teardown consumers in the same Action pass do (per **`SimulationController.update()` calls**, **A powered-off train's transaction**). The **Observe, Plan, and Action Table** owns this early-Action consumer order.
1b. `5c1e` — Obtain any open calibration's drive value against that state through `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)`. It returns a drive value whenever a speed-calibration pass or a lighting run is open for the train — `0` while a pass is between legs or still acquiring a leg's authority — and `None` when no leg or run is open (per **Speed calibration**, Where it runs). When it returns a value, the calibration drive is this tick's selected driving source and goes through the **Propulsion cap step**. Ending an invalid run is a separate `SimulationController` teardown step (`26f5`), run after this tick's voltage write (see the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**).
1c. `4d7c` — **Reason-code change event.** Read the distance-0 `atc_limit_reason_code` from `lookahead` and emit/store it on change per **A changed reason code is an event**. It sits ahead of the early exits (`3ec8`, `d483`) but does nothing for an `OFF` or absent controller, because an off train computes no limit. The `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code` reset at step `3ec8` lets the first powered-again tick report a change.
2. `3ec8` — If no train, return immediately. An operator command against a train that is absent from the network fails its own precondition check when it runs. Then, if `not powered` (`train_status == "OFF"`), keep the controller off, reset `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code` to `None` (see its schema row), and return from the controller tick's powered decision work. Observe has already committed an `OFF` train's detected block entries and vacates (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), so a train pushed by hand, or an unidentified train (see **Power**, Unidentified trains), remains observable. A train powered on between ticks began this transaction powered, so its Plan already ran and `TrainController.tick(...)` continues through normal powered Action logic (per **A powered-off train's transaction**).
3. `d483` — **EB hold.** If `eb.active == True` at the start of this step:
  - Hold the EB state: re-write handle = `EB`, re-zero `manual.manual_power_percent` through `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`, and force the ATC limit at distance 0 to `0`. Then, while EB remains latched, early-exit the tick's ATO and lookahead work (steps `22a9` through `924d`); the **Propulsion cap step** is not part of that exit and still runs (see its **Every EB tick** bullet). The **canonical EB activation effects** put both driver inputs at their safe rest position (`EB` and `0`) once; this step keeps them there on every later latched tick, so neither input can stick. The other activation effects are not re-applied, because none needs it while EB is latched: activation already cleared `commands.engaged`, which no command can set (`/ato/go` needs `train_status == ATO`, and **Start route** refuses a train with `eb.active`), and no path re-enters reservation. The driver may still re-command a notch on any EB tick per **Driver input acceptance**; it is accepted between ticks, but this hold wipes it back to `0` before the early exit, so it never produces movement and never survives into the release.
  - This step sees every EB tick except the ATC-escalation tick, where step `914f` raises EB after this step; the **Propulsion cap step**'s EB ceiling covers that tick (per its **Every EB tick** bullet).
  - Stay in the early-exit loop until the train has stopped.
  - Require explicit `eb.release()` to clear `eb.active`.
  - `TrainController.eb.release()` clears the latch; its effects and the status the train reads afterward are row `ad04` of the **EB workflow state machine**. The path cancel that EB activation latched (per the **canonical EB activation effects**) is committed by Action once the train is stopped.
4. `22a9` — `get_lookahead()` returns the canonical payload (the Dict shape) for the current state on every read (per **Lookahead is a pure derived value**):
  - With a received path plan, lookahead extends along the path to the current `reservation_end_block_id` boundary adjusted by the controller safety margin.
  - With a received path plan whose head cannot be mapped into `resource_sequence` (a pending deviation), the distance-0 anchor reports `atc_limit = 0` with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"`; the forward projections carry whatever geometry remains mappable.
  - Without a path plan, the canonical payload is the no-reservation empty form: `speed_curves` carries a single anchor at `distance_cm = 0.0` with `atc_limit = 0.0`, `operational_limit = 0.0`, and `atc_limit_reason_code = no_reservation`; `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, and `stations` are empty lists; `clearance_cm = 0.0` and `reservation_boundary_delta_cm = 0.0`. The controller does not project forward through the train's current occupied block when no live path exists. Movement reservation is binary on `received_path_plan`, per the **received_path_plan schema** rule that there is no second reservation source.
5. `c4c2` — Build ATC state from `lookahead`, including structured reason metadata.
6. `914f` — Apply ATC overspeed logic. Ordinarily, escalate through `TrainController.eb.activate()` when `current_speed_kmh > atc_limit_at_distance_0 + OVERSPEED_EB_THRESHOLD_KMH`. One fail-safe override replaces that margin: when the distance-0 limit is `0` and `atc_limit_reason_code ∈ {"deviation", "no_reservation"}`, escalate whenever `not TrainController.is_stopped()`. These are the only zero-limit override reasons; all other reason codes use the ordinary margin. Below the EB margin, when `current_speed_kmh > atc_limit_at_distance_0 + OVERSPEED_WARN_THRESHOLD_KMH`, emit one `kind = "warning"` event (`operation = "tick"`, `entities` naming the train) on the first tick the condition holds, and not again while it stays true. Store the emitted state on `_overspeed_warned: bool` and clear it once the margin is no longer exceeded, so the warning re-emits on the next fresh occurrence. This is the canonical home for both `OVERSPEED_EB_THRESHOLD_KMH` and `OVERSPEED_WARN_THRESHOLD_KMH`.
7. `0a4e` — Calculate ATO info.
8. `8d18` — In ATO mode, when the **ATO driving rule** selects the ATO output (`train_status == ATO`, `commands.engaged`, and `received_path_plan is not None`), calculate the handle with `controller.ato.compute_handle(delta_seconds)` and write it to `handle_position`; otherwise the commanded speed is `0`, written as `controller.ato.calculate_braking_notch_for_speed(...)` toward `0`. Both writes go to `handle_position` through `OperationalStateMachine`, per Module boundaries rule 5. **This step is skipped entirely while a calibration override is live** (`SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` is not `None`): the calibration drive owns the output (per the **Propulsion cap step** selection order), so no ATO notch is computed or written to `handle_position`.
9. `924d` — In manual mode, write a controller-owned command and let physics convert it to speed. **This step is skipped entirely while a calibration override is live** (`SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` is not `None`), so neither `handle_position` nor `manual.manual_power_percent` is written while calibration drives:
  - In `simulation` submode, store the driver's handle notch in `handle_position`. This is the raw driver command and is not itself clamped. `TrainPhysics` reads the live distance-0 `atc_limit` from controller lookahead when it integrates movement for the tick, and the notch may never raise speed above that limit: a notch commanding more than ATC currently allows produces motion capped at the limit, without `handle_position` itself being rewritten. When current speed already exceeds the limit — including the forced `0` while `eb.active` — physics decelerates toward the limit at the applicable brake rate (`SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate` while EB is latched, per EB workflow row `e67d`) rather than snapping the tick's resulting speed down to it.
  - In `power_percent` submode, store the driver's percentage power in `manual.manual_power_percent` as an integer `0..100`, and let physics map it through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` when no ceiling lowers it. It represents the absolute applied track/motor voltage and its calibrated immediate running speed, not a signed traction-vs-brake effort. `manual.manual_power_percent` is set-and-forget: it keeps the value last written by a driver `set_manual_power_percent(...)` command, or by a safety-zeroing site's reset to `0` through `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()` (the **Propulsion cap step**, the EB hold, the **canonical EB activation effects**, `TrainController.eb.release()` on acceptance, `set_mode(...)`, or `set_manual_mode_type(...)` entering `simulation`), until the next driver command or safety reset. The controller stores no second driver-command copy and never restores a pre-cap value automatically. The one physical difference between the submodes is defined in **TrainPhysics** (The two manual submodes differ in one physical way).
  - There is no handle fallback or negative power-percent command.
9a. **Propulsion cap step** (canonical home). The controller computes propulsion once per tick, on every Action — including every tick EB stays latched, because the `d483` early exit skips only the ATO and lookahead work — in three parts:
  - **One commanded speed from the selected driving source.** Exactly one source produces the tick's commanded speed. The branches are checked in this order, and the first whose condition holds wins:
    - an open calibration leg or run — the calibration drive obtained at step `5c1e` (per **Speed calibration**, Controller owns calibration output); a speed-calibration drive is a `power_percent` speed source, while a **Lighting-voltage calibration** drive is a `track_voltage`-magnitude source that carries no commanded speed (see the lighting note under **Lowest active ceiling**)
    - `train_status == "ATO"` — the ATO output (step `8d18`, per the **ATO driving rule**)
    - `train_status == "MANUAL"`, `simulation` submode — the handle notch through the profile (step `924d`)
    - `train_status == "MANUAL"`, `power_percent` submode — `manual.manual_power_percent` mapped through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` (step `924d`; momentum-free, applies the same tick)
    - `train_status == "EB"` (EB latched) — commanded speed `0` (the EB ceiling also holds it at `0`)
  - **Lowest active ceiling.** Each ceiling carries a brake rate. The step takes every ceiling that is active this tick:
    - `eb.active == True and not eb.cut_out` — ceiling `0`, at `SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate`
    - `eb.active == True and eb.cut_out` — ceiling `0`, applied the same tick in every submode (the momentum-free drop the `power_percent` submode already uses), with the emitted `track_voltage` driven to `0` (fully de-energized), per **Emergency cut-out**
    - `phase_latches.power_off == True` — ceiling `0`, at the service rate (neutral)
    - ATC — ceiling `atc_limit_at_distance_0`, at the service rate

    `effective_speed = min(commanded_speed, ceilings...)`; when the ceiling is `0` the strictest rate wins. The step emits one notch or one voltage from the effective operating point as this tick's physics command, a per-tick output that does not overwrite the stored `handle_position` (per Module boundaries rule 5). In `power_percent` submode it derives `effective_power` from the inverse `power_speed_curve` mapping and `track_voltage` from `voltage_power_curve`, so a zero ceiling produces zero speed, zero power, and the calibrated 0%-power track voltage (`lighting_voltage`, the stopped-but-lit output — see **SpeedProfile**), except under the cut-out ceiling, whose emitted `track_voltage` is `0`, not `lighting_voltage`. A lighting calibration run's `track_voltage` candidate carries no commanded speed and does not pass through the `min(commanded_speed, ceilings)` speed solution, so the ATC ceiling does not apply to it; a lighting run holds no reservation, so its ATC ceiling is always `0`. Under the EB or power-off ceiling the candidate is withheld and the ordinary capped output is emitted (per **Lighting-voltage calibration**, The candidate is the driving source while the run is open). With no EB or power-off ceiling the cap step emits the candidate `track_voltage` directly as the tick's output.
  - **Retained-field reset.** When any ceiling lowered the command, and only after capturing the effective operating point, call `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`, so the retained percentage springs to `0` for later ticks until the driver re-commands it. There is no exception list: EB, pending power-off, and ATC all follow this one rule. A positive ATC ceiling can produce a positive capped voltage for the current tick without contradicting the reset.
  - **The emitted `track_voltage` is the carrier across the tick boundary.** The capped operating point, captured before the reset, reaches the next tick through the `track_voltage` that `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` emits this Action. `TrainPhysics` holds that emitted value, and the next tick's `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` derives that tick's movement from it, not from the now-reset `manual.manual_power_percent`. So a positive capped operating point drives its one tick of movement, and the reset governs only the next Action's command computation, where the 0%-power output stands until the driver re-commands. No controller field carries the effective operating point across the tick boundary; the **Controller retained field schema** has no field for it.
  - **Every EB tick.** On the tick that raises EB from inside step `914f`, `eb.active` is already `True` when this step runs, so its EB ceiling lowers the command to `0` at `emergency_brake_rate` and the tick ends with `handle_position = EB`. On every other EB tick — the tick step `01f2` applies an Observe EB or cut-out, the first tick after an operator EB or cut-out command, and every later latched tick — the EB hold (`d483`) skips the ATO and lookahead work, and this step still applies the EB or cut-out ceiling.

  The safety layer sits above the driving source and only ever lowers the command; it never reads or cross-checks the driver's other inputs.
10. `44e9` — No standalone `effective_limit` or `target_speed` scalar is computed; consumers read controller lookahead at distance 0.
11. `89ba` — `TrainController.tick(...)` does not latch path completion. It builds the current state-machine outputs by reading `lookahead`, but it must not mutate `Path` records, release resources, clear reservation, or call route callbacks itself. Earlier in Observe, when movement calculation ran, `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` wrote the span and speed and appended its progress report to the mailbox (per **`on_physics_updated(span_update)` effects**); it did not mutate dispatcher or route state directly.
12. `32dd` — Waiting decisions read controller lookahead plus `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`, the route-owned projection of the acquired reservation target. Path completion is separate: it was decided earlier, in Plan settlement, by the **Stop-arrival check** (per the **Stop-arrival procedure**). Explicit teardown latches run only after that normal arrival opportunity; `TrainController.tick(...)` never commits completion.
13. `90d3` — A truncated path stopping at its current reservation boundary is not completion when that boundary is short of the route-owned armed stop target. The train keeps its live reservation with `is_stopped() == True` (ATC is holding the train at zero); the same `received_path_plan.path_id` remains live while `RouteExecutor` keeps retrying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on it.
14. `826a` — **Zero-limit reservation-loss / deviation protocol.** A rolling train whose reservation can no longer be used is stopped through the distance-0 zero limit, never through a service-brake-to-boundary path. **Any of these two cases** triggers it:
  - **Deviation under a still-live path.** The deviation latch is pending while the path stays `ACTIVE`, and the canonical lookahead reads `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"` (head unmappable, per step `22a9`).
  - **No live path at all** (`received_path_plan is None`). The lookahead is the no-reservation empty payload (`atc_limit_reason_code = "no_reservation"`). Because every cancellation commits only on a stopped train, this case does not arise under a rolling train in ordinary operation, so step `914f`'s escalation covers it only as a fail-safe.

  In either case, step `914f` applies its fail-safe override: `not TrainController.is_stopped()` escalates to EB despite the ordinary overspeed margin. It calls `TrainController.eb.activate()`, which performs the **canonical EB activation effects**. The operator later clears EB through `TrainController.eb.release()` under its conditions (per **EB release**). No raw `current_speed_kmh > 0` comparison exists.
**ATC speed limit**

- ATC restriction selection does not read signal state; signals are display state derived from blocks. CAUTION restriction comes from a single controller-owned global cap, `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH`, adjustable as `caution_speed_limit_kmh` in **Runtime settings**. It applies when `TrainController` samples a block whose computed `Block.state` is `CAUTION` and the train's own traversal of that block — the `exit_edge` of that block's entry in its live `Path.resource_sequence` — equals `block.caution.exit_edge`. A train crossing the block out of its other end is not capped (see **BlockManager**, A reservation never changes a block's caution).
- In manual mode with a received path plan, the controller lookahead builds the same reservation-boundary stop as step `22a9`: it brakes to the `reservation_end_block_id` boundary in the current live reservation frame using the controller safety margin.

**ATO handle calculation**

- `controller.ato.compute_handle(delta_seconds)` is the per-tick ATO handle selection; the controller calls it at step `8d18`. It gets its tick delta from the `delta_seconds` argument the controller passes, not from any stored field.
- `compute_handle(...)` reads `get_lookahead()`'s nested `lookahead.speed_curves`; it does not build a lookahead of its own.
- If the sampled operational speed curve at distance `0` is already at or below the stop threshold, it returns a direct braking notch immediately.
- It selects the notch from a two-point sampling of the operational speed curve:
  - the operational speed curve at distance `0`
  - one future point at a delta-scaled horizon (the lookahead distance grows with current motion using `delta_seconds`, e.g. `speed_cm_s * delta_seconds * LOOKAHEAD_TICKS`)
  - combined with the active ATC and block caps to choose power, coast, or brake.

**Speed curves**

- Build a unified restriction set for the full clearance/reservation area and take the minimum of all relevant curves and local limits at each sample point.
- Carry source metadata on each `lookahead.speed_curves` datapoint, such as `atc_limit_reason_code` and `atc_limit_reason_detail`, naming which restriction category produced the current minimum ATC limit, so monitor/debug UI can explain the displayed number. ATC reason reporting is this structured metadata, not only a free-form controller string.

**Driver/operator inputs**

- `TrainController.commands.set_handle()` is the active manual-driving command for `simulation` submode manual control, accepted under **Driver input acceptance**. The written `handle_position` is the raw driver command; `TrainPhysics` bounds its physical effect by the live distance-0 `atc_limit` without rewriting it (per tick step `924d` (Manual-mode command write)). The command never clears `eb.active`.
- `TrainController.commands.set_manual_power_percent()` is the active driver input for `power_percent` submode manual control, accepted under **Driver input acceptance**; the matching API endpoint/client method and train/editor UI control deliver operator input through `manual.set_power_percent(...)`. The command may be accepted while `eb.active`, but ATC and EB remain authoritative through the **Propulsion cap step**, and the next tick's EB-hold step `d483` wipes the percentage back to `0`. The command clamps to `0..100` and does not start movement by itself.

**Dispatcher/route-executor inputs**

- There is no `receive_path_plan(path_plan)` setter, cache refresh, or atomic replacement API. `received_path_plan` is a read-only property that resolves the active dispatcher-owned path into the **received_path_plan schema** (or `None`) on each read; updates to the dispatcher's `Path` registry surface automatically without any controller-side write.
- `received_path_plan` must follow the **received_path_plan schema**, and its nested reservation geometry must follow the **resource_sequence entry schema** and **path_tile entry schema**; the controller must not be asked to recover terminal-frame direction later from tile coordinates alone.
- `received_path_plan` carries no requested target (per the **received_path_plan schema**). The live stop the controller must brake to on this tick is derived from `reservation_end_block_id`, the terminal frame in `resource_sequence`, and the controller safety margin.
- `received_path_plan` must not carry a second lifecycle status enum. For the controller, movement reservation is binary: `received_path_plan is not None` means there is live reservation, and `received_path_plan is None` means there is not. The controller has no `wait_for_path(reason)` command.
- `on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)` is called by `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` after it computes the next span/speed and tile delta.
  - `TrainController.on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)` applies the update to controller-owned `current_span` / `current_speed_kmh`, then builds the progress report from the tile delta, the live `lookahead` (computed from the just-updated span/speed), and `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` when live reservation exists, and appends that report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`).
  - `TrainPhysics` samples the movement pass's `event_time` once, and the controller stores it unchanged on `ControllerProgressReport.event_time` (per the **ControllerProgressReport schema**). A single movement pass may make several `on_physics_updated(...)` calls (for example a span split across a tunnel boundary), and they all carry that one timestamp.
  - `SimulationController` drains and clears that mailbox in Observe by calling `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` in order. This method owns span storage and progress interpretation only. It does not mutate dispatcher path records or route state directly.
- A `dwell` task is the planner withholding reservation until the dwell's departure time, per **Task time semantics** (see the Planning Kernel's dwell timer step `70c3`). The controller takes no part in it: it stands with no reservation under the distance-0 limit `0` (reason `"no_reservation"`), and when reservation is granted again the selected driving source drives. The controller never reads or writes `RouteRun`.
- After a committed cancel, `PathDispatcher` calls the route callback defined under **`RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error)`**; the cancellation's `ErrorRecord` is diagnostic-only event data.
- `RouteExecutor` must not set controller path or destination fields directly.
- `TrainController.eb.release()` follows **EB release** and the **EB workflow state machine** row `ad04`; this list does not restate its preconditions.

**route/dispatcher command contracts**

- **Read-only, no setter.** `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` is the read-only property described under **Dispatcher/route-executor inputs**. `PathDispatcher` updates its own `Path` record in `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)`, and the controller observes those updates on its next read.
- **Reservation clear is a level test.** When the property reads `None`, the **ATO driving rule** produces a commanded speed of `0` on that tick's read. No previous-path field is stored, and that read writes none of `control_mode`, `train_status`, or `ato_status` (the last two are derived, per the **Controller state machine** and **ATO status**), so a reservation clear takes effect on each tick's read rather than as an edge the controller remembers. Because every cancellation/completion commits only on a stopped train, the derived status settles without depending on another movement calculation.
- **Single active path invariant.** A train holds at most one `ACTIVE` path. `create_path(...)` requires `received_path_plan is None`, and `extend_path(...)` keeps the same `path_id`, so a new `path_id` can never appear while a live path is still present: the old path always transitions to `None` first, and Plan then creates a fresh path when `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` holds.

**Read accessors**

- `get_lookahead()` is the canonical accessor for UI and debug consumers. Any consumer asking for target speed or speed-limit reason must sample this payload at distance `0`.
- `TrainController.is_stopped_at_reservation_end()` is the controller-owned derived read the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) calls. It returns `True` when **all three of these hold**:
  - the train is stopped — `TrainController.is_stopped()` is true;
  - `eb.active` is `False`;
  - live reservation exists — `received_path_plan is not None` (per **Controller state machine**, Authority to run is live reservation);

  **and either** of these two arrival conditions holds (`False` otherwise):
  - **4a** (first arrival condition) — the train has braked to rest at its braking target. It holds when **both hold**:
    - the lookahead's distance-`0` dominant restriction reason code is `"reservation_stop"`;
    - the lookahead's `target_stop_cm` (the distance from the head to the braking target, per the **canonical lookahead payload**) is at or below `RESERVATION_STOP_ARRIVAL_TOLERANCE_CM` — `2.0` cm, a constant in `constants.py`.

    It completes a train that braked to rest at the safety-margin boundary short of a very short or zero-length terminal block, which it never physically enters. The test uses distance, not `atc_limit`, because forward-Euler integration cannot land a step exactly on the boundary: the literal `atc_limit == 0` never occurs, and a train braked to rest stops under a centimetre short of the braking target at every tick length up to `MAX_SIM_DELTA_SECONDS`. The reason code alone is not enough, because it reads `"reservation_stop"` whenever the reservation end is the strictest restriction in view, which a train standing at the start of a fresh reservation (a manual train before the driver notches up, or an ATO train paused by `/ato/stop`) already shows when no block or train speed limit is lower.
  - **4b** (second arrival condition) — the train head is physically in the terminal (reservation-end) block. It completes a train held at rest inside its target block by something other than the reservation end — a manual driver's voluntary stop under positive clearance, which 4a does not complete because clearance is left in front of it.

  The dispatcher's `try_complete_active_path(...)` separately verifies the live reservation's terminal block is the served stop's target, so 4b cannot complete a path at the wrong block. Not a stored field; no writers.
- `get_current_span()` is the canonical controller accessor for occupied-span queries. It reads `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span`, the storage home for live physical occupancy and end locators.
  - The payload is geometry-first: at minimum it must expose `occupied_blocks` and `occupied_tiles` in physical span order, from one physical end of the train to the other, plus explicit end locators for both physical ends. The ordered occupancy is the block-level ownership view; the end locators are the tile-level precise geometry view.
  - `end_a` and `end_b` are the train's two physical ends and do not imply head/tail (per the **TrainSpan schema**). `RouteExecutor` and `PathDispatcher` consumers that need head-side reasoning must not assume `end_a == head`.
  - `RouteExecutor` / `PathDispatcher` must use `TrainController.get_current_span()` whenever they need the train's current span or physical ends. Who produces and writes the span is defined in **Only normal writer of `current_span` after placement** (see **Train Entity**).
- `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` produces the detected-only progress report on a **stopped pass**, and on a running pass for a ghost (`presence_unknown`) train Observe attributed a confirmed change to. A running-pass `OFF` train's identical report comes from the OFF branch of `on_physics_updated(...)` instead; both entry points build it through the same detected-only-report builder. Which entry point builds it is defined in **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**; the report shape and mailbox contract are defined under **Running and stopped**, the stopped pass.

**TrainSpan schema**

This is the canonical shape of `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` and the payload returned by `TrainController.get_current_span()`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `end_a` | `SpanEndLocator` | Stable physical end A of the consist; does not imply head/tail (the head is derived per **Reservation-side head derivation**). |
| `end_b` | `SpanEndLocator` | Stable physical end B of the consist; does not imply head/tail (the head is derived per **Reservation-side head derivation**). |
| `occupied_tiles` | `List[Tuple[int, int]]` | Tile-level coverage in physical order from `end_a` to `end_b`. |
| `occupied_blocks` | `List[str]` | Unique block IDs currently covered by the train, in first-seen `end_a` -> `end_b` order. |

`SpanEndLocator` carries exactly:

- `tile` — current tile coordinate for that physical end
- `entry_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` edge used as the end's current in-tile distance frame
- `distance_cm` — precise in-tile distance from `entry_edge`, in centimeters

Consumers that need the forward/head side derive it from the reservation-derived head and `travel_direction` (per **Reservation-side head derivation**) plus `end_a` / `end_b`; `TrainSpan` itself never relabels `end_a` or `end_b` as head/tail. The two locators' in-tile frames are always expressed in the current head-forward travel direction: each end's `entry_edge` sits on its rear side for the current head, so `distance_cm` grows the way the train travels. The head is the physical end facing the live reservation, or, with no live reservation, the end the current frame already treats as the head (per **Reservation-side head derivation**). **Reversed-frame re-expression:** whenever a new reservation flips the derived head to the other physical end, the controller re-expresses both locators in the reversed frame — `entry_edge` flips to the tile's opposite exit and `distance_cm` becomes `tile_length - distance_cm` — so the ends keep describing the same physical points. This is the single span-frame writer named in **Reservation-side head derivation**. A frame left un-flipped would make physics advance the head opposite to the direction of travel and draw the head marker pointing into the body.

`PhysicsSpanUpdate` is the canonical payload from `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` into `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`. It carries exactly:

- `new_span: TrainSpan`
- `current_speed_kmh: float`
- `added_tiles: List[TileTraversal]` in physical traversal order for tiles newly covered by the updated span
- `removed_tiles: List[TileTraversal]` in physical vacate order for tiles no longer covered by the updated span

`TileTraversal` carries exactly:

- `tile_xy` — tile coordinate
- `entry_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` traversal-frame entry edge
- `exit_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` traversal-frame exit edge; for tail-vacated block tiles this is the vacated block's forward exit edge for the traversal by which the train left that block, which `TrainController` reads as the block tail-vacate `direction`
- `resource_type` — `"block"` or `"switch"` when the tile belongs to a known resource, otherwise `None`
- `resource_id` — block or switch ID for that resource, otherwise `None`
- `block_id` — owning block ID when applicable, otherwise `None`

`TrainPhysics` computes this delta by comparing the previous controller-owned span it read at the start of the movement step with the newly integrated span. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` applies `span_update.new_span`, derives resource entry/release observations from `added_tiles` / `removed_tiles`, and packages them into one `ControllerProgressReport` for its progress mailbox (per **Dispatcher/route-executor inputs**).

`TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` must emit a `PhysicsSpanUpdate` on every running Observe batch in which this train's movement is calculated (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), even when `added_tiles` and `removed_tiles` are both empty and the integrated `new_span` / `current_speed_kmh` are unchanged. This always-callback rule keeps `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` / `current_speed_kmh` canonical and gives Observe a deterministic point for local progress consumption and the post-movement stop check. A train whose movement is not calculated follows the three-way split in **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs** instead.

- One shared neighbor/edge helper, such as `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(tile_a, tile_b) -> Optional[Tuple[str, str]]`, answers two questions at once: are the two tiles track-connected, and if so, which edge on each tile connects to the other. It resolves both ordinary grid adjacency (the two tiles share a cardinal edge whose `track_bits` connect) and tunnel adjacency (the two tiles are linked through `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` — see **Tunnels**). `TrainPhysics` and traversal helpers use it instead of re-deriving neighbor-edge pairs ad hoc. The lower-level neighbor lookup `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(x, y, edge) -> Optional[Tile]` follows the same two-step resolution: it returns the grid neighbour first, then falls through to `RailwayNetwork.tunnels.get((x, y, edge))` when the grid cell is empty.
**Tunnels**

- `RailwayNetwork.tunnels: Dict[Tuple[int, int, str], Tuple[int, int, str]]` pairs two dead-end edges so they behave as a single tile-to-tile connection. The map is symmetric: every pair is stored in both directions so lookups are O(1).
- The sole writer is the helper pair `RailwayNetwork.add_tunnel(a, b)` and `RailwayNetwork.remove_tunnel(endpoint)`. `add_tunnel` enforces the tunnel invariants:
  - Endpoints are distinct.
  - Each endpoint references an existing tile whose `track_bits` include the named edge.
  - Each endpoint is a dead-end at write time — no grid neighbour connects back on the opposite edge.
  - Neither endpoint already participates in another tunnel.
  - The two edges may be any pair, opposite or not (W↔E, N↔S, N↔W, …). A non-opposite pair is needed in layouts such as zig-zag siding loops. `Tile._update_dead_ends` uses `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(...)` rather than the cardinal opposite, so its connectivity check follows the actual recorded pair on each tile.
- `RailwayNetwork.propagate_from_tile(...)` runs `_sweep_stale_tunnels()` at the top of every propagation, so that propagation recomputes dead-end ports from the cleaned table. The sweep removes, through `RailwayNetwork.remove_tunnel(endpoint)`, any tunnel whose endpoint loses its track, loses the named edge from `track_bits`, or gains a real grid neighbour that connects back. `RailwayNetwork.remove_track(x, y)` calls the sweep explicitly, because the removed-tile path does not always touch a grid neighbour propagation.
- `Tile.dead_end_ports` is computed through `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(...)`, so a tunneled edge is automatically excluded. Other consumers of dead-end status (the `TRACK_END_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM` trigger, `TrainController.travel_direction` end-of-line fall-through) read the same `dead_end_ports` field and do no tunnel lookups of their own.
- `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` is serialised by `to_dict()` and `to_layout_dict()` as a `tunnels` list of `{"a": {"x", "y", "edge"}, "b": {"x", "y", "edge"}}` records, one per pair, and reloaded by `from_dict()` through `RailwayNetwork.add_tunnel(a, b)` after all tracks are in place. `add_tunnel`'s invariant checks are what classify a load-time entry as malformed; malformed entries are logged and skipped without aborting the load.
- Blocks remain grid-contiguous: a tunneled edge is always a block boundary, and `Block.ordered_tiles` does not walk through a tunnel.
- One shared backend network-graph candidate-query / walk-metrics home lives in the common network/pathfinding layer, such as `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]` (per **Operational pathfinding home**). Thin adapter methods such as `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...)` or `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(...)` may exist, but they must all delegate to this same operational graph home.
- **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload.** `GraphWalkCandidate` carries exactly this payload. This subsection is the home for candidate comparison; all other sites point here rather than restating keys.

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `ordered_walk` | `List[GraphWalkStep]` | Directed walk over graph steps in traversal order. Each step carries the resource/tile/frame data that dispatcher acquisition, route target comparison, and distance projection need. |
  | `ordered_tiles` | `Optional[List[Tuple[int, int]]]` | Ordered tile IDs for callers that requested tile payload. `None` when `return_tiles=False`. |
  | `ordered_blocks` | `Optional[List[str]]` | Ordered block IDs visited by the walk, with consecutive duplicate block steps collapsed only when they represent the same directed block traversal. `None` when `return_blocks=False`. |
  | `start_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Resolved tile-precise start locator the search used, including block/tile membership and the in-tile position when the caller supplied one. |
  | `terminal_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Resolved tile-precise terminal locator the candidate reaches. |
  | `terminal_block_id` | `str` | Block ID of the terminal block reached by the candidate. |
  | `terminal_block_direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Terminal block-relative traversal direction, derived from the candidate's directed frame against `Block.ordered_tiles`. |
  | `terminal_frame` | `DirectedBlockFrame` | Terminal directed block frame, including path tiles and the `entry_edge` / `exit_edge` that dispatcher/controller projection helpers need. |
  | `estimated_travel_seconds` | `Optional[float]` | Estimated travel time over the walk, `None` unless the originating query carries `GraphWalkQuery.train_max_speed_kmh`. When it does, the shared query computes the value from live segment lengths and effective speed limits and stores it on every returned candidate, so callers comparing results from separate queries keep the same ranking basis. First comparison key when populated. |
  | `tile_count` | `int` | Number of tile steps; first geometry key after travel time. |
  | `walk_length_cm` | `float` | Centimeter walk length; second geometry key. |
  | `candidate_rank` | `int` | Stable deterministic key assigned by the shared graph query; final key within that one query's own candidate list. Each query ranks only its own candidates, so the value carries no meaning against a candidate a different query returned, and `candidate_rank` never participates in a cross-query comparison. |

  Candidate comparison within one query's own candidate list is `(estimated_travel_seconds, tile_count, walk_length_cm, candidate_rank)`. Skip the first key when both candidates carry `None`; comparing a populated estimate with an absent one is a caller-contract error, because candidates from differently shaped queries must not be mixed. `candidate_rank` derives deterministically from directed-walk identity and is always decisive within one query's own list, so a comparison never reaches it with a tie. No caller substitutes UI order or layer-local heuristics.

  A caller that compares candidates from two separate queries uses only the first three keys (`estimated_travel_seconds`, `tile_count`, `walk_length_cm`) and, on a tie, falls straight through to the tie-break named at its call site. There are two cross-query comparison sites, and no other caller compares across queries. The first is the `create_path(...)` start-side flow in **Path And PathDispatcher**, which compares the best candidate from two separate per-span-end queries; when the first three keys tie, it falls to the `end_a` dead-heat tie-break, and `end_a` wins. The second is the `StationTarget` platform-end candidate list in the **Planning Kernel** (step `9c4f`'s target resolution), which merges candidates across every platform's separate per-end query, sorted by the same first three keys, with ties broken by platform-end identity (deterministic iteration order over `Station.platform_ids`) rather than by `candidate_rank` or the `end_a` rule.

- `GraphLocator` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `tile` | `Tuple[int, int]` | Tile coordinate anchoring the locator |
  | `resource_type` | `Optional["block" \| "switch"]` | Resource type containing the locator, when known |
  | `resource_id` | `Optional[str]` | Resource ID containing the locator, when known |
  | `block_id` | `Optional[str]` | Convenience block ID when the locator is inside a block; `None` for switch-only locators |
  | `edge` | `Optional["N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"]` | Tile edge when the locator is anchored at a graph boundary or the caller knows the relevant edge |
  | `distance_cm` | `Optional[float]` | In-tile distance from `edge` along the directed traversal when the caller has a precise position; `None` for tile-only searches |
  | `physical_end` | `Optional["end_a" \| "end_b"]` | Set only for current-train-span start locators, so the caller can apply the final `end_a` dead-heat tie-break outside the graph query |

- `DirectedBlockFrame` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `block_id` | `str` | Block whose directed traversal is represented |
  | `block_direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Direction relative to `Block.ordered_tiles` |
  | `path_tiles` | `List[path_tile entry]` | Ordered tile slice through the block, per the **path_tile entry schema** |
  | `entry_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge by which the traversal enters the block frame |
  | `exit_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge by which the traversal exits the block frame |

- `GraphWalkStep` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `step_index` | `int` | Zero-based step index inside `ordered_walk` |
  | `resource_type` | `"block" \| "switch"` | Resource traversed by this step |
  | `resource_id` | `str` | Block or switch ID for the traversed resource |
  | `tile` | `Tuple[int, int]` | Tile coordinate for this graph step |
  | `entry_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge used to enter this tile/resource step |
  | `exit_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge used to exit this tile/resource step |
  | `block_id` | `Optional[str]` | Block ID when `resource_type == "block"` |
  | `block_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse"]` | Block-relative traversal direction when the step is inside a block |
  | `switch_required_state` | `Optional[int]` | Required switch state for switch traversal when topology search determines one |
  | `length_cm` | `float` | Physical length contribution of this step |

- **Backend is the sole home for candidate comparison and filtering.** Operational candidate comparison, filtering, and multi-candidate enumeration live only at this backend home. The frontend editor pathfinders in `static/js/pathfinders.js` (`ConstructionPathfinder.findPath(...)` and `ExistingTrackPathfinder.findPathOnExistingTracks(...)`) answer connectivity for the track editor and return a single path. They never apply the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison, never apply the disabled-block / disabled-switch / manual-block / manual-switch filters, and never apply `Block.allowed_travel_directions` or `requested_destination_direction`.
- **One comparison implementation site.** The comparison function has exactly one implementation site, `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)`; the two cross-query callers (per the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload**) invoke that same function's ordering rather than reimplementing it.
- **Where the availability/direction filters apply.** The availability and direction filters are applied at `query_graph_walks(...)` (planning), at `RouteExecutor` target resolution, and again at `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` (acquisition). Callers that need ranked candidates or filter-aware paths — including UI features — route through `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` rather than re-implementing comparison or filtering on the client.
- **Shared switch-exit primitive.** The frontend and backend must agree on one shared primitive: entering a tile on one segment of a switch limits the valid exits to that segment's paired edge. The frontend encodes this in `ConstructionPathfinder.getExitsForEntry(trackBits, entry)`; the backend encodes it in `Tile.get_exits(entry, use_switch_state=False)`.

**Operational pathfinding home**

- The current operational backend path search, `PathDispatcher.find_paths(start_block_id, end_block_id, train_id=None) -> List[PathSegment]` / `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_paths(...)`, is block-to-block and distance-sorted only. It does not support **any of these**:
  - direction-aware terminal rejection
  - locator-level (tile-precise) start positions
  - explicit switch-handling mode
  - the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison, including estimated-travel-time ranking when a train max speed is supplied
  - measure-along-walk projection

  The refactor must extend or extract that existing backend pathfinding home so it exposes at least:
  - `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(request: GraphWalkQuery) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]` — a direction-aware network-graph search over a `GraphWalkQuery` request. It accepts tile-precise start and end locators, not just block IDs.
    - **Availability filter.** It always skips disabled blocks/switches, and also skips manual blocks/switches when `request.manual_override == False` (per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home).
    - **Topology-only search.** It plans through switches whatever their current position, because acquisition later throws them into the state the walk needs.
    - **Rejection criteria.** It rejects a candidate when **any of these holds**:
      - its terminal traversal does not satisfy `request.requested_destination_direction`
      - its traversal violates `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, when `request.manual_override == False` (per the same canonical home)
      - it traverses a block or switch leg whose curve radius is tighter than `request.train_min_radius_cm`, when that capability is set — the **Curve-radius feasibility filter**
      - a block ahead of the walk's start climbs steeper than `request.train_max_slope_percent` in the traversed direction, when that capability is set — the **Slope feasibility filter** (the walk's start block is exempt)
    - **Ranking and output.** It ranks all survivors by the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison and returns them with whichever ordered tile/block walk payload the request flags asked for.

  `GraphWalkQuery` carries exactly:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `start_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Tile-precise start locator. |
  | `end_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Tile-precise end locator. |
  | `requested_destination_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse"]` | Optional terminal direction filter, applied by the **Rejection criteria**. |
  | `exclude_resources` | `Optional[Set[str]]` | Optional set of resource IDs to exclude from the search (used by retry / extension logic). |
  | `manual_override` | `bool = False` | Operator-override flag per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home, read by the **Availability filter** and **Rejection criteria**. `True` only when forwarded from a run whose route stores `Route.manual_override = True` (operator-initiated routes). |
  | `train_min_radius_cm` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's minimum curve radius capability in centimetres, or `None` for geometry-only callers with no train context. Read by the **Curve-radius feasibility filter**; `manual_override` does not relax it. |
  | `train_max_speed_kmh` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's maximum speed in km/h, or `None` for geometry-only callers with no train context. It controls whether `estimated_travel_seconds` is populated; ranking then follows the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison. |
  | `train_max_slope_percent` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's maximum climbable gradient (percent grade), or `None` for geometry-only callers, or `0.0` (the `Train.max_slope` "unspecified" sentinel) for no limit. Read by the **Slope feasibility filter** when set above zero; `manual_override` does not relax it. |
  | `return_tiles` | `bool = True` | Whether to populate `GraphWalkCandidate.ordered_tiles`. |
  | `return_blocks` | `bool = True` | Whether to populate `GraphWalkCandidate.ordered_blocks`. |

  **Curve-radius feasibility filter.** A train must not be routed through a curve tighter than it can physically take. `query_graph_walks(...)` rejects any candidate that traverses a segment whose `Segment.min_radius_cm` is set and smaller than `request.train_min_radius_cm`, or a switch leg whose active radius (`Switch.main_radius_cm` for the main leg, `Switch.diverge_radius_cm` for the diverge leg) is set and smaller than `request.train_min_radius_cm`. The leg is the one the walk's `GraphWalkStep.switch_required_state` names; a step whose `switch_required_state` is `None` names no leg for that switch, so it carries no curve limit and never rejects. A `None` block/switch radius also never rejects, and a `None` `request.train_min_radius_cm` skips the filter entirely. This is a physical capability limit, so `manual_override` does not relax it. `PathDispatcher` resolves the routed train's `Train.min_radius_cm` and passes it as `request.train_min_radius_cm`; automatic and operator-initiated routes both carry it.

  **Slope feasibility filter.** A train stalls on a climb steeper than it can manage, so it must not be routed up such a grade. `query_graph_walks(...)` rejects any candidate that climbs a segment whose effective uphill gradient exceeds `request.train_max_slope_percent`. The effective gradient is `Segment.grade_percent` when the candidate traverses the segment in increasing `ordered_tiles` order and `-Segment.grade_percent` in decreasing order. Because block grouping enforces the stored-orientation invariant (per the **canonical block-direction helper**), increasing and decreasing order are also the block's forward and reverse direction respectively; callers must not maintain a second grade frame. Only a climb rejects; a descent never does. `None` grade, `None`/`0.0` train capability, or an unclassified traversal skips the filter. `manual_override` does not relax it. `PathDispatcher` resolves `Train.max_slope` and passes it as `request.train_max_slope_percent`.
    - **The walk's start block is exempt.** The filter gates only the blocks ahead of the walk's start; it never rejects a candidate for the grade of the block the walk starts from. That start block is one the train already occupies — its current block on a `create_path(...)` walk, or the live reservation-end block on an `extend_path(...)` walk — so the train is never routed up into it, and a train standing on a steep block must still be able to acquire reservation to move.
