The start block is also the one block whose traversal frame is inferred rather than read from a predecessor edge (a mid-walk start has no block before it, so its entry edge is taken as the opposite of its exit), which can flip the sign of `Segment.grade_percent` on a non-straight block; gating only the blocks ahead keeps that inferred frame from rejecting an otherwise feasible walk.

  - `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]` — thin adapter over `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` returning the ranked candidates, best first.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(ordered_walk, locator_a, locator_b) -> float` — in-walk centimeter distance projection between two locators on an already-chosen walk.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints(start_block_id, include_stations=True) -> List[str]` — topological reachability enumeration that returns every block (and optionally every station) reachable from `start_block_id`. The walk steps tile-by-tile, so switch tiles do not act as graph barriers. The walk does not consult current switch state, does not apply `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, and knows nothing about any train; callers that need direction filtering use `find_ordered_walk` / `query_graph_walks` instead.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints_for_span(head_seeds, occupied_tiles, occupied_blocks, include_stations=True) -> List[str]` — span-aware reachability for one placed train. `head_seeds` is the list of `(tile, outward_edge)` pairs for the train's two physical span ends. Each end's `outward_edge` is the network edge of that end's tile pointing away from the consist body: a purely geometric value computed from the span geometry (`end_a` / `end_b` tile + `entry_edge`) alone, independent of which end is the head. It is not derived from `travel_direction`, which is reservation-derived, describes only the head end, and is `None` when there is no live reservation. The walk starts only from those seeds, in those outward directions. It steps tile-by-tile through switch tiles exactly like `get_reachable_endpoints`, and it never steps onto a tile in `occupied_tiles`; `occupied_blocks` are removed from the result. `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints_for_train(train_id, include_stations=True)` resolves the train's current span and its two end-outward edges and delegates here; the Quick Route tool's destination highlighting calls it. Both span ends always have a well-defined outward edge, so the tool works whether or not the train holds reservation.
  - the `GraphWalkCandidate` table as the only candidate payload contract.
- Every layer that needs pathfinding shares this single home: `RouteExecutor` platform-end selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` start-side and forward candidate selection, `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` suffix selection, and the boundary-projection helpers all route through it.
- The implementation must use the following function table as the operational pathfinding surface. If the shared graph home is implemented as methods on `PathDispatcher` rather than an extracted `RailwayPathfinder` class, the inputs/outputs and single-home rule stay identical.

  | Function | Inputs | Output | Required callers / need | Current nearby implementation |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(tile_a, tile_b)` | tile coordinates that are either grid-adjacent or linked through `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` | `Optional[Tuple[str, str]]` edge on `tile_a`, edge on `tile_b` | `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)`, graph traversal, directed frame construction | Implemented; consolidates the grid-adjacency check and the tunnel fallback used by `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(...)` (per **Tunnels**). |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(request)` | `request: GraphWalkQuery` | `List[GraphWalkCandidate]` sorted/comparable by candidate metrics | `RouteExecutor` platform-end selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` start-side selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` candidate selection, `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` suffix selection | Closest backend code is `PathDispatcher.find_paths(...)`, `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_paths(...)`, `PathDispatcher._find_extension_paths(...)`, and `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_extension_paths(...)`; these must be extended/extracted. |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...)` | Same as `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` | `List[GraphWalkCandidate]`, best first; a caller that needs one chosen walk takes the first element | Thin convenience adapter for callers that want the ranked list without naming `query_graph_walks(...)` directly | No exact current equivalent; closest is `PathDispatcher.find_paths(...)` after sorting, but that lacks new frame semantics |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(ordered_walk, locator_a, locator_b)` | chosen `ordered_walk` and two `GraphLocator` values on that walk | signed or absolute centimeter distance as specified by caller | lookahead projection, platform-end pair comparison, graph-nearest route reconciliation | Current `PathSegment.distance_cm` is whole-path only and is not sufficient for locator-to-locator projection |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints(start_block_id, include_stations=True)` | starting block id, station-inclusion flag | `List[str]` of reachable block ids (plus station ids when included) | route-editor block-to-block feasibility highlighting (no placed train, any direction) | Lives at the pathfinder home; `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints(...)` is a thin wrapper that delegates here so existing callers keep their entry point |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints_for_span(head_seeds, occupied_tiles, occupied_blocks, include_stations=True)` | the two span ends as `(tile, outward_edge)` seeds, the train's occupied tiles and blocks, station-inclusion flag | `List[str]` of reachable block ids (plus station ids when included), excluding the train's own occupied blocks | Quick Route tool destination highlighting, via `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints_for_train(train_id, include_stations=True)` | Span-aware companion to `get_reachable_endpoints`; its head/tail outward-edge seeds are resolved through the train's `TrainController` |
  | `RailwayNetwork.project_reservation_boundary_delta(ordered_walk, head_locator, reservation_end, safety_margin_cm)` | the live reservation's ordered directed walk, `head_locator` (a `GraphLocator` carrying `tile`, `edge`, `distance_cm`), plus `reservation_end` (carrying `block_id` and `terminal_frame: DirectedBlockFrame`) | signed centimeter delta measured along the walk, forward from the head's resolved occurrence; positive means head is past safety-margin boundary, negative means still short | controller braking diagnostics and stop-boundary projection | No exact current equivalent; the geometry comes from shared graph/geometry helpers and the ordering from the live reservation walk, so a lapping route has one answer |

**Manual mode and movement-reservation boundary**

- In `simulation` submode, the driver must call `set_handle()`, the controller must store `handle_position`, and `TrainPhysics` must integrate it into speed that never exceeds the live distance-0 `atc_limit`, decelerating toward the limit at the applicable brake rate when current speed already exceeds it rather than snapping down to it, per tick step `924d` (Manual-mode command write).
- In `power_percent` submode, the driver must call `TrainController.commands.set_manual_power_percent()`, the controller must store `manual.manual_power_percent`, and `TrainPhysics` must convert it through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` in the same tick whenever no ceiling lowers it.
- In that same `power_percent` submode, the converted power-percent command is the absolute voltage/speed command and takes the place of the normal acceleration/deceleration-rate fields while no ceiling lowers it. `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` must set the `span_update.current_speed_kmh` for that tick to the calibrated effective speed. When ATC, a pending power-off, or EB intervenes, the **Propulsion cap step** samples the retained driver command, computes the current tick's capped operating point, and then resets the retained percentage through `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`. EB is included: EB re-zeroes it on every latched tick, and `TrainController.eb.release()` does not read it. There is no signed negative power-percent command.
- In manual mode with a received path plan, the controller lookahead brakes the train to the current reservation end boundary using the controller safety margin — the same reservation-boundary stop the lookahead builds in ATO mode.
- Without a received path plan, manual mode receives the same no-reservation empty lookahead defined in step `22a9` (`atc_limit = 0` at distance 0, `atc_limit_reason_code = no_reservation`). There is no fallback to the current-block boundary; a stopped train with no plan is held at rest, and a deviated rolling train is stopped through the zero-limit / EB protocol in step `826a`.

**Completion ownership and timing**

- `TrainController` is the sole owner of the post-physics stopped/reservation-boundary state (whether the train is now stopped at the usable end of live reservation), `RouteExecutor` the sole owner of the arrival decision (whether that stop serves the armed task), and `PathDispatcher` the sole owner of the release commit (the path and resource mutation).
- `TrainController` does not decide independently that a path-backed run is complete; once its reservation disappears, its derived reads show no live reservation.
- `PathDispatcher` is the sole owner of the `Path` record underlying `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan`; the controller reads that projection and never mutates reservation.
- Path completion is emitted only after two things hold: the train has already moved for that tick, and the **Stop-arrival check** says the train is standing at the stop it was sent to. `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` releases the reservation and then hands the arrival to `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, which records the finished stop.
- On an accepted completion, no controller hook runs: `train_status` and `ato_status` are derived, so once the reservation is released the train holds no live reservation (or stays held under EB). `control_mode` is untouched — the operator's ATO selection outlives the reservation, and the **ATO driving rule** commands `0` until the next reservation is granted. Cancellation calls no controller hook either.

**Controller invariants**

- There is no `self.target_speed` field. Lookahead at distance 0 is the source of target speed.
- Controller-owned live control and physical state must stay separate from persistent train data.
- Controller ATO destination state comes only from `received_path_plan`. There is no fallback read against `Train`.
- `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)` must keep the 1:1 train/controller pairing and must not recreate reservation from train-side runtime mirrors. Its only job is to make sure a controller object exists and is registered for this `train_id`. The controller must exist before any dispatcher path creation or extension: callers must make sure of this before `create_path(...)` or `extend_path(...)`. `SimulationController` must not build or write a path payload itself. There is no late-bind recovery hook such as `PathDispatcher.on_controller_available(train_id)`, because `received_path_plan` is a property that resolves live.
## TrainPhysics

**Movement-reservation input in `TrainPhysics`**

- `TrainPhysics` runs physical integration: the speed update, the span and end-locator update, occupancy tracing, and tail tracing. The live storage is `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` and `TrainController.physics_sync.current_speed_kmh`. `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` computes each `span_update` (`new_span`, `current_speed_kmh`, ordered `added_tiles`, ordered `removed_tiles`, and traversal frame metadata) and passes it to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`, which performs the controller-owned storage write. `TrainPhysics` must not own path identity, dispatcher reservation state, progress interpretation, completion, or a separate canonical position store on `Train`.
- **The two physics halves, and `tick()`.** `TrainPhysics` has two separate halves:
  - `integrate_movement(delta)` — the Observe movement calculation, run in the Observe batch (`SimulationController._observe_train(...)`). It advances the span and passes each `span_update` to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)`.
  - `apply_track_voltage()` — the Action step, run in that train's Action pass (`SimulationController._act_train(...)`). It drives the occupied blocks' track voltage for the next tick.

  The live per-tick loop calls the two halves directly and separately, so Observe never writes block voltage (per the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**, the Observe row). `TrainPhysics.tick(delta)` is a convenience composition that runs the two halves back-to-back as one movement-then-voltage step. The live loop must not call it, because movement and voltage belong to different stages.
- Each tick `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` caps the distance it moves the train so the calculated span stays inside what the block detector confirms (per **Power**, The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector). The cap limits distance only. It does not change the speed solution, it never moves the train backwards, and every consumer — the controller's braking and stopping logic, the voltage emission, the progress reports — reads the capped span as that tick's position with no branch for having been capped.
- To choose exits on ambiguous geometry, `TrainPhysics` normally needs a read-only reservation-geometry projection from the controller, derived from `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan.resource_sequence`. The least it needs is the ordered `resource_sequence` / `path_tiles` geometry from that active plan, plus enough local direction context to pick the correct next edge through the current tile. That plan is its only path-geometry movement input.
- `TrainPhysics` does not need dispatcher ownership fields such as `path_id` to step the train, nor requested or reserved centimetre stop targets for physical integration. Centimeter stop-target fields are not part of the path/controller contract. Controller braking logic uses reservation-boundary geometry plus the controller safety margin.
- `TrainPhysics` must read the current live position through the controller-owned span. It must write movement only by sending `span_update` to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`, never through a train-entity position field. Initial placement is set by the API `SimulationController.add_train(...)` flow, which writes `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` before the first tick. (Persistence and save-data migration are out of scope, per **Out of Scope**.)
- Exception for cancellation/revocation braking: if the dispatcher-owned path has already left `ACTIVE` while the train is still rolling, `TrainPhysics` must keep moving the train according to its speed and the current live network state. That movement relies on the physical `Switch.position` and live track geometry at that moment, not on retained reservation locks or a second copy of path ownership kept in the controller.
- Because live switch state is owned by `Switch`, `TrainPhysics._advance_end()` and tail tracing must call the `Tile` traversal helpers using the resolver input defined by the `Tile` helper contract (per **Tile role and traversal**).

**Block occupancy**

- Normal tail-vacated transitions go through `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` and `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`. That chain routes block releases through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()`, so `OCCUPIED -> CAUTION -> FREE` stays in one state machine.
- `TrainPhysics` must not write `Block` fields directly, and must not call block-state mutators for normal occupancy, CAUTION, or release. It computes movement `span_update` values, and the controller/dispatcher feedback chain does all block writes through `BlockManager`.
- Block tail-vacate observations come from the Observe detector (debounced no-current; see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), never from tile-level span arithmetic. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` includes a block in `tail_vacated_resources` only when the detector slice carries that block, so `PathDispatcher` calls `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` only on clears whose attribution result is `vacate` (see **Power**, A clear read from under the train is a detection fault).
- Normal CAUTION clearing happens inside `on_block_tail_vacated()` via `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()`, and on clean entry in `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`. Both are `BlockManager` writes; there is no separate `clear_block()` / `release_block()` step.

**Tail-vacate flow in `TrainPhysics`**

- **Tail-vacate reporting.** `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` carries each tail-vacate in the `tail_vacated_resources` of the `ControllerProgressReport` it appends to the controller-owned progress mailbox `physics_sync.queued_progress_reports` (per **Physical progress / deviation procedure**, step `35d0`).
- **Vacate reservation differs by resource type.**
  - **Block**: only a detector-confirmed clear is a block vacate, and block IDs arrive directly on the detector slice.
  - **Switch**: a tile-level vacate of the switch resource in the calculated span is enough. Switch IDs come from `Tile.switch_id` on switch tiles, via the same tile-lookup mechanism used for entry detection.
- **Observe routing.** `PathDispatcher` releases each tail-vacate through `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(...)`, passing a block event's `exit_edge` as `direction` (per **Tail-vacate release flow** and the **ControllerProgressReport schema**). Entry removal and the protection release on a switch are defined under **SwitchManager**, `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`.
- `TrainPhysics` does not track its own `_caution_blocks`; `BlockManager` owns the full release lifecycle.

**Voltage behavior**

- **Three distinct values.** `track_voltage`, `power_percent`, and `speed_kmh` are three different values.
- **Canonical home for `track_voltage` is `TrainPhysics`.** It is computed each tick from the authoritative source for the active mode.
  - In ATO and manual-simulation mode, that source is the train's current speed: the speed the physics speed solution produced, `physics_sync.current_speed_kmh`, mapped `speed_kmh -> power_percent -> track_voltage`. ATO takes no voltage from a target speed the train has not reached.
  - In manual `power_percent` mode, `manual.manual_power_percent` is mapped to `track_voltage` through the inverse of the train's resolved `voltage_power_curve` (the stage-1 `(track_voltage, power_percent)` curve), while the calibrated `speed_kmh` for that same operating point comes from its resolved `power_speed_curve`. Both curves are read through `SpeedProfileRegistry.resolve(...)` (see **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles).
  - While a **Lighting-voltage calibration** run is open for the train, that run's candidate voltage is the selected driving source, and it goes through the **Propulsion cap step** like every other driving source (per **Lighting-voltage calibration**, The candidate is the driving source while the run is open).

  `track_voltage` is always reached through `voltage_power_curve`, never through `power_speed_curve` (which has no voltage axis).
- **A powered train is lit whenever it is not driven.** A speed of `0` is `0%` power, and `0%` power is the profile's `lighting_voltage` (see **SpeedProfile**). So a powered train outputs at least `lighting_voltage` in every case where nothing drives it:
  - standing with no reservation;
  - standing under a live reservation, in `manual` or `ato` mode;
  - in `ato` mode while not engaged (`ato_status == READY`), because the **ATO driving rule** then commands `0`;
  - under a plain EB or the pending power-off ceiling, whose zero ceiling is `0%` power.

  Only two cases output `0`: an `OFF` train, whose blocks are driven to the safe `0` V (see **`SimulationController._act_train(...)` flow**, step 5), and an emergency cut-out (see **Emergency cut-out**). Separately, a block outside a train's emission set gets no voltage from it at all — a ghosted train's blocks and a train's blocks past its authority end — and the de-energize drain takes it to `0` (see **Power**, Energized set: where the train stands, plus one block ahead). The lit voltage keeps a standing locomotive in the lighting zone, where its current channel reads it (see **Power**, Occupancy source follows drive state).
- **ATO and manual driving read the same speed.** Both take `track_voltage` from the current speed, so the locomotive is driven at the speed its calculated span moves at and the detector and the calculated span stay together.
- **`track_voltage` is a magnitude, not a direction.** It says how hard to drive a block, not which way. Direction is added per block when the value is emitted (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction), so every mapping here runs from `0` up to the profile's `max_voltage` and no calibration curve carries a sign.
- **`track_voltage` is per-tick derived state.** It is not stored on `TrainController` and not persisted on `Train`. `TrainPhysics` must pass the current `track_voltage` value to `BlockPowerController`, the software-to-hardware output layer for block voltage emission, as that tick's hardware output. This is the Action step `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()`, which runs in the per-train Action pass after command generation.
- **A train that overran its authority is cut out.** When the attribution result for a block is `overrun_entry` (per **Power**, Block occupancy detection, Match order for a newly OCCUPIED block), Observe latches that train's emergency cut-out request on the same read. That tick's Action step `01f2` applies it (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection, An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out; effects per **Emergency cut-out**).

  The **Propulsion cap step**'s cut-out ceiling is what removes the drive voltage; `TrainPhysics.compute_track_voltage(...)` has no overrun test of its own. The train's blocks then sit at `0` (both rails floating) in the idle drive zone, where their `hc165` detector reads the locomotive, so a cut-out train stays attributed and is not ghosted (per **Emergency cut-out**).

  One overrun raises no cut-out: a calibration leg's overrun (see **Speed calibration**, A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass). Its overrun block is kept dead instead by the separate emission-set exclusion `blocks_past_authority` (see **Power**, A block past the authority end is never energized).
- **The two manual submodes differ in one physical way.** `power_percent` is momentum-free: the commanded speed applies the same tick, with no integration through the acceleration or deceleration rates and no handle-based speed-up/speed-down. `simulation` integrates through the notch model — the handle notch, `power_multipliers`, `brake_multipliers`, and the motion rates. How the two submodes accept their commands is stated once under **Driver input acceptance** (see **TrainController**).
- In manual `power_percent` mode, `TrainPhysics` receives the effective operating point the controller's **Propulsion cap step** produced from the sampled `manual.manual_power_percent`.
  - When no ceiling lowered the command, that point is the calibrated `power_percent -> speed_kmh` result for that tick.
  - When a ceiling — EB, pending power-off, or ATC — lowered it, the effective point is the capped one. The reset of the stored percentage and the capped point's use in the current tick are per the **Propulsion cap step**.

  Because the submode is momentum-free, a capped zero is written the same tick it is produced. The effective `speed_kmh` the **Propulsion cap step** produced is written into the same `PhysicsSpanUpdate.current_speed_kmh` that carries the movement result.
- In `power_percent` manual mode, `TrainPhysics` must use the profile's voltage/power/speed calibration directly. It must not use scalar target-speed fields, and must not apply the service acceleration/deceleration rates to the manual-power command. The calibration must work in both directions, so physics can convert between the authoritative value for the active mode and the derived outputs it needs to maintain. `SpeedProfile` owns both mappings (per **Speed-profile addition**).

**Physics invariants**

- `TrainPhysics` must not own manual-mode policy; it must execute controller commands and maintain physical state only.
- Future reservation is held by `Block.reserved_by_path` / `Block.reserved_for_train` on the block side and `Switch.locks` on the switch side. `TrainPhysics` holds no path-lock state of its own. Movement is geometry-driven. Once the train enters a resource, switch integrity during traversal is enforced by `Switch.physical_occupants` (read diagnostically through `Switch.occupied_by`) plus any `Switch.train_protection_claims`.

## SpeedProfile

`SpeedProfile` carries motion-rate data plus calibration measured from a locomotive, in the vocabulary the rest of the system must use directly: voltage, power percent, and speed. A record is a model profile or an instance profile (per **Model profiles and instance profiles**).
- `SpeedProfile` fields:
  - `profile_id`: unique profile identifier.
  - `name`: display name for UI/debug/profile selection.
  - `derived_from`: the model profile this record overlays, unset on a model profile and set on an instance profile.
  - `model`: the locomotive model this profile describes, written the same way `RosterEntry.model` writes it. It is what makes a measured curve worth keeping: a second locomotive of that model starts from the curve the first one produced rather than from the seeded linear default. **Train Roster**, Profiles are matched by model, is where a roster entry uses it. It is carried by model profiles only. It is blank on a model profile seeded at train creation, because nothing has yet said which model that train is.
  - `calibrated_at`: the wall-clock date and time **Speed calibration** last wrote this profile's `power_speed_curve`, unset until a speed calibration commit first writes it. A hand edit does not write it, so it dates the last measurement, not the last change (see **Editing a profile by hand**). An instance profile resolves it per **`calibrated_at` follows the curve**. It is the one field that says whether a profile's curve has been measured, and it is how a roster entry chooses between two model profiles naming one model (see **Train Roster**, Profiles are matched by model).
  - `max_voltage`: top of the usable `track_voltage` range for the first mapping stage. A model profile seeded at train creation defaults to `DEFAULT_SEEDED_MAX_VOLTAGE_V`, a `constants.py` value. It is carried by model profiles only.
  - `voltage_power_curve`: stored calibration mapping `(track_voltage, power_percent)` for the first stage. Its default is linear across the usable range, from `lighting_voltage` (0%) to `max_voltage` (100%). It is carried by model profiles only; an instance profile's resolved curve is defined under **Model profiles and instance profiles**. **Speed calibration** does not write it; **Lighting-voltage calibration** is what moves its bottom anchor, by committing a new `lighting_voltage`.
  - `power_speed_curve`: stored calibration mapping `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` for the second stage. Its default is linear from `0%` -> `0 km/h` to `100%` -> the owning train's configured `max_speed`, seeded on the model profile `SimulationController.add_train(...)` creates at train creation when placement imports no profile. **Speed calibration** is what writes a measured one, and a hand edit in the Speed Profile panel may also change it (see **Editing a profile by hand**).
  - `lighting_voltage`: the single voltage at which the train is lit but not yet moving. Every powered train that nothing drives outputs it (see **TrainPhysics**, A powered train is lit whenever it is not driven). It is also the 0%-power point (bottom) of `voltage_power_curve`: at exactly this voltage power is 0 and the train holds, and just above it the train begins to move. Every locomotive is expected to carry its own value of it, because a lamp, a motor and a gearbox differ between two items of one model. Its value is set, in the ordinary case, by **Lighting-voltage calibration**; a seeded default or an imported roster entry can also carry one. A model profile seeded at train creation defaults to `DEFAULT_SEEDED_LIGHTING_VOLTAGE_V`, a `constants.py` value chosen below the Hardware Setup default `current_sense_min_drive_v` so a freshly placed train satisfies **Occupancy source follows drive state**'s bound without immediate recalibration (see **Lighting-voltage calibration**, What a candidate may be).
  - `acceleration_rate`: service acceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `deceleration_rate`: service braking rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `emergency_brake_rate`: emergency-brake deceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `friction_rate`: passive/coasting deceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `operational_decel_ratio`: comfort-braking fraction used when ATO builds operational braking curves.
  - `air_resistance_enabled`: whether the drag model is active.
  - `drag_coefficient`: drag strength used by the drag model.
  - `reference_speed_kmh`: reference speed used to scale the drag model.
  - `power_multipliers`: per-notch table mapping each power handle position to the fraction of `acceleration_rate` that notch applies, so different train models can have different power-notch response. Stored on the profile and read directly by the physics integration and ATO (not from any module-level default); the construction default is the standard notch table.
  - `brake_multipliers`: per-notch table mapping each brake handle position to the fraction of the operational brake rate (`deceleration_rate × operational_decel_ratio`) that notch applies. Stored on the profile and read directly by the physics integration and ATO; the construction default is the standard notch table.

**Model profiles and instance profiles**

- **A record is a model profile or an instance profile, and `derived_from` is what says which.** A model profile leaves `derived_from` unset and describes a locomotive model. An instance profile names a model profile in `derived_from` and describes one physical locomotive.
- **A model profile carries the shape.** It stores base values for every field in the field list, including:
  - `lighting_voltage`, `power_speed_curve`, and `calibrated_at`
  - both mapping curves
  - `max_voltage`
  - the motion rates
  - the drag fields
  - the two notch tables
- **An instance profile carries only what belongs to that one locomotive.** That is what was measured on it, or a curve the operator edited for it by hand (see **Editing a profile by hand**). Besides its identity fields (`profile_id`, `name`, `derived_from`), it may carry three calibration fields and no others:
  - `lighting_voltage`
  - `power_speed_curve`
  - `calibrated_at`
- **A field an instance leaves unset is read from its model profile.** That is what lets a correction to a model profile reach every locomotive of that model that has not measured the field for itself. `calibrated_at` is the one exception (see the next rule).
- **`calibrated_at` follows the curve.** An instance profile's resolved `calibrated_at` comes from the record its resolved `power_speed_curve` comes from:
  - when the instance carries its own `power_speed_curve`, then its resolved `calibrated_at` is the instance's own value, which is unset when no speed calibration commit has written the instance's curve;
  - otherwise it is the model profile's `calibrated_at`.

  The date then always belongs to the record the locomotive's curve comes from, so a curve the operator drew by hand never shows the model profile's measurement date.
- **An instance profile stores no `voltage_power_curve`.** Its resolved curve is the model profile's curve with its bottom anchor moved to the instance's resolved `lighting_voltage`, because that anchor is the 0%-power point by definition. Building it drops every model-profile point below the new anchor — each one names a voltage that does not move this locomotive — and resolves the `0%` anchor point itself to the instance's `lighting_voltage`.
- **`SpeedProfileRegistry.resolve(profile_id)` is the one accessor that applies the overlay.** It returns a complete profile with every field resolved: from the instance where the instance carries the field, from the model profile everywhere else, and `calibrated_at` from whichever record supplies `power_speed_curve` (see **`calibrated_at` follows the curve**). `TrainPhysics`, the ATO computer, the hardware readiness evaluator, and the UI all read a train's calibration through it, and no other site merges the two records.
- **A train and a roster entry both name an instance profile.** `Train.speed_profile_id` and `RosterEntry.speed_profile_id` name the instance and never the model profile, so a measured locomotive keeps its own numbers across placements (see **Train Roster**).
- Why this shape: the two things a calibration pass measures sit at different levels. A power/speed sweep mostly describes a model, and a lighting voltage describes one item's lamp, motor, and gearbox. A record at each level lets each pass write the level it measured, so the operator is never asked at commit time which level a number belongs to, and moving a measurement from one item up to its model stays a deliberate act (see **Speed calibration**, What commit writes).

**Editing a profile by hand** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

- **The operator may edit a profile by hand.** The Speed Profile panel lets the operator change a profile's fields directly. A hand edit is the second way a profile's `power_speed_curve` changes, beside a **Speed calibration** commit.
- **Three fields are never edited by hand.** The panel shows them read-only, and a save must not change them:
  - `lighting_voltage` — **Lighting-voltage calibration** moves it (see **Lighting-voltage calibration**, The lighting-voltage field is read-only);
  - `calibrated_at` — only a speed calibration commit writes it (see **Speed calibration**, What commit writes);
  - `derived_from` — whether a record is a model profile or an instance profile is not an edit.
- **The panel shows the resolved profile.** It reads a profile through `SpeedProfileRegistry.resolve(profile_id)`, so an instance profile shows the values its locomotive runs on, and the panel marks which of them the instance carries itself.
- **A save writes only the fields the operator changed.** `PUT /api/speed-profiles/<profile_id>` keeps the stored value of every field the request leaves out, and the panel sends only the fields the operator changed. On an instance profile a field the operator did not change stays unset, so it goes on reading from its model profile.
- **A curve keeps at least two points.** `PUT /api/speed-profiles/<profile_id>` refuses a `power_speed_curve` with fewer than two points, because the curve maps a power percent to a speed by interpolating between its points.
- **A hand-edited curve must stay invertible.** `PUT /api/speed-profiles/<profile_id>` also refuses a `power_speed_curve` whose points are not non-decreasing in `speed_kmh` as power rises. Physics reads the curve in both directions, so a hand edit meets the same condition a calibration commit does (see **Speed calibration**, The measured curve must stay invertible).
- **On an instance profile only `name` and `power_speed_curve` may be edited by hand.** `name` labels the record itself. Every other field the panel edits belongs to the model profile (see **Model profiles and instance profiles**). On an instance profile the panel shows those fields read-only and names the model profile where they are edited, and `PUT /api/speed-profiles/<profile_id>` refuses a request that changes one of them.
- **Editing an instance profile's curve gives that locomotive its own curve.** From then on a change to the model profile's curve does not reach it, the same as for a curve **Save to this locomotive** wrote (see **Speed calibration**, What commit writes). Its resolved `calibrated_at` is then its own: unset unless a **Save to this locomotive** commit wrote it earlier (see **`calibrated_at` follows the curve**).
- Why this shape: refusing model-profile fields on an instance profile keeps each of those values in one record, where every locomotive of the model reads it.

**SpeedProfile constraint**

- `SpeedProfile` is not a speed-limit object and holds no kind of speed ceiling. Train maximum speed and block maximum speed are separate constraints, each enforced on its own.

**Speed-profile addition**

- The calibration has two bidirectional mappings and both must be stated directly in the doc:
  1. `track_voltage <-> power_percent`
  2. `power_percent <-> speed_kmh`
- `voltage_power_curve` is the stored `(track_voltage, power_percent)` mapping used by the first step. Reversing from `power_percent` back to `track_voltage` uses the inverse interpolation of this same stored curve.
- `power_speed_curve` is the stored `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` mapping used by the second step. `power_percent` is the normalized control value between voltage and speed; it is not a second name for either of them. A speed calibration commit or a hand edit later replaces the curve (see **Speed calibration** and **Editing a profile by hand**); after that, the stored curve — not the `max_speed` its default was anchored to — is what the calibration rests on. It is always stored explicitly as profile calibration data, never inferred ad hoc elsewhere. Reverse lookup from `speed_kmh` to `power_percent` uses the inverse interpolation of this same stored curve.
- The motion-rate fields (`acceleration_rate`, `deceleration_rate`) govern ATO, manual `simulation` handle integration, service/emergency braking, and coasting. They do not shape manual `power_percent` response (that submode applies the calibrated speed immediately, see TrainPhysics).
- A model profile is a shared record; an instance profile is not. Several instance profiles may derive from one model profile. **Speed calibration**, **What commit writes**, is where an operator decides whether a measurement stays on the one item or becomes the model's.
- Every train must name an instance profile, so `power_percent` manual mode always has a defined voltage/power/speed mapping, even before per-locomotive tuning. `SimulationController.add_train(...)` guarantees one at creation time:
  - When placement imports a **Train Roster** entry that names an instance profile, the train uses that instance.
  - Otherwise, `add_train(...)` creates a model profile whose `power_speed_curve` `100%` point is anchored to the train's configured `max_speed`, plus an empty instance profile deriving from it, and the train names the instance.

  An unidentified train, which Observe's layout-wide detector snapshot creates instead (see **Power**, Unidentified trains), gets that same pair and never uses it.
## Speed calibration

Speed calibration measures one locomotive's real power/speed response and writes it as measured points in place of the seeded linear `power_speed_curve`. `SpeedCalibration` is the class that owns and runs this procedure, keyed per train; it holds that train's `CalibrationRun`. The **SpeedProfile** section is the canonical home for the two stored curves (`voltage_power_curve`, `power_speed_curve`) and for the model-profile / instance-profile split; this section is the canonical home for the procedure that fills the second curve, and for **What commit writes**, which record receives the result. A hand edit is the other way the curve changes (see **SpeedProfile**, Editing a profile by hand).

- **A pass commands a power percent and measures the speed that comes back.** It must work this way round: the pass must not ask for a target speed, because `power_speed_curve`, the curve that turns a wanted speed into a control value, is the very curve the pass is building. Each step commands one `power_percent`. `TrainPhysics` drives the rails at the `track_voltage` that percent maps to through `voltage_power_curve`, and the pass reads the resulting `speed_kmh` back from measured motion.
- **The sweep runs in `CALIBRATION_POWER_STEP_PERCENT` increments up to `100%`.** At the `constants.py` value of `10`, that is ten measured steps, `10%` through `100%`. The `0%` point needs no measurement: `0%` power is `lighting_voltage` (per **SpeedProfile**), so `(0%, 0 km/h)` is the curve's origin by definition, and the pass writes it as such. That makes **Lighting-voltage calibration** the pass to run first: every step of this sweep is a percentage of a range whose bottom that one sets.
- **A pass measures the second stage only.** Each step yields one `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` point, and the finished set of points is the new `power_speed_curve`. `voltage_power_curve` is not measured and a pass must not write it. A timed run cannot see that curve: `power_percent` is the app's own normalized control value, not a physical quantity, so a step can only command the voltage the curve already assigns to its percent, and reading that voltage back would restate the curve rather than test it.
- **`CalibrationRun` is the transient working record of one pass**. It holds:
  - the ordered power steps
  - the samples gathered so far
  - the train under calibration
  - `active_leg_route_id: Optional[str]`, which names the calibration-created one-off route for the current leg or is `None` between legs
  - `crossing_started_at: Optional[float]`, the time the current crossing's clock started (the moment B was confirmed occupied for this leg), or `None` before it starts
  - `crossing_finished_at: Optional[float]`, the time the current crossing's clock stopped (the moment the far outer block was confirmed occupied after B), or `None` until then
  - `overrun_seen: bool`, set when a block past the far outer block was confirmed and credited to the calibration train on this leg, whether the train was still crossing or already stopping

  `SpeedCalibration` writes the last three inside Observe, when it reads the calibration train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks`, and Plan step `c9e1` reads them through `SpeedCalibration.plan_tick(...)`. They are `SpeedCalibration`'s own record, carried from Observe to Plan in the same tick, not a controller latch; each new leg resets all three. A leg that is not armed yet records no crossing, because it arms in Plan after Observe has run.

  Like all runtime movement state it is in-memory only (per **Out of Scope**); only its committed result persists, through ordinary `SpeedProfile` persistence.

**Auto profiling**

Auto profiling times the locomotive across one block of known length using the block detectors the layout already has, runs it back and forth across that block, and repeats that over the power sweep. It is the canonical home of the timed run and of the **Calibration leg** every crossing runs as.

- **The operator names the measured block.** A pass is set up by naming one block — the measured block, B — and `B.length_cm` must be greater than zero, because the measurement rests on that one length. The pass finds B's two neighbours, A and C, itself: it walks the track out of each end of B through the points as they are actually aligned, the same forward tile walk `TrainPhysics` uses to resolve a train's next reserved block (see **Power**, Only the next reserved block is pre-energized). The operator names one block rather than three because A and C are not a choice: they are whatever the points are set to.
- **The clock is two confirmed entries.** The train starts standing in A. The clock starts the moment B is confirmed occupied and stops the moment C is confirmed occupied, so it times the head crossing B end to end. `B.length_cm` over that elapsed time, converted through the same model-scale helper physics integrates distance with (see **Units contract**), is that crossing's measured `speed_kmh`. The pass watches only the confirmed entries attribution has credited to the calibration train (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), so another train moving elsewhere on the layout cannot start or stop its clock. `SpeedCalibration` checks the calibration train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` inside Observe, immediately after that tick's attribution has written it and before the per-train loop begins, so it sees a confirmation the same tick Observe credits it and before the train's own final Observe callback folds and clears the slice. It only reads the slice (per **A read is not a handoff**).
- **Why the middle block and not the first.** Timing from the moment power was applied to the moment B confirms would measure an unknown distance: the model never knows where inside a block a train sits (see **Power**, The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector), so the pass does not know how far the locomotive stood from A's far seam. Timing between two entry confirmations measures exactly one block, whatever the start position was. The two stamps are also the same kind of event — a confirmed OCCUPIED transition — so the detector's fixed lag, the one-tick read lag plus the `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` debounce reads, lands on both and cancels in the difference (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). A one-sided interval would carry that lag as a bias in every sample.
- **The pass turns the train around at each end.** When the far outer block confirms occupied, the pass commands `power_percent = 0`, waits for the train to satisfy the stopped predicate (see **Units**, `TrainController.is_stopped()`), and assigns the next **Calibration leg** — a one-off route back to the other outer block. That new reservation points the other way, so the derived head flips and the span re-frames (per **Reservation-side head derivation**), and the pass commands the same power step again to drive the loco back. The reversal is an ordinary new reservation the other way, not a cab command; calibration adds no reversal mechanism of its own. Driving the stretch back and forth is what lets a plain length of track measure a locomotive: a run that only ever went one way would need a loop the train can take.
- **Both directions are measured, and a step's sample is their mean.** A step runs `CALIBRATION_ROUND_TRIPS` round trips, so it collects twice that many crossings of B, half in each direction, and their mean is the step's sample. Two things make the mean the right number. A stretch is rarely dead level, and a grade makes the uphill direction measure slow by very nearly the amount it makes the downhill direction measure fast, so equal counts each way cancel it. And `power_speed_curve` carries no sign — `track_voltage` is a magnitude and neither stored curve is per-direction (see **TrainPhysics**) — so the single number the curve stores has to describe the locomotive driven either way.
- **The outer blocks are the run-up and the stopping room.** Each leg starts from a stand in an outer block, so that block is all the room the locomotive has to reach the speed the step commands, and the block at the far end is all the room it has to stop in. When the outer blocks are too short for the locomotive to finish accelerating in, the pass times a still-accelerating train across B and the curve reads low at its top steps. That is a property of the stretch rather than of the locomotive, so the panel names both outer blocks it resolved before the pass starts (see **The panel**).
- **A calibration leg holds no reservation-end standoff.** The leg's one-off route sets `zero_reservation_end_standoff = True` on its `Path` (see **Path field schema**), so `TrainController` lookahead brakes the locomotive to the far seam of the far outer block instead of counting back by the terminus-type margin from **Safety margin globals**. The whole length of each outer block is then usable: all of the run-up in A, all of the stopping room in C. The standoff is not needed here, because the rail past the far outer block is the leg's own dead reservation end (see **The stretch is energized by the ordinary power rules**) and the pass is a supervised, bounded, low-speed measurement. It removes no other protection: the ATC limit still brakes the locomotive to a stand by that far seam, and a block past the far outer block confirming still fails the pass (see **A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass**).
- **A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass.** When a block past the far outer block confirms occupied and attribution credits it to the calibration train, the locomotive needed more stopping room than the stretch has. An overrun is a speed-only measurement fault. In Plan step `c9e1`, `SpeedCalibration.plan_tick(...)` advances the leg; when it finds `overrun_seen` set, `SpeedCalibration` ends the pass through `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)`. That includes a block the detector confirms only after the train has stopped, because the record stands until the next leg arms. `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)`:
  - withholds the drive (`power_percent = 0`)
  - deactivates the leg route through `set_route_deactivate(...)` (the same helper `abandon(...)` uses)
  - sends the reason out on the command-result stream
  - drops the run

  The far outer block is the leg's reservation end, so the rail past it is dead and the overrun is bounded to the one block a locomotive can coast into. Coasting into it at all means the stretch is too short for this locomotive, so the pass reports it rather than measuring on. Attribution reports that block as an `overrun_entry` for the train, or as an `entry` when the block confirms only after the leg's path has completed; either way it raises no emergency cut-out for it, `overrun_seen` reads the entered slice whichever result it was, and the pass ending is the stop (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection, An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out).
- **A step that does not move the train records `0 km/h`.** A step whose B confirmation does not arrive within `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S` records `0 km/h`, and the pass moves to the next step. The train never left the outer block it stood in, so the pass does not turn it around: the next step commands from where it stands, facing the way it already faces. The flat bottom this leaves on the curve is that locomotive's real stall band, where the power does not overcome its stiction, and physics reading `0 km/h` back for those commands is reading what the locomotive actually does.
- **A leg that starts crossing and never arrives fails the pass.** When B has confirmed but the far outer block has not within `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S`, the locomotive stopped somewhere inside the stretch. Like an overrun, this is a speed-only measurement fault that ends the pass in Plan step `c9e1` through `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)`. It is not recorded as a slow step, because a part-crossing is no measurement at all, and timing one would put a speed on the curve the locomotive never held.
- **A sweep in which no step moved the train fails the pass.** When every step measured `0 km/h`, `SpeedCalibration` reports the stretch rather than offering the result to commit. An all-zero curve is not the curve of a locomotive that cannot move; it is a stretch the pass could not measure on, most often one too short for the consist to clear the measured block between crossings. Storing it would say the locomotive stands still at full power.
- **The train must be standing in one of the two outer blocks.** Opening checks it (per **Opening a run takes control of the train**), and it also says which way the opening leg runs: toward the outer block the head is not in. Every later leg re-reads the head's block the same way when it arms, so a leg never asks for reservation to the block the locomotive is already standing in.
- **Calibration leg.** A leg is one crossing of the stretch, driven under a route-backed reservation — its own `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route. A leg arms only when all three hold:
  - `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id is None`
  - `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is None`
  - no `RUNNING` calibration `RouteRun` remains

  At Plan step `c9e1`, `SpeedCalibration` prepares a `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route with one `stop` task at the far outer block, `manual_override = False`. `RouteExecutor` creates and assigns it, stores the leg's id in `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id`, and passes `zero_reservation_end_standoff=True` into the ordinary `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` call at step `66aa`, which sets that flag on the leg's `Path` (see **A calibration leg holds no reservation-end standoff**). `SpeedCalibration` does not call `PathDispatcher` or mutate route registries itself.
- **Plan acquires the leg under the ordinary braking-distance lock.** In that same Plan pass, the ordinary steps allocate the matching `RouteRun` and perform the ordinary `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` call. Until `controller.received_path_plan` is present, `TrainController.tick(...)` selects zero calibration power and the step timeout does not run. If acquisition is blocked, Plan retries normally, so a busy stretch delays the pass rather than failing the step. The leg's reservation then grows a braking distance ahead as the train rolls; on a long enough stretch it reaches the far outer block before the train brakes for its own reservation end, so the measured span runs at the step's commanded speed. When the stretch is too short for the step's speed even with no reservation-end standoff, or a foreign conflict caps the leg short, the ATC limit lowers the calibration drive across B and that crossing is discarded and re-measured, per **A capped crossing is discarded**.
- **A leg finishes through ordinary stop completion.** When the far outer block is confirmed and the train stops at the terminal, Plan settlement step `9d8b` completes the path and its callback finishes the one-stop `RouteRun`. Plan then performs the ordinary one-off terminal teardown and unassigns that route. On the next Plan step `c9e1`, the absence of an assigned active route or live run clears `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id` and prepares the next leg, which runs back the other way (per **The pass turns the train around at each end**). A stalled step is different: its leg route never reached the far outer block, so the pass tears that route down and re-arms a fresh leg from where the train stands (per **A step that does not move the train records `0 km/h`**), rather than holding a spent reservation.
- **An existing teardown is not duplicated.** If `pending_route_deactivate` is already set, the pass writes no second deactivation. If another writer already set `pending_path_cancel_request`, `set_route_deactivate(...)` follows the ordinary most-recent-payload rule while adding the route teardown request. The pass abandons its samples either way.
- **A route assignment is refused while the pass is open.** `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(...)` refuses any request for a train that reads `CALIBRATING` (per **Route assignment writers**). Only Plan step `c9e1` assigns a route to a calibrating train, and only the pass's own leg route.
- **The stretch is energized by the ordinary power rules.** Auto profiling adds no power rule and takes no exception from one. The leg's path reserves the stretch ahead of the train, so the block the train stands on carries `track voltage` under its span and the next reserved block carries it as the one block pre-energized ahead (see **Power**, Block power-controller role, and **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized**). A, B and C go live in turn, in whichever order the leg's direction takes them. That rule is also the protection this pass needs: the profile does not yet describe this locomotive, so nothing further ahead than the block it is entering may be live, and the rail past the far outer block — the leg's reservation end — is dead.
- **A capped crossing is discarded.** A crossing during which the **Propulsion cap step** lowered the calibration drive on any tick is discarded as a sample, because the speed the pass would time is not the speed the step commanded. The cap step itself ends nothing (per **Calibration drive is capped in propulsion; a calibration run is ended in teardown**). The pass's own `power_percent = 0` after the far outer block confirms is the driving source's command, not a ceiling, so it discards nothing: the measurement ended on that confirmation before the stop command applied. A discarded crossing is re-measured on the next crossing of the same step, and the pass counts the current step's consecutive discarded crossings. When that count reaches `CALIBRATION_CAP_RETRY_LIMIT`, the stretch is too short to measure this step at its power, so `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)` ends the pass in Plan step `c9e1` and reports it, the same measurement-fault path as an overrun (see **A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass**). A measured crossing resets the count, and one discarded crossing under the limit never fails the pass.
- **A step that measures slower than a lower-power step is measured once more.** `power_speed_curve` must stay invertible, so the samples have to rise with power (see **What commit writes**, The measured curve must stay invertible). One re-measure tells a noisy crossing apart from a locomotive that really does run slower at more power; when the re-measure is slow too, the pass fails and reports it rather than carrying a sample the commit will refuse.

- **The constants are in `constants.py`.** They are `CALIBRATION_POWER_STEP_PERCENT`, `CALIBRATION_ROUND_TRIPS`, `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S`, and `CALIBRATION_CAP_RETRY_LIMIT`.
- **Every calibration interval is measured against `AppState.operating_time`** (see **Units**, Clocks). `operating_time` carries the playback multiplier, so a Simulation pass at four times playback measures the model's own km/h rather than four times it. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, where `simulation_speed` is `1.0`, it advances at wall rate and the pass is a real-world measurement.

**The panel**

- **The calibration group names the locomotive before either pass opens.** The Speed Profile panel's calibration group carries a locomotive row, and both this pass and **Lighting-voltage calibration** drive the train it names; neither pass picks a train for itself. The row holds two things:
  - a train picker listing every placed train whose resolved profile is the profile on screen — every train naming an instance profile that derives from it, and every train naming it directly — showing each train's car number and state
  - a readiness line naming every opening condition the named train does not yet meet (per **Where it runs**, Opening a run takes control of the train)
- **The calibration group lists the runs in the order they are done.** The lighting-voltage row comes first and the Calibrate speed control after it (per **The sweep runs in `CALIBRATION_POWER_STEP_PERCENT` increments up to `100%`**). The order is guidance: opening a speed pass does not require a calibrated lighting voltage.
- **The operator does not choose a direction.** A speed leg takes its direction from the leg route (per **Reservation-side head derivation**), and a lighting run, which has no reservation, has its candidate signed by the train's span (per **Power**, A train with no live reservation is signed by its span).
- **The Calibrate speed control opens this pass.** It sits in the same calibration group, beside the lighting-voltage row that **Lighting-voltage calibration**, The panel, is the canonical home for.
- **Before the pass starts the panel holds three things**: the measured block, which the operator names; the two outer blocks the pass resolved out of that block's ends; and Start.
- **While the pass runs the panel holds three things**: which step is being measured and how many of its crossings are done, the points measured so far drawn against the profile's stored curve, and Stop. Stop ends the pass through `SpeedCalibration.abandon(train_id, reason)` (per **What ends a calibration run**, How a run is ended) and writes nothing to either profile record.
- **When every step is measured the panel holds the result and the two commit controls**: the measured curve drawn against the stored one, **Save to this locomotive**, and **Promote to model**. **What commit writes** states what each control does.
- **Nothing is written until the operator picks one of the two.** Closing the panel without picking discards the pass; a mid-run panel close ends the pass exactly like Stop, through `SpeedCalibration.abandon(train_id, reason)`. A measured curve says what one locomotive did on one stretch, and whether that is the model's curve or only this item's is a judgement about a physical locomotive that the operator is the one able to make.

**What commit writes**

- **Commit writes two fields and no others**: `power_speed_curve` from the pass's samples, and `calibrated_at` from the wall clock. It must not write `voltage_power_curve` — **Lighting-voltage calibration** is the one procedure that moves that curve's anchor — and it must not write a motion rate or a notch table, which describe how the model behaves rather than how fast the measured locomotive ran. `model` is edited on the model profile in the panel like any other model-profile field, so a commit never writes it.
- **Save to this locomotive** writes those two fields onto the instance profile the calibrated train names. That train runs on the measured curve from that moment and no other locomotive changes. It is the control for a locomotive that does not run like the rest of its model, and for keeping a working model curve while measuring one item beside it.
- **Promote to model** writes those two fields onto the model profile the calibrated train's instance derives from, and clears both fields from that instance in the same commit. Every locomotive whose instance leaves them unset runs on the new curve from that moment, the calibrated one included, because clearing them is what puts it back to following its model.
- **Commit is all or nothing.** A pass that has not measured every step writes nothing, whichever target the operator picks. A partly replaced curve would be part measured and part seeded, with nothing on the profile to say which part is which.
- **The measured curve must stay invertible.** Physics reads `power_speed_curve` in both directions, and the reverse lookup from `speed_kmh` to `power_percent` is an inverse interpolation that needs speed to rise with power (see **SpeedProfile**). On commit the assembled samples must be non-decreasing in `speed_kmh`, and a commit that finds them otherwise fails and reports it.

**Where it runs**

- **Opening a run takes control of the train** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name). A speed pass opens through `SpeedCalibration.start(train_id, measured_block_id)`, from the panel's Start, and a lighting run through `SpeedCalibration.start_lighting(train_id)`, from the lighting-voltage row's Calibrate. Opening runs between ticks, like an operator command (see **Operator-command processing slot**). It is accepted only when **all of these hold**:
  - the session is running — the session state is Live (per **Session state**);
  - the train is placed, and for a speed pass it stands in one of the measured block's two outer blocks;
  - the train is stopped and holds no live reservation;
  - the train is not ghosted — `presence_unknown == False` (a ghosted train refuses operator commands, per **Operator-command processing slot**);
  - `eb.active == False`, and no power-off is pending — `phase_latches.power_off == False`;
  - the train has no assigned route — `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id) is None`;
  - no calibration run of either kind is already open for it, and no finished speed pass is waiting for the operator to commit or discard it (per **What ends a calibration run**, A finished pass is a held result, not an open run).

  Otherwise it returns `success=False` and changes nothing; the panel's readiness line names every unmet condition. On acceptance it calls these two operator commands in this order, and then opens the run:
  1. when the train is `OFF`, `TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()`;
  2. `TrainController.commands.set_mode("manual")` (per **Set mode**).

  Both commands are accepted, because the conditions above already cover their gates: `power_on_cmd()` runs only for an `OFF` train, and `set_mode(...)` needs a stopped train and refuses only while a calibration run is open, which it is not until both calls have returned. Each command emits its own command-result event, and the two commands stay the only writers of `powered` and `control_mode` (per **Controller retained field schema** and **Driving mode**). The train then reads `train_status == CALIBRATING` until the run ends (see **Controller state machine**). Opening adds no effect beyond the run itself.
- **Opening takes the train from no other procedure.** An assigned route, an open run of the other kind, a latched EB, and a pending power-off each mean another procedure owns the train. The readiness line reports them, and resolving them is a decision the operator makes rather than a side effect of pressing Calibrate.
- **Where it runs.** Plan step `c9e1` advances the speed-calibration sequence, evaluates step progress against `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S`, and prepares the next leg route or requested reversal. During Action, `TrainController.tick(...)` calls `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` after its emergency-request step `01f2`; the value it returns is the selected driving source for that tick and enters the **Propulsion cap step** (canonical home: **TrainController**) like any other driving source. The return type is `Optional[CalibrationPropulsionOverride]`, where the closed union is `{kind: "power_percent", value: float}` for speed calibration or `{kind: "track_voltage", value: float}` for lighting calibration; the helper returns `None` when no leg or run is open for the train, including once a pass has measured every step. While it returns a value, the train reads `train_status == CALIBRATING` (see **Controller state machine**). Calibration never enters `SimulationController._act_train(...)` as a special pre-controller call and never issues pretend operator commands.
- **`SpeedCalibration.run_still_valid(train_id)`** is the one validity predicate for both run kinds — an open speed pass and an open **Lighting-voltage calibration** run. Action step `26f5` (`SimulationController._reevaluate_calibration_run(train)`) evaluates it once per tick from live state, during the Action teardown (`_commit_train_act`), after `TrainController.tick(...)` has selected propulsion and `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` has written this tick's voltage. It is true when all of these hold:
  - the train's controller is still present — a run whose train has lost its `TrainController` (the runtime torn down) is ended
  - the train is powered — `powered` (`train_status != "OFF"`)
  - `eb.active == False`
  - no power-off is pending — `phase_latches.power_off == False`

  A measurement fault is not one of these conditions. Those faults end the pass in Plan step `c9e1` through `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)`, or at commit-offer time for an all-zero sweep (per **What ends a calibration run**, The measurement fails), so `26f5` never evaluates this predicate for a failed run.

  When it is false, `26f5` ends the run on that same tick: through `SpeedCalibration.abandon(train_id, reason)` for a speed pass and `SpeedCalibration.cancel_lighting(train_id)` for a lighting run, and the train's `track_voltage` returns to what its ordinary state outputs on the following tick (per **What ends a calibration run**, How a run is ended). Leaving Live does not route through `26f5`: `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` ends every open run directly (per **What ends a calibration run**). An ordinary power-off drives the controller to `OFF` inside the same Action cleanup: `TrainController.complete_power_off()` runs at step `886a`, and `26f5` runs later in that same Action pass, so `26f5` finds this predicate false and ends the run on that same tick. `OutputSafety` never calls into calibration; the wrapper, the watchdog trip-record consumption, and the structural operations listed in **What ends a calibration run** end the runs. It is a `SimulationController`-level step because the run registry lives at that level.
- **The pass drives the train through ordinary surfaces, not new ones.** It drives the train the way an operator in manual mode drives one, through surfaces that already exist.
  - **Leg reservation uses the ordinary route path** (per **Calibration leg**). `SpeedCalibration` never creates, extends, completes, or cancels a path directly.
  - **Controller owns calibration output.** Speed and lighting calibration share the `CalibrationPropulsionOverride` mechanism; there is no speed-only control bypass. `TrainController.tick(...)` selects the returned value as the driving source during its ordinary Action decision, does not copy it into `manual.manual_power_percent` or `handle_position`, and issues no operator command; the ordinary manual-notch, manual-power, or ATO request is not selected while a leg or run is open. The speed pass's `power_percent` variant feeds the speed solution and is lowered by every active ceiling. The lighting pass's `track_voltage` variant is a magnitude-only holding voltage (handle `N`, no motion) that feeds no speed; under a zero ceiling — EB or pending power-off — it is withheld and the ordinary capped output is emitted, because the candidate is a test voltage rather than the stopped-but-lit output.
- **Every calibration path has a matching `RouteRun`** (per **Runtime reservation is route-backed**).
- **Leg completion and abandonment use ordinary route flows.** A successful leg uses terminal stop completion. Abandonment calls `set_route_deactivate(...)`; the Action consumer cancels any live path and removes the `RouteRun` through the standard teardown order, and the emptied one-off leg route is then deleted (per **`RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`**, An emptied one-off route is deleted).
- Calibration adds no persisted state of its own. It must not open a new event sink; progress and the final result are reported as ordinary command-result events on the one stream owned by `NotificationCenter` (see **Core Runtime Loop**, Runtime notifications).
- In Simulation the measured speed comes from the happy-path train model, so a calibration pass reproduces the model's own curve. In Virtual Hardware it comes from the controllable fake device, which lets the procedure and its fault handling be exercised against a complete Hardware Setup. In Real Hardware it comes from the physical locomotive's true response. The procedure is identical in all three environments; only the source of the measured response differs.

**What ends a calibration run** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

This is the one list of what ends an open run of either kind. Every other site that ends a run points here.

- **The operator ends it.** For a speed pass: Stop, or closing the panel. For a lighting run: Save, Revert, or closing the panel. For either kind: leaving the profile, or naming a different train in the locomotive row. Every operator ending other than a lighting Save discards the run.
- **The train fails the validity check.** **`SpeedCalibration.run_still_valid(train_id)`** is false at Action step `26f5` when EB is latched, a power-off is pending or completed, or the train's controller is gone (per **Where it runs**).
- **The measurement fails** (speed pass only). An overrun, a crossing that never arrives, `CALIBRATION_CAP_RETRY_LIMIT` capped crossings in a row, or a second slow re-measure ends the pass through `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)` in Plan step `c9e1`, and a sweep in which no step moved the train fails when it would be offered for commit (per **Auto profiling**).
- **The session leaves Live, or its outputs drop.** `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` ends every open run, so Pause, the layout emergency cut-out, entering Setup, `/api/server/restart` and shutdown, and entering either fatal halt each end them. When `SimulationController.update(...)` consumes a loss-of-control watchdog trip record, it ends them too. Before `/api/network/clear` or `load_layout` replaces the trains, it ends every open run and discards every held result. The bracketed pause around `save_layout` ends none: it holds `AppState.simulation_lock` and restores the running state before any tick or other request runs. Environment activation, Reset, and `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()` run only while the session is stopped, so they never find a run open. Deleting a train never finds one either: it accepts only an `OFF` train, and the power-off that left the train `OFF` already ended its run.
- **How a run is ended.** A speed pass ends through `SpeedCalibration.abandon(train_id, reason)`, or through `SpeedCalibration.fail(...)` for a measurement fault. Either commands `power_percent = 0` and deactivates the leg route through `set_route_deactivate(...)`, a latch that waits for the next running Action pass. Either also reports the reason on the command-result stream. A train whose pass ends mid-leg while the session runs brakes to a stand inside its leg reservation; when the session leaves Live or the outputs drop, the rails are already at `0` V (per **Running and stopped**, Leaving Live enters the safe state). A lighting run ends through `SpeedCalibration.cancel_lighting(train_id)`, and the train's `track_voltage` returns to what its ordinary state outputs on the following tick.
- **After the run ends.** The train reads its stored `control_mode` again. Opening set it to `manual`, so the train reads `MANUAL` once it is powered and clear of EB.
- **A finished pass is a held result, not an open run.** Once a pass has measured every step, `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` returns `None`, the train reads `MANUAL`, and **`SpeedCalibration.run_still_valid(train_id)`** is not evaluated for it. The pass issues no further command and accepts no further sample. The panel holds the result until the operator commits it with **Save to this locomotive** or **Promote to model**, or discards it by closing the panel, leaving the profile, or naming a different train. `/api/network/clear`, `load_layout`, and deleting the train (per **Train Entity**, Deleting a train) discard it too, because each removes the train it was measured on. No other ending in this list reaches it. While it waits, no new run opens on that train (per **Opening a run takes control of the train**).

A run is opened only while the session is running (per **Opening a run takes control of the train**), and every way the session leaves Live ends it, so no run is open while the session is stopped and no interval spans a time the session was stopped. Leaving Live cuts the rails mid-crossing, or freezes time mid-crossing in Simulation, so a timing that spans it could not be trusted.
## Lighting-voltage calibration

Lighting-voltage calibration finds the one voltage at which a locomotive is lit and still holds, and writes it to `lighting_voltage` on that locomotive's instance profile (**SpeedProfile** defines that field, which record carries it, and what else reads it). It is the first calibration a newly added locomotive gets: `SimulationController.add_train(...)` seeds a placeholder value, and a **Speed calibration** sweep takes its bottom step from `lighting_voltage`. `SpeedCalibration` owns this pass as it owns the speed pass, keyed per train.

**The operator's eye is the measurement**

- This pass commands a voltage and asks the operator whether the locomotive moved, because nothing on the rig can answer that question at this level. A current channel reads whether a locomotive is drawing on the block, not whether it moved. First movement is a creep of a few millimetres, far below what timing a head across two block seams can resolve. The operator's judgement is the sample this pass collects, and there is no measured value to write down.

**The panel**

- **The pass drives the locomotive the calibration group names.** The train comes from the locomotive row both calibrations share (per **Speed calibration**, The panel), and Calibrate takes control of it (per **Speed calibration**, Where it runs, Opening a run takes control of the train).
- **The lighting-voltage row is the panel.** The profile's lighting-voltage field sits in the same calibration group, and the Calibrate control beside it opens the run in place on that row. The row then holds:
  - the candidate voltage as it stands
  - a step-up control
  - a step-down control
  - Save
  - Revert

  The voltage/power curve stays on screen with its bottom anchor following the candidate, so the operator sees what Save will write before writing it.
- **The lighting-voltage field is read-only.** **Lighting-voltage calibration** is the one procedure that moves a profile's stored `lighting_voltage` in the ordinary case (see **Power**, Occupancy source follows drive state); seeded and imported values arrive with the profile itself. So the field displays the resolved value, and the step controls are the one way to move it.
- A step changes the candidate by `LIGHTING_VOLTAGE_STEP_V`, a `constants.py` value, and puts the new value on the rails at once.
- The value to save is the highest step at which the locomotive still held still: the operator steps up until it creeps, steps back down one, and saves.
- The step-up control stops at the ceiling in **What a candidate may be**, so the panel cannot show a value Save would refuse; the step-down control stops at `0`.
- **Save and discard are the two operator-driven endings.** Save commits the candidate and ends the run. Discarding also ends the run, and happens on any of these:
  - Revert
  - leaving the profile or closing the panel
  - naming a different train in the locomotive row

  Either way that train's `track_voltage` returns to what its state ordinarily outputs. **What ends a calibration run** lists every ending.

**What the run drives**

- **Opening preconditions.** A lighting run opens under **Opening a run takes control of the train** (under **Speed calibration**, Where it runs).

  Only one calibration run of either kind may be open for a train at a time. A lighting run holds no reservation, so ordinary per-block emission signs the candidate by the train's span (see **Power**, A train with no live reservation is signed by its span); no cab is needed, and the operator does not choose a direction. The `stopped` condition and the one-run-at-a-time condition are opening preconditions only: neither is re-checked while a run is open, so a run survives the train creeping under the candidate voltage.
- **A run ends as the shared list says** (see **What ends a calibration run**).
