When **`SpeedCalibration.run_still_valid(train_id)`** is false at Action step `26f5`, the step calls `SpeedCalibration.cancel_lighting(train_id)` on that same tick and the candidate is dropped. Save, Revert, and the other operator endings end a run without waiting for that step. The one voltage already written on the ending tick moves nothing (per **Calibration drive is capped in propulsion; a calibration run is ended in teardown**).
- **The candidate is the driving source while the run is open.** While the run is open, `TrainController.tick(...)` selects the run's exact candidate voltage magnitude as the driving source; the ordinary manual-notch, manual-power, or ATO traction request is not selected, and the candidate is not copied into an operator-command field. The candidate goes through the **Propulsion cap step**. Under a zero ceiling — EB or pending power-off — it is withheld before voltage application and the ordinary capped output is emitted, because the candidate is a test voltage rather than the stopped-but-lit output; the run itself ends at step `26f5` when the predicate above fails. Otherwise `TrainPhysics` treats the candidate `track_voltage` as the authoritative magnitude for that tick. It reaches that train's ordinary energized set, and ordinary per-block emission applies the block-relative sign separately to every block (see **Power**, Block power-controller role and A block voltage carries a direction). A train that may open a run is stopped with nothing reserved ahead of it, so that set is the rail under the locomotive. The candidate does not feed the speed solution, so it never moves the modelled train by itself.

**What a candidate may be**

- A candidate is at least `0`. It stays below both the profile's `max_voltage` and, in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, the Hardware Setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v` (see **Hardware setup**, Occupancy source follows drive state). This pass applies that second bound at candidate time because it is the one thing that moves `lighting_voltage` in the ordinary case.
- In Simulation the `current_sense_min_drive_v` bound is not evaluated, because Simulation never reads Hardware Setup (see **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup**). A candidate saved there is bounded only by `max_voltage`. The shared readiness evaluator under **Occupancy source follows drive state** keeps the bound against every other write path. It re-checks the stored value against `current_sense_min_drive_v` at hardware activation, so a candidate saved in Simulation that would fail the hardware bound is caught then rather than at save time.

**What Save writes**

- Committing always writes the candidate to `lighting_voltage` on the instance profile the train names; there is no promote-to-model choice. A lamp, a motor, and a gearbox differ between two items of one model, so this value describes the locomotive in front of the operator rather than the model it belongs to. No other train changes, and the model profile is untouched.
- `lighting_voltage` is also the 0%-power point of `voltage_power_curve`, so committing moves the bottom anchor of the curve this train resolves. An instance profile stores no `voltage_power_curve` of its own, so the move is in the resolved curve alone (per **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles, which defines how that resolved curve is built).

**Where it lives**

- `LightingCalibrationRun` is the transient working record of one run: the train, the instance profile the candidate will be written to, and the candidate voltage. Like `CalibrationRun` it is in-memory only; only the committed profile value persists. `SpeedCalibration` exposes the lighting start/step/commit/cancel methods and the shared read-only `get_propulsion_override(train_id)` accessor. `TrainController.tick(...)` reads that accessor as its driving source, and neither it nor `TrainPhysics` reaches into the run registry.
- The run adds no persisted state beyond that one profile field and opens no new event sink. It reports as ordinary command-result events on the one stream owned by `NotificationCenter` (see **Core Runtime Loop**, Runtime notifications).
- Real Hardware is where a run tells the operator something new: the candidate is a raw voltage substitution on the real rail, and the operator watches the real locomotive to see whether it creeps. The candidate never feeds `TrainPhysics`'s speed solution, so the modelled train's own crawl point stays at the profile's stored anchor. In Simulation and Virtual Hardware, where the model is the only thing to watch, a run is therefore a readback of the value already stored. The procedure — opening, stepping, Save — is the same in all three environments.

## Train Roster

The `TrainRoster` is the catalog of locomotives the operator owns. It is persisted layout data, not runtime state: it is edited with the layout and saved and restored in the layout snapshot. Each `RosterEntry` records one owned locomotive and the defaults used to put it on the track.

- `RosterEntry` fields:
  - `entry_id`: unique identifier for the roster record.
  - `name`: display name for the locomotive.
  - `model`: free-text description of the physical item — its manufacturer, product, and box, as written on the packaging. A measured profile is found by matching it against `SpeedProfile.model` (see **Profiles are matched by model**).
  - `purchase_date`: the date the locomotive was acquired.
  - `purchase_price`: the acquisition cost.
  - `consist_length_cm`: the physical length used to build the train's span when this entry is placed (see **Train Entity**).
  - `max_speed`: the locomotive's top speed.
  - `min_radius_cm`: the locomotive's minimum curve radius — the train-side value the pathfinder's curve filter reads (see **Train Entity**).
  - `max_slope`: the locomotive's maximum climbable grade as a percent, `0.0` meaning unspecified (see **Train Entity**).
  - `speed_profile_id`: the instance profile this locomotive runs on (see **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles). **Speed calibration** and **Lighting-voltage calibration** both write that instance, so a measured curve and a measured lighting voltage stay with the locomotive across placements. Several entries naming one model each carry their own instance and derive them from one model profile (see **Profiles are matched by model**).
- **Profiles are matched by model.** When a `RosterEntry` is created, or its `model` is edited, and it names no `speed_profile_id`, the roster looks for the model profile whose `model` equals the entry's, comparing the two strings exactly, then does one of the following:
  - When exactly one model profile matches, it creates an empty instance profile deriving from it for the entry to name.
  - When more than one model profile matches, the instance derives from the one with the most recent `calibrated_at`; a model profile with none set loses to any model profile that has one.
  - When no model profile matches, the entry keeps no profile link, and placement seeds the model profile and the instance under it that **SpeedProfile** describes.

  The match is made once, when the entry's model is written, and the stored `speed_profile_id` is the link every later read follows: a placement resolves a profile by id, never by string, so renaming a model afterwards moves nothing that is already linked.
- Placing a train may import a `RosterEntry`. When the placement input names one, `SimulationController.add_train(...)` (the placement home in **Train Entity**) seeds the new `Train`'s persistent fields and its instance-profile link from that entry rather than from blank defaults. A roster entry is a template for placement: the placed `Train` is a separate runtime instance, and editing one after placement does not change the other. The one record they share on purpose is the instance profile, that locomotive's own calibration, which both the entry and the placed train name.
- The roster carries the locomotive's identity, purchase record, placement defaults, and profile link only. Cumulative usage stays on the live `Train` and its block and switch counters per **Maintenance counters**; the roster stores no second usage total.

## Power

**Hardware interface boundary**

- The runtime drives and reads the physical-world boundary only through abstract interfaces addressed by logical id (`block_id`, `switch_id`), never by pin or wire. There are three:
  - `TrackOutput` for block track voltage
  - `SwitchOutput` for switch throw
  - `OccupancyInput` for detector reads
- Simulation constructs its three happy-path model implementations directly and does not read Hardware Setup. Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware construct the same setup-aware HAL implementations as one complete set; their only device difference is in-memory versus physical. A missing role or interface fails the Virtual/Real build — `None` never asks the runtime to install a simulated fallback.
- `BlockPowerController` holds `TrackOutput` and `SwitchPowerController` holds `SwitchOutput`. During operation they are the only callers of the two output interfaces, and they hold no wiring knowledge themselves. This includes the per-channel zero and de-energize writes of the safe state (see **Safe state / fail-safe**). A Setup tool is the one other caller, and only while it holds the outputs (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**).
- **No wiring knowledge above the interface.** No runtime, control, route, physics, or manager code names a GPIO pin, expander chip, shift-register bit, or bus type. A concrete implementation owns the map from logical id to physical channel and is the only place that knows the wiring. The map itself is data — the binding table in **Hardware setup** — that the concrete implementation loads. Direct GPIO, a 74HC595 / 74HC165 shift-register chain, and an I²C expander such as MCP23017 are interchangeable implementations of the same interfaces; choosing one changes which implementation is constructed and nothing else.
- **Fault injection belongs to Virtual Hardware.** Simulation's default interfaces model happy hardware: every write succeeds and every read agrees with the model. Tests may inject a stub directly into the interface seam, but operator-facing hardware faults are modeled by Virtual Hardware's in-memory device, below the real chip and HAL implementations. The injectable fault kinds are exactly these:
  - `transaction_refusal`
  - `timeout`
  - `device_disconnect`
  - `invalid_reading` (`OccupancyInput` and the block-voltage readback)
  - `input_hold_or_flicker` (`OccupancyInput`)
  - `output_disagrees_with_command` (`TrackOutput` readback)

  `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/fault` takes one of these values. This keeps Simulation focused on algorithms while proving the same hardware-failure path Real Hardware uses.
- **Input / sensing boundary.** `OccupancyInput` is the read side for sensors that no software output drives. It reads one thing: block current detection, via `read_block_currents()`. Block current detection is the block-occupancy reservation; its read, debounce, attribution, and position reconciliation are defined in **Block occupancy detection**.
  - The block track-voltage readback is not an `OccupancyInput` read: it is the output interface reading back its actual output, `TrackOutput.get_readback_voltage`. Its one consumer is the diagnostic block-voltage read `BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(block_id)` (see **Block power-controller role**).
  - The separate `TrackOutput.get_actual_voltage`, the app's last commanded output, is what the track output driver classifies into the drive zone — not what that diagnostic reads.
  - `OccupancyInput` also names the blocks it can answer for, through `detected_block_ids()`. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, activation requires both occupancy bindings for every layout block, so this set is the complete layout block set. For `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` it is empty, because Simulation senses nothing physical and derives occupancy from the model. **Block occupancy detection** reads the set to decide whether detector-gated movement applies.
  - Switch alignment has no sensor read: reservation is the commanded `Switch.position`. Treating any sensor as a fault-detection, verification, or recovery source is **Out of Scope**.
- **Safe state / fail-safe.** Each output interface defines a safe state, but one session-level entity owns the sequence, so track and point outputs cannot disagree about whether the rig is driving. That entity is `OutputSafety`, and its one method, `enter_safe_state()`, performs the whole sequence itself, in order:
  1. de-energize every point motor through `SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`
  2. command every block voltage to `0` through `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()`

  Both are each controller's non-recording device write: they command the device transport directly and do not touch the block voltages `BlockPowerController` records, `Switch.position`, or any other recorded model field, so `enter_safe_state()` is safe to call from any thread, including the Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` daemon thread (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**). Both non-recording writes still pass through the driver, so the safe state itself updates to `0` the per-channel last-commanded voltage the drive zone is classified from (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**), and every block reads as the idle zone; only the recorded model fields wait for the separate, later reconciliation. Point motors go first because a solenoid is the output that destroys itself if left energized; track voltage only keeps a train moving.
- **Every chip is attempted even when one fails.** A single dead chip cannot leave the rest energized, and the failures are reported together.
- **Reconciling the recorded model fields is a separate, later step.** Reconciling the block voltages `BlockPowerController` records and the other recorded model fields to match is always owned by the runtime thread, never `enter_safe_state()` itself. `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` performs that reconciliation synchronously, immediately after `enter_safe_state()` returns, for every runtime-thread caller; the watchdog path reconciles instead at trip-record consumption, on the runtime thread's next tick (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**).
- **Runtime-thread callers reach the sequence through `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`.** That wrapper first advances `safe_state_generation`. The Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` is the sole direct caller of `enter_safe_state()`, and the runtime advances that generation when it later consumes the watchdog trip. Pause, the layout emergency cut-out, entering Setup, restart/shutdown, and fatal runtime/hardware entry all use the wrapper. The wrapper also ends every open calibration run (per **What ends a calibration run**). A Setup tool's ending is not a caller: it zeros the outputs the tool drives through its own writes (per **Hardware setup**, Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state).
- **Environment behavior for safe state.** Virtual Hardware performs the same sequence against the fake device; Simulation only zeroes its stored values.
- **Safe state is a de-energize, not a lock.** Nothing is withheld from the outputs afterwards: Play after Pause, and Reset after Emergency stop, drive the layout again with no reactivation. It is the whole physical safety mechanism, and its limit is that reaching the safe state is a write, so it needs a live process and a working transport. A process or host that dies leaves each board holding its last commanded value.
- **A process shutdown writes the safe state before it closes the device.** When the server process exits, then it must run the safe state through the session's device while that device is still open, and must close the device only after the safe state returns. No other step of the exit may close the device. The order matters because a closed device refuses every write, the safe state included.
- **Loss-of-control watchdog.** Real Hardware only: activation starts one safety-only daemon, `OutputWatchdog`, that reaches the safe state when the runtime thread stops refreshing the outputs. Simulation and Virtual Hardware drive no physical motor, so neither starts it. A landed ordinary output transaction refreshes the deadline; expiry runs only `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()` under the same transport lock used by ordinary device transactions.
- **The daemon writes only below the model.** The daemon calls `enter_safe_state()` directly, which performs its whole sequence through each controller's non-recording device write (per **Safe state / fail-safe**). Those writes go straight to the device transport, below the model, and the daemon records their transport results in its own thread-safe trip record. It must not read or mutate `SimulationController`, trains, routes, notifications, or any other runtime model state; calling only the non-recording writes, never the ordinary model-recording write, is what guarantees that.
- **Trip-record consumption escalates a failed drop to hardware failure.** Consuming the trip record is the one step `SimulationController.update(...)` performs even behind a fatal gate, because a failed safe-state attempt must still escalate to `hardware_failure`. On the next runtime-thread tick the controller:
  - consumes that trip record
  - reconciles every block's recorded `track_voltage` to `0` (see **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage**)
  - ends every open calibration run (per **What ends a calibration run**)
  - enters hardware failure if the safe-state attempt failed
  - otherwise emits one `kind = "warning"` event through `NotificationCenter`
- **A successful drop does not end the session.** A successful safe-state drop protects the layout; a recovered loop may drive again on its next write.
- **Arming and disarming the watchdog.** `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` disarms the watchdog before delegating to `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`; the watchdog's own expiry call disarms it too. In both cases the next landed ordinary output write re-arms it.
- **Hardware I/O failure is fatal to the physical session.** When any of these occurs, it reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`:
  - a failed output write
  - a failed detector transaction
  - a lost controller
  - an inability to complete safe state
- **`SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)` is the sole true writer.** That method, not the reporting entity, is the only writer of `hardware_failure = True`. In order it:
  - calls `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`, which advances the generation and delegates to the sequence that attempts every de-energize and zero action even when one of them fails
  - records every failure in the emitted event payload
  - deactivates the environment (`environment_active = False`)
  - latches the flag
  - emits one `kind = "error"` event with `operation = "enter_hardware_failure"`

  The session then reads Halted for `hardware_failure`, or Setup when it was in Setup (per **Session state**). The halt retains no `ErrorRecord` or second diagnostic payload across ticks.
- **The affected hardware-backed operation loop stops.** `SimulationController.update(...)` refuses advancement while `hardware_failure` is set only when `active_environment` is `virtual_hardware` or `real_hardware`, apart from consuming the watchdog trip record (per **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**, step `ee19`). An active `simulation` environment continues its full Observe → Plan → Action loop while the latch remains visible; this is full Simulation operation, not a fallback inside a failed hardware-backed session. The failed Virtual/Real session does not log-and-retry its tick and never replaces its interface with a simulated one.
- **Recovery is reactivation** (canonical home). The way back from Halted for `hardware_failure` is a successful `POST /api/operation/activate` of Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware, and nothing else clears the latch.
  - **What activation proves.** It rebuilds every interface, verifies the environment, and passes the readiness check, so a success shows the device answers again.
  - **What a success does.** It clears `hardware_failure`, starts the railway over, and goes Live with every train `OFF` (per **Activation starts the railway over**). A refused or failed activation leaves the latch set.
  - **Diagnosing first.** The operator may enter Setup to find the fault before activating (see **Hardware setup**, Setup). The latch stays set in Setup, and a successful Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware activation out of Setup clears it.
  - **Simulation is not blocked by the latch.** A latched `hardware_failure` does not stop the operator from activating or running Simulation (per **Session state**, A latched hardware failure does not halt Simulation), so an operator whose Hardware Setup is broken or incomplete can still run Simulation while repairing the hardware, per **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup**. Activating Simulation leaves the latch set, because running Simulation proves nothing about the rig.
  - `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()` does not clear the hardware latch.
- Virtual Hardware follows the same latch and recovery flow so it can be tested without the rig.
**Hardware setup**

- Hardware Setup is the physical description shared by Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware: a `controller` (the transport bridge), a `chips` list, the binding maps that wire logical ids to chip ports, and detector calibration. It contains no `enabled`, `develop`, or selected-environment flag, and Simulation never reads it.
- **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy.** An incomplete setup may be saved and exercised in Setup while a rig is being built, but it cannot activate Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware operation. Until the setup is complete, the only operating environment that may run the railway is Simulation. Completeness is checked against the loaded layout, and holds when all of these hold:
  - every block has one `block_track` binding plus both required occupancy bindings (`block_occupancy` and `block_occupancy_current`)
  - every switch has one `switch_output` binding and one `switch_track_source` binding
  - every binding names a present compatible chip and unique in-range port
  - no binding names a deleted entity
  - every required device is reachable
  - every `SpeedProfile` assigned to a placed train has `lighting_voltage` strictly below the setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v` (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**)

  Absence of a required item is always a readiness blocker. A missing binding, chip, device, or detector source is never interpreted as a clear input, an unpowered/undetected exception, or a request for a simulated fallback.
- **Controller.** The transport a real session drives through. The one controller is `ch347` — a USB-HID bridge that carries an I²C bus, an SPI bus, and GPIO. It may carry a `device_port`, but `ch347` opens by USB VID/PID, so the port is optional. The controller list stays open, so another bridge is one added entry.
- **Chips.** Each chip has a `chip_id`, a `kind`, a `bus`, and the parameters that kind needs. There are five kinds:
  - `pca9685` (PWM) drives track power
  - `hc595` (shift-out) drives switch throws
  - `hc165` (shift-in), the digital detector, is one of block occupancy's two sources
  - a current monitor, which reads block supply current directly, is the other source — either an `ina3221` or an `ina219`, which differ only in how many blocks one chip covers
- **A chip's interface `role` is derived from its `kind`, never stored.** The occupancy kinds share the `occupancy_input` role and differ by port kind.
- **A chip's `bus` is user-set, not derived.** It is stored, chosen from the buses its kind allows: `pca9685`, `ina3221`, and `ina219` are I²C only, while a shift register (`hc595` / `hc165`) is `spi` or `gpio`. A shift register clocks its data over the SPI peripheral on either bus; its `bus` names where its **latch line** sits — one of the two hardware chip-select pads (`spi`), or a general-purpose pin (`gpio`). The `gpio` bus exists because the bridge carries only two chip-select pads, so a third shift register must latch somewhere else.
- **The rest of a chip's parameters are user-set as well.** An `i2c_address` for an I²C chip; a latch line (`spi_select`) plus a cascade count (`chain_length`) for a shift register on either bus.
- **Each chip kind contributes a fixed number of channels or bits.** A `pca9685` contributes 16 PWM channels, of which a block's track takes two; a shift register contributes `8 × chain_length` bits; an `ina3221` contributes 3 current-sense channels and an `ina219` 1.
- **A block's track is two PWM channels.** A commanded block voltage is signed — the sign is the block-relative direction the train runs through that block (see **Block power-controller role**, A block voltage carries a direction) — so a block's track is an H-bridge whose two inputs are driven by two `pca9685` channels. The binding names them `forward` and `reverse`, and its `reversed` flag states which of them a positive voltage drives (see **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity**). The driver maps voltage magnitude to duty cycle and voltage sign to which of the two channels drives, holding the other at zero, so the two inputs are never driven together. The two are chosen independently, not as a fixed adjacent pair, because a bench build may wire a block's rails to any two channels on the chip.
- **A block at `0` has nothing applied to it.** Zero is a commanded voltage like any other: the channel matching the sign carries the magnitude and the other rests at zero, so at zero neither channel drives and the H-bridge is given no input at all. That is what an un-energized block is — one the app applies no voltage to. It is not a claim about what a meter reads on those rails: while a locomotive's wheelbase bridges an insulated joint, the block it is leaving feeds the block it is entering through the locomotive itself. Energizing one block ahead is what bounds which block can be fed that way (see **Block power-controller role**, Only the next reserved block is pre-energized).
- **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity.** A block's tile order and its rail polarity are independent facts: the order comes from how the layout was drawn, and which rail a channel drives comes from how the rig was wired. A block driven with the wrong polarity runs its trains backwards.
- **The `reversed` flag is the bond.** It states which of the two bound channels drives the block in its `forward` direction, so a positive `track voltage` drives the binding's `forward` channel when the flag is clear and its `reverse` channel when the flag is set. Neither value is a fault — they are the two ways a block can be wired — and the **track direction sweep** under **Self-test** is the measurement that establishes which one this block is.
- **The bond is wiring, not layout.** It lives with the Hardware Setup like every other binding and persists independently of the layout.
- **The bond stays below the hardware interface.** The commanded voltage keeps its block-relative sign everywhere above, so **Occupancy source follows drive state** reads that same value and no layer above the driver carries a wiring branch.
- **The `forward` and `reverse` channels themselves must not change.** They name two physical rails, and one of those rails may carry the block's idle detection feed, so rebinding to flip a block would move that feed. A channel edit that does not name the flag keeps its stored value, so re-picking the rails never silently resets a bonded block.
- **The flag covers the whole block.** A block is fed as one: the binding feeds every member segment, and a segment carries no polarity of its own.
- **The sweep resolves the flag the same way the driver does.** It first drives the channel a positive `track voltage` would drive on that block, which is the channel that must move a locomotive toward that block's higher tile indices. A block whose flag does not match its wiring runs the locomotive the wrong way on that first leg; with the flag corrected it runs the right way, which is the operator's check that the bond is right.
- **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils.** A solenoid point motor has one coil per side, so a `switch_output` entry names two `hc595` output bits: `port_main` throws toward MAIN and `port_diverge` throws toward DIVERGE. A throw energizes one coil, waits the fixed throw pulse width, and de-energizes it, so both coils rest low between throws and the points themselves hold the alignment. The pulse is short — a coil left energized burns out — and its width is one value in the driver, used unchanged by an operating session and by the commissioning throw test, so a bench test proves the same drive the runtime issues. `port_standby` is the optional bit wired to a motor driver's standby/enable pin, for drivers that ignore their inputs until it is high; a build whose driver needs no such pin leaves `port_standby` unset. Every shift-out bit the commissioning surface drives is driven this same way, because any bit may be wired to a coil.
- **The order of a throw's writes is part of the contract.** The two coil bits are the motor driver's two inputs, so a throw must write them in this order:
  1. raise `port_standby`
  2. drive the target coil high
  3. drive the *other* coil low
  4. wait the pulse width
  5. drop `port_standby`
  6. drop the target coil

  Two rules in that sequence keep the motor alive.
  - **The other coil is always driven low, never assumed low.** This makes a throw correct from any prior bit pattern — including the one a shift-register chain powers up in — and it never drives both inputs at once.
  - **`port_standby` drops before the coil.** That write puts the driver's outputs into high impedance. When the coil input drops first, the driver stays enabled with both inputs low, which is its brake mode and shorts the coil. The final coil write then only settles the resting pattern, except on a driver with no standby bit, where it is the de-energize — which is why it is unconditional.

  The de-energizing writes must happen even when the throw fails part-way, so a failed throw leaves no coil driven.
- **Latch lines are named by pad.** A shift register latches on a line named by the CH347 board pad, and the line set depends on its bus: the SPI bus offers `cs0` and `cs1`; the GPIO bus offers `gpio0`–`gpio7`. The `ch347api` library names the SPI lines off by one — its `set_CS1` drives pad `cs0`, its `set_CS2` drives pad `cs1` — so the driver holds the pad-to-library map and the correct active polarity per chip kind. No layer above the driver names a pad or a library call.
- **A GPIO-latched chip borrows a chip-select pad.** The bridge clocks SPI data only while a chip-select is asserted, and it releases that select when the transfer ends. A shift register latched on a GPIO pin must therefore borrow one of the two pads for the length of its transfer. The driver borrows a pad that no `hc595` latches on, because releasing a `hc595`'s latch pad would clock stray bits into that chip and may throw a switch; an `hc165`'s load pad is safe to borrow, since a transfer only freezes and reloads its parallel inputs. A build in which every chip-select pad latches an `hc595` must not also carry a GPIO-latched chip.
- **Bindings.** The binding maps carry the logical-id-to-chip-port wiring, each keyed by logical id:
  - `block_track` (`block_id` to the two PWM channels driving its rails, `forward` and `reverse`, plus the `reversed` flag bonding those channels to the block's tile order — see **A block's track is two PWM channels** and **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity**)
  - `switch_output` (`switch_id` to its two coil ports plus an optional standby port, see **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils**)
  - `block_occupancy` (`block_id` to a digital-detector port on an `hc165`, see **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer**)
  - `block_occupancy_current` (`block_id` to a current-sense channel on an `ina3221` or an `ina219`, plus `calibration_id`; `OccupancyInput` resolves `baseline_ma` and `threshold_ma` from `detector_calibration[calibration_id]`)
- **`switch_track_source` wires a switch to its feed block.** This further required map wires every `switch_id` to the `block_id` whose feed powers that switch's rails. It is the one binding whose value is another logical id rather than a chip port, because a switch's rails have no channel of their own (see **Switch power-controller role**). It must name the block at the switch's main entrance. `SwitchPowerController` is its only reader.
- **The rest of this binding table is read by the concrete driver alone, with one exception.** It is the physical-channel map named under **Hardware interface boundary**. The exception is `block_occupancy_current`, which Real Hardware's block-voltage readback (`TrackOutput.get_readback_voltage`, see **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage**) also reads where that chip provides a bus-voltage measurement.
- **A binding must name a valid, uniquely-used chip port.** A binding must name a configured chip whose role matches the map — and, for the two occupancy maps, whose port kind matches (a digital detector bit for `block_occupancy`, a current-sense channel for `block_occupancy_current`) — at a port within that chip's range. Three uniqueness rules also hold:
  - a port must not be bound more than once
  - the two channels of one `block_track` entry must differ
  - the two coil ports and the standby port of one `switch_output` entry must all differ
- **An incomplete setup may be saved and tested in Setup, but not activated.** The editor may save any of these maps incomplete, and the Setup tools may exercise the entries that exist, but the readiness report keeps hardware-backed operation blocked until the cardinality and validity rules pass.
- **A binding is read per write.** A binding names a port; a session is built from chips, and the two have different lifetimes. The chips, their transport, and the maps the chips are constructed and range-checked against are captured when Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware is activated. These three values are looked up on every write instead, from the setup as it stands at that moment:
  - a switch's `port_main`, `port_diverge`, and `port_standby` (`switch_output`)
  - a block's `reversed` rail-polarity flag on its `block_track` binding
  - a switch's `switch_track_source` rail feed

  These three are the values a rig being wired gets wrong and corrects, and none of them changes which chips a session builds — each only re-aims an existing chip, or names a block. An operator who re-picks a coil port must see the next throw land on the new bit: a correction that waits for the next activation reads as a control that does nothing, and the operator changes the wiring instead of the setting. Every other part of the setup — the controller, the chip list, a `block_track` binding's two channels, both occupancy maps and their calibration, and the shared drive-zone levels — is captured at activation, because changing it means building different chips. `GET /api/operation/environment` reports whether the saved setup holds captured changes the running session was not built with; the per-write values never raise that flag, because they are already in use.

- **Occupancy source follows drive state.** A block bound in both occupancy maps is read from whichever source is trustworthy this tick. The block's drive zone decides which one, because how hard software is driving the rails is what makes a detector believable. The drive zone comes from the magnitude of the last-commanded voltage on that block's track channel; the sign is direction and has no bearing on it.
- **The track output driver owns the drive zone.** In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, the `TrackOutput` driver classifies each block's last-commanded voltage into one of the three zones and reports it through `drive_zone(block_id)`. The `OccupancyInput` asks that driver for the zone and does not compare a voltage against the zone levels itself, so the two configured levels are handed to the track output driver. The driver that put a block's rails in a state reports which state they are in, so what a commanded voltage means for the rails and for detection is decided in one place. The **Block occupancy test** builds no track output driver, so it applies the same classification to the voltage it reads back off the PWM chip.
- **The last-commanded voltage is tracked below the hardware interface.** It is held in one place, the track output driver, and written by whichever owner currently drives the channel:
  - `BlockPowerController` during operation
  - a Setup tool while it holds the outputs (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**)
  - the safe-state zero (see **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe, which updates this same store)

  A reconnect re-initialization zeroes every PWM channel, so it zeroes this store too. The drive zone therefore always reflects the voltage the rail actually carries, whichever owner put it there.
- **Two configured levels split that range into three zones.** Both are one value for the whole Hardware Setup: `idle_deadband_v`, at or below which nothing is driving the rails, and `current_sense_min_drive_v`, at or above which the drive is strong enough to put a readable load on a current channel.
  - **Idle** (at or below `idle_deadband_v`): no drive. The track output driver holds both inputs of the block's H-bridge low, and the H-bridge must leave both rails undriven in that state, because the `hc165` digital detector senses the locomotive through an undriven rail. A DRV8871 does so: with both inputs low it lets both outputs float. There is no drive current to sense, so the digital detector decides.
  - **Driven** (at or above `current_sense_min_drive_v`): the rail drive swamps the digital detector, but a motor under real drive draws a current the sense channel reads cleanly, so the current channel decides — current is present when `abs(current - baseline_ma)` reaches the channel's `threshold_ma`.
  - **Lighting** (between the two): a stopped-but-lit locomotive. The required current channel decides, as in the driven zone, and the digital detector is not read at all. A missing or unavailable current binding is an activation blocker or hardware I/O failure, never a digital fallback. Current present is returned as raw `true` to `BlockOccupancyDetector`, which still applies `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD`; it does not confirm occupancy on one interface read. A block's presence is established once its deciding source has read current on `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` consecutive reads, in any zone, since the interface last returned raw `false` for it. When the presence is established, then a raw clear must first be earned inside the hardware-backed `OccupancyInput`: that source must read clear on every one of `LIGHTING_CLEAR_HOLD_READS` consecutive reads while the interface continues to return its last reported value. Only after the hold releases does it return raw `false`, at which point `BlockOccupancyDetector` begins its separate `OCCUPANCY_OFF_THRESHOLD` debounce. When the presence is not established, then the interface returns raw `false` on the first clear read. `LIGHTING_CLEAR_HOLD_READS` is `30`, in `constants.py`. Any current-present read resets the lighting hold, and so does leaving the zone.

  The digital detector is not read in this zone because it reads the drive rather than the train. Lighting voltage reaches the rails as the full supply switched on for a fraction of each cycle (a duty cycle), so the detector's comparator asserts on roughly that fraction of reads whether or not a locomotive is there. The current channel tells the two cases apart across the same band by close to a factor of ten.

  The lighting hold exists because a locomotive can still go quiet on the current channel: one drawing less than its channel's `threshold_ma` at standby reads the same as an empty block. Occupancy and drive are a loop — a block that reads clear is released, releasing it cuts its voltage, and cutting its voltage changes its zone and therefore which detector answers. Holding the last reported value until the deciding source has read clear for a whole window keeps a release slow enough that a marginal locomotive cannot ride that loop around, and still gives the hold an exit.

  Only an established presence is held, because the hold answers every read of its window with the last reported value. Holding a single current-present read would hand `BlockOccupancyDetector` the consecutive reads `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` asks for, so one noisy sample would confirm an empty block — and a locomotive starting on the next block puts exactly such samples on this block's channel. The run counts reads in any zone so that a train confirmed while driven or idle is held when it stops in this zone.
- **`current_sense_min_drive_v` must sit above `lighting_voltage`.** `current_sense_min_drive_v` must sit above the profile's `lighting_voltage` (**SpeedProfile**), so a lit but motionless train lands in the middle zone rather than reading as driven. **Lighting-voltage calibration**, the one procedure that moves `lighting_voltage` in the ordinary case, keeps that bound by capping its accepted candidate at that ceiling in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware. In Simulation the bound is not evaluated (per **What a candidate may be**). That cap does not by itself guard every other way a profile's `lighting_voltage` or the setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v` can change.
- **This constraint is enforced by the shared readiness evaluator.** It is part of the layout-aware readiness report that `GET /api/operation/environment`, `GET /api/operation/readiness`, and `PUT /api/operation/environment` all return (see **Hardware setup**, the REST surface, and **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy**). The shared readiness evaluator checks every placed train's resolved `lighting_voltage` against the setup's current `current_sense_min_drive_v`, the same way it checks a missing occupancy binding, and reports a blocker when that value does not sit below it — whether that value came from calibration, an imported roster entry, an adoption-seeded default, or a placeholder profile from `add_train`. `POST /api/operation/activate` re-runs the same evaluator and refuses activation on the same blocker. The check is evaluated live at each of those calls; a `PUT /api/hardware/config` or profile edit made while already active takes effect on the next such check, not retroactively against the running session.
- **Both occupancy sources are mandatory.** This holds for every block in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware. A missing binding blocks activation; a source that becomes unavailable after activation is a hardware I/O failure. The choice of source lives inside the hardware-backed `OccupancyInput`; the per-block `current present` boolean it returns is the same shape whichever zone answered, so **Block occupancy detection** consumes it without knowing the source.
- **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer.** A shift-in chip carries an `active_low` flag describing how its detector drives the line: a comparator with no inverter stage pulls its output low when a train draws current, so that chain's raw bit reads 0 occupied and 1 clear, while a detector with an inverter reads the other way. Polarity is stated once per chip, because a detector chain is wired one way throughout: every block bound to that chip reads the same way, and a binding carries no polarity of its own. The real `OccupancyInput` applies the chip's polarity as it reads each bit. The boolean it returns must always mean `current present`, whichever way the detector is wired, so no code above the interface, and no other physical source, carries a polarity branch. Polarity applies to the digital detector only: a current-sense channel is judged on the magnitude `abs(current - baseline_ma)`, which has no polarity to resolve.
- **Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware share one setup.** Both environments build every required chip, binding, interface, occupancy rule, and safety-supervisor contract from the same Hardware Setup. Virtual Hardware supplies an in-memory transport and emulates whatever safety gate the setup maps; Real Hardware supplies the physical transport and external gate. The build is all-or-nothing. Missing roles, bindings, chips, or required safety facilities are activation blockers, never requests for simulated fallbacks.
- **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup.** Simulation constructs its model interfaces without opening, validating, pruning, or changing Hardware Setup. A broken or incomplete setup therefore cannot prevent Simulation from running, and running Simulation cannot be mistaken for successfully activating a requested Real Hardware environment.
- **Self-test.** It opens the selected device and scans the I²C bus: an I²C chip is proven present when its address answers. A shift register (`hc595` / `hc165`) cannot be auto-detected — it has no acknowledgement and no id register, so it reads the same wired as unwired — and is proven by hand instead (matching **`POST /api/hardware/scan`**). The ports of every configured chip form the pool the binding maps draw from.
- **A shift register is proven only when the operator confirms it.** The operator runs the port test or the commissioning session against the chip, watches the board, and confirms it worked. Running a test is not proof on its own: a shift-out test that drives a dead chain and a shift-in read of an unwired chain both complete without an error. When a later test of that chip fails, then the panel takes the confirmation back. Proof is a panel record for the operator; it is not an activation blocker, because no device read can check it.
- **Setup** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name). Setup is the session state for building and testing the rig (see **Session state**). It exists only in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, because Simulation has no rig. It is not an operating environment, and it never borrows outputs from live operation.
  - **Entering it.** `POST /api/operation/setup` enters Setup for the selected environment. It is accepted while Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware is the selected environment and the session state is Live, Paused, or Halted for `not_activated`, `hardware_failure` or `layout_emergency_cut_out`. It is refused with `409` in three cases:
    - Simulation is the selected environment;
    - the session is Halted for `runtime_failure`, which the operator clears first;
    - the session is already in Setup.
  - **What entering does.** In order:
    1. from Live or Paused, it performs the **Layout emergency cut-out**, so every train is stopped and holds no reservation;
    2. it drives the outputs to their safe state through `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`;
    3. it deactivates the environment (`environment_active = False`), so `BlockPowerController` and `SwitchPowerController` give up the outputs, and makes the selected environment the `active_environment`. When the session's interfaces were built for that same environment, its device handle and its `OccupancyInput` stay open (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**). Otherwise the session's interfaces are released, and no `OccupancyInput` is open until an activation succeeds;
    4. it sets `AppState.setup_active`, and the session reads Setup.
  - **Leaving it.** Activate is the only way out of Setup (see **Activation starts the railway over**, An open Setup tool is closed first). A refused activation leaves the session, and any open tool, in Setup; one that fails to build after closing the tool leaves the session in Setup with no tool open.
  - **What it may work on.** Setup may inspect an incomplete setup. It cannot run trains or grant ordinary operation ownership.
  - **The tools.** Inside Setup the operator uses these tools: the commissioning session, self-test, port-test, track direction sweep, switch throw test, block occupancy test, and the occupancy bench. A tool owns the outputs only while it drives them, and the detectors go on being read throughout (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**), except while a hardware failure is latched or while no `OccupancyInput` is open (see **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs).
- **The commissioning session.** It is the bounded raw-port tool, accepted only in Setup. `POST /api/hardware/commission/open` opens it and builds the chips it drives from the posted setup. Its idle timeout is the request's `timeout_seconds`, or a default when the request names none: when no action reaches the session for that long, it closes. Its `output`, `pulse`, `inputs`, and `currents` actions drive and read raw chip ports, and `close` ends it.
  - **Switch bits.** `open` reads the `switch_output` bindings of the chips it builds, from both the posted setup and the saved one, and every port such a binding names (`port_main`, `port_diverge`, and `port_standby`) is a switch bit. It reads the saved setup too because the Hardware Setup panel posts its chips without their bindings. `output` refuses to hold a switch bit on, because a held coil burns out. `open` lists the switch bits in its response, so a caller walking the bits pulses a switch bit only for the switch-coil width and may pulse every other bit for longer.
  - **Every failure reaches the operator.** A failed action returns `ok == false` with its error. A current channel that cannot be read fails the whole `currents` action; it is never reported as `0` mA.
- **Occupancy bench.** It is the Setup tool for setting detector calibration, accepted only in Setup. It holds every block that has a rail binding at one track voltage, and reports both occupancy sources for every bound block side by side, with each current channel's peak reading, so the operator can choose each channel's `baseline_ma` and `threshold_ma` (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**). `POST /api/hardware/bench/open` opens it and `POST /api/hardware/bench/close` closes it; its idle timeout also closes it.
- **Port-test.** A port-test drives one output port or reads one input port so a single wire can be confirmed before binding. An output pulse is accepted only in Setup, because it drives an output that an active environment's power controllers would otherwise own (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**); an input read drives nothing and is accepted in any state.
- **Track direction sweep.** It runs only in Setup. It drives the block's two bound channels one way, off, then the other way, with a hard duration bound and safe-state cleanup. It resolves the block's `reversed` flag as the driver does (see **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity**).
- **Switch throw test.** It pulses one coil of a bound switch through the same write order and pulse width an operating throw uses, then records that alignment on the switch through `SwitchManager.record_bench_alignment(switch_id, position)`. That entry applies the `Switch.position` and runs the `BlockManager` block-reachability notify (`on_switch_position_changed`) but drives no coil, because the bench already pulsed it. It writes model state, and only that: it drives no train and grants no operation ownership. It exists because the operating throw `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)` refuses while no operating environment is active (the operating-throw gate under **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**), and no environment is active in Setup — the state every bench throw runs in — so recording the already-driven alignment cannot go through that entry, and would double-drive a coil the Setup tool has taken if it did. `record_bench_alignment(...)` passes `manual_override = True`, so a `manual` switch's alignment is recorded too, because the operator explicitly asked for the test throw.

  The app must record the new alignment because the points have moved, and the app must not go on describing the layout the way it was before the operator watched them move.
- **Block occupancy test.** It drives nothing. When both required bindings exist, it reports both sources, the drive zone, and the resulting verdict. Otherwise it reports the missing source as a readiness blocker rather than synthesizing a result.
- **Virtual Hardware** exercises the identical workflow against its fake device.
- **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared.** A session opens one device handle and every owner reaches the rig through it. What a Setup tool takes is the exclusive right to **write**: while it holds the outputs, no other ordinary owner may drive a track channel or a coil. It does not take the reads.
- **The detector pipeline keeps running throughout Setup.** `OccupancyInput.read_block_currents()` is served for the whole time the session is in Setup, so the global read, the debounce, the attribution, and the Observe commit keep running and `Block.occupied_by` stays live (see **Block occupancy detection**, The read does not stop in Setup). An operator opens a bench to find out why a block reads wrong, so the layout beside it must go on saying what the app currently believes, because that comparison is the diagnosis.
- **The operational loop moves no train in Setup.** Setup is a stopped session state, so the route/controller loop performs no movement calculation or propulsion output. A bounded Setup tool may physically move a locomotive — the track-direction sweep does so deliberately — but that movement is not an operational train command or an extra physics pass.
- **Ordinary reads and writes run on the runtime thread, with one exception.** The exception is the Real Hardware watchdog's safety-only de-energize/zero sequence, which shares the same transport lock, so device transactions never collide.
- **A Setup tool's writes select the same occupancy zone as operation.** A Setup tool writes the same last-commanded voltage that **Occupancy source follows drive state** reads, so a rail a bench is driving is read in the `driven` zone and its current channel decides, as it would under operation. Detector processing and model commits continue, but the stopped-pass de-energize drain issues no device write in Setup. It clears any queued block IDs as logically handled, because each tool's closing safe-state sequence zeros every output before another owner may take them; the de-energize stores remain same-tick queues and never become retained latches.
- **Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state.** Closing, timing out, disconnecting, or failing a Setup tool completes the tool's own safe-state sequence, which zeros all outputs before another tool or an activation may take them. The tool performs it itself: it writes `0` to every output channel of the chips it drives — every track channel, coil, and raw port it touched, whether bound to a block or not — through the session's device handle, then gives up the outputs. It is not `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`, which reaches only the bound outputs of `BlockPowerController` and `SwitchPowerController`, and it does not advance `safe_state_generation`, because the runtime's power controllers do not own the outputs while a tool holds them. A failure of one of these writes is a hardware I/O failure (per **Hardware I/O failure is fatal to the physical session**). The session stays in Setup.
- **A timeout closes the tool on time.** Every iteration of the runtime loop, whatever pass it runs or none, closes any Setup tool whose idle timeout has passed, through that tool's own safe-state sequence. A tool that no request reaches therefore still closes on time, so an operator who walks away from an open bench does not leave the blocks driven.
- **Persisted setup; separate selected environment.** A setup `PUT` writes the whole Hardware Setup to an app-managed JSON file. Setup changes never rewire a running session in place. The selected environment is stored independently. Activating Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware with a blocker returns its readiness blockers and leaves no environment active (per **Session state**) rather than falling back. Activation owns rebuild, reconnect, verification, and starting the railway over (per **Activation starts the railway over**); the operator-facing workflow never requires a raw "restart server" step.
- **Saved with the layout.** Saving a layout writes its Hardware Setup into the layout file because bindings are keyed by that layout's `block_id` and `switch_id`. Loading the layout may adopt that setup after validation, but does not import or change the selected operating environment and never activates physical output. A loaded setup replaces the previous setup as a whole: absent sections become empty/default edit-state values and therefore remain explicit readiness blockers wherever required, dangling bindings are reported, and invalid setup is reported without preventing the geometry from loading.
**Hardware REST payload schemas**

- Unknown fields and unknown discriminator values are rejected. These validity rules all hold:
  - every referenced layout entity and `chip_id` must exist
  - ports must be integers inside the selected chip's advertised range
  - numeric values must be finite
  - one physical port may appear in only one binding of the same output/input role
- `HardwareSetupRequest` carries exactly `controller`, `chips`, `detector_calibration`, `block_track`, `block_occupancy`, `block_occupancy_current`, `switch_output`, `switch_track_source`, and the two drive-zone levels `idle_deadband_v` and `current_sense_min_drive_v` (validated `0 <= idle_deadband_v < current_sense_min_drive_v` at request time; the requirement that `current_sense_min_drive_v` sit above every placed train's `lighting_voltage` is a readiness blocker, not a PUT rejection, per **Occupancy source follows drive state**):
  - `controller` is `{ "kind": "ch347", "device_port": Optional[str] }`.
  - each I²C chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "pca9685" | "ina3221" | "ina219", "bus": "i2c", "i2c_address": int }`;
  - each shift-output chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "hc595", "bus": "spi" | "gpio", "spi_select": int, "chain_length": int }`, with `chain_length >= 1`;
  - each shift-input chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "hc165", "bus": "spi" | "gpio", "spi_select": int, "chain_length": int, "active_low": bool }`, with `chain_length >= 1`; `active_low` is stored only on this chip variant and applies to every digital detector bit in its chain;
  - `detector_calibration` maps detector calibration id to `{ "baseline_ma": float, "threshold_ma": float }`, with both values nonnegative and `threshold_ma > baseline_ma`;
  - `block_track` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "forward_port": int, "reverse_port": int, "reversed": bool }`; both ports address PWM channels on that chip and must differ;
  - `block_occupancy` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int }`; the referenced `hc165` chip supplies polarity;
  - `block_occupancy_current` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int, "calibration_id": str }`;
  - `switch_output` maps `switch_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port_main": int, "port_diverge": int, "port_standby": Optional[int] }`; `port_main` and `port_diverge` must differ, and a populated `port_standby` must differ from both. No binding carries a pulse duration; the throw width is one driver-wide value (per **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils**);
  - `switch_track_source` maps `switch_id` to a `block_id` string. Unlike the other binding maps, its value is a logical id, not a chip port, so it carries no `reversed`: a switch has no rails of its own, and its rail polarity is whatever the feed block's `block_track` binding sets.
- Commissioning-session bodies address raw chips and ports, not entities, because a bench brings up an incomplete setup whose entity bindings may not exist yet. The commissioning session is a server-side singleton, so no action body carries a `session_id`.
  - `POST /api/operation/setup` carries an empty body (see **Hardware setup**, Setup).
  - `POST /api/hardware/commission/open` carries `{ "config": HardwareSetupRequest, "timeout_seconds": Optional[float] }`. A given `timeout_seconds` must satisfy `0 < timeout_seconds <= COMMISSION_MAX_SESSION_SECONDS` and is the session's idle timeout; without it the session uses its default idle timeout.
  - `output` carries `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int, "duty": float }`, where `duty` in `0.0..1.0` is the PWM level (or on/off).
  - `pulse` carries `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int, "standby_port": Optional[int], "off_port": Optional[int], "pulse_s": Optional[float] }`. It drives one shift-out bit for the switch-coil pulse width, raises `standby_port` for the pulse when the motor driver needs it, and holds `off_port` low. A supplied `pulse_s` must be no greater than `COMMISSION_MAX_PULSE_MS`; an omitted one uses the driver-wide fixed throw width. `COMMISSION_MAX_SESSION_SECONDS` and `COMMISSION_MAX_PULSE_MS` live in `constants.py`.
  - `inputs` and `currents` each carry `{ "chip_id": str }`, reading every bit of an `hc165` and every channel of the named current monitor (an `ina3221` or `ina219`) respectively.
  - `close` carries an empty body.
  - Every `/hardware/commission/*` response is `{ "ok": bool }`, plus `"error": str` on failure; `open` adds `"switch_ports": { chip_id: [int] }` (see **The commissioning session**, Switch bits), `inputs` adds `"ports": [{ "port": int, "value": bool }]` and `currents` adds `"currents": [{ "port": int, "current_ma": float }]`.
- The raw virtual-hardware input bodies address a block, not a chip port. `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/occupancy` takes `{ "block_id": str, "occupied": bool }` — the endpoint resolves the block's `block_occupancy` binding to the chip and latch line. `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/current` takes `{ "block_id": str, "current_ma": float }` (nonnegative), resolved through the block's `block_occupancy_current` binding.
- `VirtualHardwareFaultRequest` is `{ "action": "inject" | "clear", "target_kind": "controller" | "chip" | "port" | "transaction" | "readback", "target_id": str, "operation": Optional[str], "fault": Optional[VirtualHardwareFaultKind] }`, where `VirtualHardwareFaultKind` is the set defined under **Fault injection belongs to Virtual Hardware**: `transaction_refusal`, `timeout`, `device_disconnect`, `invalid_reading`, `input_hold_or_flicker`, or `output_disagrees_with_command`. `fault` is required for `inject` and must be `None` for `clear`; an incompatible target/fault pair is rejected rather than translated to another name.
- `VirtualHardwareScenarioRequest` is one of `{ "action": "place", "train_id": str, "block_id": str, "direction": "forward" | "reverse" }`, `{ "action": "move", "train_id": str, "to_block_id": str }`, `{ "action": "stop", "train_id": str }`, or `{ "action": "remove", "train_id": str }`.

- **REST surface.**

| Endpoint | Body | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/hardware/config` | — | Returns the saved Hardware Setup: `controller`, `chips` (including stored bus plus derived role/direction/port metadata), detector calibration, binding maps, and the two drive-zone levels `idle_deadband_v` and `current_sense_min_drive_v`, plus a session summary saying which environment the session is built for, its session state (per **Session state**), and whether the saved setup holds changes the running session was not built with. The layout-aware readiness report is served by `GET /api/operation/environment` and `GET /api/operation/readiness`, not here. It contains no selected-environment flag beyond that session summary. |
| `PUT /api/hardware/config` | `HardwareSetupRequest` | Validates the fields and bindings that exist and writes the whole setup, returning the stored config. Incompleteness is allowed while editing or in Setup, and the readiness report (`GET /api/operation/environment` / `GET /api/operation/readiness`) surfaces it, but it blocks Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware activation (per **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy**). Malformed fields, incompatible chips, out-of-range or duplicate ports, and dangling references are rejected. The running session keeps the chips and maps it was built with until explicit activation; the values named in **A binding is read per write** reach the rig on the next write. |
| `GET /api/operation/environment` | — | Returns `requested_environment` and `active_environment`, each one of `"simulation" \| "virtual_hardware" \| "real_hardware"`, the session state as `{value, halt_reason}` from `AppState.session_state()` (per **Session state**), readiness blockers, device health, and whether the saved setup holds changes the running session was not built with (the captured parts only — see **A binding is read per write**). This is the single session truth the header and diagnostics read. |
| `GET /api/operation/readiness` | — | Returns the same layout-aware readiness report as `GET /api/operation/environment` — readiness blockers and device health, evaluated live against the loaded layout and Hardware Setup (see **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy**). It activates nothing. |
| `PUT /api/operation/environment` | `{ "environment": "simulation" \| "virtual_hardware" \| "real_hardware" }` | Selects the requested environment but does not silently rewire a running session. Simulation needs no setup. Virtual/Real selection returns the readiness blockers that would prevent activation. |
| `POST /api/operation/activate` | — | Refused with `409` while the session is Live or Halted for `runtime_failure` (per **Session state**). Otherwise it validates the requested environment, closes any Setup tool that still holds the outputs, builds all interfaces atomically, reconnects, verifies the active environment, starts the railway over, and goes Live (per **Activation starts the railway over**). A successful Virtual/Real activation clears `hardware_failure` (per **Power**, Recovery is reactivation). A refused or failed activation returns the readiness blockers, leaves no environment active, and never activates Simulation as a fallback. |
| `POST /api/runtime/clear-fatal` | — | Calls `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()`. Refused when the runtime is not halted (`failed_runtime` unset). On success it runs the step-`7c41` (Clearing the halt) cleanup, and the session state is derived again from the other flags (per **Session state**); it does not clear `hardware_failure`. |
| `POST /api/simulation/control` | `{ "action": "start" \| "stop" \| "set_speed", "speed": float }` (`speed` only with `set_speed`) | Play, Pause and playback speed, only while Simulation is the active environment. `start` is accepted only while the session is Paused and writes `simulation_running = True`; `stop` is accepted only while it is Live, enters the safe state, and writes `simulation_running = False` (per **Session state** and **Running and stopped**). `set_speed` writes `simulation_speed`, which must be positive (per **Session mode and operating environment**, Pacing). Every other case is refused with `409` and changes nothing, including every request in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware. |
| `POST /api/simulation/emergency-cut-out` | — | Emergency stop: calls `SimulationController.layout_emergency_cut_out()` (per **Emergency cut-out**, Layout emergency cut-out), in every environment. |
| `POST /api/simulation/reset` | — | Reset: calls `SimulationController.reset_layout_cut_out()` (per **Emergency cut-out**, Reset). Refused with `409` unless the session is Halted for `layout_emergency_cut_out`. |
| `POST /api/simulation/hold-all` | — | Hold all: calls `SimulationController.hold_all()` (per **Hold all**) and returns the IDs of the trains it stopped. Accepted in every session state and environment. |
| `GET /api/hardware/catalog` | — | Returns the selectable controllers and chip kinds — the buses each kind allows, role, direction, port count, and required parameters — that the setup UI reads. |
| `POST /api/hardware/scan` | `{ "config": {…} }` | Opens the controller and reports which I²C addresses answer — per-chip reachability for the I²C chips (the Hardware Setup Detect / Rescan button). It does not probe shift-register (`hc595` / `hc165`) transactions; those chips and individual output ports are exercised through the port-test, track-test, switch-test, and occupancy-test endpoints and commissioning. It borrows the running session's output-owning device under `simulation_lock` when there is one, and otherwise opens a transient device of its own. |
| `POST /api/hardware/port-test` | `{ "config": {…}, "chip_id": str, "port": int, "action": "pulse_output" \| "read_input", "pulse_s": Optional[float] }` | Drives one output port or reads one input port on a named chip, so a single wire is confirmed before it is bound to any entity (see **Hardware setup**, Port-test). `pulse_output` is accepted only in Setup and refused with `409` otherwise; `read_input` is accepted in any state. |
| `POST /api/hardware/occupancy-test` | `{ "config": {…}, "block_id": str }` | Reads both of a block's occupancy detectors — the `hc165` bit and the current-sense channel — reads the block's drive state back off its PWM chip, applies the **Occupancy source follows drive state** rule for which source decides, and reports the verdict. Drives nothing. |
| `POST /api/hardware/track-test` | `{ "config": {…}, "block_id": str }` | Sweeps a block's two bound PWM channels forward / off / reverse, mirroring each leg onto the voltage `BlockPowerController` records for the block so the layout shows what the rails carry, then zeros every channel of that chip (the block editor's track Test). It is a Setup tool of its own: it drives the channels itself through the session's device handle, not through the commissioning session (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared** and **Closing a Setup tool restores the safe state**). It runs only in Setup, a stopped session state, so the runtime writes no block voltage during the sweep. |
| `POST /api/hardware/switch-test` | `{ "config": {…}, "switch_id": str, "position": int }` | Throws one switch to the named position (`0` = MAIN, `1` = DIVERGE) — the switch editor's Test throw. When the session owns the switch coils it is an operating throw through `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)`; otherwise the coil is pulsed through the commissioning session using the switch's binding and the alignment is recorded through `SwitchManager.record_bench_alignment(...)` after the pulse lands (see **Hardware setup**, Switch throw test). Either way it passes `manual_override = True`, because a test throw is an alignment the operator explicitly asked for. |
| `POST /api/operation/setup` | — | Enters Setup (per **Hardware setup**, Setup), through the steps in the Enter Setup row of **Session state**. Refused with `409` in Simulation, while Halted for `runtime_failure`, and while already in Setup. It changes no setup. |
| `POST /api/hardware/commission/{open,output,pulse,inputs,currents,close}` | The commissioning body for that action under **Hardware REST payload schemas** | The commissioning session (per **Hardware setup**, The commissioning session), accepted only in Setup. `open` builds the session's chips from the posted config, giving it exclusive **output** ownership. The `output` / `pulse` / `inputs` / `currents` actions drive and read raw chip ports through the same output interfaces and drivers, with the same duration limits, as operation. The occupancy read is shared and keeps running throughout (see **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**). `close` — or a timeout, disconnect, or failure — completes the safe state before releasing ownership, and the session stays in Setup. These endpoints change no setup. |
| `POST /api/hardware/bench/{open,close,drive,threshold,peaks/reset}` and `GET /api/hardware/bench/state` | as the current code has them | The occupancy bench (per **Hardware setup**, Occupancy bench), accepted only in Setup. `open` takes exclusive output ownership; `drive` sets the held level, `state` reads both sources per block, and `threshold` and `peaks/reset` help pick each channel's calibration. `close`, or its idle timeout, completes the safe state and leaves the session in Setup. It never activates an environment. This document changes only when the bench is accepted and what closing it does. |
| `GET /api/virtual-hardware` | — | Virtual Hardware only. Returns fake-device connection state, raw inputs, measured/current values, output commands/readback, injected faults, and active high-level scenario. Each block reports which outputs and detectors it is bound to, the raw detector bit alongside that bit resolved through the chain's polarity, and the commanded duty on both of its rails alongside the signed voltage those duties mean once the binding's `reversed` flag is applied. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/occupancy` (`{ "block_id": …, "occupied": bool }`) and `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/current` (`{ "block_id": …, "current_ma": float }`) | see left | Change fake device input state only; the ordinary occupancy pipeline observes it on its next read. Each call writes one raw source and leaves the block's other source saying whatever it said before, which is how a deliberate disagreement between the two is set up. `/input/occupancy` sets the block's digital detector bit at the raw level, so on an `active_low` chain the bit that means `current present` is 0 (see **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer**). `/input/current` sets the block's fake current-sense reading in mA. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/presence` | `{ "block_id": …, "present": true \| false }` | Puts a virtual object on one block's detectors, or lifts it off. It writes every occupancy source the block is bound to in one call — the digital bit resolved through the chain's polarity, and a current clear of that channel's `threshold_ma` above its `baseline_ma` — so the block reads the same way whichever source **Occupancy source follows drive state** selects. A block bound to no occupancy source is rejected. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/fault` | `VirtualHardwareFaultRequest` | Injects or clears a fake controller, chip, port, transaction, or readback failure below the real HAL implementation. |
| `POST /api/virtual-hardware/scenario` | `VirtualHardwareScenarioRequest` | Converts a topology-aware virtual train action into raw fake detector/current transitions, one block at a time through the same write `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/presence` performs. A step across a block boundary confirms the entered block's detectors and clears the left block's in the same call. It never writes `Block.occupied_by`, controller span, or another operational state directly. |
**Block occupancy detection**

- Each block has its own current detector and is its own occupancy section; its member segments are geometry only and are not detected on their own (see **Block**, Detection isolation is separate from geometry). Current on a block means a train is standing on it; no current means no train is. This detection is the reservation for `Block.occupied_by`: it replaces any guess from the calculated train position. Switch occupancy is not detected this way: switch-alignment reservation stays the commanded `Switch.position` (see **Out of Scope**), and a switch's physical entry and exit come from the train's calculated traversal.
- **One global read per tick.** At the top of each tick the runtime reads every block's detector at once through `OccupancyInput.read_block_currents()`, which returns a plain `block_id -> current present` map with no train identity. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, **Hardware setup** defines which physical source produces that boolean: an `hc165` digital detector or a current-sense channel selected by drive state. In Simulation, `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` derives the same-shaped map from live train spans. The read reflects where trains were at the end of the previous tick, so a block the locomotive just entered is confirmed no earlier than the next tick, and in practice after the `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` debounce reads on top of that (see **Debounce with on/off thresholds**). That lag is sensor latency. Each pass's read is also written to the **Detector reading log** (see **Event log**).
- **The read does not stop in Setup.** A Setup tool takes the outputs, not the detectors, so the global read, the debounce, the attribution, and the Observe commit keep running throughout Setup whenever an `OccupancyInput` is open (see **Hardware setup**, Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared). A session that entered Setup without interfaces built has nothing to read until an activation succeeds (see **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs). Train motion stops, because Setup is a stopped session state. A block a locomotive stands on therefore reads OCCUPIED throughout.
- **Debounce with on/off thresholds.** Real contacts flicker: a block a train is standing on can briefly read open. `BlockOccupancyDetector` keeps a per-block counter and confirms a block OCCUPIED only after `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` consecutive current reads, and CLEAR only after `OCCUPANCY_OFF_THRESHOLD` consecutive no-current reads. Both thresholds live in `constants.py`. The bias is fail-safe: occupy quickly, clear slowly. Debounce rides out a dropout shorter than the off-window; the gate on committing a clear covers a dropout that outlasts it (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**). Each tick the detector compares the whole confirmed-occupied set against the previous one, so a fast train that enters or clears several blocks in one tick is reported in one pass.
- **Placement is seeded, not re-detected.** `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` sets `Block.occupied_by` directly when a train is initially put on the track. This initial placement is the one sanctioned exception to the "runtime entry writes `occupied_by` only through `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`" rule, because it runs before the first tick (as `SimulationController.add_train(...)` seeds `current_span` before the first tick). Adoption of an unidentified train reuses `place_train(...)` for the span and `Switch.physical_occupants` seed only; it does **not** write `Block.occupied_by` there — mid-session block ownership moves through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(...)` then `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)` (see **Adoption**, The same `Train` record survives, re-keyed). At the top of each tick the detector seeds every already-occupied block as already confirmed, so a block a train was placed on is not reported as a fresh entry; it still clears normally once its current drops for the off-window. The one block the seed skips is a block held under a detection fault — one the model still holds only because a clear read under its train is being held: re-seeding it would overwrite that clear read and restart its off-window (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**). Runtime-state save/load is out of scope.
