- **Placement seeds switch occupancy too.** A placed span may cover a switch tile (see **Adoption**, The body must not reach a block reading no current — a switch tile has no detector to read clear, and a body may cover it). For every switch tile the seeded span covers, `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` also seeds a `Switch.physical_occupants[route] = train_id` entry, deriving `route` from the span's own traversal through that tile (the same `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` shape `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)` records — see **Switch entity**, `Switch.physical_occupants`). It runs before the first tick at initial placement, and between ticks when adoption rebuilds an adopted train's span (per **Adoption**). These two placements are the only sanctioned exceptions to "`Switch.physical_occupants` is written only through `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)`". A switch seeded this way carries no `Switch.locks` entry, because seeded already-covered switches are never newly locked (see **SwitchManager**, Intrusion check); the switch-integrity guarantee for a seeded train rests on the seeded `physical_occupants` entry alone, the same as for a train that entered the switch normally and consumed its main lock. Such a switch clears the ordinary way: `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` removes the entry once the train's tail vacates the tile.
- **The occupancy chain runs one way.** Occupancy is four layers, and each layer reads only the layers above it:
  1. **Detection** — the debounced confirmed-occupied set from the global read.
  2. **Attribution** — which train each confirmed change belongs to, decided from the confirmed set, each train's block list, each train's head side, and the reservations; never from the calculated position inside a block.
  3. **The block list** — the blocks a train stands on at block resolution: the blocks whose `Block.occupied_by` names the train, ordered rear to front by the connectivity walk from the train's tail side. It is written only through the `BlockManager` entry and vacate writers that commit attribution's result.
  4. **The span** — the centimetre position (`physics_sync.current_span`), which adds where inside its block list the train sits. It must never cover a block outside the block list, and its head and tail seams are the block list's outer seams (see **The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector**).

  When a higher layer changes, the layers below it change on the same read: a confirmed entry attributes, joins the block list, and moves the span's head in one Observe pass. Nothing reads the span to attribute a block, except the frozen span of a ghosted train (see **A ghosted train's retained span stands in for its block list**). A moving calculated position is the one input that is wrong exactly when it matters most: a locomotive running ahead of its `SpeedProfile`.
- **Touching.** A block touches a train when it is adjacent to a block in that train's block list, adjacency being the connectivity walk through switch tiles at their current `Switch.position` with no other block in between (the same walk unidentified-train identity uses, see **Unidentified trains**). It touches on the head side when it is the first block that same walk meets past the front block of the list, going away from the rear of the list; the head is the reservation-side end (see **Reservation-side head derivation**). A train is directional when it holds a live reservation (`received_path_plan` is set) and is not stopped (`is_stopped()` is false); a directional train is touched on its head side only. A train that is stopped or holds no reservation is touched on either side, because it is not being driven away from anything and a stationary locomotive may bridge an insulated joint the model shows it clear of. An unidentified train touches no block: current next to one resolves by rank 4, and `UnidentifiedTrainTracker` joins it to that train by connectivity (see **Unidentified trains**, Creation and identity).
  - **A ghosted train's retained span stands in for its block list.** A ghosted train's block list is empty, because the rising edge released its blocks (see **Ghosted trains**). For attribution only, the blocks of its retained span stand in for that list: a block of the retained span touches the ghosted train, and so does a block adjacent to one. A ghosted train is stopped and holds no reservation, so it is touched on either side. When detection returns on its retained span, the block therefore resolves to the ghosted train by rank 3 as an `entry`, which gives the train its blocks back. This is the one place attribution reads a calculated position, and that position does not move: a ghosted train integrates no motion, so its retained span is the last position a detector backed, not an estimate the app advances.
- **Attribution.** The raw read carries no train identity, so each confirmed change is matched to a train by this evidence order. `BlockOccupancyDetector` owns the order; `SimulationController` supplies it the block lists, head sides, and reservations it reads.
  - **Match order for a newly OCCUPIED block.** The block is resolved by the first rank that applies:
    1. **Held** — the block is already in some train's block list. The result is `held` for that train and nothing changes.
    2. **Entry** — exactly one train it touches has the block reserved (`Block.reserved_for_train` names that train). The result is `entry` for that train.
    3. **Overrun entry** — no touching train has it reserved, and exactly one train touches it. The block is that train's, because it stands there. Which result it gets depends on where the block is:
       - **In front of a train that holds a path** — the block touches the train on its head side, and the train holds a path (`received_path_plan` is set). The result is `overrun_entry` for it, because it has run past its authority to get there.
       - **Otherwise** — the train holds no path, or the block touches only its rear side. The result is `entry` for it. A train with no authority has none to run past, and a block behind a train is not one it ran into: it is the train's own body, such as a locomotive or a lit car bridging the joint behind a stopped train. A block behind the span is held, not reconciled (see **A confirmed block behind the span is held, not reconciled**).
    4. **Unidentified** — no train touches it. The result is `unidentified`, and the block goes to an **unidentified train** (see below).
    5. **Conflict** — no touching train has it reserved, and more than one train touches it. The result is `conflict`, naming every candidate, and the block goes to no train.

    A reserved touching train outranks an unreserved one, so a train arriving on its own reservation next to a train that overran is rank 2 alone, not a conflict. Ranks 3 to 5 all take the block out of the reservation of any train that does not touch it, whether the block went to one train or to none (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, Reservation truncation).
  - **The attribution result.** Every resolved block yields one result record with these fields:
    - `kind` — for a newly OCCUPIED block one of `held`, `entry`, `overrun_entry`, `unidentified`, `conflict`; for a newly CLEAR block one of `vacate`, `held_clear`, `unowned_clear` (see **A newly CLEAR block** below)
    - `block_id`
    - `train_id` — the matched train for `held`, `entry` and `overrun_entry`; the unidentified train the block joined or was minted as for `unidentified`; the holder for `vacate` and `held_clear`; absent for `conflict` and `unowned_clear`
    - `candidates` — the tied trains, present only for `conflict`

    Every consumer reads `kind` and nothing else about how the match was made: the block-list commit reads `entry`, `overrun_entry` and `unidentified` identically; reservation truncation reads those three and `conflict`; the emergency cut-out reads `overrun_entry` and `conflict`; the vacate commit reads `vacate`; the detection-fault report reads `held_clear`.
  - **A reservation is evidence among touching trains only.** A train reserves the corridor in front of it before it gets there, so a reservation never admits a train that does not touch the block. Current on a block reserved for a train that does not touch it is a different object: the block resolves by ranks 3 to 5 against the trains that do touch it.
  - **Matching runs until it stops resolving blocks**, rather than in one pass: a train fast enough to cross several blocks between two reads has them all confirmed in the same comparison, and each block a train gains in this pass joins its block list for the next one, so the second block across is matched to the train that just gained the first. Clears resolve the same way: each `vacate` takes its block out of the list and leaves the next block the rearmost, so a train that clears several blocks between two reads vacates them all.
  - **One locomotive is one record.** A locomotive standing across a block boundary draws current on both blocks. The far block touches the train, so it resolves to that train by rank 2 or 3 rather than becoming a second object.
  - **A newly CLEAR block** is matched to its current holder (`Block.occupied_by`) and yields one of three results:
    - `vacate` — the block can clear for its holder. For an unidentified train that is every block it holds (see **An unidentified train's clears commit at once**). For any other train it is the end block of the holder's list that can clear: the list's rearmost block, stopped or moving, including the only block of a one-block list. The block leaves the list. For a train that is not unidentified, the span end in it moves (see **A vacated block moves the span end to the seam**); an unidentified train's span becomes exactly its remaining blocks.
    - `held_clear` — the holder is not an unidentified train, and the block is not such an end block: it is in the middle of the holder's list, or it is the front block of a list that holds more than one block. The block stays held (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**).
    - `unowned_clear` — no train holds the block. Nothing changes; `SimulationController` records one `kind = "info"` event.
  - **A confirmed entry that no train touches** is attributed to an **unidentified train**: a `Train` Observe's layout-wide detector snapshot creates for it, with its own `train_id` and its own `TrainController` (see **Unidentified trains**). From that point it is an ordinary train to every other rule in this document.
    - A different train that physically enters a block an unidentified train holds is not detected: the block already reads current, so it stays the unidentified train's by rank 1 (see **Block**, A second train on a held block is not detected). Claiming what a locomotive is standing on is adoption's job, not a second train's (see **Unidentified trains**, Adoption).
    - Under Simulation no unidentified train appears: its current map is built from live train spans, so every confirmed-occupied block already matches a train the app controls. An unidentified train may appear in Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware when the hardware-backed input reports current on a block no controllable train covers.
  - **An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out.** On the read whose attribution result is `overrun_entry`, Observe latches a cut-out request for that train through `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_emergency_request("cut_out", error)`; on a `conflict` result it latches one for every candidate. The same tick's Action step `01f2` applies it through `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()`, whose effects are the **Emergency cut-out**.
    - On an `overrun_entry`, the overrun block still joins the overrunning train's block list and its head still moves to that block's entry seam, so the position stays true while the train is cut out.
    - On a `conflict`, the block joins no list, and each candidate keeps the blocks it already held. The block stays confirmed-occupied and owned by no train, so it re-resolves as a `conflict` on each later read — re-latching the request, which Action step `01f2` applies as a no-op on the candidates already cut out (the `eb.active == False` gate) — until an operator moves the trains so that at most one still touches it; there is no automatic resolution.
    - A train with a speed-calibration pass open is the one exemption: an `overrun_entry` for it latches no cut-out request, because the pass drives that train at an unmeasured step into a stretch whose far end is dead rail by construction, and the pass itself is the stop — it ends as a measurement fault on that same read (see **Speed calibration**, A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass). The block still joins the train's block list and the head still moves to its seam.
    - Both results are also recorded as one event each with `kind = "warning"` and an `ErrorRecord` naming the overrun or the conflict, with the block and train ids on the event's entities.
- **The confirmed change flows through the normal Observe path.** Observe writes the affected train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` and never writes `Block.occupied_by` itself, for every train. The train's final Observe callback folds those sets into its progress report and clears them; Observe commits block entry/vacate through the ordinary coordinator/manager path. Unidentified trains take this same path, which is why a detected occupant the app does not control is modelled as a train rather than as a second kind of occupant. `physics_sync.pending_block_exit_edges` is the separate direction buffer, holding an entry across ticks when detector clear lags calculated tail exit and holding one within a single tick for an unidentified train.
- **Physical detection outranks the calculated position.** When an attribution result of `entry` or `overrun_entry` adds a block to a train's block list, Observe calls `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(train, controller)` directly for that train; the method itself computes a forward-only corrected span whose head sits on that block's entry seam and writes it onto `physics_sync.current_span`, before route ordering/Plan. The correction reads that train's block list alone.
- **Correction and integration compose sequentially.** The same tick's movement calculation, later in the Observe batch, runs from that corrected span, and its `span_update.new_span` replaces it with the ordinary movement result.
- **The correction walks through the train's own blocks only.** The corrected span is found by walking forward from the current head, tile by tile, until the head has entered the newly attributed block. The correction runs only for a block that touches the front of the block list, because a block behind the span is held instead (see **A confirmed block behind the span is held, not reconciled**). So every tile the walk crosses lies in a block the train already holds — including a block reading clear that is still held under a detection fault (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**) — or on the switch tiles between its front block and the newly attributed block, and never in a block no detector vouched for under this train. A switch tile the walk carries the head across is entered all the same: the train's next movement report lists it as entered, the way it lists a switch tile the head crosses under power, so `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)` records the train on the switch (see **Switch entity**, `Switch.physical_occupants`). With every block detected, this walk is how a head reaches the block beyond a switch, because the head waits at the exit seam of its own block until that block confirms (see **A held head always ends up inside a block**).
- **A confirmed block behind the span is held, not reconciled.** A confirmed block behind the span — the locomotive is further back than the calculated position put it, and attribution has just given that block to this train — cannot be reconciled by a forward-only walk, so the span does not move for it and the block is simply held.
- **A vacated block moves the span end to the seam.** When the attribution result for a clear is `vacate` and the span's tail stands in the vacated block, then `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` moves the tail forward to that block's seam with the neighbouring block still in the list, and the head moves with it by the same distance, because a span is rigid. The move is forward for every train, stopped or moving. The move never carries the tail past the vacated block's exit seam: when undetected track lies between the vacated block and the next block, the tail stops at that seam, and ordinary integration carries it over the switch. A 0 cm switch tile has its entry and exit on that same seam, so a tail stopped there has left the switch, and the next movement report lists it as vacated (see **A switch tile a correction carries the tail off is vacated all the same**). The head may move only over the train's own blocks: when the move would carry it onto a switch tile or into a block outside the list, the head is held at the exit seam of the block it is in, and the tail stops short of its seam by the same amount (see **The tighter cap wins**). When the vacate empties the block list, the span does not move (see **Ghosted trains**).
- **A switch tile a correction carries the tail off is vacated all the same.** When a correction by `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` leaves a switch tile the span covered before it and no longer covers, then the train's next movement report lists that tile as tail-vacated, the way it lists a switch tile the tail leaves under power, so `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` removes the train's entry from the switch (see **Switch entity**, `Switch.physical_occupants`). Both corrections can do it:
  - the entry correction slides the whole span forward, so the tail can cross a switch behind the head (see **The correction walks through the train's own blocks only**);
  - a vacate's seam is also the far seam of a 0 cm switch tile (see **A vacated block moves the span end to the seam**).

  A correction moves the span without a movement report of its own, and a switch is released only by a reported tail-vacate, so this report is what frees a switch the train has left.
- **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault.** When the attribution result for a clear is `held_clear`, then the block is not vacated: `Block.occupied_by` stays with its holder, the block keeps its `track voltage`, and the span does not move. A train cannot leave its middle block while still standing on the blocks either side of it, and a moving train cannot leave its front block before the blocks behind it, so a clear read there is the detector losing the train rather than the train leaving. A stopped train's front block reading clear is held the same way, because a span is never moved backward (see **Forward-only protects integrated motion from being snapped backwards**).
- **The fault is reported once per block.** `SimulationController` emits one event on the read where a block first reads clear under its holding train, with `kind = "warning"`, an `ErrorRecord` naming the lost detection, and the block and train ids on the event's entities. It emits nothing further for that block while the fault holds, and reports it again only after the block has read current again in between.
- **A held clear is re-offered until it is an end block.** Release follows the confirmed-clear state, not the single read on which the block first went clear. On every later read, a `detected block` the detector still confirms clear and a train still holds through `Block.occupied_by` is matched again, and it vacates on the first read where it has become an end block that can clear for its holder.
- **The two sources settle the disagreement themselves.** When a clear is held, then one of exactly two things ends it:
  - the block reads current again — attribution resolves that read as `held` for the holder (rank 1 of the match order), so it is never an entry or an overrun entry, even though the train's first entry onto the block consumed its reservation
  - the blocks behind it clear so that it becomes the rearmost block, an end block that can clear for its holder, and it vacates; when that vacate empties the block list, the train is ghosted (see **Ghosted trains**)

  Neither needs an operator.
- **An unidentified train's clears commit at once.** Every clear on an unidentified train's blocks is a `vacate`, wherever the block sits. It integrates no motion, so it has no second source to say a clear came too early, and it has no rear to tell an end block from. Its span is exactly the blocks it holds (see **Unidentified trains**, Span), so a clear leaves its span and its `Block.occupied_by` on the same read. A vacate that leaves its remaining blocks in two separate connected groups splits it into two unidentified trains (see **Unidentified trains**, Creation and identity).
- **Span-writer roles.** `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` is the Observe correction span writer; `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` is the ordinary Observe span writer for continuing integration.
- **Forward-only protects integrated motion from being snapped backwards.** A stopped train's span is forward-only too: a vacate moves its tail forward (see **A vacated block moves the span end to the seam**), and a clear on its front block is held (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**). An unidentified train integrates no motion of its own, so it has none to protect (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector.** This rule is the mirror of the forward correction: it holds a span back from where the detector has not yet said the train is. A train's calculated span must not claim a `detected block` the detector has not confirmed occupied, and must not release a `detected block` the detector still confirms. `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` enforces both by capping the distance it moves the train that tick:
  - the head stops at the entry seam of the next `detected block` and waits there until that block confirms occupied
  - the tail stops at the exit seam of the rearmost `detected block` the span holds and waits there until that block confirms clear
- **A held head always ends up inside a block.** Switch tiles belong to no block and carry no detection, so a run of them between two blocks is track nothing can vouch for. When the next `detected block` lies beyond such a run, the head is held at the exit seam of the block it is in rather than at that block's edge. A head that is already outside every block is left free to run to the next block boundary, where the hold applies again, rather than pinned where nothing can release it.

  Holding the head on undetected track would claim a position no detector supports, and a head in no block has no current block to resolve, so `PathDispatcher.create_path` could no longer plan for the train.
- **The tighter cap wins.** A span is rigid, so the tighter of the two caps decides the whole tick, and a cap never moves a span backwards — it only shortens the step, down to standing still.
- **A confirmed entry is an exact position fix.** A confirmed entry puts the head on that block's entry seam. A confirmed vacate moves the span end that stood in the vacated block to its seam (see **A vacated block moves the span end to the seam**). Between two entries, the position inside the block is integrated from the speed solution and is an estimate, because the speed solution describes the locomotive the profile was calibrated for rather than the one on the track.

  The cap is what bounds that estimate: the model may be wrong about where a train sits inside a block, and never about which blocks it is on.
- **Environment differences.** In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, every layout block is in `detected_block_ids()`; losing a detector after activation is fatal rather than a reason to bypass its cap. Under Simulation the set is empty, so no train is detector-capped and this rule is inert. An unidentified train integrates no motion of its own, so it has nothing to cap (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **The pending-entry block stays live.** The block a capped head is waiting on is that train's `pending-entry block`, and it carries `track voltage` for as long as the cap holds, because the train has to be driven onto the very block whose detector releases the cap (see **Block power-controller role**). Only the detector releases a cap.
- **Every forward span correction is reported.** A span correction here is the forward move made after the detector confirms a block the calculated span had not reached. `TrainPhysics` emits one event for every such correction that moved the span, and its level is set by how many blocks the correction gained:
  - a gain of one block is reported with `kind = "info"` and no `ErrorRecord`
  - a gain of `OVERRUN_REPORT_MIN_BLOCKS` or more blocks is reported with `kind = "warning"` and an `ErrorRecord` naming the profile lag

  Both levels carry the same payload: the blocks the detector read the train onto (`blocks_gained`), the blocks the calculated span held before the correction (`span_blocks_before`), and the distance the span was moved forward (`correction_cm`).

  A one-block gain is routine: the cap parks the head on the entry seam of the block it is entering, so every ordinary block entry gains exactly that one block once its detector confirms it. That is sensor latency, so it is reported at info level rather than as a fault. A gain of `OVERRUN_REPORT_MIN_BLOCKS` or more blocks is not latency: the locomotive is running faster than its `SpeedProfile` says, so every estimate built on that profile — arrival time, braking distance, where the train sits inside its current block — is wrong in the same direction, and will be wrong again on the next block. The correction is the same at either level; the report means the app never corrects the position silently. `OVERRUN_REPORT_MIN_BLOCKS` lives in `constants.py`.
- **A held confirmed block behind the span pins the train.** A train can hold a confirmed block its span does not cover and its head cannot reach by going forward: the locomotive is standing behind the calculated position. A directional train is never handed one, because it is touched on its head side only (see **Touching**). One arrives the other ways a train comes to hold a block: initial placement, adoption, or a block credited to it while it stood still that a later reversal (a new reservation the other way) puts behind it. The forward-only correction does not move the span for such a block, but the tail rule still applies: the span must not run away from a block whose detector says this train is standing there. While the train holds such a block, `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` caps the step to zero, so the whole span stands still with its tail against the detected locomotive. The pin releases through the ordinary vacate path — the locomotive leaves, the block's current stops, the confirmed clear releases `Block.occupied_by` — and the cap lifts on the next tick. Such a block is the rearmost block of the train's block list, so its clear is a `vacate` and is never held.
- **Not a latch.** Debounce is a filter; the detector slice is a named within-tick handoff with a final-callback clear point; the span correction is immediate; the distance cap is recomputed from the confirmed set every tick and retains nothing. A held clear retains nothing either: the set of blocks reading clear under their holding train is recomputed from the confirmed set and the block lists on every read, and the once-per-block report is the difference between that set and the previous read's. None waits across ticks on a gating predicate, so none belongs in the Latch Table.
- **Two views of occupancy.** The block list is what the detector confirms, held until the block is an end block that can clear and reads clear. The calculated span's `occupied_blocks` is where the model puts the train, and over `detected block`s it is the block list at the end of every tick: the span adds only a block attribution has added to the list and refuses to add or drop a block it has not, and the list refuses to drop a block that is not such an end block. The one thing the list may hold that the span does not is a confirmed block behind the span, and the pin keeps the span parked against it until it clears (see **A held confirmed block behind the span pins the train**). On top of the list, the span carries where inside those blocks the train sits, an estimate between confirmed changes. In Simulation the detector set is empty and the model span is the sole occupancy source. Block track voltage tracks the calculated span in addition to the block list, so the rail under the train is never dead while a block is still clearing (see **Block power-controller role**).
- **Ghosted trains.** A train's evidence set is its span's `occupied_blocks` plus the blocks it holds through `Block.occupied_by`, intersected with `detected_block_ids()`. When that set is non-empty and none of it is confirmed occupied, no physical reading backs the calculated position — for example, the locomotive may have been lifted off the rails. Such a train is **ghosted**: an identity the app still holds with no current behind it, the mirror image of an **unidentified train** (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **`presence_unknown` is recomputed each Observe pass, not latched.** Observe computes this pass's verdict, overwrites the stored `presence_unknown`, and publishes it on the controller payload, so detection returning anywhere in the evidence set clears it on the next pass. Observe detects the rising edge by comparing the fresh verdict with the stored value before overwriting — the stored `presence_unknown` is its own edge memory, and there is no separate previous-value field.
- **The rising edge triggers the ordinary power-off teardown.** On the rising edge Observe calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_power_off(reason, has_active_path=...)` through `TrainController._apply_power_off_request(...)`, so the inclusive `phase_latches.path_cancel_request` and `phase_latches.power_off` latches drive the same teardown every other power-off does (see the **Power-off procedure**). While `phase_latches.power_off` is set:
  - the **Propulsion cap step** (see **TrainController**) lowers the train's command to zero
  - future block reservations and switch locks release
  - the `RouteRun` is removed
  - `TrainController.complete_power_off()` performs only its general OFF cleanup

  The ghost-only work stays outside that general helper.
- **The rising edge also releases the train's block occupancy.** On the same rising edge Observe calls `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)`, clearing every block the train holds through `Block.occupied_by` and synchronously reevaluating caution because no detector observation will ever arrive to vacate those holdings; that occupancy release exercises `BlockManager`'s own occupancy-release writer into its `_blocks_pending_deenergize` store (see **Power**, De-energize against the same source) for the just-cleared holdings.
- **The rising edge excludes the train from the energized set.** Observe also excludes the train from the energized set, so this train's emission set reads empty for the rest of the tick; the ordinary per-tick `TrainPhysics` emission-set difference then queues the rest of the train's prior emission set — including its retained span — into the same de-energize drain, with no separate Observe write.
- **An operator-initiated power-off does not perform these ghost-specific steps.** It leaves `occupied_by` untouched.
- **The rising edge retains switch-side protection.** This rising edge does not release any `Switch.physical_occupants` entry or `train_protection_claims` the train holds, because the locomotive may still be bodily on the points even though its evidence set reads unconfirmed. They clear through the ordinary tail-vacate release (`SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`, see **SwitchManager**) once detection returns and the train moves off the switch under ordinary operation; a ghost frozen mid-switch keeps its physical protection until then, or until the operator deletes the train (see **Train Entity**, Deleting a train).
- **The freeze makes the pending cancel commit at once.** Observe forces the ghosted train's speed to `0` on the rising edge (see **The ghost-only freeze runs from the rising edge**), so the `is_stopped()` gate every cancellation uses already holds. Action therefore commits the inclusive `phase_latches.path_cancel_request` the rising edge latched on that same tick's Action pass.
- **The ghost-only freeze runs from the rising edge.** `SimulationController._freeze_lost_train_controller(train_id)` performs the ghost-only freeze on the rising edge and again on every later Observe pass while `presence_unknown` remains true — both before and after the teardown commits the controller to `OFF`. It clears movement-derived controller progress reports and forces the retained speed to `0`, and every operator command to the train other than EB is refused while the flag holds (per **Operator-command processing slot**), and `SimulationController._observe_train(...)` skips this train's movement calculation while the flag holds (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**). It does not suppress the layout-wide detector snapshot, attribution, occupancy reconciliation, or detector-derived progress delivery: those Observe steps run for every train regardless of controller state, and they are what notice detection returning. It does not clear route/resource state or call `TrainController.complete_power_off()` again. The last span stays as the retained position used for attribution (see **A ghosted train's retained span stands in for its block list**) and the question-mark display, never as a prediction the app advances.
- **Detection returning admits the train back to ordinary operation.** Detection returning clears the flag on the next Observe read; once the controller is `OFF`, that lets `power_on_cmd()` run between ticks as for any `OFF` train (per **Operator-command processing slot**) and ordinary operation resumes from the retained position.
- **UI marker.** The UI marks a ghosted train with a question mark for as long as `presence_unknown` reads true.
- **The runtime never removes a ghosted train.** The train stays until detection returns or the operator deletes it. The absence of current does not prove the locomotive was physically removed, so only the operator can say it is gone. Once the ghost's teardown has left it `OFF`, the operator may delete it (see **Train Entity**, Deleting a train).
- **Environment differences.** In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware the evidence set covers every block in the span; in Simulation it is empty because `detected_block_ids()` is empty, so the flag stays off.
- **An unidentified train is never ghosted.** It has no identity to outlive its occupancy, so one that loses its blocks is retired instead (see **Unidentified trains**, The gap).
**Unidentified trains**

- An **unidentified train** is a `Train` the runtime creates for current it detects on track that no train the app controls is standing on — a locomotive placed on the rails by hand, a car left behind, a train from before the app started. The app cannot drive it as it stands, because it was never set up with a speed profile or a route. The app keeps track of it, which keeps every other train clear of it, and the operator can turn it into an ordinary train (**Adoption**). It is the mirror image of a **ghosted** train: current on the rails with no identity behind it, rather than an identity with no current behind it (see **Ghosted trains**).
- **Creation and identity.** Observe creates one when it confirms a block OCCUPIED that attribution matches to no existing train, because no train touches it (see **Block occupancy detection**, Touching). Adjacency is decided first because an unidentified train is never energized: handing a train's own block to one would drive that block to `0` under the locomotive the app is driving. It gets a fresh `train_id` from the runtime, its own `TrainController`, `is_unidentified = True`, and blank persistent train data with the default `SpeedProfile` described in **SpeedProfile**.
  - Identity follows connectivity: one unidentified train per connected group of blocks held by unidentified trains. When two such groups grow together they are one train, and it keeps the older `train_id`. When one group splits in two, the older `train_id` stays with the part holding the block it held longest, and the other part becomes a new unidentified train.
  - The `UnidentifiedTrainTracker` mints each unidentified `train_id` from a counter that only ever counts up, which is the canonical home of the never-reuse rule: a `train_id` an unidentified train was retired with (**The gap**) or adopted away from (**Adoption**) is never handed out again within the session. The mint also skips any id a train in the registry already holds.
  - The counter is not saved, so a restart starts it fresh (**Runtime only**); a fresh session holds no unidentified trains, so restarting the count reuses no live id.
- **Span.** Its span is exactly the blocks it holds. Its length, and where inside those blocks it sits, are unknown, so its `current_span` end locators sit at the outer boundaries of its end blocks and `occupied_tiles` lists every tile of every block it holds. This claims the most track the detector allows, the safe reading for a train nobody is driving.
- **Movement.** `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` integrates nothing for it: it is never powered, so its speed is `0`. Detection is its only span source, through the ordinary Observe call to `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)`. Everything downstream is the normal per-train chain — Observe `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)`, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`, `ResourceCoordinator`, and the two managers.
- **Direction.** It has no travel direction when it first appears: it holds no reservation, so `travel_direction` is `None` (per **Reservation-side head derivation**). Once it moves, its direction is the block it moved into. When it vacates a block while still holding a neighbour, the `direction` passed to `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` is the vacated block's `exit_edge` toward that neighbour, and the block it left behind takes normal `CAUTION`. When the vacated block has held neighbours on both sides — a middle block, whose clear splits the train — no single edge leads toward the train, so the vacate passes `direction = None` and the block goes straight to `FREE`. Observe writes that edge into `physics_sync.pending_block_exit_edges`, the one carrier for a per-block tail-vacate direction, and the final Observe callback consumes it on the same tick. For an unidentified train that entry never waits across ticks, because the edge comes from the detected blocks rather than from a calculated tail exit it does not have.
- **The gap.** Switch tiles carry no detection, so an unidentified train rolling through a switch can hold no blocks at all for a moment. When its last block clears, that block's tail-vacate passes `direction = None` and the block goes straight to `FREE` (see **BlockManager**), but the train itself is held, with an empty span, for `UNIDENTIFIED_GAP_HOLD_S`, which lives in `constants.py`.
- **A held train reclaims a reachable confirmed entry within the gap window.** Within that window, a confirmed entry no existing train accounts for, on a block reachable from its last held block through undetected track, is that same train continuing its run: it keeps its `train_id`. If more than one held train could account for the entry, the one whose hold began most recently takes it.
- **A train retires when the gap window ends with no blocks held.**
- **Retirement teardown.** Retirement is a runtime-owned teardown in this order:
  1. clear the train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks`, `pending_detected_vacated_blocks`, and `pending_block_exit_edges`
  2. drop the `Train` from the train registry, its `TrainController` from the controller registry, and its physics instance from the physics registry
  3. remove the seeded default `SpeedProfile` pair it was created with (**Creation and identity**), which nothing else holds

  The train holds no blocks, reservations, locks, or `RouteRun` at this point, so nothing further is released, and nothing about it was ever written to saved state (**Runtime only**).
- **Retirement is the one teardown the runtime performs on a train by itself.** Deleting a train the operator placed is an operator request, defined in **Train Entity**, Deleting a train, and an unidentified train refuses it.
- **Never driven while it is unidentified.** While `is_unidentified` is `True` the train is never assigned a route, never given a `RouteRun` or a `Path`, and never accepts an operator command; the API rejects every such request for its `train_id`, and `PathDispatcher` never creates a path for it. The one command its `train_id` does accept is adoption, which is not a driving command. It takes its place in the runnable order like any train without a `RouteRun` (per **Per-train tick transaction**), its Plan is a no-op, and its controller stays `OFF`. The Observe occupancy commit runs for it on the ticks Observe attributed a block change to it, which is how its entries and vacates commit (see **Per-train tick transaction**).
- **Adoption.** `SimulationController.adopt_unidentified_train(...)` takes the three facts the train is missing and the operator can see on the layout — which locomotive it is, how long it is, and which way it is pointing — plus the `train_id` the train keeps from then on, and turns it into an ordinary train.
- **Adoption is refused when any of these holds:**
  - the train is not unidentified
  - the `train_id` is already held by another train
  - the head tile named is not one the train is standing on
  - the train is holding nothing because it is in the gap
  - the declared consist would reach into a block reading no current
  - the declared consist would reach into a block another train holds — one whose `Block.occupied_by` names a different train

  Under Simulation no unidentified train ever exists, so the first refusal rejects every adoption attempt (see **Block occupancy detection**).
- **What adoption does, once it is not refused:**
  - **The same `Train` record survives, re-keyed.** Adoption does not delete the unidentified train and add a train in its place. `Block.occupied_by` follows the detector, which reports changes rather than levels (**Block occupancy detection**), so releasing a block that still draws current would leave it `FREE` under the locomotive standing on it, with no later entry to correct it. Instead the `train_id` moves to its new value across every registry that keys on it: the train registry, the controller and physics instances, and the blocks the train holds. Block ownership moves through the ordinary `BlockManager` release-then-occupy writers — `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(old_train_id)` first, then `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(<the rebuilt span's blocks>, new_train_id)` — so no block is ever owned by two ids. `is_unidentified` becomes `False`, and no later unidentified train is handed the old `train_id` (**Creation and identity**).
  - **Placement is the operator's declaration.** `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` rebuilds the adopted train's span from the declared consist length and facing. With no head tile given, the consist must be centered in the track the detector confirmed, with as much unaccounted-for track in front of the train as behind it. The detector reports only that the train is somewhere in these blocks, so standing it at the first tile of the first block would claim a position the detector gives no reason to believe. An operator who can see where the train stands may give a head tile, which must be one the train claims; the front then sits at that tile's exit edge in the declared facing. Placement is validated before anything commits, so a consist that does not fit the track behind the head leaves the train the unidentified train it was. That `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` call also seeds `Switch.physical_occupants` under the adopted `train_id` for every switch tile the rebuilt span covers (per **Placement seeds switch occupancy too**), but unlike a pre-first-tick placement it writes no `Block.occupied_by`: block ownership moves through the release-then-occupy writers of **The same `Train` record survives, re-keyed**, so the detector-following occupancy is never bypassed.
  - **The body must not reach a block reading no current.** A block the detector reports clear has nothing standing on it, so no adopted train's body can extend into one. A declared consist that would is refused and the train is left as it was; the operator gives a shorter length, a different facing or a different head tile, or waits until every block the train stands on reads current. Track that carries no detection at all is not such a block: a switch tile has no detector to read clear, and a body may cover it.
  - **What the consist does not reach goes back to being unidentified.** Blocks the train held that the rebuilt span does not cover are current on track no train the app controls stands on, so `SimulationController.adopt_unidentified_train(...)` hands them to an unidentified train through the ordinary Observe attribution and reports which blocks it gave back. They must not stay on the adopted train: a block with `occupied_by` set is not an eligible reservation candidate for anyone, its own holder included (see **BlockManager**), and the dispatcher excludes only the train's span blocks from the candidate set, so a train holding track it does not stand on walls itself off from its own route and never acquires a path. They must not simply be released either: they draw current and the detector reports changes rather than levels, so nothing would re-occupy them and another train could be routed straight in. An operator who meant those blocks to be part of the train adopts it again with the full consist length.
  - **It is a real train from that moment.** It takes an instance profile — the one the operator named, or a fresh model profile and instance anchored to the declared `max_speed`, replacing the blank pair it carried. It accepts every operator command, is energized like any other train, and is written to saved state. Nothing downstream has a branch for an adopted train; `is_unidentified` is `False`, which is the whole of what the other rules test.
- **Never energized.** An unidentified train commands no `track_voltage`, and its span is excluded from the energized set and from the de-energize test (see **Block power-controller role**). Voltage on the rail under a train the app cannot steer or stop is the hazard this rule contains.
- **Runtime only.** Unidentified trains are not written to saved state and not restored. A restart re-detects whatever still draws current and creates fresh ones for it. An adopted train is saved like any ordinary train, so adoption is also how an operator makes a hand-placed locomotive survive a restart.
- **Shown as itself.** An unidentified train appears in the train list and on the layout marked apart from the trains the operator controls, offering none of their controls. Its detail panel reports which blocks it was detected on and carries the form that adopts it.

**Block power-controller role**

- `BlockPowerController` is the software-to-hardware boundary for block voltage and owns only voltage emission and readback: it applies an already-computed voltage to the hardware-facing block outputs. `TrainPhysics` computes `track_voltage` from the current authoritative mode input (see **TrainPhysics**, Voltage behavior), and the controller and physics layers supply all manual-mode decisions.
- **A block voltage carries a direction.** `track_voltage` is a magnitude, and a DC locomotive's direction is the polarity on its rails. So the value `BlockPowerController` commands on a block is that magnitude given a sign: positive when the train runs the block in its `forward` direction, negative when it runs it in `reverse`, where forward and reverse are the block-relative directions over `Block.ordered_tiles` (see **Block**). The sign is per block, not per train, because each block's tile order is drawn on its own: two blocks a train holds at the same moment may run opposite ways against the train's line of travel, and one sign for the whole train would drive the locomotive backwards on every block whose order was drawn against it.
- **A held block's direction comes from the canonical block-direction helper.** The direction for a held block is the block-relative direction of the train's line of travel through that block, computed by the **canonical block-direction helper** (see **Segment**) — the same value `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction` carries for a reserved block (see **BlockManager**).
- **The line of travel** is the ordered walk from the train's tail end through its head end and onward through its pending-entry block and reserved corridor, oriented by `TrainController.travel_direction` (see **TrainController**). A block held through confirmed occupancy that the calculated span does not cover sits at one end of that walk, and extending the walk through it by the connectivity that attributed it gives that block its direction.
- **A train with no live reservation is signed by its span.** It has no path to read directions from, so its span walk, ordered from its tail end to its head end, signs every block the calculated span covers, and that walk continued forward from the head signs a block held through confirmed occupancy just past the span (see **The line of travel**). A block neither reaches is driven positive.
- **A reservation change re-signs every held block.** A new reservation — or the loss of one — recomputes `travel_direction`, so the next emission re-signs every block that train holds; being granted a new reservation the other way is how a train reverses.
- **The signed value is recorded on the block.** `BlockPowerController.set_block_voltage(...)` records it, so the layout reports which way each block is being driven as well as how hard.
- **Which physical channel a sign reaches is wiring.** It is resolved below the hardware interface (see **Hardware setup**, The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity); no layer above the driver names a channel.
- **Energized set: where the train stands, plus one block ahead.** For every train `T` the app controls — every train that is neither unidentified (see **Unidentified trains**) nor ghosted (`presence_unknown`, see **Ghosted trains**) — the exact emission set is `T.controller.physics_sync.current_span.occupied_blocks ∪ {block_id | Block.occupied_by == T.train_id} ∪ {T's `pending-entry block`} ∪ {T's `next reserved block`}`, less the blocks past `T`'s authority end (see **A block past the authority end is never energized**). Each tick `TrainPhysics` drives that train's one computed `track_voltage` onto every block in this set, signed per block (see **A block voltage carries a direction**). Each term is in the set for its own reason:
  - **The calculated-span term**, not debounced `Block.occupied_by`, keeps a newly entered unreserved/deviated block powered immediately.
  - **The confirmed-occupancy term** is there because the two views of occupancy can disagree about where a train is, and the rail must not go dead under a locomotive on either reading. It powers a block the train holds through `Block.occupied_by` that its calculated span does not cover — a confirmed block behind the span (see **A held confirmed block behind the span pins the train**), which a forward-only correction cannot bring the span back onto — so it is the only term that powers that block, and the locomotive standing there needs it in order to move at all.
  - **The pending-entry term** covers the train the detector cap is holding at a block seam: its calculated span stops short of the block it is entering, so without this term the rail the locomotive has to roll onto to release its own cap would be dead.
- **A block past the authority end is never energized.** When a train holds a path plan and has no reserved block ahead of its head, then `TrainPhysics` leaves out of its emission set every block not on that path's `resource_sequence`, whether the block reached the set through the calculated-span term or the confirmed-occupancy term. Such a block is the one the locomotive overran onto, which attribution credits to the train by joining it to both the train's block list and its calculated span (see **Block occupancy detection**, An overrun entry or a conflict raises the emergency cut-out). It stays at `0`, so its drive zone is idle and its `hc165` detector reads it (see **Hardware setup**, Occupancy source follows drive state). `TrainPhysics` reports these blocks through `blocks_past_authority`, and the drain leaves them unheld (see **A block is driven to `0` only when it fails all four emission-set terms**). For an overrun that raised the emergency cut-out this exclusion is redundant, because the cut-out already drives the whole train to `0`; it is what keeps a calibration leg's overrun block dead, since that overrun raises no cut-out (see **TrainPhysics**, A train that overran its authority is cut out). Any voltage there keeps driving a locomotive that has already run past where it may go, and dead rail past the reservation end is what bounds an overrun to that one block (see **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized**).
- **A block's feed is never asked for two voltages.** A block shares one feed across its segments, and block exclusion prevents another modeled train from owning the same calculated block. This covers the voltages the app commands, not where a locomotive coasts: one that physically runs onto a block another train holds is not detected (see **Block**, A second train on a held block is not detected).
- **A ghosted or unidentified train's emission set is empty for that tick.** It controls no `track_voltage`, so `TrainPhysics`'s difference against `TrainPhysics.previous_tick_emission_set_by_train_id` (see **De-energize against the same source**) queues every block of its last non-empty set, its retained span, with no additional writer.
- **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized.** A train's **next reserved block** is the first block of its reserved-ahead corridor (`Block.reserved_for_train`) that its head reaches by travelling forward, passing over the blocks it already stands on. This is the braking-distance-lock floor (per the **Braking-distance lock**), the one block the lock always reaches. `TrainPhysics` resolves it each tick with the same forward tile walk the seam cap uses, so it follows the points as they are actually aligned rather than as a plan describes them; it is `None` for a train with nothing reserved ahead of it. The rest of the corridor carries no voltage. One block ahead is the whole of what pre-energizing is for — a locomotive must not cross an insulated boundary into dead rail — and it is also the most that may be live at once. **Rail energized further ahead than the locomotive is allowed to be this instant is rail a train running fast keeps accelerating over.** A speed profile describes the locomotive it was calibrated for, so a real train reaches a seam before the model says it has; with the whole corridor live it would run on through every block of it while the app still believes it is a block back. Energizing the next reserved block bounds a reserved-corridor overrun to one block and puts dead rail immediately past the reservation end, so the layout itself enforces the limit the app is computing.
- **A train with no reservations is unaffected by the pre-energizing rule.**
- **De-energize against the same source.** This subsection is the canonical home of the de-energize mechanism. A block leaves the energized set two ways, and each source holds its dropped blocks in its own owner's store — `BlockManager._blocks_pending_deenergize` and each `TrainPhysics` instance's `_blocks_dropped_from_energized`. The two stores are world-level collections, not latches: they hold no **Latch Table** row and are not governed by the latch Writer-helper rule. `SimulationController` reads the two stores through their take-methods and keeps no combined queue or merged copy in any field.
- **The stores drain once per tick.** `SimulationController` takes both stores — `BlockManager.take_blocks_to_deenergize()` and every `TrainPhysics.take_blocks_dropped_from_energized()` — once per tick, after every train has emitted and before the signal refresh, unions their contents, and clears both, so nothing survives to the next tick.
- **`BlockManager` queues a block when any of these holds**:
  - a calculated span drops the block
  - a reservation on it clears
  - a confirmed-occupancy holding on it is released through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(...)` (a ghost rising edge, an adoption re-key, or a train deletion)

  `BlockManager` adds it to `_blocks_pending_deenergize` through its writer `BlockManager._mark_for_deenergize(block_id)`, and `BlockManager.take_blocks_to_deenergize()` returns only the blocks still unheld at drain time — a block vacated and re-held within the same tick is not returned.
- **`TrainPhysics` queues a block that silently drops out of the next-reserved-block term.** When a block stays reserved but stops being its train's `next reserved block` — the train reversed on its corridor, or a replan reordered it — nothing about the block changed, so `BlockManager` cannot see it. `TrainPhysics` adds it instead to `_blocks_dropped_from_energized`, from the difference between this tick's emission set and the emission set it stored per train from the previous tick (`TrainPhysics.previous_tick_emission_set_by_train_id`).
- **A block is driven to `0` only when it fails all four emission-set terms.** `SimulationController` drives a block from either store to `0` only when all four of these hold, where a block in a train's `blocks_past_authority` counts as absent from all four of that train's terms (see **A block past the authority end is never energized**):
  - it is absent from every controller's current `current_span.occupied_blocks`
  - it has no `Block.occupied_by` naming that controller's train
  - it is no controller's `pending-entry block`
  - it is no controller's `next reserved block`
- **The drain tests both views of occupancy, never one alone.** It tests the calculated span **in addition to** debounced `Block.occupied_by`, so neither view of occupancy alone can zero a rail, and a same-tick re-entry prevents zeroing.
- **A reservation the train has not reached is not part of the test.** It is not part of the emission set either: holding it would leave a block driven and zeroed on the same tick.
- **Ghosted and unidentified trains are excluded from all four tests.** A block held only by an unidentified train, or only by a `presence_unknown` train no detector can find, is therefore driven to `0` (see **Unidentified trains** and **Ghosted trains**).
- **This makes the routine energized set the global union of steerable trains' four terms.** Each train's blocks past its authority end are left out of it, as they are of that train's emission set.
- **A whole-layout sweep is the no-`BlockManager` fallback and the admin/test primitive.** `BlockPowerController.deenergize_unheld_blocks(skip=None)` drops every block no train physically holds (`Block.occupied_by`) to `0` in one pass over all blocks, with `skip` naming the calculated-span, pending-entry, and next-reserved blocks the runtime keeps energized. A normally-wired runtime drives the two event-driven stores instead and never reaches it.
- **This differs from the loss-of-control safe state, which zeroes every output at once.**
- **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage.** Simulation's `TrackOutput.set_voltage(...)` is the happy-path model and accepts a valid block command. Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware cannot activate with a missing binding or chip, so a refusal or exception after activation means the device contract has failed at runtime. `BlockPowerController.set_block_voltage(...)`, the ordinary model-recording write, records the commanded voltage only when the write landed; otherwise it reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`, which drives the safe state itself (see **Hardware I/O failure**), latches the halt, and emits one `kind = "error"` event with an `ErrorRecord` naming the failed device. The first time it cannot reach a given block, `BlockPowerController.set_block_voltage(...)` also emits one `kind = "warning"` event with `ErrorRecord.origin = "block_track_output_unreachable"` naming that block, so a silently dead rail is diagnosable per block; that warning is emitted at most once per block.
- **A write that fails inside `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter it.** That sequence calls the non-recording device writes (`SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`, `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()`; see **Safe state / fail-safe**), not the ordinary model-recording writes, but the two report failures into the same per-channel failure-tracking shape. When the caller is that sequence itself, a failed per-channel write is recorded in that run's failure set and the sequence continues to the next channel. The aggregate result is reported once, through the "inability to complete safe state" entry of **Hardware I/O failure** (see **Power**, Hardware I/O failure is fatal to the physical session), never by a second call into `enter_hardware_failure(...)` or a second `enter_safe_state()` from inside the first.
- **The runtime drives nothing again until a successful activation.** While the latch is set, a Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware session reads Halted for `hardware_failure`, or Setup once the operator enters it, and the runtime runs no pass (per **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs). Only a Setup tool may drive an output meanwhile. Only a successful activation of Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware clears the latch (see **Recovery is reactivation**).
- **The model never reports a block energized while the rail is dead.** The runtime never continues operating around missing hardware.
- **A watchdog-driven safe-state drop is reconciled on the next runtime-thread tick.** It is the one path that writes the physical rail to `0` before any model write records it; the runtime-thread tick that consumes the trip record reconciles the recorded voltages to match (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**), so the invariant holds again from that tick onward.
- The block-voltage read surface (`BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(block_id)` over `TrackOutput.get_readback_voltage(block_id)`) reports the actual voltage on a block: in Simulation the last value the happy-path model accepted, in Virtual Hardware the controllable fake device's readback, and in Real Hardware the bus voltage of the block's bound `block_occupancy_current` channel where that chip provides one. Neither hardware-backed environment silently substitutes the commanded value for a failed read. It returns `None` where the rig has no measurement facility, and `None` plus one `kind = "warning"` event on a failed readback transaction. It is a diagnostic read: it never enters the hardware-failure lifecycle, which is why the fatal "failed detector transaction" of **Hardware I/O failure** does not cover it. `TrackOutput.get_actual_voltage(block_id)` is a separate, commanded read-back — the app's last commanded output, never `None` — and is what the track output driver classifies into the drive zone that decides which occupancy source is read (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**). The two must not be conflated, because on Real Hardware the commanded value and the measured rail voltage can differ.

**Switch power-controller role**

- `SwitchPowerController` is the switch-side counterpart of `BlockPowerController` and covers a switch's two separate electricals: the `throw voltage` it drives onto the point motor, and the block feed its rails run on. It holds `SwitchOutput` and is its only caller during operation, including the safe-state call, so `SwitchManager` requests a throw through the controller and never touches the interface itself. A Setup tool is the one other caller, and only while it holds the outputs, through the same output interfaces and drivers (see **Hardware interface boundary** and **Setup tools own the writes; the detectors stay shared**).
- **The two electricals are different wires.** `SwitchOutput` is the software-to-hardware boundary for switch *throw* output: it accepts a target alignment (`0 = MAIN`, `1 = DIVERGE`, matching `Switch.position`) and drives the point motor. It holds no wiring knowledge — how a target alignment reaches the motor is the driver's business, defined under **Hardware setup** (see **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils**) — and owns no routing, lock, or availability policy. The rails are the other wire: they carry the `track voltage` of the switch's feed block, which `BlockPowerController` emits. The two are never compared. Simulation supplies `SimulatedSwitchDriver`; Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware supply the setup-aware driver against their respective device.
- **A switch's rails are fed from one nearby block.** A switch has no track feed of its own: its rails are wired to one nearby block and carry that block's `track voltage`. The wiring is the `switch_track_source` binding in **Hardware setup** (`switch_id` to `block_id`), and `SwitchPowerController` is that map's only reader. The bound block must be the one at the switch's **main entrance**.
  - A train crossing the switch from its main-side entrance is standing on the feeding block itself.
  - A train crossing from the diverge side is entering the switch out of its pending-entry / next-reserved block, which the one-block-ahead rule (see **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized**) already pre-energizes as the feeding block before the train reaches the switch.

  Either way the feeding block is one the ordinary energized set already carries — the block the train stands on, or the block it is about to enter — so a switch is live under a train without any emission, reservation, or channel of its own, and switches add nothing to the energized set defined under **Block power-controller role**.
- **Rail voltage is read, never written.** `SwitchPowerController.get_switch_voltage(switch_id)` reports the voltage on a switch's rails by reading its feed block through `BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(source_block_id)`. While an incomplete setup is being edited or tested in Setup, it returns `None` for a switch with no `switch_track_source` entry; that state is an activation blocker and cannot occur during Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware operation. It is a UI/diagnostic read — the per-switch hardware view shows which block feeds the switch and whether those rails are live — and no control, routing, or physics decision reads it. `SwitchPowerController` drives nothing onto the rails: the bond is physical, so there is no output to write.
- **Why the switch has its own controller.** A switch's one output is an alignment, not a voltage, and its one voltage is sourced from a block rather than commanded. Holding both facts in `SwitchPowerController` gives every switch-side electrical question a single answer site, and leaves `BlockPowerController` owning exactly one thing: the voltage on a block.
- **Acquisition always throws.** Lock acquisition drives the coil for every switch it acquires, whether or not `Switch.position` needed changing and whether or not that alignment was the last one commanded. A throw is blind, so having driven a coil once is no evidence the points seated: a solenoid can stall, bounce back, or be moved by hand afterwards, and nothing reports it. Points left on the wrong side carry the train's `track voltage` down the other branch, which both denies the train the rail it is about to run on and lights the current detector on a block the train is nowhere near. One extra pulse removes that whole class of failure. Outside acquisition the throw is emitted whenever the `Switch.position` mutation workflow (see the **Switch entity** section) issues an alignment the output has not last driven.
- **A throw is blind.** A point motor reports no position back — it has no contact, encoder, or sensed alignment — so `Switch.position` is the commanded alignment and nothing confirms the points seated. `SwitchManager` must not infer a physical alignment from any other reading, and must not treat a successful throw as evidence the switch moved. The rail-voltage read is no exception: it reports the feed block's voltage and says nothing about where the points are.
- **An unissued throw is fatal to a hardware-backed session.** `SwitchPowerController.set_throw(switch_id, target_state)` returns `True` when the command reached the device and `False` when it did not. A missing port binding or chip is rejected before Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware activation, so a refusal or exception after activation means the device contract has failed at runtime. The controller reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`, which drives the safe state itself, and reports the failed command through `NotificationCenter`. It is the only reporter of an unissued throw: `SwitchManager` sees the `False` return and rolls back its software locks, but reports nothing itself. A throw that fails while it is itself part of `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter that sequence (see **A write that fails inside `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter it**). Any partial lock acquisition rolls back its software locks, but operation does not continue and the throw is never auto-retried. `Switch.position` remains the commanded alignment rather than being rewritten as an inferred physical position.
- **Environment behavior.** Simulation accepts every valid throw and records it. Virtual Hardware can inject any of the fault kinds listed in **Hardware interface boundary** to prove the same observable hardware-failure lifecycle without physical equipment; it does not pretend to observe an uninstrumented point motor mechanically sticking after a successful pulse. Real Hardware enters the hardware-failure lifecycle when the physical device refuses or fails.
## Data Flow To UI

**API payload ownership**

- Each runtime/entity owner must expose its own API payload through its own `to_dict()` (or equivalent read-model method), rather than merging changed live fields back into another entity's payload. `Train.to_dict()` owns persistent train data. `TrainController.to_dict()` owns live onboard, control, and physical diagnostics, including the stored `presence_unknown`.
- **A composite runtime snapshot exposes six sibling payload groups.** Any composite runtime snapshot that returns the network/train view must expose them with this ownership split:
  - **`trains`**: the list of `Train.to_dict()` payloads.
  - **`controllers_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> TrainController.to_dict()`.
  - **`dispatcher_progress_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> {path_id, status, current_resource_index, reservation_end_block_id, waiting_for_block_id, resource_sequence}`. The dispatcher-owned path fields come from `PathDispatcher.get_active_path_progress(train_id)`; `waiting_for_block_id` comes from the complete `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` request assembled by `RouteExecutor`. Each `resource_sequence` entry in this progress projection is a lightweight subset — `sequence_index`, `resource_type`, `resource_id`, `entry_edge`, `exit_edge` — and carries no nested `path_tiles`. A consumer that needs per-step tile geometry reads the controller payload's `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` (the full **resource_sequence entry schema**, with its nested `path_tiles`) instead.
  - **`assigned_routes_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> route_id` (or `None`), resolved from `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)`.
  - **`route_runs_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> {route_id, run_number, state, display_state, last_error}` — a lightweight live-run summary.
    - `state` is the run's `current_route_status` value.
    - `display_state` is the derived UI projection, resolved in this read model per **Route-run state**, `display_state`.
    - `last_error` is the derived `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)` read for the run, never a stored field.
    - **The full run record is served on demand, not inlined.** The armed requested-target pair (from `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id).stored_resolved_target`), `start_mode`, and the per-walk-position `task_runs` timing projection are served by the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` detail endpoint, under its `tasks` key.
    - **The `tasks` projection schema.** For each walk-position it carries `{task_index, task_kind, walk_direction, started_at, finished_at, delay_class, elapsed_basis_seconds, elapsed_wall_seconds, resolved_target}`. `task_kind` is derived from `Route.tasks[task_index].task_kind`, and `walk_direction` is stored on `RouteTaskRun`. `elapsed_wall_seconds = finished_at - started_at` for a finished row, and under `timing_basis == "operating"`, `elapsed_basis_seconds = finished_at_operating - started_at_operating` (equal to the wall result under `"realtime"`). Both elapsed fields are `None` until the row finishes, including an active dwell, and are serialization-only.
    - `RouteRun` owns both the summary and the detail; `TrainController.to_dict()` never merges route-owned fields into its payload.
  - **`operator_status_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> {ato_status, pending_actions, hold_reason}` — the three read-model projections that need both controller state and route state, assembled each read (see **ATO status**, **Pending actions**, and **Hold reason**). No entity stores them.
- **The two route-side maps answer different questions, and both are carried.** `assigned_routes_by_train_id` is the lightweight "which route is this train on?" map the frontend reads to tell assigned trains from unassigned ones; it is non-`None` even between runs, before Plan has allocated a `RouteRun`. `route_runs_by_train_id` is the live run summary (`None` whenever there is no `RUNNING` run). When a run is live, the `route_id` in both agrees.
- **`waiting_for_block_id` is recomputed, not retained.** During composite read-model assembly, `RouteExecutor` resolves `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` and the run's manual override, then passes that request to the `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` projection with `reservation_cap_block_id=None` and `required_candidate_resource_keys=None`, matching the tick-start contention view. The read model does not reimplement the walk or ask the dispatcher to discover route-owned target state. Acquisition retries may change the result tick to tick, which is why it is recomputed rather than retained; it feeds the "show stuck" overlay.
- **Other endpoints must preserve the ownership split.** Other detail endpoints may present the same owned data in a different wrapper, but they must preserve this ownership split and must not merge controller-owned, dispatcher-owned, or route-owned live fields back into `Train.to_dict()`.

**Layout version** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

- **The `GET /api/network` endpoint serves the composite runtime snapshot in two parts.** The layout part is every field that changes only when the layout is edited, as the table lists. The live part is every other field.
- **`layout_version` names one layout.** It is a hash of the layout part, and the endpoint computes it on every read. No component stores it or bumps it. Two reads of the same layout carry the same `layout_version`, across a server restart too.
- **When a request's `layout_version` query parameter equals the current `layout_version`, then the reply leaves the layout part out.** That reply:
  - carries `layout_unchanged: true` and the current `layout_version`;
  - omits the sections in the table's first row, and the `blocks`, `switches`, and `tracks` keys;
  - carries `live_blocks` (`block_id` -> that block's live fields), `live_switches` (`switch_id` -> that switch's live fields), and `live_tracks` (one entry of `x`, `y`, and the live fields for each tile that holds a switch or a signal);
  - carries every other snapshot key unchanged, the six sibling payload groups included.
- **Any other request gets the full snapshot.** When the parameter is missing or names another version, then the reply is the full snapshot plus `layout_version` and `layout_unchanged: false`.
- **The frontend rebuilds the full snapshot from a live-only reply.**
  - The frontend keeps the layout part of the last full reply and lays each `live_*` entry over the matching cached entity.
  - When an entity's live fields did not change, then the frontend keeps the same object for it, so its change check skips that entity without comparing fields.
  - When a live-only reply names a version other than the one the frontend holds, then the frontend asks for the full snapshot instead of using that reply.
  - The frontend fetches station groups (`GET /api/station`) again only after a full reply, or after its last fetch of them failed.

| Snapshot key | Layout part |
| --- | --- |
| `platforms`, `station_groups`, `tunnels`, `speed_profiles`, `train_roster` | the whole section |
| `blocks` | per block: `block_id`, `name`, `length_cm`, `min_radius_cm`, `grade_percent`, `is_holding_point`, `speed_limit_kmh`, `allowed_travel_directions`, `ordered_tiles`, `segment_ids`, `segments` |
| `switches` | per switch: `switch_id`, `x`, `y`, `main_length_cm`, `diverge_length_cm`, `main_radius_cm`, `diverge_radius_cm`, `switch_type`, `name`, `notes` |
| `tracks` | per tile: every field, except `switch_state`, `switch_states`, and `signals` on a tile that holds a switch or a signal (`is_switch`, or a non-empty `signal_ids`) |

- Why this shape: the frontend receives this snapshot several times a second while a session runs (per **Network stream**), and the layout is most of the snapshot. A hash means no edit path has to remember to bump a version. A field wrongly placed in the layout part costs a full reply or message each time it changes, and never leaves the frontend showing stale data.

**Network stream** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

- **`GET /api/network/stream` pushes the composite runtime snapshot to the frontend.** It is a server-sent event stream: one long-lived response on which the server writes a message each time it sends, and the browser reads each message as it arrives. Data flows only from the server to the browser. While the stream is open, the frontend reads the snapshot from it; `GET /api/network` serves one-off reads.
