- **Each message is one `GET /api/network` reply.** A message's data is the JSON reply `GET /api/network` would give at that moment, in the two-part shape defined under **Layout version**, with `layout_version` and `layout_unchanged`.
- **The layout part goes out only when it changed.**
  - The first message on a connection follows the `GET /api/network` rule: it leaves the layout part out only when the connection's `layout_version` query parameter equals the current `layout_version`. So a new connection gets the full snapshot first, unless the frontend already holds the current layout.
  - Each later message leaves the layout part out when the current `layout_version` equals the one that connection's previous message carried.
- **When the server sends.** The server sends a message on every open connection when any of these holds:
  - `NETWORK_STREAM_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (0.2 s) has passed since that connection's last message;
  - a request that can change state (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`) finished after that connection's last message was built.
- **One build serves every connection.** The server builds each message's snapshot once and sends it on every open connection, so a second browser tab adds no second build. It builds the snapshot holding `AppState.simulation_lock`, between ticks, and waits for the next send without holding it, so an open stream never holds up a tick or another request.
- **The frontend lays every message over the same cached layout.** A stream message and a `GET /api/network` reply go through the one cache and merge described under **Layout version** (The frontend rebuilds the full snapshot from a live-only reply), including asking for the full snapshot when a live-only message names a version other than the one the frontend holds.
- **When the stream drops, the frontend polls until a new one works.**
  - The stream counts as dropped when it fails to open, when it closes, or when no message arrives on it for 5 s.
  - While it is dropped, the frontend reads `GET /api/network` every 0.2 s, passing the `layout_version` it holds, and tries a new stream every 2 s, naming that same version.
  - When a message arrives on a new stream, then the frontend stops polling.
- **A hidden tab may close its stream.** While the browser tab is hidden, the frontend may close the stream; it opens a new one when the tab shows again.
- Why this shape: the snapshot changes every tick and every open tab needs it. Building it once per send costs one build per 0.2 s however many tabs are open, where a poll costs one build per tab. Sending right after a state-changing request shows a command or an edit in every tab without waiting for the next interval. Polling while the stream is down keeps the frontend live when only the stream fails.

**Elapsed values are server-owned**

- A payload that carries a duration carries it as a number the runtime computed. A client renders it and never derives one from its own clock, because a browser clock cannot see a stop, a playback multiplier, or the server's own time (see **Clocks** under the **Units contract**).
- A client may still format a wall instant the payload carries — `started_at`, `finished_at`, `target_time` — as a local clock time, because those are absolute and need no elapsed arithmetic.
- The run panel reads its per-walk-position elapsed figures from the `tasks` projection, which carries both the `timing_basis` elapsed figure and the elapsed wall time, because a run that was stopped for ten minutes is honestly described only by both numbers.

**`Train.to_dict()` payload**

- `to_dict()` must expose all fields owned by the `Train` entity.
- `Train.to_dict()` exports only the persistent train fields owned by `Train`. Live physical/control diagnostics (position, span, speed, `train_status` / `ato_status`, target speed, ATO info, lookahead, path/destination IDs, reserved blocks) are not in this payload — they live on the controller payload and the read model.

**`TrainController.to_dict()` payload**

- `to_dict()` must expose all fields owned by the `TrainController` entity.
- **Export all live operational state.** That includes:
  - the derived `train_status` (see **Controller state machine**)
  - `handle_position`
  - `powered` — the stored power flag
  - `control_mode` — the operator's ato/manual selection (see **TrainController**, Driving mode)
  - `commands.engaged` — the ATO go/stop bit
  - `manual.manual_mode_type`
  - `manual.manual_power_percent`

  The `ato_status` projection is not a controller field: the read model assembles it (see **ATO status**) and serves it in `operator_status_by_train_id`.
- Export live physical state from the controller-owned storage, including `current_span` and `current_speed_kmh`, for UI/debug consumers that need position or occupied tiles.
- Export ATO state using `ato_destination_block_id` derived from `received_path_plan.reservation_end_block_id`.
- Export `received_path_plan` when present using the **received_path_plan schema**. This is the controller/UI projection of active dispatcher reservation, and its nested reservation geometry must follow the **resource_sequence entry schema** and **path_tile entry schema**.
- `TrainController.to_dict()` does not own live path-progress state, and `PathDispatcher` is the only owner of `current_resource_index`. The UI reads that progress through `PathDispatcher.get_active_path_progress(train_id)` (in `dispatcher_progress_by_train_id`), resolved from the dispatcher's own active-path registry for that `train_id`. Do not copy ownership into `TrainController`, and do not write per-tick sequence-index updates into the controller.
- UI/debug consumers that need active reservation geometry must read `received_path_plan.resource_sequence`; consumers that need current physical occupancy must read `TrainController.get_current_span()`.
- Expose the full canonical lookahead payload as the single source of truth for current target speed, ATC limit, speed-limit reason, and forward curve rendering.

**Pending actions** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

- **`pending_actions` lists what a train has accepted but can only finish later.** It is a derived read-model list with one entry for each Action latch currently set on the train's `phase_latches`, plus one entry while `RouteExecutor._pending_route_assignments[train_id]` is set. Each latch entry carries the latch name and the label in the **Latch Table**'s "Operator sees (pending action)" column. The held-assignment entry reads "switching to route `<requested_route_id>` once stopped", or "leaving its route once stopped" when `requested_route_id` is `None`. Entries are listed in this order: `emergency_request`, `power_off`, `route_deactivate`, `route_abort`, the held-assignment entry, then `path_cancel_request`, so the latch that explains the hold comes first.
- **It is display-only.** No component writes it and no control logic reads it.
- Why this shape: a latch is a request the train has accepted but not yet carried out — a teardown that can finish only once the train stops, or an emergency request that waits for the next running Action. Showing it as a pending action lets the operator see that the train is waiting, and for what, without the UI keeping its own copy of the latch rules.

**Hold reason** (canonical home; referenced elsewhere by name)

- **`hold_reason` says why a train is not moving.** It is a derived read-model value, assembled each read into `operator_status_by_train_id`. It is `None` while the session is running and the train is moving (`TrainController.is_stopped()` is `False`). Otherwise it is the first row of the table whose condition holds, as `{code, question, detail}`; it is `None` when no row holds. A stopped session moves no train, so a train it froze with speed still stored reads its question-1 row like a standing one.
- **Every operator-facing explanation of a stopped train reads `hold_reason`.** No UI, API diagnostic, or button keeps its own list of hold conditions. A refused command's reply carries the train's current `hold_reason`.
- **The rows follow the four questions in order, except `driver_idle`, which comes last.** Each question has one owner, and each row reads that owner's answer rather than recombining stored flags:
  - question 1, "Is the layout live?", is answered by the session state, `AppState.session_state()` (see **Session state**);
  - question 2, "Who is driving this train, and is it asking to move?", is answered by `train_status` (see **Controller state machine**) and the selected driving source's input;
  - question 3, "How far may it go?", is answered by the live reservation `RouteExecutor` and `PathDispatcher` grant in Plan, and by the train's pending actions;
  - question 4, "How fast may it go right now?", is answered by the distance-`0` ATC limit and its reason code in the **canonical lookahead payload**, which the **Propulsion cap step** applies.

| Order | `code` | Question | Condition | `detail` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `halted` | 1 | the session state is Halted (see **Session state**) | the `halt_reason`: `layout_emergency_cut_out`, `hardware_failure`, `runtime_failure`, or `not_activated` |
| 2 | `setup` | 1 | the session state is Setup | — |
| 3 | `paused` | 1 | the session state is Paused | — |
| 4 | `unidentified` | 2 | `Train.is_unidentified` (see **Power**, Unidentified trains) | — |
| 5 | `detection_lost` | 2 | `presence_unknown` (see **Power**, Ghosted trains) | — |
| 6 | `powered_off` | 2 | `train_status == OFF` | — |
| 7 | `emergency_cut_out` | 2 | `train_status == EB` and `eb.cut_out` | — |
| 8 | `emergency_brake` | 2 | `train_status == EB` | — |
| 9 | `calibrating` | 2 | `train_status == CALIBRATING` (see **Speed calibration**, Where it runs) | the run kind, `speed` or `lighting` |
| 10 | `ato_not_engaged` | 2 | `train_status == ATO`, not `commands.engaged`, and `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` is not `None` (see **ATO status**) | — |
| 11 | `pending_action` | 3 | `pending_actions` is not empty (see **Pending actions**) | the first entry's label |
| 12 | `no_route` | 3 | `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id) is None` | — |
| 13 | `dwelling` | 3 | the route's current walk task is a started, unfinished `dwell` row (see **Dwell timer step**) | — |
| 14 | `no_reservation` | 3 | `received_path_plan is None` | the `origin` of `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for("train", train_id)`, when one is retained |
| 15 | `reservation_end` | 3 | the distance-`0` `atc_limit` is `0` and its `atc_limit_reason_code` is `"reservation_stop"` | the `origin` of `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for("train", train_id)` when one is retained; otherwise the train's `waiting_for_block_id` from `dispatcher_progress_by_train_id` |
| 16 | `atc_limit` | 4 | the distance-`0` `atc_limit` is `0` | the distance-`0` `atc_limit_reason_code` |
| 17 | `driver_idle` | 2 | `train_status == MANUAL` and the driver's input commands no traction: the handle is at neutral or a brake notch in the `simulation` submode, or `manual.manual_power_percent == 0` in the `power_percent` submode | — |

- **An environment that is not active reads `halted`.** When the session state is Halted for `not_activated` (per **Session state**) — a hardware environment was never activated, or its activation was refused, as with Real Hardware and no controller attached — every train reads `halted` with `not_activated`. Question 1 comes first, so the train does not read `no_reservation`, which would point the operator at routing instead of at Activate.
- **The order puts the cause before its effects.** A train under EB also has no reservation, and a powered-off train also has no driving source, so the earlier, more basic answer is the one the operator acts on first.
- **`driver_idle` comes last.** The **Propulsion cap step** springs a capped power percentage back to `0`, and a power-off sets `manual` mode at once, so idle driver input is often the result of another row's hold. The driver is the reason only when no other row holds.

**UI data-flow anchor**

- A UI asking "what is the train's target speed right now?" must call `controller.get_lookahead()` and sample at distance `0`.
- **"At station" is a derived read.** A UI shows a train as at a station when the route's current walk task is a `dwell` row whose `started_at` is set and whose `finished_at` is not (read from the `tasks` projection of the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` detail endpoint). No controller field stores it, and the controller payload carries no station flag.

**Signals (display-only)**

- Signals are display-only UI state. `SignalRegistry` stores them and owns their lookup surface (`add_signal`, `get_signal`, `get_signal_at`, `get_signal_at_direction`, `remove_signal`, `update_signal`); `RailwayNetwork` reaches signals only through it. `RailwayNetwork.update_signals_from_blocks()` produces aspect values for the UI once per tick, at the tick tail (see the **Per-train tick transaction**). No controller or physics layer uses them as a speed restriction. The CAUTION speed restriction is owned by `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` through the lookahead / ATC path (see **TrainController**, ATC speed limit).

## Event log

The event log is the operator-facing record of what happened during a run: the structured stream `NotificationCenter` owns (see **Core Runtime Loop**, **Runtime notifications**), kept on disk and presented for review, so an operator can scroll back through a run instead of catching events only as they pass.

**What it records**

- The log carries every event `NotificationCenter` emits, at every level:
  - command results
  - the error events defined in **Error events**
  - the latch writes and consumptions defined by the **Writer-helper rule**
  - the operational events that mark what each train did — train placed, deleted, arrived, entered a block, vacated a block, threw a switch, path created / completed / cancelled, and EB activated / released

  Each one is a single event with the fields defined by the **Event schema**, and each names the function that produced it in `operation` (`"add_train"`, `"remove_train"`, `"occupy_blocks"`, `"on_block_tail_vacated"`, `"request_position_change"`, `"apply_position_change"`, `"create_path"`, `"try_complete_active_path"`, `"cancel_path"`, `"handle_path_completion"`, `"activate"`, `"activate_cut_out"`, `"release"`). A train standing at a platform during a `dwell` emits no event of its own: "at station" is the derived read defined under **Data Flow To UI**, UI data-flow anchor.
- **`apply_position_change` is distinct from the operator/API `request_position_change` throw.** `"apply_position_change"` is the Plan dispatcher acquisition-time throw (`SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)`, see **Switch entity**).
- **Emitter attribution for the named operations.** `"handle_path_completion"` is emitted by `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`; `"activate"`, `"activate_cut_out"`, and `"release"` are emitted by `TrainController.eb.activate()`, `TrainController.eb.activate_cut_out()`, and `TrainController.eb.release()`. The stored `operation` is the unqualified function name, per the **Event schema**.
- **Operational events carry `kind = "info"` and no `ErrorRecord`, with one exception.** The `cancel_path` event carries the cancellation's `ErrorRecord` (for a deviation cancel, `origin = "out_of_sequence"`) per **Cancellation** under **Path And PathDispatcher**. That event is the only thing that remembers a cancellation happened; `RouteRun.display_state` derives `"CANCELLED"` from it (see **Route-run state**, `display_state`).
- Components must not write the log directly. They emit each event through `NotificationCenter` at the points they already report from, the same way as any other notification, so the "no separate sink" rule in **Runtime notifications** still holds.

**Persistence**

- The event log persists to disk, so an operator can review an earlier run's incidents after the session ends. It holds the same `NOTIFICATION_RETENTION_ROWS` window the in-memory stream holds (see **Runtime notifications**, Retention), so a row an operator can no longer see in the viewer is a row no query can reach. This is a persisted record, separate from live runtime state — occupancy, locks, the train span — which stays in memory per **Out of Scope**. It is runtime-written data saved alongside the maintenance counters (see **Maintenance counters**).

**Viewer**

- The event-log viewer is a read-only panel in the operator UI. It reads the persisted stream and lets the operator filter it by:
  - entity
  - `kind`
  - `source`
  - `operation`
  - `ErrorRecord.origin`
  - time

  Selecting an entry highlights the entities it names on the canvas. It presents the record only; it never mutates runtime state.

**Replay**

- Replay is an event-timeline visualization, not state reconstruction. It steps or scrubs through retained events, shows the selected event's message and payload, and highlights the entities named by that event on the matching saved layout. When an operation's closed payload contains explicit geometry or before/after values, the viewer may draw those recorded values; it never infers missing train positions, block occupancy, or switch alignment, and it never interpolates motion between events. The viewer makes no promise to reconstruct world state at an arbitrary time, because retention may remove the beginning of a run and no replay checkpoint is stored. Re-running the simulation engine forward or backward is **Out of Scope**.

**Detector reading log**

The detector reading log is a file of what the block detectors told the runtime, one line per pass. The event log records what the runtime decided; this log records the readings it decided from, so a run that went wrong can be read back as the exact readings the runtime acted on and when it read them. It records inputs, not events: no `NotificationCenter` event is written to it, and nothing in it is an event.

- **Who writes it.** `SimulationController` owns one `DetectorReadingLog` (`SimulationController.detector_reading_log`) for the life of the process. It is off until the server enables it at boot with a folder, so a unit test or scenario run writes nothing. Nothing reads it at runtime.
- **When a line is written.** Every pass that reads the detectors gets one line: each running tick and each stopped pass (see **Running and stopped**, Which pass runs). `SimulationController` calls `DetectorReadingLog.record_pass(...)` right after `BlockOccupancyDetector.step()` returns and before attribution runs (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection, One global read per tick). `record_pass(...)` writes the line. A pass whose read fails gets no line, because that failure is a hardware I/O failure (see **Power**, Hardware I/O failure). An iteration that runs no detector read gets no line.
- **What every line carries.**
  - `pass` — counts the passes the log recorded in this process, from 1. A gap in `pass` means lines were lost to a failed write.
  - `pass_kind` — `"tick"` for a running pass, `"stopped"` for a stopped pass.
  - `wall_time` — the wall time (`time.time()`) at which the pass started.
  - `simulation_time` — `SimulationController.simulation_time` after this pass advanced it.
  - `delta_seconds` — the capped step this pass advanced `simulation_time` by; `0` on a stopped pass.
  - `operating_delta_seconds` — the uncapped step this pass advanced `AppState.operating_time` by; `0` on a stopped pass. The log never records an `operating_time` reading (per **Clocks**).
  - `readings` — a map from block id to that block's reading, holding the blocks **Only changed readings are written** selects.
- **A block's reading.** `present` is the boolean `OccupancyInput.read_block_currents()` returned for the block, the value the debounce counts (see **Debounce with on/off thresholds**). In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware the reading also carries what the driver reports about that read:
  - `source` — `"current"` or `"digital"`, the detector that answered (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**);
  - `zone` — the block's drive zone;
  - `current_ma` and `threshold_ma` — when the current channel answered, the measured current and the threshold it was judged against, each rounded to 0.1 mA;
  - `raw_bit` — when the digital detector answered, its bit before polarity is applied (see **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer**);
  - `held_from_previous: true` — when the lighting hold kept the block present.

  A Simulation reading is `present` alone.
- **Only changed readings are written.** A line lists only the blocks whose reading differs from the reading the file last holds for that block, and leaves out `readings` when none differs.
- **Some lines list every block.** A line lists every block the read returned, and adds `full` naming why, `environment` (the active environment), `on_threshold`, and `off_threshold`, when **any of these holds**:
  - it is the first line the process writes — `full = "start"`;
  - it is the first line of a new file — `"new_file"`;
  - the detector or the operating environment changed since the last line — `"environment"` (an activation builds a new detector);
  - a layout was loaded, or the set of blocks the read returned changed — `"layout"`;
  - the previous write failed — `"write_failure"`.

  So reading a file forward from any line that carries `full` gives every block's reading at every pass after it.
- **Where it is kept.** The server writes the files into the per-machine `.runtime/detector_readings/` folder beside the code, where the shutdown record also lives. Each file is named for the local time it was opened. Each line reaches the operating system as it is written, so a crash loses no line already written. A file past `DETECTOR_READING_LOG_MAX_FILE_BYTES` is closed and the next line opens a new file. Opening a file deletes the oldest files until the folder holds no more than `DETECTOR_READING_LOG_MAX_TOTAL_BYTES`. Both values live in `constants.py`. The files are not part of a layout save.
- **A failed write never stops the session.** `DetectorReadingLog` catches every failure of its own write, and the pass carries on. It reports the failure as one `kind = "warning"` event with `source = "DetectorReadingLog"`, `operation = "record_pass"`, and an `ErrorRecord` naming the failure, under one condition key, so a run of failing passes produces one event (per **Error events**, Suppression mechanism). It resolves that key on the next successful write.

## End-To-End ATO Path Run

**End-to-end path-reservation projection**

- `PathDispatcher` stores the active dispatcher-owned `Path`. `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` reads the **received_path_plan schema** projection from that active record. `controller.assigned_path_id` is a derived read of that projection's `path_id`.
- `RouteExecutor` must ensure the train's `TrainController` exists before path reservation is created or extended in Plan.
- `RouteExecutor` must not write `assigned_path_id` or `ato_destination_block_id` directly.

**End-to-end ATO run**

This is a high-level walk-through; the contracts live in the sections it names (see **Stop-arrival procedure**, **Planning Kernel**, **Route-run state**, **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**). Movement reservation is the one "may move" signal in this walk-through: the planner grants it, the engaged ATO uses as much of it as exists, and a train with none stands and waits.

1. The operator powers the train, assigns a route, selects `TrainController.commands.set_mode("ato")`, and issues `/ato/go` — or issues **Start route**, which makes the same writes in one command. `set_mode("ato")` sets `control_mode = "ato"` (per **Driving mode**), and `/ato/go` sets `commands.engaged`, which opens the **ATO engage gate**. Nothing moves yet: there is no reservation.
2. Observe runs once before runnable-train ordering. It samples every layout detector into one retained snapshot, then, across the whole layout and for every train regardless of controller state, it:
   - debounces and attributes that snapshot
   - creates, extends, holds, or retires unidentified trains
   - latches the emergency cut-out for an overrun entry or a conflict
   - truncates conflicting reservation, latching an emergency brake on a train whose locked block was taken
   - reconciles affected train spans to the detector
   - computes each train's `presence_unknown` verdict and performs the ghost rising-edge occupancy/power cleanup and latch writes per the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**

   Then, for each train whose movement is calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), it calculates movement from the reconciled span. Then, for every train, whether or not its movement was calculated, it:
   - drains the train's progress mailbox to commit block entry and tail-vacate, and records the tick's head-entered blocks for Plan settlement
   - latches any movement-derived deviation (`origin = "out_of_sequence"`, committed later in Action once the train is stopped)

   Observe finishes no route task; head-advance and stop arrival run in Plan settlement. Its detector-derived handoff and committed positions are ready before any train's Plan begins.
3. Plan runs settlement first, then planning (per the **Planning Kernel**).
   - **Settlement.** It consumes the tick's head-entered `waypoint` tasks (step `640a`). When the **Stop-arrival check** holds, it finishes the served `stop` or expired `run` and releases its reservation (step `9d8b`, skipped when a cancel is pending).
   - **Planning.** It creates or extends reservation on every pass on which `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)`, the one planning gate, holds. That gate's one driving-source condition is the ATO engage gate (an ATO train must be engaged), and it does not require the train to be stopped, so a train finishes its stop and acquires the next reservation in one pass. Planning runs the **Covered-task index advance**, then resolves the next task via `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id)` to one exact `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)`: a `run` task resolves per **Run task resolution**, and a `dwell` row is handled by the **Dwell timer step** (Plan step `70c3`) before any target is resolved. Plan then calls `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` (or `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` if a live path exists), bounding acquisition at any meet ceiling and the next holding point (per the **Reservation-cap rule** and **Reservation termination rule**), and locks the reserved blocks within braking distance (per the **Braking-distance lock**). If a resolved pass-through (`waypoint`) target block is already covered, the index advance skips it; it finishes a resolved stop target block once the train is stopped with its head in that block and has no active path — the covered-stop rule.
4. Action runs for each train, after Plan (per the **`SimulationController._act_train(...)` flow**). In order, it:
   - applies any emergency request Observe latched (step `01f2`)
   - consumes `pending_path_cancel_request` through the stopped-gated early-Action dispatcher callback
   - runs the **Controller tick order** — the selected driving source produces one commanded speed, and the **Propulsion cap step** takes the lowest active ceiling — and sets the block track voltage
   - consumes `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, and `pending_route_deactivate`

   In ATO (`train_status == ATO`), the driving source is the **ATO driving rule**. When the train is engaged (`commands.engaged`) and `received_path_plan` is present, the ATO output drives toward the reservation end, with the head derived from the reservation (per **Reservation-side head derivation**). When not engaged, or when `received_path_plan is None`, the ATO output is `0` and the train waits. The voltage drives movement calculated in the next tick's Observe.
5. Extension retries use the same `path_id` until reservation reaches the requested target (per the **Planning Kernel**); a `no_viable_path` failure latches cancel-and-replan.
6. The **Stop-arrival check** finishes the `stop` task via `RouteExecutor.advance_walk_position(...)`, which writes its `finished_at`. The path completes, so no live path remains and the ATO output is `0`. When the route's next task is `dwell`, the same pass's **Dwell timer step** (`70c3`) starts the dwell row's timer. While `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` is not yet satisfied (per **Task time semantics**), it returns without resolving a target: the train stands at the platform with no reservation, and ATC holds it (distance-0 limit `0`, reason `"no_reservation"`). When the dwell time has elapsed, `70c3` finishes the dwell row and Plan continues to the next target in the same pass: the planner grants the next reservation and the engaged ATO goes.
7. A `run` task is a stop whose location is decided by time (**Run task resolution**). While `task_runs[walk_position].run_elapsed_seconds < task_time` (accrued by Plan step `6a0d`), it behaves as a waypoint, and the planner keeps extending reservation through the route's next geometry. Once it reaches `task_time`, its resolved target is the target it is armed for (per **Expired-run precedence**). The planner keeps extending toward that target, the train brakes to it under the ordinary `reservation_stop` path, and the **Stop-arrival check** finishes it.
8. When `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns `None`, Plan calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` per **Terminal route completion**. No live path remains at this point, since the last stop's arrival already cleared it.

**End-to-end cancellation note**

- When reservation is cancelled — an operator cancel, a system revoke, or the deviation cancel — the cancel commits only once `TrainController.is_stopped()` holds (see **Action latched-cancel consumption: stopped-train gating and no-active-path skip**).
- **Whether the train resumes under ATO on its own depends on what the cause of the cancellation wrote** (per **Driving mode** and **ATO status**):
  - An internal re-plan — a system revoke, a live-path re-resolution, or a structural extend-failure — writes neither `control_mode` nor `commands.engaged`. The next Plan pass on which `is_clean_for_create(train_id)` holds creates fresh reservation, and ATO drives.
  - Power-off sets `control_mode` to `"manual"`, and its Action cleanup removes the route run, so nothing re-plans: the train is `OFF` with no route until the operator assigns one and starts it (for example with **Start route**). `set_mode("manual")` cancels nothing; the route re-plans as a manual train, and the driver drives, until the operator selects ATO again.
  - EB, including the EB a deviation raises, keeps `control_mode` and clears `commands.engaged`. After release a manual train re-plans and its driver drives; an ATO train re-plans after the operator issues `/ato/go`.

**End-to-end manual-arrival note**

- Manual trains use the same route-committed arrival and the same **Dwell timer step** as ATO trains. The only difference is the driving source: in `manual` mode the driver's input drives (**Driver input acceptance**) and ATC caps it to the reservation (**Manual mode and movement-reservation boundary**). `is_clean_for_create(train_id)` has no driving-source condition in `manual` mode (per **Planning Kernel**); when the planner grants reservation after a dwell, the driver goes.

**End-to-end EB note**

- EB activation applies the **canonical EB activation effects** (under the **EB workflow state machine**). An ATP trip voids the reservation, which is why re-establishing reservation is a fresh `create_path(...)`.
- On every later tick where `eb.active` holds at tick start, the EB hold (tick step `d483`) keeps both driver inputs at their safe rest position and the distance-0 ATC limit at `0` (per **Controller tick order**).
- `TrainController.eb.release()` accepts under its four conditions (per **EB release**). Its effects, and the mode the train reads afterward, are row `ad04` of the **EB workflow state machine**.
## Glossary

This section defines words that are overloaded across the document: words that mean similar but different things in different layers, and words used in prose with no stored field behind them. Each is defined once here, so every other site can point to it by name instead of restating it.

Three rules govern this glossary:

1. **If a word appears in prose but in no schema, it goes in the glossary, or it does not appear in prose at all.**
2. **If two words mean the same thing across layers, pick one as the main word and mark the other as a synonym.**
3. **If a word means different things in different contexts, qualify it every time it appears.** Never write a bare `forward`; write "block-relative forward" or "train-relative forward."

**Group A — Action verbs.** Each row names the entity acted on, who initiates the action, and the resulting state.

| Verb | Entity / initiator / resulting state |
| --- | --- |
| `cancel` | `Path` (`status: ACTIVE -> CANCELLED`); initiated by `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`. Writers and gating per the **Latch Table** (`c832`) and the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**. |
| `complete` | `Path` (`status: ACTIVE -> COMPLETED`); initiated by `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` per the **Stop-arrival procedure** |
| `finish` | `RouteRun` deleted, and a `ONE_OFF` route left with no assigned train deleted with it; initiated by `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` per the terminal route completion procedure (`879a`) |
| `deactivate` | `RouteRun` (`current_route_status -> DEACTIVATED`); initiated by `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` from the Action abort/power-off/deactivate consumers |
| `abort` | `RouteRun`; operator-driven teardown via the `pending_route_abort` latch per the **Latch Table** (`bc5d`) |
| `revoke` | `Path`; system-driven cancel via `pending_path_cancel_request(revoked)` from route reconciliation, a route deactivate latch (structural route edit, route deletion, or speed-calibration abandonment), structural extend failure, a path left with no valid reservation after another train takes a block it reserved (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, Reservation truncation), or the broken-skip terminal-walk cancel (steps `c481` / `592a`, latched while a live path still exists on an all-broken or terminal walk — see **Unreachable and broken task handling**) |
| `cancel (operator)` | `Path`; operator-driven cancel via `pending_path_cancel_request(operator_cancelled)` — an operator cancelling their own live path, either through Plan cancel-and-replan or the between-tick API/UI/admin path-cancel request service (procedure-table row `148a`); `kind = "info"` |
| `deviate` | `Path`; system-driven cancel via `pending_path_cancel_request` with `deviation = true`, whose `cancel_path` event carries one `ErrorRecord` (`origin = "out_of_sequence"`); writer and gating per the **Latch Table** (`c832`) and the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**. As for every cancellation, the derived `RouteRun.display_state` shows `"CANCELLED"` while the run has no live path, and the reason is read from that event's `ErrorRecord.origin` (see **Route-run state**, `display_state`). |
| `select ATO / manual` | `control_mode -> "ato"` / `"manual"`; set by `TrainController.commands.set_mode(...)`, to `"ato"` also by **Start route**, and to `"manual"` also by power-off acceptance and OFF cleanup. These are its only writers (per **TrainController**, Driving mode). EB, including the EB a deviation raises, path cancellation, and preemption leave it unchanged. It is an input to the derived **`train_status`**. |
| `start route` | `TrainController.commands.start_route()`: on a stopped train with a route assigned, powers it up when `OFF`, selects ATO, and engages it, as one command. Full contract under **TrainController**, **Start route**. |
| `engage / pause (ATO)` | `commands.engaged`; `/ato/go` (`TrainController.commands.ato_go()`) sets it `True` to start ATO driving once the train has a route assigned (per **ATO go**), and `/ato/stop` (`TrainController.commands.ato_stop()`) sets it `False` to pause. **Start route** also sets it `True`, and the **canonical EB activation effects** clear it. A not-engaged ATO train reads `ato_status == READY`, stands with the ATO output `0`, and keeps its reservation. Full writer set and the **ATO engage gate** under **TrainController**, **ATO status**. |
| `dwell` | `RouteRun` task (`task_kind == "dwell"`); the planner grants no reservation until the dwell's departure time (`task_time` or `target_time`), then continues. Started and finished by the **Dwell timer step** (Plan step `70c3`). No controller state records it. |
| `throw` | `Switch` (moves the point motor to a new alignment and writes the commanded `Switch.position`); owned by `SwitchManager` per the **Switch entity** mutation workflow and **Power**, Switch power-controller role |
| `skip` | `RouteRun` (`task_runs[walk_position].finished_at` set, the route-progress cursor advances past a broken task); initiated by Plan step `c481`, or step `592a` for a task a mid-pass cursor move landed on. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `stall` | `RouteRun` (`no_reachable_task = True`, derived `display_state == "STALLED"`, the train holds idle); initiated by Plan step `c481` (or step `592a`) when every task on a `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` walk is broken and no live path remains — while a live path still exists the step latches the ordinary cancel instead and sets the flag on a later pass. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |

**Group B — Geometry terms.** Each row names the frame of reference.

| Term | Frame of reference |
| --- | --- |
| `forward` | Block-relative (matches `Block.allowed_travel_directions`; the tile order is the concatenation of the block's constituent `Segment.ordered_tiles`) OR train-relative (the head end the train is heading toward). Always qualify which. |
| `reverse` | Block-relative or train-relative. Always qualify which. |
| `head` | Train-relative; the physical end of the current span on the reservation side, i.e. closer to `reservation_end_block_id`. With no live reservation, the end the span's current frame already treats as the head (per **Reservation-side head derivation**). |
| `tail` | Train-relative; the physical end of the current span opposite the `head`. |
| `frame` | Generic term for a directed coordinate context; always qualify with one of: block-relative, traversal, terminal, or travel. |
| `traversal direction` | Block-relative; `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for one block as walked by a path. |
| `travel direction` | Network-relative; the train's current motion direction in the network frame, derived from the live reservation and span per **Reservation-side head derivation** (`None` when there is no live reservation). |
| `terminal frame` | The directed `path_tiles` / `entry_edge` / `exit_edge` of the terminal block in a `Path.resource_sequence`; used for braking and for completion direction match. |

**Group C — Aggregate nouns.** Each row gives the type, or marks the word as informal prose only and points to the real concrete artifact behind it.

| Noun | Type / canonical schema |
| --- | --- |
| `path` | Stored entity (`Path` record); canonical schema in **Path field schema**. |
| `reservation` | The corridor a train has claimed ahead of it — the `Path.resource_sequence` held as per-block `Block.reserved_by_path` claims (and `Switch.locks`). There is no single `Path.reservation` field; use `Path` / `received_path_plan` for the whole corridor, `Block.reserved_by_path` for one block. Contrast `reservation` vs `lock`. |
| `plan` | Informal prose synonym for `received_path_plan`; canonical schema in **received_path_plan schema**. |
| `run` | Bare, the `RouteRun` runtime instance; canonical schema in the RouteRun section. Always write "`run` task" for the `task_kind == "run"` entry — a stop whose location is decided by time, resolved per **Run task resolution** (canonical home **Canonical Next-Target Selection**). |
| `walk` | The directed sequence of walk-positions (`task_runs` entries) of a `RouteRun`, each carrying a `task_index` back-reference; not a stored field. |
| `task` | `RouteTask` authored entry (with `task_kind`); runtime instance is `RouteTaskRun`. |
| `start mode` | Which stop a fresh `RouteRun` begins at (`FIRST` / `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC`). It comes from the route-level default `Route.start_mode` plus a per-assignment one-shot input. Canonical home **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `broken task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose `task_location` ID is not in the network (it resolves with `failure_kind == missing_target`). It is skipped, never waited on. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `unreachable task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose target exists but cannot be served this tick (`failure_kind == target_unavailable`, or a live `PathAcquisitionFailureKind`). It is waited on, not skipped. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `valid task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose `task_location` ID is in the network, whether or not it can be served right now. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `holding point` | A block a user marks with `Block.is_holding_point = True` as a safe place to wait. The field lives in the **Block** field schema. It has three consumers: the holding-point chunking of the **Reservation termination rule**, the truncation holding-point preference (a truncation-terminal rule under **Path And PathDispatcher**), and **Meet coordination**'s passing places, where the waiting train's `meet_ceiling_block_id` is set. |
| `passing place` | In a meet, a holding point where the waiting train can stop, can get to before the other train takes the way, and that the other train's route does not use — often one road of a passing loop. Canonical home **Meet coordination**, Passing place. |
| `lock end` (`lock_end_block_id`) | The furthest block a powered run has **locked** this tick. Each reserved block within the train's stopping distance ahead of the head is flagged `Block.locked_by_path`, floored at the next block ahead of the head. When no block ahead of the head is locked, the lock end is the head's block. The lock does not bound how far reservation is acquired: the holding-point chunking and any meet ceiling (`reservation_cap_block_id`) do. Canonical home **Braking-distance lock**. |
| `reservation` vs `lock` | The **reservation** is the path a train has claimed toward its target (`Block.reserved_by_path`), soft-exclusive and preemptible above the lock. The **lock** is the braking-distance subset of that reservation (`Block.locked_by_path`), hard-exclusive and uncancellable. A train brakes toward its reservation end; the lock guarantees it can stop within the reservation and marks which reserved blocks **Preemption** may not take. Canonical homes **Braking-distance lock** and **Preemption**. |
| `preemption` | A strictly higher-priority run taking a reserved-but-not-locked block, or a future switch claim beyond the holder's lock end (a crossover included), from a lower-priority run, which truncates the victim's reservation from that resource onward (keeping the victim `ACTIVE`, its committed span, and its `control_mode`). Committed track — a locked block, or a switch at/before the lock end or already entered — is never taken, and neither is a meet's waiting train's way to its passing place. Canonical home **Preemption**. |
| `adoption` | The operator turning an **unidentified train** into an ordinary, driveable train by supplying the identity, consist and facing the detector cannot know. Canonical home **Power**, Unidentified trains. |
| `unidentified train` | A `Train` the runtime creates by itself for a detected block with no app-controlled train accounting for it. It is never driven while it stays unidentified. Canonical home **Power**, Unidentified trains. |
| `ghosted` | Said of a train the operator placed whose detected blocks all read clear. Canonical home **Power**, Ghosted trains. |
| `configuration` | A category word, not one schema, file, mode, or API surface. Do not use it bare. Name the actual owner: **persistent train data**, **layout geometry**, **Hardware Setup**, or **runtime settings**. These have different lifetimes and activation rules. |

**Group D — Electrical / switch-hardware terms.** These separate the two voltages and the two meanings of switch alignment.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `track voltage` | The DC voltage put on a block to drive the train. Each train uses one magnitude, applied to the blocks it stands on plus the block it is entering and the next block reserved ahead of it, never to a block past its authority end (see **Power**, Energized set). Each of those blocks gets its own sign: which way the train runs through that block (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction). A block shares one feed across its segments, so the whole block is powered (see **Block**, one-train-per-Block power domain). Canonical home `TrainPhysics` (see **TrainPhysics**). `BlockPowerController` emits it to the block outputs (see **Power**). A switch's rails carry the voltage of its `switch feed block`. |
| `throw voltage` | The DC drive put on a switch point motor to move it. Which coil it is put on picks which alignment to move to (see **Power**, Hardware setup). Emitted by `SwitchPowerController` (see **Power**, Switch power-controller role). This is a separate output from `track voltage`: the two are different wires and are never compared. |
| `switch feed block` | The block whose feed also powers a switch's rails. A switch carries no `track voltage` of its own: its rails are wired to the block at its main entrance, so a train standing on the switch is driven by that block's voltage. The wiring is the `switch_track_source` binding in **Hardware setup**, and `SwitchPowerController` owns the relation (see **Power**, Switch power-controller role). |
| `physical channel` | One addressable line on a chip — a PWM channel, a shift-register output bit, a shift-register input bit, or a current-sense channel — that a logical `block_id` or `switch_id` maps to on a given hardware build. A logical entity may take more than one: a block's track takes two PWM channels, a switch takes two coil bits. The physical-channel maps in the binding table in **Hardware setup** (see **Power**) carry it; only the concrete `TrackOutput` / `SwitchOutput` / `OccupancyInput` driver reads them, and no other layer names a channel. |
| `safe state` | Every switch point motor is powered off and every block's `track voltage` is `0`. Canonical home **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe. |
| `detected block` | In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, every layout block is a detected block. Canonical home **Power**, Hardware interface boundary. |
| `pending-entry block` | The detected block a train's head is being held out of while it waits for that block to confirm occupied. A train has at most one, and only while the cap holds. Canonical home **Power**, Block occupancy detection. |
| `block list` | The blocks a train stands on at block resolution: the blocks whose `Block.occupied_by` names the train, ordered rear to front. Canonical home **Power**, Block occupancy detection, The occupancy chain runs one way. |
| `touching` | Said of a block adjacent, through switch tiles at their current position, to a block in a train's block list. A moving train holding a reservation is touched on its head side only; a stopped or unreserved train on either side. For a ghosted train, the blocks of its retained span, and blocks next to them, touch it. Canonical home **Power**, Block occupancy detection, Touching. |
| `attribution result` | The `kind` / `block_id` / `train_id` / `candidates` record attribution yields for each confirmed change. Canonical home **Power**, Block occupancy detection, The attribution result. |
| `emergency cut-out` | An emergency stop that removes traction power — drives the train's `track voltage` to `0` and drops commanded speed to `0` on the train's next Action, with no brake curve — rather than braking down `SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate`. It is the emergency-brake latch with `eb.cut_out` set. Canonical home **TrainController**, Emergency cut-out. |

**Group E — Session-mode and operating-environment terms.** These name two different layers: the Editor/Operation session-mode split, and the three environments in which Operation may run. Canonical home is **Session mode and operating environment** under **Core Runtime Loop**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `session` | One run of the app in one session mode, Editor or Operation (per **Session mode and operating environment**). An operation session is built for one operating environment by activation, and has one session state at a time. A **commissioning session** is a different thing: the bounded raw-port tool that owns the outputs inside Setup (per **Hardware setup**, The commissioning session). |
| `session state` | The one value that answers "is the layout live?": Setup, Live, Paused, or Halted, where Halted always carries a `halt_reason` (`layout_emergency_cut_out`, `hardware_failure`, `runtime_failure`, or `not_activated`). Derived on every read by `AppState.session_state()`. Canonical home **Session state** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
| `Reset` | The layout-wide action that leaves Halted for `layout_emergency_cut_out` and returns the session to Live, or to Paused when it was Paused before Emergency stop. Canonical home **Emergency cut-out**, Reset. |
| `Hold all` | The layout-wide action that sends ATO stop to every train that reads `ATO`; each keeps its route and its reservation and resumes with `/ato/go`. Canonical home **Hold all** under **TrainController**. |
| `editor mode` / `operation mode` | The two session modes; a session is in exactly one. Editor mode places and wires geometry; operation mode runs the railway — it brings up the runtime (`SimulationController` and its per-tick loop) and drives the trains. |
| `Simulation` | The algorithm-focused operating environment. It needs no Hardware Setup, derives occupancy and train motion from the model, and uses happy-path simulated interfaces whose writes succeed. It does not emulate chips, ports, buses, or wiring. |
| `Virtual Hardware` | The hardware-integration operating environment. It requires the same complete Hardware Setup as Real Hardware and runs the real chip drivers, bindings, HAL, and occupancy pipeline against an in-memory device. Its inputs, responses, disconnects, and failures are controllable. It never opens or energizes the physical controller. |
| `Real Hardware` | The physical-layout operating environment. It requires a complete, validated Hardware Setup. Every required interface is physical; a missing binding, chip, or device blocks activation or faults the session. It never substitutes a simulated interface. |
| `SimulationController` | The runtime engine shared by operation in all three environments. The `Simulation` in its name is historical; it is not a Simulation-environment-only object, and it is not itself a mode. |
| `running` / `stopped` | Running means the session state is Live; stopped means any other session state. A stopped session runs at most the observing steps, and leaving Live drives the outputs to their `safe state`. A stopped session is not a frozen railway: in the two hardware environments the layout goes on carrying whatever is on it, and in Setup and after Emergency stop the detectors go on reporting it. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
| `authoring step` / `observing step` | The two halves every step of the tick falls into. An authoring step decides what happens next and drives the layout to make it happen; it runs only while the session is running. An observing step reads the detectors and makes the model agree with them; it cannot invent motion, so it runs running or stopped. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
| `stopped pass` | One turn of the runtime loop in a Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware session that is in Setup or Halted for `layout_emergency_cut_out`: the observing steps and nothing else. A stopped Simulation session runs no such pass, and neither does Setup with `hardware_failure` latched or with no `OccupancyInput` open. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
